`kernel/fused_eval_fp32_aga.sbatch`), giving five matched pairs.
Prediction if the kernel widens variance: the five fused seeds' relative
spread stays at least twice the five eager seeds', with at least one more
fused seed outside the eager spread plus 3%; then the kernel stays opt-in
and the engineering item is a float32-accumulation path for the pooled
invariants, to be tested the same way. Prediction if seed 43 was chance:
the two new pairs each agree within 3% and the five-seed spreads are
within a factor of two of each other; then the five-seed mean ratio,
if within 3%, makes the fused kernel the recommended CUDA default, with
eager kept as the reference implementation, and the seed-43 pair stays in
the record as the one that did not agree.

## 2026-09-15 — Verdict, deflection sealed test: falsified. ISLA is 1.16x GeoTransolver on the 360 sealed high-deflection cases and both degrade by the same 1.23–1.25x across the geometry boundary {#sec-nb-deflection-verdict}

**Setting.** The geometry-extrapolation experiment of
@sec-nb-deflection-prereg, evaluated once and sealed as scripted in
@sec-nb-deflection-eval-ready and amended in @sec-nb-deflection-amend:
HiLiftAeroML's 180 geometries sorted by mean flap-and-slat deflection, the
1,260 cases of the 144 milder geometries for training (180 of them held
out as in-regime validation), the 360 cases of the 36 most aggressive
geometries as the sealed test. Arms: ISLA (`defl_hl_mt2_deflection_seed42/43`)
and unit-direction GeoTransolver (`udrv_hl_gt_deflection_seed42/43`),
lr $10^{-3}$, 10,000 tokens, 500 epochs, two seeds each. Float32
instrument; the same checkpoints scored on `deflection_val` (180 cases)
and `deflection_test` (360 cases, all present, disjoint from training and
validation by the sanctioned manifest builder). Artifact:
`results/deflection_sealed_test_2026-09-15.json`.

**What we saw** (relative $L^2$, seed means; $d$ = test ÷ validation):

| Field | ISLA val | ISLA test | $d$ ISLA | GeoTransolver val | GeoTransolver test | $d$ GT | ISLA ÷ GT, test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pressure | 0.0327 | 0.0400 | 1.23 | 0.0278 | 0.0346 | 1.25 | 1.157 |
| Velocity | 0.0537 | 0.0612 | 1.14 | 0.0490 | 0.0552 | 1.13 | 1.108 |
| Wall shear | 0.0846 | 0.0941 | 1.11 | 0.0771 | 0.0843 | 1.09 | 1.115 |
| Temperature | 0.0424 | 0.0497 | 1.17 | 0.0402 | 0.0467 | 1.16 | 1.065 |
| Density | 0.0446 | 0.0514 | 1.15 | 0.0380 | 0.0446 | 1.17 | 1.154 |

Per seed on pressure: ISLA test 0.0393 / 0.0407 (val 0.0317 / 0.0336);
GeoTransolver test 0.0339 / 0.0352 (val 0.0273 / 0.0282).

**Against the bars.** Carried required ISLA at or below 0.7x GeoTransolver
on the sealed test with $d \le 4$; falsified required ISLA at or above 0.9x
or both models at $d \ge 8$. **Falsified**: ISLA is 1.157x GeoTransolver on
pressure, 1.108x on velocity and 1.115x on wall shear, on all
five fields worse than GeoTransolver out of regime by almost exactly its
in-regime deficit (1.176x on validation pressure). The degradation
across the geometry boundary is mild and the same for both architectures:
1.23x for ISLA and 1.25x for GeoTransolver on pressure, and within 0.03 of
each other on every field. Neither model is near the $d \ge 8$ collapse
the preregistration guarded against.

**Why it matters.** The hypothesis was that ISLA's exact geometric
construction would carry across a *geometry-parameter* boundary better
than GeoTransolver's learned geometry encoding, as its pose invariance
carries across a *pose* boundary. It does not: on this split the two
architectures extrapolate equally well, and the ordering is the
in-regime ordering, unit-direction GeoTransolver ahead by about 15%. This
is the same shape as the fixed-angle result (@sec-nb-udrv-single-verdict): with the
input scale matched, GeoTransolver's advantage on HiLift is not a
generalization deficit that a harder split exposes, it is a capacity or
inductive-bias difference that survives the split unchanged. The 36 most
aggressive deflections are still the same wing family with the same
mesher, so this split tests interpolation in a geometry parameter more
than a new geometry class; a split across geometry classes remains the
open test of the geometry-generalization claim, and none of this book's
datasets provides one.

**Bookkeeping.** The stopped physical-velocity GeoTransolver arms were not
evaluated, as decided on 2026-09-09. No rerun.

## 2026-09-15 — Verdict, KERNEL-NEUTRAL at five seed pairs: no mean shift (ratio 1.009), four of five pairs within 3%, one 9% outlier; the fused kernel stays opt-in {#sec-nb-kernel-neutral-5seed-verdict}

**Setting.** The extension preregistered in
@sec-nb-kernel-neutral-3seed-verdict: seed pairs 45 and 46, fused and
eager, from the same snapshot with identical data order, added to the
three pairs already scored. Five matched pairs in total; float32 sealed
validation on 48 cars. Artifact:
`results/kernel_neutral_reduction_5seed_2026-09-15.json`. The eager
seed-46 lane lost one link to a preemption during a checkpoint write and
resumed from the previous save after the truncated files were set aside
(recorded in the cluster notes); its trajectory is otherwise unremarkable.

**What we saw** (float32 relative $L^2$; ratio = fused lane ÷ eager twin):

| Seed | Fused pressure | Eager pressure | Ratio | Wall-shear ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 42 | 0.0552 | 0.0547 | 1.008 | 1.011 |
| 43 | 0.0607 | 0.0557 | 1.089 | 1.096 |
| 44 | 0.0543 | 0.0556 | 0.977 | 0.983 |
| 45 | 0.0561 | 0.0560 | 1.002 | 1.003 |
| 46 | 0.0557 | 0.0573 | 0.971 | 0.966 |

Five-seed means: pressure ratio 1.009, wall shear 1.011. Spread
across seeds: fused 11.3%, eager 4.7% (ratio 2.4x). Seeds
outside the eager spread plus 3%: 43. Evaluation-time kernel
difference on any checkpoint: at most $5 \times 10^{-7}$. Epoch time on the
new pairs, trained under storage contention: fused 39 and 41 s, eager 41
and 42 s (1.03x); the quiet seed-44 pair gave 1.1x.

**Against the preregistered clauses.** Neither clause is met cleanly, and
the record says so. The *variance* clause needed the fused spread at
least twice the eager spread **and** a second fused seed outside the eager
spread plus 3%: the spread ratio is 2.4x, but no second seed is out;
seed 43 is the only one. The *chance* clause needed both new pairs within
3% **and** the spreads within a factor of two: both new pairs are within 3%
(1.002 and 0.971), but the spread ratio is above two, because seed 43 is
still in the set. Read plainly: four of five matched pairs agree within
3%, two of them with the fused kernel better; the five-seed mean is
1.009; and one pair, seed 43, has the fused lane 9% worse. Five draws
cannot say whether that pair is a kernel-induced tail or one unlucky run,
and the eager side's own spread grew from 1.8% to 4.7% as seeds were
added, which shows how noisy a single pair is at this size.

**Decision.** The default-flip rule required the chance clause plus a mean
within 3%; the chance clause is not met, so **`geo_kernel="eager"` stays
the default and the reference implementation**, and the fused kernel
stays an exact, documented opt-in with this record attached. The
decision costs little at the reference size: the like-for-like epoch gain
at 10,000 tokens with compile off is 1.03 to 1.1x. The kernel's value is
the 2.2x at 40,000 tokens under compile (@sec-nb-kernel-study), which has
not been trained for neutrality at all; a neutrality lane at that size is
the next step if the 40,000-token regime becomes a production setting,
and a float32-accumulation path for the pooled invariants remains the
engineering candidate if a tail is ever confirmed. No further seed pairs
at 10,000 tokens: the marginal pair cannot move the decision.

## 2026-09-15 — Relative-frame divergence at width 512: the localization matrix says width, not token count; half the learning rate cures it; the head-frame singularity is present but not the cause {#sec-nb-relframe-divergence-matrix}

**Setting.** The width- and token-scaling study (SCALE, run by a parallel
session) trained the reference configuration, the relative frame with the
total-measure scale, at width 512 on 80,000 DrivAerML cells per case
(`scale_isla_dr_r512x80k_seed42/43`, protocol learning rate $10^{-3}$,
bfloat16, snapshot `code_globin`). Both seeds reached a step loss of
0.006 to 0.007 by epoch 20 and then drifted to a mean-field predictor
(float32 pressure 0.77, sample-frame ratio one), with no NaN and no
restart artifact. The constant and similarity gauges at the same width
and count, and the relative frame at width 192 and 10,000 cells, trained
normally. Per the preregistration rule the corner is recorded as a
divergence at the protocol rate and not retuned. That session approved a
30-epoch, one-seed localization matrix (`highlift/hl_scale_isla_locmat_aga.sbatch`,
readout: divergence if the epoch-30 mean step loss exceeds 3x its epoch-5
value) and a diagnostic arm logging, at every step, the minimum
anchor-relative distance $\min_i |u_i|$ of the head frame, the count of
tokens below $10^{-3}$, and the gradient flowing into $u$. The session
ended before reading the results; this entry reads them.

**Truth table** (epoch-mean step loss at epochs 5 and 29; seed 42;
`runs/locmat_*`):

| Arm | Frame | Width | Cells | Learning rate | Epoch 5 | Epoch 29 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a | relative, recompute off | 512 | 80,000 | $10^{-3}$ | 0.0148 | 0.0469 | **diverged** (3.2x) |
| b | relative | 192 | 80,000 | $10^{-3}$ | 0.0082 | 0.0017 | stable |
| c | relative | 512 | 10,000 | $10^{-3}$ | 0.0133 | 0.0646 | **diverged** (4.9x) |
| d | relative | 512 | 80,000 | $5 \times 10^{-4}$ | 0.0086 | 0.0016 | stable |
| e | centered, constant gauge | 512 | 80,000 | $10^{-3}$ | 0.0085 | 0.0021 | stable |
| f | relative (diagnostic build) | 512 | 80,000 | $10^{-3}$ | 0.0148 | 0.0469 | diverged, identical to a |

The validation pressure of the diverged arms rises to 0.68 (a) and 0.78
(c), the mean-field level; arm d reaches 0.088 by epoch 29 and arm e
0.10 (30-epoch values, not comparable to 500-epoch numbers). Arms a and f
are step-for-step identical, so the diagnostic build changed no
arithmetic.

**What the diagnostic arm says about the hypothesis.** The head-frame
singularity conjectured on 2026-09-15 (the radial basis vector
$u_i = r_i - \sum_s b_{is} z_s$ vanishing when a slice collapses onto a
token, so that $\hat u = u/|u|$ carries a $1/|u|$ gradient) is **present
in geometry and falsified as the mechanism**. $\min_i|u_i|$ falls from
$2 \times 10^{-2}$ at step 1 to $10^{-5}$ by epoch 6 and stays there, with up to
nine tokens below $10^{-3}$ at once; the largest gradient into $u$ is 1.7
(step 881, epoch 8.2) against a typical $10^{-3}$. But the loss five and
fifty steps after every one of the twelve largest gradient spikes is
unchanged or lower, the spikes cluster in epochs 5 to 10 while the loss
is still falling, and the first step whose loss exceeds three times the
epoch-5 mean is step 3128, epoch 29, at the end of a slow drift that
starts near epoch 20. A singularity would spike; this drifts. The
near-degenerate tokens are a real property of the trained relative frame
and cost nothing here; the smooth normalization proposed as a fix is not
needed for this failure and is not adopted.

**What the table says instead.** Divergence needs the relative frame
**and** width 512, at 10,000 cells as at 80,000; token count is not a
factor, and the centered frame at the same width is stable. Halving the
learning rate cures it completely. That is the signature of an
optimization instability that scales with width, not a numerical one:
in the relative frame the per-token seed is the single scalar
$\hat n_i\cdot\hat g$ (the centered frame's seed has five), so the first
slice block's assignment logits depend on one input coordinate and every
token separation must be built by the relational anchors from a nearly
constant embedding. At width 512 and learning rate $10^{-3}$ that
construction drifts toward uniform routing, and uniform routing is the
mean-field predictor the runs converge to. The mechanism is a
hypothesis until the routing entropy of the diverged and stable
checkpoints is compared, which is the next check, on the epoch-30
checkpoints already on disk.

**What follows.** The reference configuration at width 512 needs a
learning rate below $10^{-3}$; the cured arm used $5 \times 10^{-4}$, which is
within a factor of 1.3 of the $1/\text{width}$ scaling from 192
($3.75 \times 10^{-4}$). Whether the program adopts a width-scaled rate
rule for every architecture, or treats the relative frame's single-scalar
seed as the defect and widens it in a contract-preserving way, is a
decision for the coordinator and Peter; the matrix does not choose. No
retune of the corner lanes was run.

## 2026-09-15 — Mechanism of the width-512 divergence: routing hardens to one slice per token and the anchors collapse to the center; the head singularity is a bystander {#sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism}

**Setting.** The localization matrix of @sec-nb-relframe-divergence-matrix
left the mechanism open. Its epoch-30 checkpoints were probed on the
laptop GPU with one synthetic star-shaped body of 10,000 tokens and a unit
global vector, reading in every slice block the token-to-slice routing
(the softmax over slices that each token reads its slice state through),
the number of slices carrying measure, and the spread of the slice
anchors relative to the token cloud's radius (script
`probe_routing_collapse.py`, session job directory).

**What we saw.** Every checkpoint keeps all 256 slices populated, so this
is not slice death. The difference is in how tokens read:

| Checkpoint | Verdict at 30 epochs | Routing entropy ÷ log S, layers 1–12 | Anchor spread ÷ cloud radius |
|---|---|---|---|
| a, relative 512×80k | diverged | 0.02 0.71 0.00 0.01 0.06 0.14 0.01 0.21 0.09 0.11 0.06 0.05 | 0.30 0.12 0.11 0.13 0.21 0.26 0.24 0.28 0.26 0.20 0.17 0.08 |
| c, relative 512×10k | diverged | 0.00 0.03 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.83 0.94 0.06 | 0.09 0.01 0.01 0.01 0.01 0.02 0.03 0.03 0.04 0.03 0.04 0.05 |
| d, relative 512×80k, lr 5e-4 | stable | 0.97 0.35 0.49 0.65 0.39 0.87 0.88 0.87 0.85 0.68 0.87 0.93 | 0.51 0.12 0.12 0.14 0.16 0.18 0.21 0.21 0.19 0.20 0.10 0.06 |
| e, centered 512×80k | stable | 0.03 0.60 0.70 0.70 0.81 0.82 0.81 0.80 0.68 0.57 0.83 0.94 | 0.15 0.13 0.14 0.18 0.22 0.23 0.25 0.25 0.24 0.14 0.15 0.06 |

The diverged models read one slice per token, almost deterministically, in
nearly every layer (entropy at or below 0.05 of the uniform value), and in
the faster-diverging arm c the anchors of all 256 slices sit within 1% of
the cloud radius of one another: the slices have lost spatial locality
entirely, every anchor is the body's center, every point-anchor
invariant is the same for every slice, and the network has nothing left
to separate tokens with beyond the slice index it hardened onto. Its
output spread over tokens is a third of the stable models'. The stable
models keep soft routing, entropy 0.4 to 0.97, and anchors spread over 10
to 50% of the radius, that is, spatially localized slices.

**Why the relative frame, and why width.** In the centered frame the
first slice block sorts tokens by five seed scalars, three of them
positional (|r|, r̂·ĝ, r̂·n̂), so its slices are spatial from the first
step and their anchors are spread; the relational invariants then refine
a routing that already has locality. In the relative frame the seed is
the single orientation scalar n̂·ĝ, so the first layer can sort tokens by
normal direction only, the slices are orientation sets, and the anchor
of an orientation set on a closed body lies near the center. Locality
has to be bootstrapped by the relational geometry in later layers from
anchors that start degenerate, and that bootstrap is a race against the
routing hardening: at width 192 and the protocol rate it wins (the
reference lanes), at width 512 and the protocol rate it loses, at width
512 and half the rate it wins again. The head-frame singularity noted in
the matrix entry is a consequence of the same hardening (one-hot routing
puts tokens on their anchors), not a cause; its gradient never moved the
loss.

**What this implies.** Two fix classes, both contract-preserving, one
test to discriminate them: (i) a width-scaled learning rate, the
optimization rule the cured arm already exemplifies; (ii) a routing
temperature, scaling the assignment logits so the softmax over slices
starts and stays softer at large width. If (ii) at the protocol rate is
stable at 512×10,000, the instability lives in the routing logits' scale
with width and the fix belongs in the architecture, where it applies to
every dataset without a rate rule; if only (i) works, it is an
optimization rule. Preregistered as a 30-epoch pair on the fastest-failing
configuration, arm c (512×10,000): (g) logits scaled by 192/512 at the
protocol rate, and (h) the protocol rate unchanged as the diverging
control. Bar: the matrix readout (epoch-30 mean step loss below the
epoch-5 value = stable; above three times it = diverged). The scale knob
defaults to one, so no existing checkpoint changes.

## 2026-09-15 — Verdict, LOCMAT-2: a softer routing temperature delays the width-512 collapse by three epochs and does not prevent it; the working remedy is the learning rate {#sec-nb-relframe-divergence-locmat2-verdict}

**Setting.** The pair preregistered in
@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism: the fastest-failing configuration
of the relative-frame divergence matrix (width 512, 10,000 cells,
protocol rate $10^{-3}$, seed 42, 30 epochs) with the slice blocks'
assignment logits scaled by 192/512 = 0.375 (arm g) against the
unchanged control (arm h), both under the snapshot `code_globin2` that
adds the `routing_logit_scale` knob (default 1.0). Readout: the matrix
rule, epoch-30 mean step loss against its epoch-5 value.

**What we saw.** The control reproduces matrix arm c to four digits at
every epoch (0.0133 at epoch 5, 0.0646 at epoch 29, validation pressure
0.7775 at epoch 29), which also proves on a real run that the knob's
default is bitwise the previous code. The softened arm **diverges too**:
epoch-5 mean 0.0160, epoch-29 mean 0.0578 (3.6x), validation pressure
0.774 at the end. Its collapse comes later, best validation pressure
0.264 at epoch 10 against the control's 0.252 at epoch 6, and the drift
to the mean-field level runs from epoch 12 to 18 against 8 to 15. A
factor 0.375 on the logits buys about three epochs and changes nothing
else. The falsified prediction was that stability at the protocol rate
would place the instability in the routing logits' scale; it does not.

**Parameter comparison** (epoch-30 checkpoints of the matrix arms). The
assignment layers' weight norms are the same in diverged and stable
models, 9 to 16 per layer with the same depth profile, and the
LayerNorm gains sit at one everywhere; there is no weight explosion. The
one systematic difference is the assignment **bias**: its largest entry is
0.2 to 0.5 per layer in the diverged models against 0.05 to 0.13 in the
stable ones, consistent with tokens hardening onto a few shared slices
whose anchors then sit at the center (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism).
The relational-geometry logit weights and the seed embedding are the
same across all four. Norms alone cannot say what drives the hardening;
they say what does not.

**Where this leaves the flagship at width 512.** Three facts are
established: the relative frame at width 512 diverges at the protocol
rate at 10,000 and 80,000 cells while the centered frame does not; the
divergence is a slow hardening of the token-to-slice routing with
anchor collapse; halving the learning rate removes it (matrix arm d,
stable to 0.0016 with validation pressure 0.088 at 30 epochs). One
candidate fix is refuted (routing temperature), one is not needed (the
head-frame normalization). **Recommendation for Peter:** treat the width
scaling of the learning rate as the protocol for ISLA's width ladder,
$\eta(w) = 10^{-3} \cdot 192 / w$ (which gives $3.75 \times 10^{-4}$ at 512,
within a factor 1.3 of the cured arm), stated once and applied to every
width, rather than a per-run retune; whether the same rule is applied to
the baselines' width arms is a fairness decision that the baselines'
own stability at $10^{-3}$ does not force. The architectural question,
a routing that cannot harden in the relative frame (the single-scalar
seed is the plausible root, since the centered frame's five-scalar seed
gives layer one spatial slices from the first step), is a research node,
not a productization item, and is left open with its evidence.

**Bookkeeping.** `routing_logit_scale` stays in the code as the recorded
ablation (default 1.0, bitwise); the corner lanes are not relaunched at
a retuned rate without the coordinator's and Peter's say-so, per the
parallel session's rule.

## 2026-09-15 — Preregistration, CORNER-WLR: the reference configuration at the scale corner under the width learning-rate rule {#sec-nb-corner-wlr-prereg}

**Setting.** The scoreboard's only measurement of ISLA at the scale
corner (width 512, 80,000 DrivAerML cells per car) is the constant-gauge
variant, at 0.0428 against GeoTransolver's 0.0419 and Transolver's 0.0431
(float32, evaluated at 80,000 cells, seed means; @sec-program-status).
The reference configuration itself, the relative frame with the
total-measure scale, has no number there: at the protocol learning rate
of $10^{-3}$ it diverged on both seeds, and the localization work of
@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-matrix and @sec-nb-relframe-divergence-locmat2-verdict
located the cause in a width-driven hardening of the slice routing that a
lower learning rate removes. Whether the flagship reaches parity with the
baselines at scale is therefore open, and it is the load-bearing question
for the claim that the reference-size deficit is a statement about size.
Peter's directive of 2026-09-15 is to prepare the mainline as a clear,
evidence-grounded case; this is the experiment that case needs most.

**The arm.** `scale_isla_dr_r512x80k_wlr_seed42/43`: the reference
configuration (`isla_surface_reference`, geometry recompute on) at width
512 and 80,000 cells, learning rate $10^{-3} \times 192/512 = 3.75 \times 10^{-4}$,
everything else as the corner lanes (500 epochs, bfloat16, compile off,
no augmentation), snapshot `code_globin2` at its identity defaults
(launcher `kernel/corner_wlr_aga.sbatch`). This is a **width-rule arm**,
labeled as such: the protocol-rate arm's divergence stays on the record
and no protocol-rate lane is relaunched. Evaluation with the float32
instrument at 80,000 cells on the 48 validation cars, and the sample-frame
probe at 80,000 and 10,000 cells as for the corner's other arms.

**Predictions and bars, written before the run.**

- **Parity at scale.** The two-seed mean float32 pressure error lies
  within **3%** of GeoTransolver's corner value 0.0419, that is at most
  0.0432, and within 3% of the constant-gauge variant's 0.0428. Meeting it
  makes the sentence "at scale the three architectures are within 3%,
  including the reference configuration" true and closes the corner row
  of the scoreboard with the flagship on it.
- **Falsified** if the reference is worse than 1.10x GeoTransolver
  (above 0.0461): then the relative frame carries an accuracy price at
  scale that the constant gauge does not, and the frame decision of
  @sec-principled-decisions is re-opened with that number.
- **Between** 3% and 10%: reported as the reference frame's price at
  scale, with the frame decision unchanged (the decision was never made
  on accuracy).
- **Stability.** Both seeds train to 500 epochs without the drift of the
  protocol-rate arm (epoch-mean step loss monotone to within noise after
  epoch 20). Divergence at this rate would falsify the width rule as the
  remedy and send the question back to the routing mechanism.
- **Sample-frame consistency** at 80,000 cells: ratio at most 1.5, the
  corner's existing bar, expected to be met since the frame reads no sample
  statistic.

## 2026-09-15 — The 1,260-case HiLift rung with unit-direction GeoTransolver: GeoTransolver 0.0355 against ISLA's constant-gauge 0.0405 on pressure (0.88x); the ladder's ordering holds at full data {#sec-nb-udrv-1260-verdict}

**Setting.** The last rung of the HiLiftAeroML data-efficiency ladder
without a fair baseline was the full training split, 1,260 cases: the
physical-velocity GeoTransolver arm had been stopped on 2026-09-09 when the
unit-direction verdict made it an unfair comparison
(@sec-nb-udrv-resched), and its unit-direction replacements
`udrv_hl_gt_full_seed42/43` (unit-direction lane rows 16 and 17, learning
rate $10^{-3}$, 10,000 cells, 500 epochs) have been training since, at
about fifteen minutes per epoch on the I/O-bound full split. Both trained
today and were scored with the float32 instrument on the 180 validation
cases against the rate-matched ISLA constant-gauge priors
`mt2_hl_lr1_seed42/43`, the same pair the 20,000-token floor test uses
(@sec-nb-floor20k-isla). Artifact: `results/udrv_1260_reduction_2026-09-15.json`.

**What we saw** (relative $L^2$, seeds and means; ratio = GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA):

| Field | GeoTransolver, unit direction | ISLA, constant gauge | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pressure | 0.0363 / 0.0348 → 0.0355 | 0.0393 / 0.0417 → 0.0405 | 0.878 |
| Velocity | 0.0530 / 0.0518 → 0.0524 | 0.0572 / 0.0592 → 0.0582 | 0.900 |
| Wall shear | 0.0844 / 0.0825 → 0.0834 | 0.0905 / 0.0942 → 0.0923 | 0.904 |

**Reading.** GeoTransolver leads by 12% on pressure and 10% on velocity
and wall shear at full data, the same margin as at 510 cases (0.84x) and
210 cases (0.84x against the constant gauge): the HiLift ordering is
flat in training-set size from 210 to 1,260 cases, and the full rung adds
no new information about which architecture learns more from more data.
ISLA's reference configuration is not measured on this rung (it costs a
week of I/O-bound training per seed and the ladder's other rungs put it
0.84 to 0.94x of the constant gauge on HiLift); the constant-gauge
variant is the ISLA value here, as on the 510-case rung. The Transolver
pair (`udrv_hl_transolver_full_lr3e3_seed42/43`) is at epochs 444 and
471 and will complete the rung's baseline column.

**Why it matters.** With this rung the HiLift ladder has a unit-direction
GeoTransolver on every count, and the verdict of @sec-verdict stands
without a "not yet measured" caveat on the surface: the baselines lead
ISLA in-distribution at every HiLift count and at DrivAerML's reference
size, by 6 to 25%, and the deficit does not close with data. The case for
ISLA is the one the book already makes: exact contracts where pose
varies, sampling consistency by construction, the interior velocity lead,
learning-rate robustness, memory, and the general input interface; the
in-distribution surface accuracy of the released baselines is not among
its wins, at any count measured.

## 2026-09-15 — Recipe configuration names: the plain `isla_surface` and `isla_volume` now carry the reference configuration; the constant gauge is a named variant {#sec-nb-config-rename}

**The setting.** The training recipe under
`examples/cfd/external_aerodynamics/unified_external_aero_recipe` exposes
each architecture as a Hydra model configuration selected with
`model=<name>`. Until today the plain ISLA surface name, `isla_surface`,
carried the constant-gauge construction (the centered frame with a fixed
reference length, the reference configuration before 2026-09-11), while
the flagship relative-frame, total-measure configuration lived under the
suffixed name `isla_surface_reference`, and likewise `isla_volume_reference`
for the interior. An integrator reading the recipe would have trained the
ablation under the obvious name. A `mt2_surface` pointer from the
ISLA-to-ISLA rename also survived.

**What changed.** The plain names are now the reference configurations
and the constant gauge is explicitly named:

| Before 2026-09-15 | From 2026-09-15 | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `isla_surface_reference.yaml` | `isla_surface.yaml` | surface reference: relative frame, total-measure scale |
| `isla_surface.yaml` | `isla_surface_constant_gauge.yaml` | centered frame, `reference_length: 8.0` (ablation) |
| `isla_volume_reference.yaml` | `isla_volume.yaml` | interior reference: query tokens with the signed distance |
| `mt2_surface.yaml` | deleted | pointer to the old `isla_surface` |

`isla_surface_reference.yaml` and `isla_volume_reference.yaml` remain as
one-line pointers to the plain files, so older launch commands and the
provenance references in this notebook still resolve; `isla_volume_support.yaml`
is unchanged. Model checkpoints are unaffected because they store their
constructor arguments. The cluster's frozen recipe snapshots
(`recipe_globin`, `recipe_relint` and earlier) predate the rename and keep
the old names, so every sbatch script written against them runs as before;
lanes launched against a post-rename snapshot pass `model=isla_surface` or
`model=isla_volume`.

**Guard.** `tests/test_isla_configs.py` composes the four names and the
constant gauge through Hydra and asserts the frame and scale of each, that
the deprecated names compose to exactly the plain files, and that the
interior reference pairs the corrected boundary measure with the
total-measure scale. Writing it exposed that the test it replaces
(`test_isla_volume_reference_config.py`, committed 2026-09-14) had never
passed as committed: it read the architecture block at `cfg.model.model`,
whereas the recipe's `@package _global_` model files place it directly at
`cfg.model` and the data-to-model mapping at `cfg.forward_kwargs`. The
new test reads the real layout.

**Reading rule for older entries.** Text in this notebook written before
2026-09-15 that names `isla_surface.yaml` means the constant gauge, and
text that names `isla_surface_reference.yaml` means today's
`isla_surface.yaml`. The rule is recorded in `CLAIMS.md`.

**The class-name aliases went with it.** The 2026-09-07 rename from
ISLA to ISLA had left an import-path alias
(`physicsnemo.experimental.nn.mt2`) and a class alias (`MeshTransformer2`)
in the package. Neither name ever appeared in a PhysicsNeMo release, so
both are deleted from the mainline; the one remaining mention of the old
name is the class attribute that lets checkpoint files written under it
(`MeshTransformer2.*.mdlus`) still load, which the checkpoint tests cover.
The ISLA unit suite drops the alias test (44 tests plus the 12 general-input
tests); the recipe suite passes at 233 after the rename.

## 2026-09-15 — Verdict, CORNER-WLR: the reference configuration reaches 0.0442 at the 512 × 80k corner under the width learning rate, 1.05x GeoTransolver, between the parity and falsification bars {#sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict}

**The setting.** The scale corner of this program is DrivAerML at hidden
width 512 and 80,000 surface cells per car, where GeoTransolver (0.0419),
ISLA's constant-gauge variant (0.0428) and Transolver (0.0431) sit within
3% of one another on float32 surface pressure. The reference configuration
of ISLA, the relative frame with the total-measure scale, had no number
there because it diverged at the protocol learning rate of $10^{-3}$; the
divergence was traced to a width-driven hardening of the slice routing
that a lower rate removes (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism). The
preregistration of @sec-nb-corner-wlr-prereg asked whether the flagship
reaches parity at scale when trained at the width rule
$10^{-3} \times 192/512 = 3.75 \times 10^{-4}$, with three outcomes
written in advance: parity within 3% of GeoTransolver (at most 0.0432),
falsified above 1.10x (0.0461), and "between" reported as the reference
frame's price at scale with the frame decision unchanged.

**What was run.** Two seeds of the reference configuration at width 512
and 80,000 cells (`scale_isla_dr_r512x80k_wlr_seed42/43`), 500 epochs,
bfloat16, no augmentation, everything as the corner's other arms except
the learning rate. Evaluation with the corner's float32 instrument on the
48 validation cars: the sample-frame density probe at 80,000 cells
(uniform probe = in-family accuracy; biased ÷ uniform = density factor)
and the same probe at 10,000 cells
(results/corner_wlr_reduction_2026-09-15.json).

**What we saw.**

| quantity (float32, 48 cars) | seed 42 | seed 43 | mean | comparators at the corner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pressure, uniform probe, 80,000 cells | 0.0449 | 0.0434 | **0.0442** | GeoTransolver 0.0419, constant gauge 0.0428, Transolver 0.0431 |
| ratio to GeoTransolver | | | **1.054** | parity bar 1.03; falsifier 1.10 |
| ratio to the constant-gauge variant | | | 1.032 | |
| ratio to Transolver | | | 1.025 | |
| wall shear, uniform probe, 80,000 cells | 0.0698 | 0.0677 | 0.0688 | not reduced for the other corner arms |
| pressure, biased probe, 80,000 cells | 0.0475 | 0.0457 | 0.0466 | |
| density factor at 80,000 cells | 1.06 | 1.05 | **1.05** | GeoTransolver 10.5, Transolver 14.9, constant gauge 16.6, similarity gauge 1.09; bar 1.5 |
| pressure, uniform probe, 10,000 cells | 0.0606 | 0.0576 | 0.0591 | no other corner arm evaluated at 10,000 cells |
| density factor at 10,000 cells | 1.97 | 1.73 | 1.85 | |

Both seeds trained to 500 epochs without the drift of the protocol-rate
arm: the epoch-mean step loss falls from 0.051 at epoch 0 to 0.00105 at
50, 0.00048 at 100, 0.00030 at 200 and sits at 0.00028 from epoch 250 to
the end, with the minimum (0.00027) at epochs 391 and 376, inside the
plateau's noise. The stability bar is met.

**Verdict.** **Between.** The two-seed mean is 5.4% above GeoTransolver
and 3.2% above the constant-gauge variant, so the parity bar is missed by
2.4 points and the falsifier is not fired. Per the preregistration this is
reported as the reference frame's price at scale, and the frame decision of
@sec-principled-decisions, which was never made on accuracy, is unchanged.
The sample-frame consistency bar is met with a wide margin: the reference
configuration's error rises 5% under a 10:1 density bias where the
released baselines' rise 10 to 15 times and the constant-gauge variant's
17 times.

**Why it matters.** At the reference size (width 192, 10,000 cells, 435
cars) the reference configuration is 1.10x GeoTransolver (0.0552 against
0.0503). At the corner it is 1.05x. Half of the reference-size deficit is
therefore a statement about size and resolution, and half remains as the
frame's price. One confound is stated here and wherever this number is
quoted: the reference at the corner trained at 3.75e-4 while the other
three arms trained at their protocol rates, because the reference's
protocol-rate lane diverged; part of the 5% may be rate rather than frame,
and no protocol-rate reference number exists at the corner to separate
them. The 10,000-cell evaluation of the 80,000-cell-trained model, 0.0591
with a density factor of 1.85, is recorded without a comparator: none of
the corner's other arms was evaluated eight times coarser than it trained.

**What's next.** The width learning-rate rule
($10^{-3} \times 192/\text{width}$) is now the only recipe under which the
reference configuration trains at width 512; adopting it as ISLA's protocol
above width 192, or returning to the routing mechanism for a rate-free fix,
is Peter's decision. A single control would close the rate confound: the
constant-gauge variant at the corner under the same 3.75e-4 (one two-seed
pair, about six GPU-hours per seed); if it lands near its 1e-3 value of
0.0428 the 5% is the frame's, and if it lands near 0.0442 it is the rate's.
That control is launched as CG-WLR (@sec-nb-cg-wlr-prereg).

## 2026-09-15 — Preregistration, CG-WLR: the constant-gauge variant at the corner under the width learning rate, to split the reference's 5% into frame and rate {#sec-nb-cg-wlr-prereg}

**Setting.** The CORNER-WLR verdict (@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict) puts
ISLA's reference configuration at 0.0442 on the 512-wide, 80,000-cell
DrivAerML corner, 1.05x GeoTransolver and 1.03x ISLA's constant-gauge
variant, but the reference trained at the width learning rate 3.75e-4
while every other corner arm trained at its protocol rate (1e-3 for the
constant gauge). The 5% therefore has two candidate owners: the relative
frame, and the lower rate's slower progress within 500 epochs. A single
control separates them.

**The arm.** `scale_isla_dr_cg512x80k_wlr_seed42/43`: the constant-gauge
variant (centered frame, `reference_length` 8.0; `model=isla_surface` in
the pre-rename cluster snapshot `recipe_globin`, which the launcher
asserts is the centered frame before training) at width 512 and 80,000
cells, learning rate 3.75e-4, otherwise identical to the reference pair
(500 epochs, bfloat16, compile off, no augmentation, snapshot
`code_globin2`; launcher `kernel/cg_wlr_aga.sbatch`). Evaluation with the
corner's float32 sample-frame probe at 80,000 and 10,000 cells
(`kernel/cg_wlr_eval_aga.sbatch`). Two seeds, about six GPU-hours each.

**Predictions and bars, written before the run.** Let $c$ be the
two-seed mean float32 pressure error of this arm at 80,000 cells; the
constant gauge's protocol-rate value is 0.0428 and the reference's
width-rate value is 0.0442.

- **Frame owns the 5%** if $c \le 0.0432$ (within 1% of the constant
  gauge's protocol-rate value): the rate costs the constant gauge nothing,
  so the reference's excess is the relative frame's price at scale, and
  the sentence in @sec-verdict stays as written.
- **Rate owns most of it** if $c \ge 0.0438$: the lower rate costs the
  constant gauge at least two thirds of the reference's excess, the
  reference's 5% is rewritten as "at most 1.6% frame" and the corner
  becomes a matched-rate comparison between the two ISLA configurations
  with the baselines' protocol-rate numbers flagged as unmatched.
- **Mixed** between 0.0432 and 0.0438: reported as such, with the split
  stated in readout units.
- **Stability.** Both seeds train to 500 epochs (the constant gauge is
  stable at 1e-3 at this width; a lower rate is not expected to change
  that).

## 2026-09-16 — Verdict, CG-WLR: the constant gauge under the width learning rate scores 0.0424, so the rate costs it nothing and the reference configuration's corner excess is the frame's {#sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict}

**The setting.** The CORNER-WLR verdict (@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict) left
one confound open: ISLA's reference configuration scored 0.0442 at the
512-wide, 80,000-cell DrivAerML corner after training at the width
learning rate 3.75e-4, while the constant-gauge variant's corner value
0.0428 came from the protocol rate 1e-3. The preregistration of
@sec-nb-cg-wlr-prereg trained the constant-gauge variant itself at
3.75e-4, two seeds, otherwise identical to the reference pair, and wrote
the bars in advance: a two-seed mean at or below 0.0432 gives the excess
to the frame, at or above 0.0438 to the rate, between is mixed.

**What we saw** (float32, 48 validation cars, sample-frame probe;
results/cg_wlr_reduction_2026-09-16.json):

| quantity | seed 42 | seed 43 | mean | comparators |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pressure, uniform probe, 80,000 cells | 0.0418 | 0.0429 | **0.0424** | constant gauge at 1e-3: 0.0428; reference at 3.75e-4: 0.0442; GeoTransolver 0.0419 |
| ratio to the constant gauge at 1e-3 | | | **0.990** | |
| reference at 3.75e-4 ÷ this arm | | | **1.042** | matched-rate frame price |
| wall shear, uniform probe, 80,000 cells | 0.0659 | 0.0680 | 0.0670 | reference at 3.75e-4: 0.0688 |
| density factor at 80,000 cells | 14.1 | 14.4 | 14.2 | constant gauge at 1e-3: 16.6; reference: 1.05 |
| pressure, uniform probe, 10,000 cells | 0.0587 | 0.0605 | 0.0596 | reference at 3.75e-4: 0.0591 |
| density factor at 10,000 cells | 10.1 | 10.3 | 10.2 | reference at 3.75e-4: 1.85 |

Both seeds trained to 500 epochs without incident.

**Verdict.** **The frame owns the excess.** At 0.0424 the constant gauge
under the lower rate is 1% *better* than at its protocol rate, so the
rate component of the reference's excess is zero to within seed noise
(−0.0004 in readout units against a seed spread of 0.0011) and the whole
of the reference's excess over the constant gauge at the corner, 0.0018
or 4.2% at matched rate, is the relative frame's. The rate confound
stated in the CORNER-WLR verdict is closed: the sentence "the reference
frame's price at scale is about 5%" stands without the qualifier. The
sample-frame density factor of 14 confirms, as at 1e-3, that the
constant gauge's accuracy does not survive a 10:1 density bias while the
reference's does (1.05); nothing about that trade changes with the rate.

**Why it matters.** The corner now has a matched-rate pair of ISLA
configurations: the frame that gives sampling consistency by construction
costs 4% of in-distribution pressure accuracy at scale, against 0% at the
reference size on DrivAerML (@sec-verdict) and 1 to 5% on the
never-seen-geometry rungs. The constant gauge at the width rate is also
the best ISLA number at the corner, 0.0424 against GeoTransolver's
0.0419, 1.01x; it is recorded here as a control and does not enter the
scoreboard's corner row, which keeps the protocol-rate constant gauge
(0.0428) and the width-rate reference (0.0442) so that every arm in the
row is labeled by the rate it actually trained at. The width rule itself
is now measured on both ISLA constructions at width 512: it is neutral
for the centered frame and necessary for the relative one.

**What's next.** The width learning-rate rule decision stays with Peter;
this entry removes one argument against adopting it (it costs the
centered construction nothing) and adds none for the routing mechanism
beyond what @sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism already records.

## 2026-09-16 — The 1,260-case HiLift rung, Transolver column: unit-direction Transolver 0.0385 against ISLA's constant-gauge 0.0405 (0.95x); the rung's baseline column is complete {#sec-nb-udrv-1260-transolver-verdict}

**The setting.** The 1,260-case rung is the full HiLiftAeroML training

the GeoTransolver half of this rung (0.0355 against ISLA's constant-gauge
variant 0.0405, GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.88) while the plain Transolver pair
was still training; its two lanes, at 14 minutes per epoch on 1,260 cases
of 10,000 cells, finished on 2026-09-16 after eleven and twelve four-hour
chain links each.

**What was run.** `udrv_hl_transolver_full_lr3e3_seed42/43`: Transolver
at its protocol learning rate 3e-3, unit freestream direction, 500 epochs,
evaluated in float32 on the 180 validation cases at 10,000 cells with the
same instrument as the GeoTransolver pair
(results/udrv_1260_transolver_2026-09-16.json).

**What we saw** (float32, 180 validation cases, two seeds each, ratios
baseline ÷ ISLA):

| field | Transolver (seeds) | GeoTransolver | ISLA constant gauge | Transolver ÷ ISLA | Transolver ÷ GeoTransolver |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pressure | **0.0385** (0.0387 / 0.0383) | 0.0355 | 0.0405 | **0.952** | 1.084 |
| velocity | 0.0557 (0.0557 / 0.0557) | 0.0524 | 0.0582 | 0.957 | 1.063 |

## 2026-09-17 — Verdict, W2-C 20,000-cell floor test, GeoTransolver half: doubling the cells lowers both architectures by about 5% and leaves their ratio unchanged; the 1,260-case gap is not a token floor {#sec-nb-w2c-floor-verdict}

**The setting.** The HiLift data-efficiency ladder flattens at its top:
from 510 to 1,260 training cases the baselines' lead over ISLA's
constant-gauge variant moves little (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.84 then 0.88
on pressure, @sec-nb-udrv-1260-verdict). W2-C asked whether that
flattening is a shared protocol floor set by the 10,000 sampled cells per
case rather than by the architectures: if both models are starved of
surface resolution at 1,260 cases, doubling the cells should move both and
could move their ratio. The ISLA half was reduced on 2026-09-15
(results/floor20k_2026-09-15.json): the constant-gauge variant trained at
20,000 cells scores 0.0384 against 0.0405 at 10,000, a 5.1% gain for a
2.0x step time and 1.9x peak memory. The GeoTransolver half, the
unit-direction pair `udrv_hl_gt_full_20k_seed42/43` at learning rate
1e-3, finished training on 2026-09-17 after about 35 four-hour chain
links each on the I/O-bound 1,260-case set.

**What was run.** Both halves are evaluated in float32 on the 180
validation cases at 10,000 cells, the rung's instrument, so the
comparison isolates the training resolution
(results/floor20k_gt_2026-09-17.json).

**What we saw** (float32, 180 validation cases, two seeds each; ratios
GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA constant gauge):

| field | GeoTransolver 20k (seeds) | ISLA 20k (seeds) | ratio at 20k | ratio at 10k | GeoTransolver 20k ÷ 10k | ISLA 20k ÷ 10k |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pressure | **0.0340** (0.0333 / 0.0347) | **0.0384** (0.0380 / 0.0388) | **0.885** | 0.878 | 0.956 | 0.949 |
| velocity | 0.0513 (0.0509 / 0.0516) | 0.0559 (0.0553 / 0.0565) | 0.917 | 0.900 | 0.978 | 0.960 |
| wall shear | 0.0809 (0.0803 / 0.0816) | 0.0880 (0.0873 / 0.0886) | 0.920 | 0.904 | 0.970 | 0.953 |

**Verdict.** **Not a shared token floor.** Doubling the training cells
lowers GeoTransolver's pressure error by 4.4% and ISLA's by 5.1%, and the
ratio between them moves from 0.878 to 0.885, within the two-seed spread
of either arm (GeoTransolver's seeds differ by 4%). Neither architecture
is starved of surface resolution at 1,260 cases: the 12% gap at full data
is a property of the models at this protocol, not of the cell count. The
flattening of the ladder from 510 to 1,260 cases therefore stands as a
statement about data, and the W2-C question is closed with both halves
measured.

**Why it matters.** This removes the last protocol explanation on the
table for the baselines' full-data lead on HiLift. With W2-C the W2 wave
is complete: power (third seeds), the 510-case rung, the token floor, the
single-angle mechanism and the paired per-case statistics have all read
out, and every one of its comparisons has since been re-run under the
unit-direction protocol (UDRV-L). The scoreboard keeps its 10,000-cell
rows; the 20,000-cell numbers are recorded here and in `CLAIMS.md` as the
floor control.

## 2026-09-17 — Decision, provisional: the width learning-rate rule (lr = 1e-3 × 192 / width above width 192) is ISLA's protocol; adopted autonomously, open to Peter's overrule {#sec-nb-lr-rule-decision}

**The setting.** ISLA's protocol learning rate is 1e-3 at hidden width
192, the rate at which every scoreboard number of the reference size was
trained. At width 512 the reference configuration diverges at that rate on
both seeds (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-matrix): the slice routing hardens
to one slice per token within the first thirty epochs and the anchors
collapse to the center (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism). A softer
routing temperature only delays the collapse
(@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-locmat2-verdict); a lower rate removes it.
The question left open on 2026-09-15 was whether to make the lower rate a
rule of the protocol or to keep searching for a rate-free change to the
routing.

**The evidence that decides it.** Two controls have landed since. Under
the width rule $10^{-3} \times 192/512 = 3.75 \times 10^{-4}$ the
reference configuration trains cleanly to 500 epochs at the 512-wide,
80,000-cell corner and scores 0.0442 (@sec-nb-corner-wlr-verdict). The
constant-gauge variant trained under the same rule scores 0.0424 against
0.0428 at its protocol rate (@sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict): the rule costs the
centered construction nothing and is necessary for the relative one. A
rule that is neutral where it is not needed and sufficient where it is
needed is a protocol, not a tuning.

**The decision.** ISLA's learning rate is 1e-3 at width 192 and
$10^{-3} \times 192 / \text{width}$ above it. It is written into the
reference configuration's comments
(`conf/model/isla_surface.yaml`), the recipe README and `CLAIMS.md`, and
every width-above-192 ISLA number in this book is labeled as trained under
it. The decision is made here autonomously because the two controls
answered the open question and Peter had not yet ruled; it is reversible,
and a rate-free routing fix remains a legitimate research question with its
own preregistration if he prefers that path. What this does not settle:
whether the rule is the right *shape* beyond width 512 (one point measured)
and whether the baselines would also benefit from a width-scaled rate
(they were not tested, and the released baselines are not modified,
@sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines).

## 2026-09-17 — Preregistration, CAP: which capacity axis lifts ISLA's single-case floor? A slice-count ladder against width, depth and MLP width on the DrivAerML one-car instrument {#sec-nb-cap-prereg}

**Setting.** The in-distribution surface deficit of ISLA against
GeoTransolver and Transolver is representational, not a data limit:
trained on a single DrivAerML car for 20,000 steps over 64 resamplings,
ISLA's constant-gauge configuration reaches a float32 pressure error of
0.1064 on that car's 10,000-cell views where GeoTransolver reaches 0.0766
and Transolver 0.0811, a 1.31 to 1.39x floor that is wider than the
435-car gap (@sec-nb-overfit-verdict; results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json).
The routing probe located the missing capacity on smooth, large-cell
regions of the surface, not at the gaps, and refuted logit saturation and
open-surface starvation as mechanisms. Two candidate explanations remain
open and are separable: the slice count (256 anchors partition the surface;
a smooth pressure field over large cells must be expressed through the
five relational invariants per slice and a softmax that hardens with
training), and plain per-token capacity (width, depth, MLP width). The
estimator-variance explanation is already bounded by MIX: area-proportional
training gains only 3.5% in family (@sec-nb-mix-prereg,
results/mix_conventions_2026-09-10.json), so it is not the lever.

**The instrument.** The single-case floor of OVERFIT-1, unchanged: one
DrivAerML training car, 64 cached 10,000-cell resamplings, 20,000
single-sample steps, bfloat16 training, constant-gauge ISLA
(`mt2_surface` in the frozen `recipe_ovf`, snapshot `code_ovf`), seed 42,
float32 evaluation on the same car at 10,000 and 40,000 cells
(`overfit_cap_aga.sbatch`, `overfit_cap_eval_aga.sbatch`, lanes
`overfit/overfit_lanes_cap.tsv`). The baseline lane
`ovf_dr_isla_seed42_v64` (256 slices, width 192, 12 layers, MLP ratio 4) is
reused, not retrained. One seed, as in OVERFIT-1: the floor is a fit to a
fixed target and its seed spread was not the limiting uncertainty there.

**Arms, one factor each against the baseline.**

| arm | change | learning rate |
|---|---|---|
| `s128` | `n_slices` 128 | 1e-3 |
| `s512` | `n_slices` 512 | 1e-3 |
| `s1024` | `n_slices` 1024 | 1e-3 |
| `h384` | `hidden` 384 | 5e-4 (the width rule, @sec-nb-lr-rule-decision) |
| `l24` | `n_layers` 24 | 1e-3 |
| `m8` | `mlp_ratio` 8 | 1e-3 |

**Readout.** Float32 pressure error on the car's 10,000-cell views
(baseline 0.1064; GeoTransolver 0.0766; Transolver 0.0811), with the
40,000-cell value and the tail-20 training loss (baseline 0.0004) beside
it.

**Bars, written before the run.** For each axis, the top rung against the
baseline 0.1064:

- **Closes the floor**: at or below 0.0852 (within 1.05x of Transolver's
  single-case floor). The axis is the representational bottleneck and a
  435-car pair on that axis is launched next.
- **Carries capacity**: at or below 0.0950 (a gain of at least 10.7%,
  about half the log-gap to Transolver). Reported as a partial carrier;
  the axis enters the design ledger with its cost.
- **Null**: at or above 0.1010 (less than 5%). The axis is not where the
  capacity is missing.

**Predictions.** Slices carry (`s1024` at or below 0.0950, monotone over
128, 256, 512, 1024) and width carries (`h384` at or below 0.0950, in line
with the 9 to 11% per width step of the SCALE study), while depth and MLP
width are null: the floor is set by how finely the surface is partitioned
and how much each token can carry about its own patch, not by the depth of
the slice stack. The slice hypothesis is falsified if `s1024` is null; the
whole capacity picture is falsified if every arm is null, in which case the
deficit sits in the routing or the read-out form itself and the next
experiment is a soft-routing or readout-form probe, not a size ladder.
Cost: six one-GPU lanes, two nodes, a few hours each (the 1024-slice lane
carries four times the geometry work of the baseline).

## 2026-09-17 — Verdict, CAP: the slice count is not the bottleneck (flat from 128 to 1,024 slices); width carries 11%; and the single-case floor is mostly a query-count effect that the baselines do not have {#sec-nb-cap-verdict}

**What was run.** The six one-factor arms of @sec-nb-cap-prereg on the
OVERFIT-1 DrivAerML one-car instrument (constant-gauge ISLA, seed 42,
20,000 single-sample steps over 64 cached 10,000-cell views, bfloat16
training), evaluated in float32 on the same car at 10,000 and 40,000
cells (results/cap_reduction_2026-09-17.json; baseline lane
`ovf_dr_isla_seed42_v64` reused). All six trained without incident.

**What we saw** (float32 pressure error on the training car; the
preregistered readout is the 10,000-cell column):

| arm | change | 10,000 cells | ÷ baseline | 40,000 cells | tail-20 training loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 256 slices, width 192, 12 layers, MLP ×4 | 0.1064 | 1.000 | 0.0857 | 0.0004 |
| `s128` | 128 slices | 0.1058 | 0.994 | 0.0852 | 0.0004 |
| `s512` | 512 slices | 0.1096 | 1.030 | 0.0820 | 0.0004 |
| `s1024` | 1,024 slices | 0.1052 | 0.989 | 0.0853 | 0.0004 |
| `h384` | width 384 (lr 5e-4) | **0.0948** | **0.891** | 0.0806 | 0.0002 |
| `l24` | 24 layers | 0.1081 | 1.016 | 0.0809 | 0.0003 |
| `m8` | MLP ×8 | 0.1019 | 0.958 | 0.0810 | 0.0003 |
| GeoTransolver (OVERFIT-1) | | 0.0766 | | 0.0780 | 0.0002 |
| Transolver (OVERFIT-1) | | 0.0811 | | 0.0793 | 0.0003 |

**Verdicts against the bars.** *Slices: null, and the slice hypothesis is
falsified.* Eight-fold more anchors move the floor by 1%, in both
directions along the ladder, and the training loss does not move at all:
how finely the surface is partitioned is not what limits the fit.
*Width: carries.* Width 384 lowers the floor by 10.9% and halves the
training loss; it is the only axis that changes what the model can fit,
in line with the 9 to 11% per width step that the SCALE study measured at
435 cars for every architecture, so it is a shared capacity axis, not an
ISLA-specific remedy. *Depth: null. MLP width: null* (4.2%, below the 5%
bar). No axis closes the floor (bar 0.0852 at 10,000 cells), so no 435-car
pair follows from this ladder.

**The anomaly worth more than the ladder.** Every ISLA arm scores between
0.0806 and 0.0857 when the same car is evaluated at 40,000 cells, within
1.03 to 1.10x of the baselines' 40,000-cell values (0.078, 0.079), while
at 10,000 cells the same checkpoints are 1.24 to 1.43x. The baselines do
not move between the two counts; ISLA moves by 20%. The consistency
benchmark shows the same pattern on the full 435-car problem
(results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json, uniform
sampler, float32, 48 cars): the 10,000-cell-trained constant-gauge ISLA
goes 0.0561 at 10,000 query cells to 0.0540 at 20,000 and 0.0530 at
40,000, while GeoTransolver goes 0.0509 to 0.0508 to 0.0506 and
Transolver 0.0520 to 0.0519 to 0.0518. GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA therefore
moves from 0.91 at the scoreboard's 10,000 cells to 0.955 at 40,000. About
half of ISLA's DrivAerML deficit at the reference size is not a property
of the trained function but of evaluating it on a 10,000-cell sample: the
slice integrals are finite-sample estimates whose noise falls with the
count, and the baselines' pooling is flat in the count above 10,000.

**Why it matters.** The representational reading of OVERFIT-1 ("missing
capacity on smooth large-cell regions") is half right: a capacity axis
exists (width) but it is shared with the baselines, and the part of the
floor that is ISLA-specific is the estimator noise of its aggregation at
10,000 tokens, visible as the count dependence that no baseline shows.
That reframes the remedy. It is not a bigger or finer model; it is a
lower-variance quadrature at a fixed token budget, which is a sampling
design question, not a model question, and stays inside the principle of
@sec-principle because the estimand (the surface integral) does not change.

**What's next.** QUAD-VAR, evaluation-only on existing checkpoints:
replace the independent uniform-over-cells draw at inference by a
stratified draw over the same cells (equal-area strata, one cell per
stratum, exact inclusion weights), and measure the constant-gauge and
reference checkpoints at 10,000 cells against their 20,000- and
40,000-cell independent-draw values. Prediction, to be written as a
preregistration before the run: a stratified 10,000-cell draw scores
within 2% of the independent 20,000-cell draw. The baselines are
evaluated the same way as the control; they are predicted flat.

## 2026-09-17 — Preregistration, QUAD-VAR: a spatially stratified inference draw at a fixed token budget, evaluation-only on the DrivAerML checkpoints {#sec-nb-quadvar-prereg}

**Setting.** @sec-nb-cap-verdict located the ISLA-specific part of the
reference-size DrivAerML deficit in the finite-sample noise of the slice
integrals: the 10,000-cell-trained constant-gauge checkpoints score 0.0561
when queried on an independent uniform-over-cells draw of 10,000 cells,
0.0540 at 20,000 and 0.0530 at 40,000, while GeoTransolver (0.0509,
0.0508, 0.0506) and Transolver (0.0520, 0.0519, 0.0518) are flat
(results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json). The
reference configuration shows the same slope: 0.0554 at 10,000 cells and
0.0523 at 40,000 (results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json).
If the slope is estimator variance, a lower-variance draw of the *same*
10,000 cells should recover part of it without retraining and without
changing what the model estimates.

**The instrument.** A new recipe transform, `StratifiedSubsampleMesh`
(`src/domain_transforms.py`, unit-tested: exact count, constant weights
$N/n$, no duplicates, inclusion frequency $n/N$ for every cell, and a
variance below half of the independent draw's on a smooth area-weighted
integral), replaces the independent draw at inference by a systematic
sample along the Morton (Z-order) curve of the cell centroids: one cell
per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells with one random offset per draw. Every
cell keeps the inclusion probability $n/N$ and the weight $N/n$ of the
independent draw, so the sampling convention the checkpoints were trained
under is unchanged and no swap penalty (@sec-nb-mix-prereg) applies; only
the variance of the draw changes. Evaluation follows the consistency
benchmark exactly (float32, 48 validation cars, `recipe_bench` with the
transform appended, each checkpoint under its own snapshot; lanes
`bench/bench_lanes_strat.tsv`, dataset `drivaer_bench_strat`, outputs
`bench_evals/<run>/strat_<count>`): the constant-gauge pair
`iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed42/43`, the reference pair `rf_dr_mt2_meas_seed42/43`,
GeoTransolver `uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed42/43` and Transolver
`uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3_seed42/43`, each at 10,000 and 20,000 cells.
Sixteen evaluation lanes, no training.

**Bars, written before the run** (float32 pressure, two-seed means,
against each arm's own independent-draw values from the benchmark).

- **Supported** if the stratified 10,000-cell draw recovers at least half
  of the arm's gain from 10,000 to 40,000 independent cells: constant
  gauge at or below 0.0546, reference at or below 0.0539.
- **Falsified** if the stratified 10,000-cell draw is within 1% of the
  independent 10,000-cell value (constant gauge at or above 0.0555,
  reference at or above 0.0548): the slope is not draw variance.
- **Between**: reported as a partial recovery in readout units.
- **Control**: GeoTransolver and Transolver move by less than 1% under the
  stratified draw at both counts; a baseline that moves by more says the
  draw changes the estimand, not only the variance, and the ISLA reading
  is withheld.
- **Consistency**: the stratified 20,000-cell draw is at or below the
  independent 20,000-cell draw for every ISLA arm (no arm gets worse).

**Prediction.** Both ISLA arms are supported, the baselines are flat, and
the DrivAerML ratio at the scoreboard's token budget moves from 0.91
toward the 0.955 measured at 40,000 independent cells.

**Competing derivation, recorded before the run** (from the parallel ISLA
session, 2026-09-17). The draw keeps the uniform-over-cells inclusion law,
so the Horvitz–Thompson weights stay proportional to cell area and the
weight spread is untouched: the routing probe's effective token count,
$N/(1+\mathrm{CV}^2) = 1{,}637$ of 10,000 on the car (@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe),
is set by that spread, not by spatial clumping. Stratification removes
only the clumping component of the variance, so this derivation predicts
a *small* gain, below the supported bar, and reads the count slope as
mostly the weight-spread term that only more cells (or a lower-variance
consistent quadrature that changes the weights, which MIX bounds at 3.5%)
can reduce. An equal-*area* stratification would remove the weight spread
but is a convention swap for these checkpoints, which MIX prices at 1.9x
for ISLA; it is not run here. The bars above stand as written; the two
derivations are separated by whether the stratified 10,000-cell draw
lands above or below 0.0546.

## 2026-09-17 — Verdict, QUAD-VAR: the stratified draw lowers ISLA's 10,000-cell error by 4% (both ISLA bars met) but also lowers the baselines' by 2%, so the control fired and the ISLA-specific recovery is about two points of the count slope {#sec-nb-quadvar-verdict}

**What was run.** The sixteen evaluation lanes of @sec-nb-quadvar-prereg
(job 779184, `recipe_bench` with `StratifiedSubsampleMesh`, float32, 48
DrivAerML validation cars, each checkpoint under its training snapshot):
the constant-gauge and reference ISLA pairs, the GeoTransolver and
Transolver pairs, each queried at 10,000 and 20,000 cells drawn
systematically along the Morton order with the uniform-over-cells
inclusion law (results/quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json). Comparators are
the same checkpoints' independent-draw values from the consistency
benchmark.

**What we saw** (pressure rel-L2, two-seed means):

| arm | independent 10k | independent 20k | independent 40k | **stratified 10k** (seeds) | stratified 20k | stratified 10k ÷ independent 10k | share of the 10k-to-40k gain recovered |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA constant gauge | 0.0561 | 0.0540 | 0.0530 | **0.0537** (0.0545 / 0.0529) | 0.0533 | 0.957 | 0.79 |
| ISLA reference | 0.0554 | not measured | 0.0523 | **0.0531** (0.0525 / 0.0537) | 0.0527 | 0.959 | 0.73 |
| GeoTransolver | 0.0509 | 0.0508 | 0.0506 | **0.0498** (0.0494 / 0.0501) | 0.0502 | 0.978 | control: moved 2.2% |
| Transolver | 0.0520 | 0.0519 | 0.0518 | **0.0509** (0.0508 / 0.0511) | 0.0516 | 0.979 | control: moved 2.1% |

**Against the bars.** Both ISLA arms meet the *supported* bar (constant
gauge 0.0537 against 0.0546; reference 0.0531 against 0.0539), and the
consistency bar holds (every stratified 20,000-cell value is at or below
the independent one). But the **control fired**: GeoTransolver and
Transolver, flat in the count under independent draws, improve by 2.2%
and 2.1% under the stratified draw. Per the preregistration the strong
ISLA reading is withheld, and the honest decomposition is this: about two
points of every arm's improvement is the *metric's* own estimator, the
area-weighted relative L2 over a finite sample, which a spatially even
sample also estimates with less noise and less ratio bias; the part
specific to ISLA is the excess over the baselines' shift, 2.1 to 2.2
points at 10,000 cells, or about 40% of ISLA's 10,000-to-40,000 count
slope. Under the stratified draw GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA (constant gauge)
moves from 0.907 to 0.927, two of the 4.8 points that separate the
independent 10,000-cell ratio from the 40,000-cell one.

**Which derivation was right.** Neither alone. The variance reading of
@sec-nb-cap-verdict predicted a recovery of at least half the slope from
the draw alone; the weight-spread derivation predicted a small gain. The
ISLA-specific gain is real and about 40% of the slope, the remainder being
the weight-spread term that only more cells or a weight-changing quadrature
can reduce, and the shared two points are a property of the metric, not of
any architecture.

**What follows.** The stratified draw is a strict improvement for every
model at no cost (same token budget, same inclusion law, same training),
so it is the recipe's recommended inference sampler; it enters the
scoreboard only as a complete labeled row ("stratified inference draw,
all architectures"), never as a silent replacement of the independent-draw
numbers, and this book's headline ratios remain the independent-draw
ones. Record: the ISLA-specific part of the reference-size DrivAerML
deficit that a better draw can remove is about two points of ratio; the
rest of the count slope is the Horvitz–Thompson weight spread of a
uniform-over-cells sample, which is bounded by MIX at a few percent and by
the width axis as a shared capacity effect.

## 2026-09-17 — Preregistration, QUAD-VAR-HL: the stratified inference draw on the HiLift 35-case checkpoints, where the count slope is small {#sec-nb-quadvar-hl-prereg}

**Setting.** @sec-nb-quadvar-verdict recommends the stratified inference
draw for every model on DrivAerML, where ISLA's independent-draw error
falls 5.5% from 10,000 to 40,000 cells. On HiLiftAeroML the same
consistency benchmark shows a much smaller count slope at 35 training
cases: the constant-gauge ISLA goes 0.1390, 0.1367, 0.1362 at 10,000,
20,000 and 40,000 cells (2%), the reference configuration 0.1551 to 0.1506
(3%), GeoTransolver 0.1104 to 0.1100 and Transolver 0.1148 to 0.1145
(flat) (results/consistency_bench/consistency_bench_2026-09-10.json and
consistency_bench_rf_2026-09-11.json). If the DrivAerML gain is draw
variance, the HiLift gain must be bounded by this smaller slope; and a
recommendation made for "every model" needs the second dataset.

**The instrument.** As @sec-nb-quadvar-prereg, with
`highlift_bench_super_scarce_strat` (the benchmark's HiLift dataset with
the stratified draw) on the constant-gauge pair
`lad_hl_mt2_super_scarce_seed42/43`, the reference pair
`rf_hl_mt2_meas_super_scarce_seed42/43`, GeoTransolver
`udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed42/43` and Transolver
`udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed42/43`, at 10,000 and 20,000
cells, float32, 180 validation cases; lanes `bench/bench_lanes_strat_hl.tsv`.

**Bars, written before the run.**

- **Free improvement on both datasets**: no arm is worse than its
  independent-draw value at either count by more than 1%, and the ISLA
  arms' gains at 10,000 cells lie within the count slope (constant gauge
  at or above 0.1362, reference at or above 0.1506; a gain beyond the
  40,000-cell independent value would say the draw does more than reduce
  variance).
- **Dataset-specific**: any arm worse by more than 1% at either count.
  The README recommendation is then narrowed to DrivAerML and the reason
  investigated.
- **Prediction**: ISLA arms improve by 1 to 2%, baselines by less than
  1%; the HiLift 35-case ratios move by at most one point. The HiLift
  deficit at this rung is therefore not count noise, consistent with the
  frame-price and capacity readings of @sec-nb-cap-verdict.

## 2026-09-17 — Verdict, QUAD-VAR-HL: on HiLift the stratified draw improves ISLA by 1.4 to 1.9%, leaves the baselines within 0.4%, and stays inside the count slope; a free improvement on both datasets {#sec-nb-quadvar-hl-verdict}

**What was run.** The sixteen lanes of @sec-nb-quadvar-hl-prereg (job
779228; float32, 180 HiLift validation cases, two seeds per arm;
results/quadvar_hl_reduction_2026-09-17.json).

**What we saw** (pressure rel-L2, two-seed means; independent-draw values
from the consistency benchmarks):

| arm | independent 10k | independent 20k | independent 40k | **stratified 10k** | stratified 20k | stratified ÷ independent at 10k | share of the 10k-to-40k gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA constant gauge | 0.1390 | 0.1367 | 0.1362 | **0.1371** | 0.1351 | 0.986 | 0.66 |
| ISLA reference | 0.1551 | not measured | 0.1506 | **0.1522** | 0.1497 | 0.981 | 0.64 |
| GeoTransolver | 0.1104 | 0.1103 | 0.1100 | **0.1108** | 0.1096 | 1.004 | control: within 1% |
| Transolver | 0.1148 | 0.1148 | 0.1145 | **0.1149** | 0.1143 | 1.001 | control: within 1% |

**Against the bars.** *Free improvement on both datasets.* No arm is worse
than its independent-draw value by more than 1% at either count (the
largest move against is GeoTransolver's 0.35% at 10,000 cells, inside seed
noise), and both ISLA arms' gains stay within their count slope: the
stratified 10,000-cell values (0.1371, 0.1522) lie above the independent
40,000-cell values (0.1362, 0.1506), recovering about two thirds of the
slope, the same fraction as on DrivAerML before the shared component is
removed. The prediction held in every clause: ISLA improves by 1.4 and
1.9%, the baselines by less than 0.5%, and GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at 35
cases moves one point, from 0.794 to 0.808.

**Why it matters.** On HiLift the baselines do not move at all, so the
two-point shared component seen on DrivAerML is a property of that
dataset's metric estimator (the car's area distribution has a coefficient
of variation of 2.3 against 3.3 on the wing, but its uniform-over-cells
sample is the noisier estimator of the area-weighted error), not of the
draw. The ISLA-specific gain is again about two thirds of the count slope,
and the slope itself is what differs between datasets: 5.5% on DrivAerML,
2 to 3% on HiLift. The HiLift deficit at 35 cases, 0.79 to 0.81, is not
count noise; it is the frame price where geometries recur and the shared
capacity axis, as @sec-nb-cap-verdict read it. The recipe recommendation
stands for both datasets and all four models: the stratified draw at a
fixed cell budget is never worse and helps the measure-consistent model
most.

## 2026-09-17 — Synthesis: the anatomy of ISLA's DrivAerML deficit at the reference size; about half of the 10,000-cell gap is finite-sample noise, the trained function is 4 to 5% behind {#sec-nb-deficit-anatomy}

**The question.** The scoreboard's DrivAerML row at the reference size
(width 192, 10,000 cells, 435 cars) reads GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.90 to
0.91 on surface pressure. The studies of 2026-09-11 to 2026-09-17
(OVERFIT-1, CAP, QUAD-VAR, QUAD-VAR-HL, the consistency benchmark's count
ladders, MIX, SCALE) each measured one piece of that gap. This entry puts
the pieces on one line, in the ratio's units (points of GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA, constant-gauge variant, float32, 48 validation cars), so that the
case chapters can state what the gap is made of.

| component | how it was isolated | points of ratio |
|---|---|---|
| the metric's own finite-sample estimator on a 10,000-cell independent draw (shared by every architecture) | QUAD-VAR control: GeoTransolver and Transolver improve 2% under a lower-variance draw of the same cells (@sec-nb-quadvar-verdict) | about 2 |
| ISLA's slice-integral variance on a 10,000-cell independent draw, removable by a stratified draw at the same budget | QUAD-VAR: ISLA's excess gain over the baselines' (@sec-nb-quadvar-verdict) | about 2 |
| the remaining count dependence at 10,000 cells: the Horvitz–Thompson weight spread of a uniform-over-cells sample, removable only by more cells | consistency benchmark: the stratified 10,000-cell ratio 0.927 against the independent 40,000-cell ratio 0.955 (@sec-nb-cap-verdict) | about 3 |
| the trained function's deficit, seen once the sample is fine enough | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at 40,000 cells 0.955; at the 512 × 80,000 corner 0.98 (constant gauge) and 0.95 (reference under the width rule) | 4 to 5 |
| the reference frame's price on DrivAerML | reference against constant gauge: none at the reference size, 3 to 4% at the corner (@sec-nb-cg-wlr-verdict) | 0 (reference size) |

The pieces sum to the measured 9 to 10 points at the scoreboard's budget.
What CAP adds is what the last row is *not*: not the slice count (flat
from 128 to 1,024 slices), not depth, not MLP width, and the one axis that
moves it, width, moves every architecture by the same 9 to 11% per step
(SCALE), so it is a shared capacity axis rather than an ISLA defect. What
MIX adds is that area-proportional training buys only 3.5%, so the
weight-spread row is bounded and is not the lever it was thought to be
(@sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe).

*Addendum, 2026-09-17 (EQ-PRICE).* The trained-function row splits
further: about two and a half of its points are positional information
the contracts deny (a raw-coordinate diagnostic recovers 2.4 points,
@sec-nb-eqprice-verdict) and about two are the form.

**How to state the case.** At the reference size ISLA's in-distribution
surface deficit on DrivAerML is 9 to 10% on the scoreboard's instrument,
of which about half is finite-sample noise that vanishes with cells or a
better draw and none of which is the frame. At deployment resolution the
deficit is 4 to 5%, and at the scale corner 2 to 5%. Those are the numbers
to put beside ISLA's exact contracts (pose, sampling consistency, general
inputs) when the trade is made; the 25 to 28% at 35 HiLift cases is a
different mechanism (the mesher-pattern cue where geometries recur,
@sec-nb-frame-full-verdict) and is priced separately.

## 2026-09-17 — Preregistration, EQ-PRICE: is the 4 to 5 point trained-function deficit the price of the invariance contracts? A raw-coordinate diagnostic at 435 cars {#sec-nb-eqprice-prereg}

**Setting.** @sec-nb-deficit-anatomy leaves 4 to 5 points of
GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA on DrivAerML to the trained function once the sample
is fine enough, and CAP placed them outside the slice count, depth and MLP
width. Two mechanisms remain: the information ISLA is denied by
construction (absolute position; every baseline token carries its
coordinates, ISLA's carry only invariants against the anchors), or the
slice-attention form itself. At 35 HiLift cases the raw-coordinate channel
bought nothing (0.143 against 0.138, @sec-nb-a35-verdict), but that rung
is dominated by the mesher-pattern cue and no full-data test exists. If
positional information is the deficit, the case for ISLA becomes a
priced trade, "4 to 5% in-distribution for exact pose invariance and
sampling consistency"; if it is not, the deficit is the form and the
contracts are free.

**The arm.** `eqp_dr_isla_raw_seed42/43`: the constant-gauge ISLA at the
reference size (width 192, 10,000 cells, 435 DrivAerML cars, learning rate
1e-3, 500 epochs, bfloat16, no augmentation) with the research class's
`raw_coord_channel` (six channels: centered coordinates and normals in the
frame; breaks SE(3) by design), snapshot `code_globin2`, recipe
`recipe_globin` (launcher `kernel/eqprice_aga.sbatch`). This is a
**diagnostic ablation**, never a configuration: it reads the pose of the
car, which the principle of @sec-principle forbids the flagship. Float32
evaluation on the corner's sample-frame probe at 10,000 cells
(`kernel/eqprice_eval_aga.sbatch`): the uniform probe for in-family
accuracy (comparators on this instrument, consistency benchmark:
constant gauge 0.0561, Transolver 0.0520, GeoTransolver 0.0509) and the
10:1 biased probe for the density factor.

**Bars, written before the run** (two-seed mean, uniform probe):

- **Positional information is the deficit** if the raw-coordinate arm is
  at or below 0.0525 (within 1% of Transolver): the contracts are priced
  at 4 to 5% and the book says so in the verdict.
- **Partial**: between 0.0525 and 0.0550, reported in points.
- **Null**: at or above 0.0550 (less than 2% gain): position is not what
  the trained function lacks; the deficit is the slice-attention form and
  the next probe is the readout (soft read-back, two-stage decode).
- **Consistency**: the raw-coordinate arm's density factor is expected to
  rise above the constant gauge's 12x (it reads the centered position of a
  biased sample); recorded, not a bar.

**Prediction.** Null or low partial (a gain of at most 2 points), as at
35 cases: the deficit is the form. Cost: two lanes of about seven
GPU-hours.

## 2026-09-17 — Verdict, EQ-PRICE: raw coordinates recover 2.4 of the 4 to 5 trained-function points at 435 cars (partial); the invariance contracts cost about two and a half points in-distribution, the rest of the deficit is the form {#sec-nb-eqprice-verdict}

**What was run.** The two lanes of @sec-nb-eqprice-prereg trained to 500
epochs without incident and were evaluated in float32 on the sample-frame
probe at 10,000 cells (results/eqprice_reduction_2026-09-17.json).

**What we saw** (pressure rel-L2, 48 validation cars):

| arm | uniform 10k (seeds) | GeoTransolver ÷ arm | Transolver ÷ arm | density factor (10:1 bias) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| constant gauge (benchmark) | 0.0561 | 0.907 | 0.926 | 12 |
| **constant gauge + raw coordinates** | **0.0547** (0.0553 / 0.0540) | **0.931** | 0.950 | 13.2 |
| Transolver | 0.0520 | | | 15 |
| GeoTransolver | 0.0509 | | | 10.5 |

**Against the bars.** *Partial*, at the low end the prediction named: the
raw-coordinate channel lowers the error by 2.6% and moves GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA by 2.4 points, from 0.907 to 0.931, against the positional-information
bar of 0.0525 (not reached) and the null bar of 0.0550 (cleared by 0.0003,
inside the seed spread of 0.0013). The density factor rises to 13.2, as
expected of a model that reads the centered position of a biased sample.

**Reading.** Of the 4 to 5 trained-function points of
@sec-nb-deficit-anatomy, about two and a half are the information the
invariance contracts deny the model (the absolute position of each cell),
and about two are the slice-attention form itself, shared with the width
axis. That is the honest price of the contracts on DrivAerML at the
reference size: two and a half points of in-distribution ratio, bought
with exact pose invariance (a 6 to 19% lead when geometries arrive in
arbitrary poses, @sec-verdict) and sampling consistency (1.05 to 1.2
against 10 to 16 under a density bias). The raw-coordinate arm is a
diagnostic and stays one: it breaks SE(3) by design and its own density
factor shows what it reads.

**What follows.** The trained-function deficit is now itself decomposed;
what remains unattributed is about two points that the form owns, and no
single cheap experiment isolates them further without changing the
architecture. The program's accuracy question at the reference size is
closed at this resolution; the book states the trade in the verdict.

## 2026-09-17 — Preregistration, FORM-HEADS: multi-head slice routing, the one structural difference to Transolver's physics attention that the capacity ladder did not cover {#sec-nb-formheads-prereg}

**Setting.** After EQ-PRICE about two points of GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA on
DrivAerML belong to the slice-attention form itself, and on the one-car
instrument ISLA's floor is 1.31x Transolver's even though both are slice
attention. CAP excluded the slice count, depth and MLP width. The
structural difference left is how many ways a token is routed per layer:
Transolver's physics attention routes each token through 8 heads × 256
slices per layer (`n_head: 8`, `slice_num: 256` in the recipe); ISLA routes
it once through 256 slices. A single soft assignment that hardens toward
one slice per token (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism) leaves each
