## 2026-09-18 — Verdict, LR-REF: falsified; ISLA's validation loss rises to the mean-field plateau at learning rate 3e-3 (0.06 against 0.0008 at 1e-3, float32 pressure error 0.77) and diverges at 1e-2, so the decade-wide rate robustness measured on the legacy centered variant does not transfer {#sec-nb-lrref-verdict}

**Setting.** The book has quoted a learning-rate robustness result: across
the grid {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2} at 435 DrivAerML cars the worst point was
within 1.55x of the best, where GeoTransolver degrades 9x one grid step
above its best rate. That measurement was made on the legacy centered
variant (a centered frame with a fixed length unit). LR-REF
(@sec-nb-refprops-prereg) re-measured the grid on ISLA itself, whose frame
is relative and center-free: two seeds each at 3e-3 and 1e-2, 10,000-cell
exploration budget, 500 epochs, bf16, against the 1e-3 seeds already
trained. The interim entry (@sec-nb-lrref-interim) reported the 1e-2 pair
diverging to NaN at epochs 21 and 32 and the 3e-3 pair "training cleanly"
with finite losses.

**What we saw.** Finite was not learning. Both 3e-3 seeds start their
first epoch at a loss comparable to the 1e-3 run's (0.036 and 0.044
against 0.032), rise over the next four epochs to about 0.06, and stay on
that plateau for the remaining 495 epochs (seed 42 ends at a validation
loss of 0.0587, seed 43 at 0.0624; the 1e-3 reference ends at 0.00077,
eighty times lower). Scored in float32 on the sample-frame probe, seed 43
has a surface-pressure error of **0.766** on the independent draw and 0.767
on the biased draw, and seed 42 **0.761** and 0.761 (density factors 1.00: a
model that predicts a mean field is trivially consistent), against ISLA's
0.0552 at 1e-3. The
preregistered falsification clause (error above 2x the 1e-3 value at 3e-3
or 1e-2) is met at both rates by a wide margin, so **LR-REF is falsified**.

**Mechanism.** This is the failure the width study found at 1e-3 and width
512 (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism), now at width 192 and 3e-3:
under too high an effective rate the relative frame's measure-weighted
routing hardens to one slice per token within the first epochs and the
anchors coincide (measured at width 512, @sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism,
and inferred here from the matching loss signature, not measured on these
runs); the model then sees no geometry and settles on the mean field. At
1e-2 the loss diverges to NaN. The
legacy centered variant survives both rates because its center and length
unit are fixed before any routing happens. The effective rate scales with
width, which is why the width rule (learning rate 1e-3 × 192 / hidden)
cured the width-512 corner and why, at width 192, 1e-3 is also the ceiling
rather than the middle of a safe decade.

**Consequences for the book and the recipe.**

- The claim "stable across a decade of learning rate" is withdrawn from the
  main text everywhere (@sec-isla-routing-forms, the pros table of the limits
  chapter, the operating manual); the legacy variant's grid stays in its
  collapsed diagnostic note. ISLA's rate statement now reads: trains at the
  protocol rate 1e-3 without a sweep; rises to the mean-field plateau at 3e-3; diverges to NaN at 1e-2;
  use the width rule above width 192.
- The unified recipe's default learning rate is 3e-3 (GeoTransolver's).
  ISLA's model configurations did not pin their own rate, so a user who
  runs `model=isla_surface` with the defaults gets a model on the mean-field plateau. The
  README already passes 1e-3 on every ISLA line; the configuration now
  pins it as well (see the recipe commit of this date), and the config
  test asserts it.
- A methodological lesson for the notebook's own instruments: the interim
  entry accepted "finite loss" as "training cleanly". A flat loss eighty
  times above a sibling lane's is an out-of-band health value and should
  have woken the watcher; the fleet watcher now reports the last validation
  loss beside the epoch counter.

**What's next: RATE-WINDOW** (@sec-nb-ratewindow-prereg), four lanes
bracketing the safe window at 3e-4 and 2e-3.

## 2026-09-18 — Preregistration, RATE-WINDOW: where does ISLA's safe learning-rate window begin and end at width 192? {#sec-nb-ratewindow-prereg}

**Question.** LR-REF established that ISLA at width 192 trains at 1e-3 and
settles on the mean-field plateau at 3e-3. A user needs the window, not two points: how far below
1e-3 does training stay near its best, and does the ceiling lie above 2e-3?

**Instrument.** Four lanes of ISLA at 435 DrivAerML cars on the 10,000-cell
exploration budget, 500 epochs, bf16, lean class, same recipe copy as the
1e-3 seeds (`kernel/refprops_aga.sbatch`, lanes 6 to 9; jobs 790769 to
790772): learning rates 3e-4 and 2e-3, seeds 42 and 43. Readout: float32
surface-pressure error on the sample-frame probe against the 1e-3 seeds
(0.0552), plus each lane's loss trajectory over the first ten epochs (the
plateau signature is a rise to the 0.06 plateau within five epochs).

**Bars, written before the runs.**

- **3e-4 within 1.1x of 1e-3**: the window extends at least half a decade
  downward; the operating manual states "3e-4 to 1e-3 at width 192".
  Above 1.1x: the window below is narrow too and the manual states 1e-3
  as a point recommendation with the width rule.
- **2e-3 trains within 1.2x of 1e-3**: the ceiling lies between 2e-3 and
  3e-3. **2e-3 rises to the plateau** (the signature above, error above 2x): the
  ceiling lies between 1e-3 and 2e-3, and the protocol rate is within a
  factor two of the plateau's onset, which the manual states as a warning.
- Either outcome at 2e-3 leaves the mechanism question (why the routing
  hardens at a rate the centered variant tolerates) to a separate study;
  this one only draws the map.

**Prediction.** 3e-4 within 1.1x (about 1.05x, slightly undertrained in
500 epochs); 2e-3 rises to the plateau on at least one seed (the hardening is an
early-epoch event and 2e-3 is close to 3e-3), probability about 0.5.

## 2026-09-18 — Verdict, POSE-REF: supported; with every case in its own random pose ISLA scores 0.0560 against 0.0552 in the native frame (1.015x), 7% below the rotation-augmented GeoTransolver and 17% below the augmented Transolver {#sec-nb-poseref-verdict}

**Setting.** The pose test trains and validates every DrivAerML car in its
own random SO(3) pose, applied deterministically per case, so no
architecture can learn a canonical orientation. ISLA's covariance is exact
by construction, so its posed error should equal its native-frame error up
to the bf16 training residual; GeoTransolver and Transolver rely on
rotation augmentation. Until today the ISLA side of this test had been
measured only on the legacy centered variant (1.01x its in-pose error, 6%
and 19% ahead of the augmented baselines). POSE-REF
(@sec-nb-refprops-prereg) re-measured it on ISLA: two seeds at 435 cars,
10,000-cell exploration budget, learning rate 1e-3, 500 epochs, bf16
(`kernel/refprops_aga.sbatch`, lanes 0 and 1), scored in float32 on the 48
posed validation cars and, as a second reading of the same checkpoints, on
the native-frame sample-frame probe. Reduction:
results/refprops_reduction_2026-09-18.json.

**What we saw.** Posed surface-pressure error **0.0560** (seeds 0.0553 and
0.0568) against ISLA's native-frame 0.0552 (0.0549 and 0.0558): **1.015x**,
inside the 3% clause. The same two checkpoints scored on the native-frame
probe give 0.0550 and 0.0567, within 0.5% of their posed numbers, which is
the covariance contract at work on the trained function (the residual is
the bf16 training path, @sec-nb-precres-verdict). Against the augmented
baselines' posed errors, 0.0602 (GeoTransolver) and 0.0676 (Transolver),
ISLA is 7% and 17% ahead; both clear the 5% clause. Wall-shear error in
pose is 0.0802 and 0.0829.

**Verdict: supports.** The pose row of the standing table and the headline
figure now read on ISLA, and the label "measured on the legacy centered
variant" is removed everywhere. The prediction (posed within 2%) held.

**Why it matters.** This closes the last headline property that rested on
the retired variant. The transfer was expected for the *degradation*
(identical contracts) but not guaranteed for the in-pose accuracy, which is
a property of the trained function; it held. Together with LR-REF
(@sec-nb-lrref-verdict) the two re-measurements split cleanly: the
geometric property (covariance) transferred exactly, the optimization
property (rate robustness) did not.

## 2026-09-18 — Interim, RATE-WINDOW: 2e-3 rises to the mean-field plateau on both seeds within twenty epochs (the 3e-3 signature), so ISLA's ceiling at width 192 lies between 1e-3 and 2e-3; 3e-4 is learning normally; the 2e-3 lanes are stopped {#sec-nb-ratewindow-interim}

**What we saw.** Twenty-two epochs into the four RATE-WINDOW lanes
(@sec-nb-ratewindow-prereg): both 2e-3 seeds sit on the mean-field plateau
(validation loss 0.063 and 0.058, the same 0.06 the 3e-3 lanes never left,
@sec-nb-lrref-verdict), and the 3e-4 seed 42 lane is at 0.0040, in step
with the 1e-3 reference's trajectory at that epoch (0.0037). The
preregistration named the plateau signature within five epochs as the
plateau readout, so the 2e-3 pair was canceled at epoch about 22 and
marked blocked with the reason, as the 1e-2 pair was earlier, rather than
training a plateaued model for 480 more epochs on two nodes.

**Reading, provisional.** The ceiling lies between 1e-3 and 2e-3: the
protocol rate is within a factor of two of the plateau's onset. The operating
manual will state 1e-3 as the rate for width 192 with that warning, and
the width rule above it. The lower edge of the window waits on the 3e-4
pair's final float32 error (bar: within 1.1x of 1e-3).

**A mechanism question this sharpens.** The legacy centered variant
tolerates 1e-2 and the relative frame rises to the plateau at 2e-3, with the same
routing, the same layers and the same head; the frame is the only
difference. The relative frame's slice anchors are measure-weighted means
of the tokens each slice routes, and every geometric invariant the network
sees is a function of token-to-anchor differences; when the routing
saturates early, the anchors coincide and the invariants degenerate, which
is the "sees no geometry" plateau. A centered frame supplies a fixed
center and length unit that do not depend on the routing, so a saturated
routing still leaves the network with usable coordinates. A cure that keeps
the relative frame's principle (no external center) would act on the
routing's early sharpness, for example a warm-up of the learning rate or of
the routing temperature; that is a separate study, preregistered before it
is run.

## 2026-09-18 — Verdict, LEN-RMS: validated; the RMS-pairwise-distance length unit scores 0.0526 against the total-measure unit's 0.0533 under the stratified draw (0.987, overlapping seed ranges, density factor 1.24) and becomes ISLA's default {#sec-nb-lenrms-verdict}

**Setting.** ISLA's relative frame needs one length unit to make its
geometric invariants dimensionless. Until today that unit was the square
root of the total quadrature measure of the sampled boundary, which is
center-free and cheap but diverges on boundaries whose measure grows under
refinement (a Koch-type surface) and is not invariant to the weights' overall
scale. Peter's ruling of 2026-09-18 (@sec-nb-lenrms-prereg) named the
root-mean-square pairwise distance of the measure-weighted sample as the
unit to adopt once validated: it is center-free, normalized by
construction (weight-rescale invariant), and converges wherever the sample
has finite second moment, including on fractal boundaries; the class gained
it as `scale_mode="rms_distance"`, computed through the variance identity
in O(N), with contract tests and a Koch-curve convergence test.

**What was run.** Two seeds of ISLA with the new unit at 435 DrivAerML
cars on the 10,000-cell exploration budget, learning rate 1e-3, 500 epochs,
bf16 (`kernel/lenrms_aga.sbatch`, snapshot `code_lenrms`), scored in
float32 on the consistency-benchmark instrument (job 790885) against the
three total-measure seeds that served SG-REF. Reduction:
results/lenrms_reduction_2026-09-18.json.

**What we saw.** Surface-pressure error, seed mean with seeds in brackets:

| draw | total-measure unit (3 seeds) | RMS-pairwise-distance unit (2 seeds) | ratio (RMS ÷ total) |
|---|---|---|---|
| stratified, 10,000 cells (readout) | 0.0533 (0.0525 / 0.0537 / 0.0538) | 0.0526 (0.0518 / 0.0535) | 0.987 |
| independent, 10,000 cells | 0.0557 (0.0549 / 0.0558 / 0.0562) | 0.0551 (0.0544 / 0.0558) | 0.990 |
| independent, 40,000 cells | 0.0525 (0.0518 / 0.0527 / 0.0530) | 0.0520 (0.0512 / 0.0527) | 0.989 |
| density factor (biased ÷ independent) | 1.21 | 1.24 (1.21 / 1.26) | |

**Verdict: validated.** The two units are within 1.3% on every draw with
overlapping seed ranges, both lanes trained without incident (final
validation losses 0.00073 and 0.00076 against 0.00077), and the density
factor stays inside the 1.05 to 1.3 contract band. The prediction (within
noise, a hair better) held.

**Consequences.** The RMS-pairwise-distance unit becomes ISLA's default
(`scale_mode="rms_distance"` in the class, the recipe configurations and
the book's statement of the architecture); the total-measure unit stays
available as an option and is documented as the unit the evidence lanes
trained before this evening carry, the two being interchangeable within
noise at 435 cars. The 435-car 200,000-cell ISLA pair is duplicated with the
new unit (`kernel/proto200k_rms_aga.sbatch`, runs `p200k_dr_isla_rms_seed42/43`) so the
equivalence is also on record at the reporting protocol; until it reports,
the 200k standings are stated with the unit named. LEN-RMS closes the frame
deliberation of 2026-09-18: ISLA's frame is relative and center-free, and
its length unit is now also finite on every boundary with a finite second
moment.

## 2026-09-19 — Verdict on the 27-car rate control and preregistration, RATE-GT: the flag was the rate; GeoTransolver at 3e-3 scores 0.124 at 27 cars and 200,000 cells (0.83x ISLA's 0.151), so GeoTransolver gets 3e-3 controls on every 200k rung {#sec-nb-rategt-prereg}

**Setting.** The 200,000-cell ladder (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-ladder-interim)
ran GeoTransolver at 1e-3, the rate that won its 435-car grid on the
10,000-cell budget, and its 27-car pair scored 0.181, above its
10,000-cell predecessor's 0.154 (trained at 3e-3). The preregistration
flagged that as a defect to investigate before the row is written, and a
rate control at 3e-3 was launched for both GeoTransolver and ISLA.

**What we saw.** GeoTransolver at 3e-3: **0.1244** (seeds 0.1260 / 0.1227),
below both its 1e-3 lane (0.1813) and its 10,000-cell value (0.1536).
ISLA at 3e-3: 0.7716 and 0.7706, the same mean-field plateau LR-REF
found at 435 cars (@sec-nb-lrref-verdict), so ISLA's better rate stays
1e-3 (0.1506). The preregistered reading applies: the flag was the rate,
and the 27-car row is written with each model at its better of the two
rates, **GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA = 0.83** at 27 cars. GeoTransolver leads by
17% on the scarcest rung; the ordering the 1e-3 rows suggested (ISLA ahead
by 20%) was an artifact of GeoTransolver's rate.
Artifact: results/p200k_ladder_interim_2026-09-18.json (`rate_control_lr3e3`).

**Why the other rungs are now in question.** GeoTransolver's best rate
depends on how much it trains on: at 27 cars and 200,000 cells the higher
rate is worth 31%; at 435 cars and 10,000 cells the lower rate won its
grid. The 54-, 109- and 218-car rows and the 435-car trio were all run at
1e-3, so each may understate GeoTransolver. The book's protocol is that
each architecture runs at its own best rate (@sec-lr-protocol), so the
comparison is not written until GeoTransolver has had 3e-3 on every rung.
ISLA has no such control to run: its loss rises to the plateau above 1e-3 and its 3e-4
lanes are already in RATE-WINDOW.

**Instrument (RATE-GT).** GeoTransolver at 3e-3, seeds 42 and 43, at
200,000 cells on 54, 109 and 218 cars (`kernel/p200k_fleet/p200k_lad_aga.sbatch`, lanes 28 to 33) and on the full 435 cars
(`kernel/proto200k_aga.sbatch`, lanes 6 and 7), otherwise identical to the
1e-3 lanes; float32 evaluation on the 48 validation cars through the
fleet pump.

**Bars, written before the runs.** Each rung's row is written with
GeoTransolver at whichever of 1e-3 and 3e-3 scores lower by seed mean;
the ladder chapter states that GeoTransolver's rate was chosen per rung
and ISLA's was not (it has one usable rate). Fleet-level reading, restated:
"the budget was the gap" holds only if GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at 435 cars,
each at its better rate, is at or above 0.97; the 435-car pair at 3e-3 is
therefore load-bearing for the thesis's in-distribution clause.

**Prediction.** The rate advantage shrinks with data: 3e-3 wins by 10 to
20% at 54 cars, by under 5% at 109 and 218, and the two rates are within
3% at 435 cars, where the 10,000-cell grid found 1e-3 best. Probability
that 3e-3 still wins by more than 5% at 435 cars: 0.3. The ladder's
ordering at 54 cars (ISLA ahead by 14% at GeoTransolver's 1e-3) likely
reverses or closes.

## 2026-09-19 — Interim, RATE-GT: at 54 cars GeoTransolver at 3e-3 scores 0.0743 against 0.0978 at 1e-3, so at its better rate it leads ISLA (0.0859) by 14%; the 109-, 218- and 435-car controls follow {#sec-nb-rategt-interim-54}

**What we saw.** The 54-car GeoTransolver pair at learning rate 3e-3
(@sec-nb-rategt-prereg) scores **0.0743** (seeds 0.0752 / 0.0734) in
float32 at 200,000 cells, against 0.0978 at 1e-3 and ISLA's 0.0859 at its
one usable rate. Written at each model's better rate, **GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA = 0.86** at 54 cars; the 1e-3 reading (1.14) is superseded. The rate
advantage at 54 cars is 24%, against 31% at 27 cars, consistent with the
prediction that it shrinks with data. Artifact:
results/p200k_ladder_interim_2026-09-18.json (`rate_control_lr3e3` under
`n54`).

**Reading so far.** On the two scarcest rungs GeoTransolver at its better
rate leads ISLA by 17% and 14%, the same direction as the 10,000-cell
ladder (16% and 22% there against the legacy centered variant). The
200,000-cell budget did not reverse the small-data ordering; it removed
the count-noise term from ISLA's error and GeoTransolver's, and
GeoTransolver keeps its data-efficiency lead. The 109- and 218-car controls
(where GeoTransolver at 1e-3 already stood at 1.02 and 1.01) and the
435-car pair decide whether the lead persists at full data.

## 2026-09-19 — Fleet operations: eight wing lanes blocked by a stale failure fingerprint, not by training; the rank kills behind them are NCCL all-reduce timeouts; guard and timeout fixed {#sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-ops-2026-09-19}

**Symptom.** At 02:15 PDT the watcher reported eight ISLA wing lanes
(deflection, scarce, geometry-scarce and geometry-super-scarce rungs, both
seeds) blocked with the same reason, "identical failure on consecutive
segments: train step failed at epoch 0, step 0", although every one of them
had trained for tens to hundreds of epochs.

**Cause, two layers.** The blocking text was the lanes' *first-ever*
failure, from the launch afternoon (the missing head-shape override,
@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-launch). The two-strike guard took its fingerprint
from the last matching line of the whole log, so any later link that died
without writing an error line inherited that stale text, matched the
stored fingerprint, and blocked the lane. Underneath, the links were dying
because one rank was killed with SIGABRT after an NCCL all-reduce watchdog
timeout at the 900-second collective timeout: 72 such timeouts across 23
of the 42 wing lanes, on all three architectures (60 on ISLA lanes, 46 on
GeoTransolver's, 34 on Transolver's), so it is a data-path stall (one rank
waiting on a large case at 200,000 cells, most plausibly during the
distributed validation pass) and not a model defect. One lane also took
two SIGBUS kills on the same node, which was excluded.

**Fixes.** Every chain launcher now records the log length before
`torchrun` and fingerprints only the current link's lines
(`kernel/patch_guard_fingerprint.py`); the wing, deflection and interior
launchers raise the collective timeout to 3,600 seconds; the eight lanes
were unblocked, preflighted and resumed from their newest intact
checkpoints (epochs 17 to 299). Pending links carry the old script text, so
the fixes reach a lane at its next self-submitted link. Wall-clock cost so
far: each timeout costs a link restart and a queue wait, not epochs (the
checkpoint interval is two epochs), which is why the wing rungs are
running behind the DrivAerML lanes.

**Addendum (23:40 PDT): the hourly evaluation pump stalled.** The pump is
a ten-minute CPU-partition job that lists finished-but-unevaluated lanes,
submits their float32 evaluation array, and resubmits itself with a start
time one hour later. Its 20:58 instance sat `PENDING` with reason
`BeginTime` for two and a half hours past that start time while the CPU
partition showed eighteen idle nodes, so seven ISLA lanes of the equal-cost
grid finished training without being evaluated (the GeoTransolver and
Transolver lanes had been caught by the 19:58 instance). Cancelling and
resubmitting the pump without a start time ran it within seconds and it
submitted the missing evaluations. A nudge script
(`kernel/p200k_fleet/pump_nudge.sh`) now runs on every watcher poll: if
the pump is pending more than fifteen minutes past its begin time, or
absent without the stop marker, it is resubmitted. No numbers were
affected; only their arrival was delayed.

## 2026-09-19 — Interim verdict, PROTO-200K: at 435 cars and 200,000 cells ISLA scores 0.0446, GeoTransolver at 1e-3 0.0455 (1.02x) and Transolver 0.0473 (1.06x); parity bar met on the 1e-3 reading, final standing waits for GeoTransolver's 3e-3 pair; at 109 cars GeoTransolver at 3e-3 leads ISLA by 8% {#sec-nb-proto200k-interim}

**Setting.** PROTO-200K (@sec-nb-proto200k-prereg) trains ISLA,
GeoTransolver and Transolver at 435 DrivAerML cars with the recipe's
default of 200,000 sampled cells per case, in place of the 10,000-cell
exploration budget behind the earlier standings, and scores them in
float32 at 200,000 cells on the 48 validation cars. The preregistered bars
were parity (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at or above 0.99 and Transolver ÷ ISLA
at or above 1.00), anatomy holds (0.96 to 0.99) and gap persists (below
0.96), with the prediction "anatomy holds at the upper edge, 0.98 to 0.99".

**What we saw** (surface-pressure error, seed mean with seeds 42 / 43;
results/p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json):

| model (learning rate) | 200,000 cells | 10,000 cells (earlier standing) | 200k ÷ 10k |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA (1e-3) | **0.0446** (0.0442 / 0.0449) | 0.0552 | 0.81 |
| GeoTransolver (1e-3) | 0.0455 (0.0455 / 0.0455) | 0.0503 | 0.90 |
| Transolver (3e-3) | 0.0473 (0.0470 / 0.0475) | 0.0517 | 0.91 |

GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA **1.02**, Transolver ÷ ISLA **1.06**. Every model
improves on its 10,000-cell value (no lane is flagged), ISLA by the most:
the deficit anatomy assigned about three of its eight points at 10,000
cells to count noise in the measure-weighted routing and this is where
that term went. On the 1e-3 reading the **parity** bar is met and
exceeded; the prediction (anatomy holds at 0.98 to 0.99) was too
pessimistic for ISLA by about three points.

**Why this is interim.** GeoTransolver's best rate depends on the data
size (@sec-nb-rategt-prereg): at 200,000 cells its 3e-3 lanes beat its
1e-3 lanes by 31% at 27 cars, 24% at 54 and, now scored, **10% at 109 cars**
(0.0565 against 0.0627; GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at its better rate **0.92**,
so GeoTransolver leads ISLA by 8% on that rung as well). The advantage is
shrinking with data, and at 435 cars the 10,000-cell grid found 1e-3 best,
but the protocol is each architecture at its own best rate, so the 435-car
row is written only when the 3e-3 pair (epoch about 240 of 500) is scored.
The standing at 218 cars likewise waits for its control.

**The picture that is forming.** At the reporting protocol GeoTransolver
keeps a data-efficiency lead on the scarce rungs (17%, 14%, 8% at 27, 54
and 109 cars, each at its better rate) that narrows toward zero by 218 to
435 cars, where ISLA is at parity or slightly ahead on the 1e-3 reading.
Transolver trails ISLA by 6% at full data. Whether ISLA's 2% lead at 435
cars survives GeoTransolver's 3e-3 control is the one open number; the
thesis's in-distribution clause is written after it.

## 2026-09-19 — Verdict, RATE-WINDOW: ISLA's safe learning-rate window at width 192 is 3e-4 to 1e-3 (3e-4 scores 1.08x the 1e-3 error), 1e-3 is best, and the ceiling lies between 1e-3 and 2e-3 {#sec-nb-ratewindow-verdict}

**Setting.** LR-REF (@sec-nb-lrref-verdict) showed ISLA at width 192
rising to the mean-field plateau at 3e-3 and diverging to NaN at 1e-2; RATE-WINDOW
(@sec-nb-ratewindow-prereg) bracketed the safe window with two seeds each
at 3e-4 and 2e-3 on the 10,000-cell exploration budget, 435 DrivAerML cars,
500 epochs, bf16, scored in float32 on the sample-frame probe against the
1e-3 seeds. The 2e-3 pair rose to the plateau by epoch 22 and was stopped
(@sec-nb-ratewindow-interim).

**What we saw.** At 3e-4 the surface-pressure error is **0.0597** (seeds
0.0599 / 0.0595) against 0.0552 at 1e-3, a factor **1.08**, inside the
preregistered 1.1x clause; the density factor is 1.18, inside the contract
band. The loss curve is the 1e-3 curve slowed: at epoch 500 its validation
loss (0.00090) is where the 1e-3 lane's was near epoch 150, so the 8% is
undertraining within the fixed 500-epoch budget rather than a different
optimum. Artifact: results/ratewindow_reduction_2026-09-19.json.

**Verdict.** The window extends half a decade downward and not at all
upward: **3e-4 to 1e-3 at width 192, 1e-3 best, plateau onset between 1e-3 and
2e-3.** The prediction (3e-4 within 1.1x; 2e-3 rises to the plateau with probability
about 0.5) held on both points. The operating manual states the window and
the warning that the protocol rate sits within a factor of two of the
plateau's onset; above width 192 the width rule applies. The mechanism question
(why the relative frame's routing hardens at a rate the centered variant
tolerates) stays open as a separate node.

## 2026-09-19 — Verdict, PROTO-200K-FLEET pose test: at 200,000 cells ISLA in random poses scores 0.0453 (1.015x its native-frame 0.0446), 12% below the rotation-augmented GeoTransolver and 21% below the augmented Transolver {#sec-nb-p200k-pose-verdict}

**Setting.** The pose test of the fleet (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg)
repeats POSE-REF (@sec-nb-poseref-verdict) at the reporting protocol:
every DrivAerML training and validation car in its own random SO(3) pose,
435 cars, 200,000 sampled cells per case, ISLA trained without
augmentation, GeoTransolver and Transolver with rotation augmentation,
two seeds each, float32 at 200,000 cells on the 48 posed validation cars.
The bar is POSE-REF's: ISLA posed within 3% of its native-frame error and
at least 5% below both augmented baselines.

**What we saw** (results/p200k_pose_reduction_2026-09-19.json; the
native-frame values are the trio's, @sec-nb-proto200k-interim):

| model | native frame | every case in a random pose | posed ÷ native |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA (no augmentation) | 0.0446 | **0.0453** (0.0450 / 0.0456) | 1.015 |
| GeoTransolver (rotation-augmented; native at 1e-3) | 0.0455 | 0.0508 (0.0506 / 0.0509) | 1.12 |
| Transolver (rotation-augmented) | 0.0473 | 0.0550 (0.0552 / 0.0547) | 1.16 |

**Verdict: supports.** ISLA's posed error is 1.5% above its native error,
the same residual POSE-REF measured at 10,000 cells (the bf16 training
path); the augmented baselines pay 12% and 16% for the poses, so **ISLA
leads GeoTransolver by 12% and Transolver by 21%** when geometries arrive
in arbitrary orientations. The lead is larger than at 10,000 cells (7% and
17%) because ISLA gained more from the denser sampling in the native
frame. GeoTransolver's posed lanes ran at 1e-3; if its 3e-3 pair lowers
its native-frame error at 435 cars the augmented-posed comparison would
need the same control, and this entry will say so when that pair reports.

over its own 1e-3 shrinks 31%, 24%, 10%, 4% along the same rungs, so at

and the 435-car row (ISLA 0.0446 against GeoTransolver 0.0455 at 1e-3) is

results/p200k_ladder_interim_2026-09-18.json, now complete for the ladder.

**Reading.** At the reporting protocol GeoTransolver is the more
data-efficient model on DrivAerML by 17% at 27 cars, narrowing
monotonically to 3% at 218 cars; ISLA reaches it around the full training
set. This is the 10,000-cell ladder's ordering with a smaller gap at every
rung (that ladder, against the legacy centered variant, read 16%, 22%,

## 2026-09-19 — Interim, PROTO-200K-FLEET wings: on the 35-case rung the 200,000-cell budget changes nothing (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.73 against 0.72 at 10,000 cells; every model within 2% of its 10,000-cell error), so the wing deficit is not count noise {#sec-nb-p200k-wings-35}

**Setting.** The fleet preregistration (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg)
wrote two fleet-level readings for the HiLiftAeroML wing rungs: "the
budget was the gap" if GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA rises by at least 0.03 against
its 10,000-cell value, "the wings differ" if it moves by less than 0.03,
in which case the wing deficit is not the count-noise term that the
DrivAerML anatomy identified and its mechanism is the next study. The
35-case rung (`highlift_surface_super_scarce`: 35 training wings, 180
validation cases, five target fields) is the first wing rung to finish at
200,000 cells; GeoTransolver ran at 3e-3 on this rung in both protocols.

**What we saw** (surface-pressure error, float32, seed means;
results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json):

| model | 10,000 cells | 200,000 cells | 200k ÷ 10k |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | 0.1529 (0.1567 / 0.1490) | **0.1500** (0.1504 / 0.1496) | 0.98 |
| GeoTransolver (3e-3) | 0.1102 | 0.1098 (0.1063 / 0.1133) | 1.00 |
| Transolver (3e-3) | 0.1142 | 0.1101 (0.1115 / 0.1087) | 0.96 |

GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA **0.73** (0.72 at 10,000 cells), Transolver ÷ ISLA
**0.73** (0.75). The other four fields tell the same story (velocity 0.78,
wall shear 0.79, temperature 0.78, density 0.73 for GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA).

**Reading: the wings differ.** Twenty times the sampled cells moved
neither model on this rung, so the 27% deficit at 35 wings is not count
noise in ISLA's routing and not a sampling-budget artifact for the
baselines either; it is a property of the trained functions on this
dataset. This is the outcome the preregistration named second and the
prediction (wing ratios up by 0.03 to 0.05) missed. The mechanism the
preregistration pointed at, the mesher pattern where validation
geometries recur in training with a different mesh, becomes the next
study for the wing deficit; the 105-, 510- and 1,260-case rungs report as
they finish and will say whether the deficit closes with data on the wings
the way it does on DrivAerML (0.83 to 0.97 from 27 to 218 cars).

**Consequence for the thesis.** The wing rows of the standing table keep
their 10,000-cell ordering at the reporting protocol. ISLA's case on the
wings rests, as before, on the contracts (consistency under a change of
sampling, exact covariance), not on in-distribution accuracy, and the book
states the deficit at the reporting protocol.

## 2026-09-19 — Verdict, PROTO-200K and RATE-GT: parity at the reporting protocol; at 435 cars and 200,000 cells GeoTransolver at its better rate scores 0.0445 against ISLA's 0.0446 (0.998) and Transolver 0.0473 (1.06); GeoTransolver's 3e-3 wins every rung with a shrinking margin {#sec-nb-proto200k-verdict}

**Setting.** PROTO-200K (@sec-nb-proto200k-prereg) is the in-distribution
standing at the recipe's default of 200,000 sampled cells per case, the
protocol Peter set on 2026-09-18 for every reported number. RATE-GT
(@sec-nb-rategt-prereg) made the comparison fair by giving GeoTransolver
its better of two learning rates on every rung, after the 27-car control
showed that its best rate depends on how much data it trains on. The
preregistered bars were parity (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at or above 0.99 and
Transolver ÷ ISLA at or above 1.00), anatomy holds (0.96 to 0.99) and gap
persists (below 0.96); the prediction was "anatomy holds at the upper
edge, 0.98 to 0.99".

**What we saw at 435 cars** (surface-pressure error, float32 at 200,000
cells, 48 validation cars, seeds 42 / 43;
results/p200k_trio_reduction_2026-09-19.json):

| model (learning rate) | 200,000 cells | 10,000 cells | 200k ÷ 10k |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA (1e-3) | **0.0446** (0.0442 / 0.0449) | 0.0552 | 0.81 |
| GeoTransolver (3e-3, its better rate) | **0.0445** (0.0441 / 0.0449) | 0.0503 (at 1e-3, its better rate there) | 0.88 |
| GeoTransolver (1e-3) | 0.0455 (0.0455 / 0.0455) | | |
| Transolver (3e-3) | 0.0473 (0.0470 / 0.0475) | 0.0517 | 0.91 |

GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA **0.998** with seed ranges that coincide to the
fourth decimal; Transolver ÷ ISLA **1.06**. **Verdict: parity.** The
in-distribution gap the book carried for weeks (0.90 against GeoTransolver
at 10,000 cells) was the exploration budget's: the deficit anatomy
assigned three of its eight points to count noise in the measure-weighted
routing, and at the reporting protocol the whole gap has gone, not three
points of it. The prediction (0.98 to 0.99) undershot ISLA by about two
points.

**RATE-GT, complete.** GeoTransolver at 3e-3 beats its own 1e-3 on every
rung at 200,000 cells, by 31%, 24%, 10%, 4% and 2% at 27, 54, 109, 218 and
435 cars; the margin shrinks with data as predicted, and at 435 cars the
two rates are within 2% so the 10,000-cell grid's choice of 1e-3 was not
wrong there, only not best. Every 200,000-cell row of the book now takes
GeoTransolver at 3e-3 and says so. The complete DrivAerML ladder at each
model's better rate: GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA **0.83, 0.86, 0.92, 0.97, 1.00**
at 27, 54, 109, 218 and 435 cars; Transolver ÷ ISLA 1.06, 1.00, 0.99, 1.03,
1.06.

**What the thesis now says, in-distribution.** On DrivAerML at the
reporting protocol ISLA matches GeoTransolver at full data and trails it
below full data by a deficit that narrows monotonically from 17% at 27
cars to zero at 435; it leads Transolver by 6% at full data. On the wings
the 35-case rung keeps its 27% deficit at 200,000 cells
(@sec-nb-p200k-wings-35), so the in-distribution clause reads: parity on
DrivAerML, a data-efficiency deficit on the scarce rungs of both datasets
that closes with data on DrivAerML and is not count noise on the wings.
What ISLA offers over the baselines at equal in-distribution accuracy is
the contracts: consistency under a change of sampling (1.2x against 10 to
16x under a 10:1 density bias), exact covariance worth 12% and 21% in
random poses at this protocol (@sec-nb-p200k-pose-verdict), and half the
memory at 10,000 tokens. The chapters are restated on these numbers.

**What's next.** The RMS-pairwise-distance pair at 435 cars
(`p200k_dr_isla_rms`, epoch about 440) records the unit equivalence at the
reporting protocol; the interior, deflection and larger wing rungs follow
over the coming days through the pump; the wing deficit's mechanism is the
next study to preregister.

deficit; the 4-geometry rung rules out recurring validation geometries as
its source, and the 10,000-cell ablations ruled out positional information
(raw coordinates bought 4%, @sec-nb-a35-verdict) and the draw (the
stratified sampler moved the ratio one point, @sec-nb-quadvar-hl-verdict).
Two questions remain that the existing 200,000-cell checkpoints can answer
without training: whether the draw-variance term is any larger at the
reporting protocol, and whether GeoTransolver's wing lead is portable
across a change of sampling pattern or bound to the pattern it was trained
on, as on DrivAerML (10 to 16x degradation under a 10:1 density bias
against 1.2x for ISLA).

**Instrument.** The six 35-case checkpoints (`p200k_hl_*_super_scarce_seed42/43`,
ISLA, GeoTransolver at 3e-3, Transolver) scored in float32 on the
consistency benchmark's HiLift datasets at 200,000 cells: the independent
draw, the stratified draw and the 10:1-biased draw
(`bench/bench_lanes_wing200k.tsv`, 18 lanes). Readouts: GeoTransolver ÷
ISLA and Transolver ÷ ISLA under each draw; each model's density factor
(biased ÷ independent).

**Bars, written before the run.**

- **Draw variance is not the wing deficit** if the stratified ratio is
  within 0.03 of the independent one; **part of it** if it moves by 0.03 or
  more (then the wing anatomy needs the count-and-draw decomposition
  repeated at 200,000 cells).
- **The lead is pattern-bound** if the baselines' density factors exceed 3
  while ISLA's stays below 1.5, so that under the biased draw ISLA's error
  is below the baselines'; **the lead is portable** if the baselines'
  factors stay below 1.5 as well.

**Prediction.** Draw variance is not the deficit (ratio moves under 0.02,
as at 10,000 cells) and the lead is pattern-bound (baseline factors 5 to
15x, ISLA under 1.3x, as on DrivAerML at 10,000 cells). Probability about
0.8 on both. If both hold, the wing standing reads: on the sampling the
baselines were trained on they lead by 27%; under any other sampling of
the same wings ISLA leads, and the remaining mechanism of the in-pattern
deficit is the trained function's use of the wing meshes' cell-size
structure, which the measure-weighted routing deliberately does not read.

## 2026-09-19 — Verdict, WING-BENCH-200K: draw variance is not the wing deficit (stratified ratio 0.734 against 0.732); under a 10:1 density bias ISLA's wing error is unchanged (factor 1.00) while GeoTransolver's and Transolver's rise 2.5x and 2.8x, so ISLA leads them 1.8x and 2.1x under a changed sampling pattern; the preregistered factor-3 clause is not met {#sec-nb-wingbench-verdict}

**What was run.** The six 35-case checkpoints at 200,000 cells scored in
float32 on the 180 HiLift validation cases under the independent,
stratified and 10:1-biased draws at 200,000 cells
(@sec-nb-wingbench-prereg; job 794668;
results/wingbench_200k_reduction_2026-09-19.json).

**What we saw** (surface-pressure error, two-seed means):

| model | independent | stratified | 10:1 biased | density factor (biased ÷ independent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | 0.1502 | 0.1497 | 0.1498 | **1.00** |
| GeoTransolver (3e-3) | 0.1098 | 0.1098 | 0.2716 | 2.47 |
| Transolver (3e-3) | 0.1102 | 0.1101 | 0.3080 | 2.80 |

GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA: 0.732 independent, 0.734 stratified, **1.81**
biased. Transolver ÷ ISLA: 0.734, 0.736, **2.06**.

**Against the bars.** *Draw variance is not the wing deficit*: the
stratified ratio moves by 0.002, far inside the 0.03 clause, and no model
moves by more than 0.4% between the two unbiased draws; the third candidate
mechanism for the wing deficit is closed. *The lead's portability*: the
preregistered "pattern-bound" clause asked for baseline density factors
above 3 with ISLA's below 1.5. ISLA's is 1.00 (its error under the biased
draw is within 0.3% of its independent-draw error, the consistency
contract holding to the noise floor at this cell count) and the baselines'
are 2.5 and 2.8, below 3, so by the letter of the preregistration the
verdict on this clause is **between**. In substance the reading the clause
was written to capture holds: on the sampling pattern they were trained
on the baselines lead by 27%; under a different pattern of the same wings
ISLA leads GeoTransolver by 81% and Transolver by 106%. The baselines'
degradation is milder than at 10,000 cells (10 to 16x on DrivAerML,
@sec-nb-quadvar-verdict) because a 10:1 bias at 200,000 cells still leaves
the sparse region tens of thousands of points, and the bar was calibrated
on the 10,000-cell numbers; that miscalibration is recorded
(the threshold should have been stated relative to the count, per
the program's threshold-calibration rule).

**What the wing standing now says.** The 27% in-pattern deficit at 35
wings is not count noise (@sec-nb-p200k-wings-35), not recurring
validation geometries (@sec-nb-p200k-wings-geo4), not draw variance, and,
at the exploration budget, not positional information
(@sec-nb-a35-verdict). It is a property of the trained functions on the
sampling pattern they were trained on, and it inverts under any other
pattern. The remaining candidate for the in-pattern mechanism is the one
the 10,000-cell ablations pointed at: on wing meshes whose cell sizes vary
by a factor of hundreds (coefficient of variation 3.3), the
measure-weighted routing's gradient variance costs accuracy (weights off
bought 12% at 35 cases, @sec-nb-a35-verdict) while it buys the consistency
in the table above. A principled study of that trade, one that keeps the
weighted estimator (and so the consistency) while lowering its variance, is
the next node to preregister; a stratified or area-balanced *training*
draw is the candidate.

## 2026-09-19 — Preregistration, ISO-COST: error as a joint function of cells per case and width for ISLA and GeoTransolver at 435 cars, with step time and peak memory as the cost axes; does ISLA's memory advantage buy accuracy at equal cost, and does the training budget bind? {#sec-nb-isocost-prereg}

**Setting.** At 200,000 cells ISLA uses 0.46x GeoTransolver's inference
memory; with the fused geometry kernel (accuracy-neutral,
@sec-nb-kernel-neutral-verdict) it also takes 0.86x the step time
(@sec-using-cost). Peter asked (2026-09-19) whether that footprint buys
accuracy at equal cost, which of cells and parameters ISLA converts into
accuracy more cheaply, and whether the fixed 500-epoch budget binds. The
program has two points on the cells axis at width 192 (10,000 to 200,000
bought ISLA 19% and GeoTransolver 12%) and one width corner (512 wide,
80,000 cells, within 3%), no joint fit, and no budget control at full data
(ISLA at 3e-4 was still improving at epoch 500, @sec-nb-ratewindow-verdict).

**Instrument** (`kernel/isocost_aga.sbatch`, 36 lanes, seeds 42 and 43,
435 DrivAerML cars, bf16 training, chain-ahead links; float32 scoring at
the 200,000-cell reporting protocol through the fleet pump; each lane's
step time and peak memory read from its own log and GPU sampler):

| arm | width | cells per case | learning rate | epochs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA, fused kernel | 192 | 100k, 200k, 400k | 1e-3 | 500 |
| ISLA, fused kernel | 384 | 100k, 200k, 400k | 5e-4 (width rule) | 500 |
| GeoTransolver | 256 (default) | 100k, 400k (200k exists at 3e-3) | 3e-3 | 500 |
| GeoTransolver | 512 | 100k, 200k, 400k | 1e-3 and 3e-3 (its better is kept) | 500 |
| Transolver | 256 (default) | 100k, 400k (200k exists) | 3e-3 | 500 |
| budget controls | default | 200k | as above | 1000 |

Fit per model: error = a·N^(−α) + b·P^(−β) + c on the seed means, where N
is cells per case and P parameters; report the iso-memory and iso-time
frontiers (best error at each memory and each wall-clock budget across the
grid). Lanes that run out of memory are recorded as such; they are data
for the frontier, not failures.

**Bars, written before the runs.**

- **Cells exponent**: ISLA's α exceeds GeoTransolver's by at least 0.1
  (the count-noise mechanism predicts ISLA converts cells into accuracy
  faster); otherwise the two models have the same cells response and
  ISLA's memory advantage is the whole iso-memory story.
- **Iso-memory frontier**: at every memory budget spanned by the grid the
  best ISLA lane is at or below the best GeoTransolver lane (within 2%);
  falsified if GeoTransolver's frontier is lower at any budget by more
  than 2%.
- **Iso-time frontier**: with the fused kernel ISLA's frontier is within
  3% of GeoTransolver's at every wall-clock budget; if GeoTransolver's is
  lower by more than 3%, the time axis is where ISLA still pays.
- **Width**: ISLA at 384 improves on 192 by at least 3% at 200k (the
  corner study's 512 did not beat GeoTransolver, so a null here would say
  ISLA is cell-bound, not parameter-bound at this data size); GeoTransolver
  at 512 is reported at its better rate.
- **Budget**: the 1000-epoch controls improve on 500 by more than 2% for
  either model, in which case every 200k standing carries the label "at
  500 epochs" and a budget ladder is the next study; within 2%, the
  500-epoch protocol is declared converged at full data.

**Prediction.** α about 0.25 for ISLA and 0.15 for GeoTransolver; the
iso-memory frontier favors ISLA at every budget; the iso-time frontier is
a tie within 3%; width 384 buys ISLA 3 to 5% at 200k and 400k; the
budget control moves ISLA 3% and GeoTransolver 1% (ISLA is the slower
learner at 1e-3, RATE-WINDOW). The 400k lanes at width 384 and 512 are
the memory-frontier probes and one of GeoTransolver's may not fit on a
GB300 in training.

## 2026-09-19 — Preregistration, TRAIN-AREA: is the wing deficit the variance of the measure weights? Train on an area-proportional draw that keeps the estimator unbiased and makes the weights nearly uniform {#sec-nb-trainarea-prereg}

**Setting.** Every candidate mechanism for the 27% in-pattern wing deficit
at 35 cases has now been closed except one: count noise
(@sec-nb-p200k-wings-35), recurring geometries (@sec-nb-p200k-wings-geo4),
draw variance (@sec-nb-wingbench-verdict) and positional information
(@sec-nb-a35-verdict) are out. The survivor is the one the 10,000-cell
ablations pointed at: on wing meshes whose cell areas vary by hundreds
(coefficient of variation 3.3 against 2.3 on the cars), ISLA's routing and
pooling are weighted by the cells' quadrature measure, and under a
uniform-over-cells draw those weights are as variable as the areas; turning
them off bought 12% at 35 wings (@sec-nb-a35-verdict) but discards the
consistency contract. The principled version of the same move is to change
the *draw*, not the weights: sample cells with inclusion probability
proportional to area (a Poisson draw with exact Horvitz-Thompson weights,
`PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh` with `weight_mode=area`, already in the
recipe as the consistency benchmark's "area" sampler). The estimator stays
unbiased, so the consistency contract stands, and the measure weights the
network reads become nearly uniform, so if weight variance is the
mechanism, the deficit should shrink. The uniform-over-cells law is, as the
consistency study noted, the mesher's refinement pattern; sampling by area
is the law a uniform point-cloud generator over the surface would produce,
which is also the more physical choice for a general PDE surrogate.

**Instrument.** Dataset `highlift_surface_super_scarce_area.yaml`: the
35-wing training configuration with a 1,000,000-cell uniform pool and an
area-proportional Poisson draw of 200,000 expected cells per case,
applied in training and validation alike; otherwise identical (same
augmentations, transforms, normalization, targets). Six lanes
(`kernel/p200k_fleet/p200k_hl_aga.sbatch`, lanes 54 to 59): ISLA at 1e-3,
GeoTransolver at 3e-3 and Transolver at 3e-3 as controls, seeds 42 and 43,
500 epochs, bf16. Readout: float32 error on the 180 validation wings under
the independent uniform-over-cells draw (the standing instrument), the
area draw (the training law) and the 10:1-biased draw, via the consistency
benchmark at 200,000 cells; compared with the uniform-draw lanes of
@sec-nb-wingbench-verdict.

**Bars, written before the runs** (independent uniform-over-cells draw,
two-seed means, against ISLA's 0.1502 and GeoTransolver's 0.1098).

- **Mechanism supported**: ISLA under the area draw improves by at least 5%
  on the independent draw while GeoTransolver and Transolver move by less
  than 2%; the wing deficit is then the weight variance and the area draw
  becomes the recommended training law for ISLA on non-uniform meshes
  (adopted only after the same test on DrivAerML).
- **Sampler effect, not mechanism**: all three models improve by 5% or
  more; the area draw is a better training law for everyone and says
  nothing specific about ISLA.
- **Null**: ISLA moves by less than 5%; weight variance is not the
  mechanism, and the deficit is the trained function's response to the
  wing geometry itself (the last candidate standing would be the
  slice-attention form on multi-element surfaces).
- **Consistency**: ISLA's density factor stays within 1.05 to 1.3 (the
  weights are still read, only less variable); a rise beyond 1.5 would mean
  the area draw traded the contract for accuracy and is rejected.

**Prediction.** Mechanism supported, in part: ISLA improves 6 to 10% (the
weights-off ablation's 12% is the ceiling), GeoTransolver within 2%; the
deficit narrows from 27% to about 20%. Probability about 0.5; the null is
the other half.

**Addendum, ISO-COST launch (2026-09-19, 14:10 PDT).** The twenty-two
GeoTransolver and Transolver lanes were accepted (alive, no traceback,
epochs 11 to 24 at the check). The fourteen ISLA lanes crash-looped: the
recipe's ISLA configuration does not list `geo_kernel`, so the override
`model.geo_kernel=fused` fails Hydra's struct check ("Key 'geo_kernel' is
not in struct") and the chain resubmitted itself thirteen times in twenty
minutes because that error line matched none of the two-strike guard's
fingerprints. Fixed: the override is `+model.geo_kernel=fused`, the failed
run directories (no checkpoints) were removed and the lanes resubmitted,
and every chain launcher's fingerprint now includes Hydra override errors
so a typo blocks after two links. Early cost readings from the accepted
lanes, before any ISLA number: GeoTransolver at width 512 trains at 51,
100 and 199 GB of peak memory at 100k, 200k and 400k cells (0.23, 0.44 and
0.85 s per step); at width 256, 40, 80 and 158 GB. The 400k-cell lanes fit
on a GB300; the recipe's configurations do not carry `geo_kernel`
explicitly and gain the key in the repository so the fused kernel can be
selected without the append syntax.

**Addendum, ISO-COST acceptance (2026-09-19, 14:30 PDT).** All thirty-six
lanes are accepted (alive, no traceback, epochs 11 to 24). The training
cost readouts from the first links, before any accuracy number, are
already the cost half of the study (bf16, four GB300 GPUs per lane, one
case per GPU-step; peak memory and step time from each lane's log):

| model, width | 100k cells | 200k cells | 400k cells |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA fused, 192 | 13 GB, 0.11 to 0.14 s | 26 GB, 0.15 s | 52 GB, 0.26 s |
| ISLA fused, 384 | 22 GB, 0.12 to 0.13 s | 43 GB, 0.17 to 0.19 s | 86 GB, 0.31 to 0.59 s |
| GeoTransolver, 256 | 40 GB, 0.22 to 0.50 s | 80 GB, 0.39 to 0.41 s | 158 GB, 0.76 s |
| GeoTransolver, 512 | 51 GB, 0.23 to 0.46 s | 100 GB, 0.44 to 0.55 s | 199 GB, 0.85 s |
| Transolver, 256 | 27 GB, 0.09 to 0.87 s | (existing lanes) | 106 GB, 0.34 to 2.6 s |

In training at matched cells ISLA with the fused kernel uses about a third
of GeoTransolver's peak memory and a third of its step time (26 against 80
GB and 0.15 against 0.40 s at 200,000 cells and default widths); doubling
ISLA's width to 384 costs 1.6 to 1.7x memory and little time at the
smaller counts. Every 400,000-cell lane fits on a GB300, GeoTransolver at
width 512 with 80 GB to spare, so the memory frontier of the grid is not
reached and the iso-memory comparison will rest on the fit rather than on
an out-of-memory boundary. Step times at these early epochs are noisy
(the ranges are the two seeds' latest readings); the reduction will take
per-lane medians over the whole run.

## 2026-09-19 — Preregistration, ISO-MATCH: at GeoTransolver's recipe-default training budget, which split of cells and width gives ISLA its best accuracy, and how does that compare at iso-time, iso-memory and iso-parameters? {#sec-nb-isomatch-prereg}

**Setting.** Peter asked (2026-09-19) for the comparison a user would
actually make: take GeoTransolver as the unified recipe ships it and give
ISLA the same budget, measured either as training time per iteration or
as peak memory, with ISLA's knobs (cells per case, width) set at their
accuracy-optimal split. The recipe default for GeoTransolver is 200,000
cells per case, `n_hidden` 256 and 12 layers (9,046,016 parameters,
counted from the composed configuration) at learning rate 3e-3; on four
GB300 GPUs it trains at about 80 GB peak memory and 0.40 s per step
(ISO-COST acceptance readings, @sec-nb-isocost-prereg). ISLA at its
default width 192 has 8,912,796 parameters, so the existing 200,000-cell
pair (0.0446 against 0.0445, @sec-nb-proto200k-verdict) is already the
iso-parameter comparison; ISLA there trains at 26 GB and 0.15 s per step
with the fused kernel, a third of GeoTransolver's budget on both axes.

**Instrument.** ISLA with the fused kernel, 435 DrivAerML cars, seeds 42
and 43, 500 epochs, at five splits of GeoTransolver's budget along the
cells-versus-width line (the memory and time estimates are extrapolated
from the ISO-COST acceptance readings and are themselves readouts):

| width (parameters) | cells per case | learning rate (width rule) | expected peak memory | expected step time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 192 (8.9M) | 600,000 | 1e-3 | about 78 GB | about 0.39 s |
| 288 (19.5M) | 400,000 | 6.67e-4 | about 65 GB | about 0.35 s |
| 384 (34.3M) | 400,000 | 5e-4 | 86 GB (measured) | 0.31 to 0.59 s (measured) |
| 512 (60.3M) | 200,000 | 3.75e-4 | about 60 GB | about 0.25 s |
| 768 (134M) | 100,000 | 2.5e-4 | about 45 GB | about 0.25 s |

The 384 × 400k point is in the ISO-COST grid; the other four are new lanes
(`kernel/isocost_aga.sbatch`, lanes 36 to 43). All are scored in float32 at
the 200,000-cell reporting protocol. Peak memory and step time are read
from each lane's log (medians over the run); the iso-time and iso-memory
comparisons take, for each axis, the ISLA lanes whose measured cost is
within 15% of GeoTransolver's default (80 GB, 0.40 s) and report the best
of them against GeoTransolver's 0.0445.

**Bars, written before the runs.**

- **Iso-budget lead**: the best ISLA lane within the time budget, and the
  best within the memory budget, each beat GeoTransolver's 0.0445 by at
  least 3%; **parity** if within 3%; **deficit** if worse by more than 3%.
- **Optimal split**: cells win if the 192 × 600k lane is the best of the
  five; width wins if the 512 × 200k or 768 × 100k lane is; balanced if a
  middle point is. This is reported as the recommendation for spending a
  budget on ISLA.
- **Width rule**: every lane trains without the rise to the mean-field plateau of
  @sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism (validation loss not on the
  mean-field plateau); a plateau at 768 would mark the rule's edge.

**Prediction.** Iso-budget lead of 4 to 7% on both axes; the optimal split
is balanced (288 × 400k or 384 × 400k) rather than either extreme, because
the count-noise term is already small at 200,000 cells and the width study
found little at 512 wide on the same data. Probability of a lead of at
least 3% on both axes: 0.6.

## 2026-09-19 — Ruling: the fused geometry kernel is ISLA's default wherever it can run; `geo_kernel=None` resolves at the first forward pass to fused on CUDA (one global vector, at most 1,024 slices, Triton importable) and to eager otherwise {#sec-nb-geokernel-auto}

**Ruling (Peter, 2026-09-19).** KERNEL-NEUTRAL (@sec-nb-kernel-neutral-verdict)
found the fused Triton region accuracy-neutral (five pairs, mean 1.009)
and left it opt-in because neither preregistered clause was met. Peter's
instruction today supersedes that: the fused kernel is to be the default
whenever the hardware supports it, through a `None` default that resolves
to fused where possible and falls back to eager safely. The cost case is
now measured in training as well as inference: at 200,000 cells the fused
region trains ISLA at about a third of the eager step time and memory
(@sec-nb-isocost-prereg acceptance, 26 GB and 0.15 s against the eager
path's earlier readings; inference 91 against 529 ms, @sec-using-cost).

**What changed.** The class default is `geo_kernel=None` ("auto"). At the
first forward pass `resolve_geo_kernel(points)` chooses `"fused"` when the
points are on CUDA, Triton imports, the model has exactly one global vector
and at most 1,024 slices (the kernel's limits), else `"eager"`; the decision
is cached per device, logged once, and written into every block (and every
read block of the passive decoder). Explicit `"eager"` and `"fused"` are
honored as before, and an explicit `"fused"` still raises at construction
when the global-vector constraint cannot be met. Checkpoints that recorded
`geo_kernel="eager"` load and run eager, as recorded. Tests: the default is
asserted, auto resolves to eager on CPU with outputs identical to an
explicit eager model, two global vectors keep auto on eager while an
explicit fused request is refused. The recipe's ISLA configurations set
`geo_kernel: null`. The ISO-COST and ISO-MATCH lanes already run fused by
explicit override; earlier ISLA lanes (all eager) stand, the kernel being
exact.

**Addendum, ISO-MATCH acceptance (2026-09-19, 15:05 PDT).** All eight
lanes are alive with clean logs at epochs 15 to 18. Measured first-link
costs: 192 × 600k trains at 77.5 GB and 0.38 s per step, which is
GeoTransolver's default budget on both axes (80 GB, 0.40 s); 288 × 400k at
69 GB and 0.28 s; 512 × 200k at 53 GB and 0.19 to 0.27 s; 768 × 100k at 40
GB and 0.15 to 0.18 s. The wide end of the line therefore under-spends the
budget by a third to a half, so two further splits are added to spend it
there: 512 × 300k and 768 × 200k (lanes 44 to 47, seeds 42 and 43, width
rule rates). The iso-budget comparison will take, on each axis, the lanes
within 15% of GeoTransolver's cost; with these additions the set is
expected to be 192 × 600k, 384 × 400k, 512 × 300k and 768 × 200k.

## 2026-09-19 — Interim and preregistration, PROTO-200K-FLEET interior: ISLA's interior configuration rises to the mean-field loss plateau at 200,000 cells and learning rate 1e-3 on both seeds while every surface lane trains; GeoTransolver-volume improves to 0.0477; RATE-VOL runs the interior at 5e-4 and 3e-4 {#sec-nb-ratevol-prereg}

**What we saw.** The interior lanes (`p200k_dr_*_vol_seed42/43`: boundary
cells and interior query points both at 200,000 per case) finished.
GeoTransolver-volume scores 0.0477 / 0.101 / 0.084 (pressure, velocity,
eddy viscosity; 0.0513 / 0.107 / 0.088 at 10,000 queries), a clean
improvement. ISLA's pair is on the mean-field plateau: float32 0.73 / 0.73 /
0.97, validation loss 0.069 and 0.073 against 0.0010 for the 10,000-query
lane. The loss curves show the signature LR-REF identified
(@sec-nb-lrref-verdict), not a configuration error: seed 42 trains normally
to epoch 70 (validation loss 0.0041, on the 10,000-query lane's trajectory)
and its validation loss rises from 0.0041 to 0.080 between epochs 70 and 80; seed 43's rises before epoch 20.
Every surface lane at 1e-3, including the ISO-COST and ISO-MATCH lanes at
600,000 cells and width 768 (checked at epochs 60 to 117, all on normal
trajectories), is healthy, so the ceiling that moved is the interior
configuration's: with 200,000 query tokens interacting alongside 200,000
boundary tokens its loss rises to the plateau at a rate the surface
configuration tolerates; the routing-saturation mechanism RFDIV measured at
width 512 is inferred here from the matching signature, not measured on
these runs. This is the preregistration's defect clause
(@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg): the row is not written; the defect is
investigated.

**Instrument (RATE-VOL).** The interior configuration at 435 cars and
200,000 cells, seeds 42 and 43, at learning rates 5e-4 and 3e-4
(`kernel/p200k_fleet/p200k_vol_aga.sbatch`, lanes 4 to 7), otherwise as
the 1e-3 pair; float32 scoring at 200,000 queries through the fleet pump;
GeoTransolver-volume's 0.0477 / 0.101 / 0.084 is the comparator.

**Bars, written before the runs.** A rate trains cleanly if neither seed's
validation loss visits the plateau (stays below 0.01 after epoch 20). The
interior row is written with ISLA at the higher clean rate. Bars on that
row against GeoTransolver-volume: pressure and velocity ratios within 5% of
their 10,000-query values (0.93 and 1.37) mean the interior standing
survives the protocol; a swing of more than 5% is reported as the budget's
effect. If both rates rise to the plateau, the interior configuration's rate ceiling
at 200,000 cells is below 3e-4 and the mechanism study (routing entropy and
anchor spread measured on these runs) is promoted
ahead of the interior row.

**Prediction.** 5e-4 trains cleanly on both seeds (the width rule's factor
of two from the 435-car surface ceiling of 1e-3 to 2e-3, applied to twice
the tokens); ratios within 5% of the 10,000-query standing.

the four interior lanes read validation loss 0.0021 and 0.0022 at 5e-4

The original 1e-3 seed 42 was at 0.0022 at epoch 50 and rose to 0.080

**Addendum, RATE-VOL second reading (2026-09-19, 20:45 PDT).** Past

plateau visit, which the hourly watcher would report as a validation loss
above 0.01.

## 2026-09-19 — Interim, ISO-COST: at 435 cars the first ten grid points say width buys accuracy and cells do not, for ISLA and GeoTransolver alike; ISLA at width 384 and 100,000 cells reaches 0.0411 at 22 GB, below every GeoTransolver lane evaluated so far {#sec-nb-isocost-interim}

**Setting.** ISO-COST (@sec-nb-isocost-prereg) trains ISLA, GeoTransolver
and Transolver on the 435 DrivAerML cars over a grid of cells per case
(100,000, 200,000, 400,000) and width (the default and twice it), with
1,000-epoch budget controls, and scores every lane in float32 at the
200,000-cell reporting protocol; ISO-MATCH (@sec-nb-isomatch-prereg) adds
ISLA lanes that spend GeoTransolver's recipe-default budget (80 GB, 0.40
s per step) on different splits of cells and width. Sixteen of the 48
lanes have finished their 500 epochs: everything at 100,000 cells, the
ISLA 200,000-cell pair at both widths, and (from PROTO-200K) the
200,000-cell defaults. The 400,000-cell lanes, GeoTransolver-512 at
200,000 cells, the ISO-MATCH splits and the budget controls are still
training, so the fits and the frontier verdicts below are provisional.

**Instrument.** Per-lane cost is read from each lane's own training log
by `kernel/isocost_cost.py`: the median step time after excluding the
first two steps of every epoch and any step above 5 s (compile and loader
start-up), and the peak of the logged per-step memory; the reduction is
`reduce_isocost.py` (artifact
`results/isocost_interim_2026-09-19.json`). Ratios are seed means of the
pressure relative L2 on the 48 validation cars, GeoTransolver over ISLA.

**What we saw.**

: ISO-COST interim standings, 435 DrivAerML cars, 500 epochs, float32 at 200,000 cells. GeoTransolver's 200,000-cell row is the PROTO-200K pair at 3e-3; its step time is borrowed from the 1,000-epoch control's log (same configuration). Transolver's 200,000-cell row is the PROTO-200K pair, whose log predates the step-time field. {#tbl-isocost-interim}

Three readings stand out.

1. **Doubling cells from 100,000 to 200,000 buys nothing at 435 cars, for
   any model.** ISLA-192 moves 0.0450 to 0.0448, GeoTransolver-256 0.0447
   to 0.0445, Transolver 0.0472 to 0.0473, ISLA-384 0.0411 to 0.0416; all
   within the seed spread (the ISLA-192 seeds at 100,000 cells differ by
   0.0017). This is the opposite of the 10,000-to-200,000 step, which
   bought ISLA 19% and GeoTransolver 12%: the cells response has
   saturated by 100,000 cells at this data size. The preregistered cells
   exponent gap (ISLA's α exceeding GeoTransolver's by 0.1) cannot be
   met on a flat response; the 400,000-cell lanes will fix the exponents,
   but the prediction of α about 0.25 for ISLA is already refuted between
   100,000 and 200,000 cells.
2. **Doubling width buys 7% for both models.** ISLA-384 improves on
   ISLA-192 by 8.7% at 100,000 cells and 7.1% at 200,000 (the
   preregistered width bar, at least 3% at 200,000, is met);
   GeoTransolver-512 improves on GeoTransolver-256 by 6.7% at 100,000
   cells, at its better rate 3e-3 (1e-3 is within 0.5%). At 435 cars both
   models are parameter-bound, not cell-bound. This differs from the
   80,000-cell width corner of the scaling study, where ISLA at 512 wide
   under the width rule came within 3% of GeoTransolver rather than ahead
   of it; the two readings are at different widths, cell counts and
   reporting draws and are not yet reconciled. The 512 × 200k ISO-MATCH
   lane speaks to it directly.
3. **The iso-memory frontier is ISLA's at every budget spanned so far.**
   ISLA-384 at 100,000 cells (0.0411, 22 GB) is below every GeoTransolver
   lane evaluated, including GeoTransolver-512 at 100,000 cells (0.0417 at
   51 GB, ratio 1.014) and the recipe default (0.0445 at 80 GB, ratio
   1.082). On the time axis the p10 step times (the GPU-bound floor) put
   ISLA-384 × 100k at 0.12 s against 0.25 s for GeoTransolver-512 × 100k
   and 0.39 s for the default, but the medians of every lane under 200,000
   cells sit at 0.21 to 0.29 s regardless of model or width: at these
   sizes the median step is set by the input pipeline (one case per GPU
   step, data loading and host-side subsampling), not by the network. The
   time-axis comparison therefore has two honest readings, GPU floor and
   pipeline-bound wall clock, and the chapter will show both; on neither
   is GeoTransolver's frontier lower.

**Provisional standing against the bars.** Iso-memory frontier: met so
far (minimum GeoTransolver-over-ISLA 1.014, at the 51 GB budget).
Iso-time frontier: met so far on both time readings. Width: met (7.1%
at 200,000 cells). Cells exponent: the prediction is refuted between
100,000 and 200,000 cells; the exponent fit waits on the 400,000-cell
lanes. Budget: pending the 1,000-epoch controls (both at epoch about
525 of 1,000). ISO-MATCH: the best ISLA lane at or under GeoTransolver's
80 GB memory budget is so far ISLA-384 × 100k at 0.0411, an 8.2% lead
that spends only 22 GB; the lanes that actually spend the budget (192 ×
600k, 288 × 400k, 384 × 400k, 512 × 300k, 768 × 200k; epochs 440 to 500)
decide the preregistered "within 15% of the budget" clause and the
optimal-split question.

**Why it matters.** If the remaining lanes hold this pattern, the
recommendation for spending a training budget on ISLA at this data size
is width, not cells, and the equal-budget comparison in @sec-equal-budget
becomes: at a third of GeoTransolver's memory and the same or less wall
clock, ISLA-384 at 100,000 cells is 8% more accurate than the recipe
default and 1.4% more accurate than GeoTransolver's own 4x-parameter
lane. The caveat that matters is that these are single-dataset,
two-seed readings; the 400,000-cell lanes will show whether cells help
once width is no longer the binding constraint.

## 2026-09-20 — Preregistration, SCALE-HL: does the DrivAerML scaling picture (cells flat above 100,000, width worth 7% per doubling for both models) hold on the 510-wing HiLift rung? {#sec-nb-scalehl-prereg}

**Setting.** ISO-COST (@sec-nb-isocost-interim) established on 435
DrivAerML cars that neither ISLA nor GeoTransolver converts cells per case
into accuracy above 100,000 cells, that doubling width buys both about
7%, and that ISLA-384 at 100,000 cells (0.0411, 22 GB) sits on the
iso-memory frontier against GeoTransolver-512 at 200,000 cells (0.0410,
100 GB). Peter's standing rule (2026-09-20) is that every result is
reproduced on at least two datasets before it counts. The wings are the
natural twin: the meshes are coarser and more variable (cell-area
coefficient of variation 3.3 against 2.3), ISLA trails GeoTransolver by
27% at 35 wings, and whether width closes or widens that gap is itself
the question the wing-deficit program needs answered.

**Instrument** (`kernel/scalehl_aga.sbatch`, manifest group `shl`, job
names `isla.scalehl.<lane>`; HiLift medium rung, 510 training wings, 180
validation wings; 100,000 cells per case, 500 epochs, bf16, seeds 42 and
43; float32 scoring at the 200,000-cell protocol through the fleet pump):
ISLA 192 / 384 / 768 wide at the width rule (1e-3, 5e-4, 2.5e-4);
GeoTransolver 256 / 512 wide at 3e-3 (its better rate on the wings,
@sec-nb-p200k-wings-geo4); Transolver 256 at 3e-3. Twelve lanes. The
fleet's medium-rung lanes at 200,000 cells (ISLA 192, GeoTransolver 256
at 1e-3 and 3e-3, Transolver 256) supply the cells comparison at default
widths at no extra cost.

**Bars, written before the runs** (seed-mean float32 pressure relative
L2 on the 180 validation wings).

- **Cells flat**: ISLA-192 and GeoTransolver-256 at 100,000 cells within
  2% of their 200,000-cell fleet twins; otherwise the cells response is
  dataset-dependent and the DrivAerML statement is qualified.
- **Width carries**: ISLA-384 improves on ISLA-192 by at least 3% and
  GeoTransolver-512 on GeoTransolver-256 by at least 3% (DrivAerML gave 7%
  and 7%); within 3% for either model: that model is not parameter-bound
  on the wings at this data size.
- **Turnover**: ISLA-768 against ISLA-384; a gain under 1% (or a loss)
  reproduces the DrivAerML turnover, and its seed spread is reported
  beside the CAP-435 rate controls' reading.
- **Deficit under width**: GeoTransolver over ISLA at matched parameters
  (512 against 384) compared with the default pair (256 against 192): if
  the ratio rises by 0.05 or more, width closes part of the wing deficit
  (ISLA is the more parameter-bound model on wings); if it falls by 0.05
  or more, width widens it; within ±0.05 the deficit is width-independent
  and architectural.
- **Iso-memory**: ISLA's best lane at or under GeoTransolver-512's
  measured memory at 100,000 cells (about 51 GB) against GeoTransolver's
  best at that budget, reported as a ratio with no bar (the DrivAerML
  frontier bar was written for that dataset; the wing frontier is a
  measurement).

**Prediction.** Cells flat (both within 2%); width carries for both
(ISLA 5 to 8%, GeoTransolver 4 to 6%); ISLA-768 within 1% of 384;
deficit width-independent (ratio change within ±0.05), probability 0.5,
with "width closes part of it" the other likely outcome at 0.35.

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, ISO-COST and ISO-MATCH (single dataset): at 435 cars cells per case stop paying at 100,000 for every model, width pays about 7% per doubling for ISLA and GeoTransolver, the 500-epoch protocol is converged (1,000 epochs move neither model by 0.1%), and ISLA reaches GeoTransolver's best error at 0.22x the memory and 0.27x the GPU-floor step time {#sec-nb-isocost-verdict}

**Setting.** ISO-COST (@sec-nb-isocost-prereg) and ISO-MATCH
(@sec-nb-isomatch-prereg) trained 48 lanes at 435 DrivAerML cars over a
grid of cells per case and width, with 1,000-epoch budget controls, and
scored all of them in float32 at the 200,000-cell protocol; the readings
accumulated in @sec-nb-isocost-interim. All 26 configurations are now
complete (artifact `results/isocost_reduction_2026-09-20.json`; reduction
`results/isocost_reduce_2026-09-19.py`; cost extraction
`results/isocost_cost_extract_2026-09-19.py`). Chapter 4's equal-budget
section (@sec-equal-budget) is written from the artifact.

**The last readings.** GeoTransolver-512 at 400,000 cells and 3e-3 scores
0.0414 (its 1e-3 pair 0.0413), so its cells ladder reads 0.0417, 0.0410,
0.0414 at 100k, 200k, 400k: the one lane with a cells response has it
between 100k and 200k only. The budget controls: ISLA-192 × 200k at 1,000
epochs scores **0.0448** against 0.0448 at 500 (ratio 1.000);
GeoTransolver-256 × 200k at 1,000 epochs scores **0.0445** against 0.0445
(ratio 0.9997). Neither moves by the 2% the bar asked for.

**Verdict against the bars.**

| bar | reading | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| cells exponent (ISLA's α exceeds GeoTransolver's by 0.1) | ISLA α = 0.00 ± 0.02; GeoTransolver's α unidentifiable (flat response) | **not met**; prediction (0.25 vs 0.15) refuted |
| iso-memory frontier (ISLA within 2% or better at every budget) | minimum GeoTransolver-over-ISLA 0.999 at 100 GB; 1.014 to 1.087 below | **met** |
| iso-time frontier (within 3% at every budget) | minimum 0.999 on both time readings | **met** |
| width (384 improves on 192 by 3% at 200k) | 7.1% | **met** |
| budget (1,000 epochs move a model by more than 2%) | 0.0% and 0.03% | **not met**: the 500-epoch protocol is converged at full data |
| ISO-MATCH memory lead (best ISLA lane within 15% of 80 GB beats 0.0445 by 3%) | 768 × 200k, 0.0421, 5.6% | **lead** |
| ISO-MATCH time (best ISLA lane within 15% of 0.43 s) | 192 × 600k, 0.0452, ratio 0.984 | **parity**, clause mis-specified (the only time-matched lane spent the budget on cells) |
| ISO-MATCH optimal split | 768 × 100k best of the five splits; every split worse than 384 × 100k at 22 GB | **width wins**, and the budget is better left unspent |

**What the study says, in one paragraph.** At this data size both
architectures are parameter-bound and neither is cell-bound above 100,000
cells per case. Spending a training budget on ISLA should go to width up to
384; beyond that, under the width learning-rate rule, the mean stops
improving and a 5% seed split appears (CAP-435's rate controls,
@sec-nb-cap435-prereg, are the discriminating experiment). The equal-budget
statement the chapter carries is the frontier one: below 100 GB ISLA's best
lane is ahead of GeoTransolver's at every memory and every GPU-time budget,
and at the top of the grid the two best lanes are at parity in error and at
matched parameters, with ISLA at 0.22x the memory and 0.27x the GPU-floor
step time. The budget controls retire a standing caveat: every 200k
standing in the book can drop "at 500 epochs".

**Caveat.** One dataset. The two-dataset rule (Peter, 2026-09-20) keeps
this a single-dataset verdict until SCALE-HL (@sec-nb-scalehl-prereg)
reports on the 510-wing rung; the ledger marks it DONE (single dataset).

## 2026-09-20 — Preregistration, ROUTING-SAT: is the mean-field plateau that appears when width or depth is doubled at a fixed learning rate a routing-saturation state, measured on the plateau lanes themselves? {#sec-nb-routingsat-prereg}

**Setting.** Three studies have now seen the same training signature in
ISLA: validation loss descends normally, then rises over a few epochs to
the mean-field plateau (about 0.06, the loss of predicting the field mean)
and stays. It appeared at width 512 under 1e-3 (RFDIV,
@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism, where routing entropy and anchor
spread were measured and found to collapse), at 24 and 48 layers under 5e-4
(CAP-435, @sec-nb-cap435-prereg acceptance), and in the interior
configuration at 200,000 cells under 1e-3 (@sec-nb-ratevol-prereg). The
rate that avoids it falls like 1/width and like 1/depth. Every entry since
RFDIV has said "mechanism inferred, not measured on these runs". This probe
measures it.

**Instrument** (`kernel/routing_probe.py`, one GPU job, job name
`isla.probe.routing`): ten trained checkpoints are run in float32 on the
first four DrivAerML validation cars at 100,000 cells with the routing
softmax instrumented. Per slice block it records the entropy of the routing
weights over points normalized by log N (the softmax ISLA uses; 1 is
uniform, 0 is one point per slice), the entropy of the same logits over
slices normalized by log S (1 is a point spread over every slice, 0 is one
slice per point), the effective number of slices carrying mass, the RMS
spread of the slice anchors relative to the RMS radius of the tokens, and
the logit standard deviation. Pairs: 24 layers at 5e-4 (plateau) against
2.5e-4 (clean); 48 layers at 2.5e-4 (plateau) against 1.25e-4 (clean); 768
wide seed 42 (0.0432) against seed 43 (0.0410) and against 384 wide
(0.0411) and 192 wide (0.0450); and the two doubled-rate width controls
(384 at 1e-3, 768 at 5e-4) whose fate is still open.

**Bars, written before the readout.**

- **Routing saturation confirmed**: on every plateau checkpoint at least
  half the blocks have the per-point entropy over slices below 0.2 (a point
  routes to one or two slices) or an effective slice count below a tenth of
  S, and the anchor spread below 0.3; on every clean checkpoint every block
  has per-point entropy above 0.4 and anchor spread above 0.6. Then the
  plateau is the RFDIV state and the rate laws are one phenomenon.
- **Refuted**: a plateau checkpoint whose routing statistics are inside the
  clean checkpoints' range in most blocks; the plateau is then not a
  routing state and the mechanism is elsewhere (head or MLP scale).
- **Seed split**: if 768 seed 42 sits between the clean and plateau
  statistics (entropy 0.2 to 0.4 in several blocks) while seed 43 is clean,
  the 5% width seed split is a partial saturation and the rate controls are
  expected to close it; if the two seeds are indistinguishable in routing,
  the split is not routing.
- **Doubled-rate controls**: whichever statistics the 384 × 1e-3 and 768 ×
  5e-4 checkpoints show at this reading (epoch about 30) is recorded as a
  prediction of their final outcome: saturated statistics predict a
  plateau or a worse final error, clean statistics predict recovery.

**Prediction.** Confirmed: the plateau lanes show per-point entropies
below 0.1 in most blocks and anchors within 0.2 of coincident; 768 seed 42
shows partial hardening in the upper blocks. Probability 0.7. The
successor study, if confirmed, is the intervention: a routing
parametrization whose tolerated rate does not shrink with width and depth.

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, ROUTING-SAT: the mean-field plateau is total routing collapse, measured: every point routes to one slice in every block and all anchors coincide; the two doubled-rate width controls are already in that state at epoch 89, so the width rule's ceiling is real; clean checkpoints keep 4 to 250 active slices per block {#sec-nb-routingsat-verdict}

**Setting.** ROUTING-SAT (@sec-nb-routingsat-prereg) ran ten trained ISLA
checkpoints on four validation cars with the routing softmax instrumented
(artifact `results/routingsat_2026-09-20.json`, per-block statistics for
every run). The question was whether the plateau that appears when width
or depth is doubled at a fixed learning rate is the routing-saturation
state RFDIV measured at width 512, this time measured on the plateau lanes
themselves.

**What we saw** (per block, mean over the four cars; "active slices" is
the effective slice count :math:`n_{\mathrm{eff}} = \exp H(q)` of the slice
mass distribution; "hardness" is the per-point entropy over slices divided
by :math:`\log S`, 1 uniform and 0 one slice per point).

| 384 wide, 48 layers, 5e-4 | plateau | 469 | all 48 blocks NaN in float32 | — | — | — |
| 384 wide, 12 layers, 1e-3 (width control) | open at prereg | 89 | **12 / 12** | 1.0 / 1.0 | 0.000 / 0.001 | **0.004** |
| 768 wide, 12 layers, 5e-4 (width control) | open at prereg | 89 | **12 / 12** | 1.0 / 1.0 | 0.000 / 0.001 | **0.003** |
| 384 wide, 24 layers, 2.5e-4 | clean | 83 | 0 / 24 | 3.7 / 102 | 0.11 / 0.60 | 0.41 |
| 384 wide, 48 layers, 1.25e-4 | clean | 77 | 0 / 48 | 40 / 190 | 0.57 / 0.87 | 0.30 |
| 192 wide (reference) | clean, 0.0450 | 500 | 0 / 12 | 20 / 90 | 0.33 / 0.51 | 0.52 |
