: ROUTING-SAT: routing statistics of plateau and clean ISLA checkpoints on four DrivAerML validation cars at 100,000 cells. {#tbl-routingsat}

**Verdict against the bars.** **Confirmed, with the criterion sharpened.**
The plateau checkpoints are not merely hardened: in the two doubled-rate
width controls every one of the twelve blocks routes every point to a
single slice (one active slice, hardness 0.000 to 0.001) and the 256
anchors of each block sit on top of each other (spread 0.003 to 0.004 of
the token radius). With one slice and one anchor per block the network can
only produce a per-case constant, which is the mean-field prediction the
plateau loss (about 0.06) corresponds to. The 24-layer plateau lane at
epoch 500 is in the same state in ten of its blocks and within two slices
of it in the rest. The clean checkpoints never reach it: no block of any
clean checkpoint has fewer than 3.7 active slices, and their medians run
54 to 190. The preregistered clean threshold (hardness above 0.4 in every
block) was too strict, however: every trained ISLA, including the 192-wide
reference, has two to six blocks that route sharply (hardness 0.19 to 0.33,
6 to 20 active slices), so "clean" means *bounded* sharpness, not uniform
routing, and the discriminator that separates the states is the effective
slice count (1 against at least 4) together with the anchor spread (below
0.01 against above 0.13). The 48-layer plateau checkpoint returns NaN
routing statistics in float32 in all 48 blocks (its bf16 training loss
stayed finite at 0.063); the weights were not inspected and the lane is
recorded as a divergence, not a plateau.

**The width controls are decided early.** Both doubled-rate lanes (384 at
1e-3, 768 at 5e-4) are in total collapse at epoch 89. The notebook records
this as the prediction the prereg asked for: their final errors will be on
the plateau. That places the rate ceiling at width 384 below 1e-3 (RFDIV
placed it at 512 below 1e-3; at 384 the 7.5e-4 control is the open point),
and at 768 below 5e-4 (3.75e-4 clean so far). The width rule is a real
ceiling, and its 1/width form is a measured fact about this routing
parametrization, not an artifact of under-training.

**The seed split is not routing.** ISLA-768 seed 42 (0.0432) and seed 43
(0.0410) have the same routing statistics within noise (six against four
sharp blocks, minimum active slices 12 against 11, median anchor spread
0.46 against 0.51); by the preregistered reading the 5% width seed split
is not a partial saturation.

**Mechanism, now measured.** Routing collapse is the failure mode of this
architecture at high learning rate, and the tolerated rate falls with
width and with depth because both raise the gain of the feedback that
sharpens the routing (each block's assignment logits are a linear map of
a normalized state whose weights are free to grow; a sharper routing
concentrates the slice states, which sharpens the next block's routing).
The intervention this suggests is structural, not a rate rule: bound the
routing logits so that no block can reach one active slice, for example
by routing on the cosine between the normalized token state and normalized
slice prototypes at a fixed temperature. That is the successor study
(ROUTE-NORM), to be preregistered with the collapse conditions measured
here (384 at 1e-3, 768 at 5e-4) as its test cases and the reference
configuration's accuracy as its null.

## 2026-09-20 — Preregistration, ROUTE-NORM: does bounding the routing logits (cosine routing at a fixed temperature) remove the learning-rate ceiling that ROUTING-SAT measured as total routing collapse, and does it change accuracy at the rule rates? {#sec-nb-routenorm-prereg}

**Setting.** ROUTING-SAT (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict) measured the
mean-field plateau as total routing collapse: every block routes every
point to one slice and all anchors coincide. The tolerated learning rate
falls like 1/width and 1/depth (@sec-nb-cap435-prereg acceptance), which
costs the wide models their training speed and, under the width rule,
leaves a seed split at 512 and 768 (@sec-nb-isocost-interim). Each block's
routing logits are an affine map of a normalized token state whose weights
are free to grow, so nothing bounds how sharp the routing can become. The
intervention is structural: route on the cosine between the token state
and a learned prototype per slice, times a fixed temperature :math:`T`, so
every logit lies in :math:`[-T, T]` and no block can reach the collapsed
state however its weights grow. The frame, measure and head contracts are
untouched (the routing consumes only invariants either way); the test file
`test_isla_routing.py` asserts the bound, the contracts and that every
parameter trains. Implementation: `routing_norm="cosine"`,
`routing_temperature=10` (the linear routing of trained ISLA has logit
standard deviations of 2.1 to 3.0 on validation cars, so a range of ±10
leaves ordinary routing sharpness available while forbidding the one-slice
state; the temperature is a hyperparameter of this study, not tuned).

**Instrument** (`kernel/routenorm_aga.sbatch`, code snapshot
`code_routenorm`, manifest group `rn`, job names `isla.routenorm.<lane>`;
100,000 cells, 500 epochs, bf16, seeds 42 and 43, float32 scoring at the
200,000-cell protocol through the fleet pump; 18 lanes):

| dataset | routing | width | rate | role |
|---|---|--:|--:|---|
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 192 | 1e-3 | accuracy null against the reference (0.0450) |
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 384 | 5e-4 | accuracy null against 0.0411 |
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 384 | 1e-3 | collapse condition (linear routing collapses by epoch 89) |
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 768 | 2.5e-4 | accuracy null against 0.0421 (seed split 0.0432 / 0.0410) |
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 768 | 5e-4 | collapse condition |
| DrivAerML 435 | cosine | 768 | 1e-3 | twice the collapse rate |
| HiLift 510 | cosine | 192 | 1e-3 | second-dataset accuracy null (against SCALE-HL's linear 192) |
| HiLift 510 | cosine | 384 | 1e-3 | second-dataset collapse condition |
| HiLift 510 | linear | 384 | 1e-3 | second-dataset collapse control (does linear collapse on wings too?) |

**Bars, written before the runs** (validation loss trajectories for the
collapse clause; seed-mean float32 pressure relative L2 for accuracy).

- **Collapse removed**: every cosine lane at a collapse rate (384 at 1e-3,
  768 at 5e-4 and 1e-3, on both datasets) keeps its validation loss below
  0.01 after epoch 20 on both seeds and finishes with routing statistics in
  the clean range (effective slices at least 4 in every block, measured with
  the ROUTING-SAT probe); the linear wing control at 384 and 1e-3 collapses
  as its DrivAerML twin did. Then the rate ceiling was the routing
  parametrization and the width rule becomes unnecessary.
- **Collapse moved, not removed**: cosine lanes survive 1e-3 at 384 but not
  at 768, or survive on the cars but not the wings; the bound helps and the
  ceiling still scales.
- **Null**: a cosine lane collapses at a rate where linear routing also
  collapses; the bound is not the mechanism's lever (the collapse then goes
  through the token states rather than the logit scale).
- **Accuracy at the rule rates**: cosine within 1% of linear at 192 × 1e-3
  (0.0450), 384 × 5e-4 (0.0411) and 768 × 2.5e-4 (0.0421) is neutral; more
  than 2% worse is a cost that the rate freedom must pay for; more than 2%
  better is a finding on its own.
- **Width beyond 384 recovers**: if cosine 768 at 5e-4 or 1e-3 scores at
  least 2% below linear 384's 0.0411 with both seeds within 1% of each
  other, the ISO-COST width turnover was optimization (rate-limited, seed-
  split) and not capacity, and the width ladder is re-run under cosine
  routing (CAP-435's 1,024 and 1,536 lanes would follow).
- **Second dataset**: the collapse and accuracy clauses are read on the
  510-wing rung as well; a verdict that holds on one dataset only is
  interim.

**Prediction.** Collapse removed at 384 × 1e-3 on both datasets and at 768
× 5e-4; 768 × 1e-3 open (0.5); accuracy neutral at the rule rates (within
1%); 768 under cosine at 5e-4 beats 0.0411 by 1 to 3% with the seed split
closed. Probability of the full "collapse removed" clause: 0.6.

**Readings against the bars.**

- **ISLA width turnover: at 384.** The gains along 192, 384, 512, 768,
  1,024, 1,536 are +8.6%, −3.6%, +1.1%, −1.9%, −5.3%: every width above
  384 is worse than 384 under the width rule, and 1,536 wide (532M
  parameters) is back at the 192-wide error. The seed spread at 768 and
  1,024 (5% and 6%) is the split @sec-nb-isocost-interim reported; 512 and
  1,536 do not show it. This is the preregistered turnover clause met at
  the first step, and it is the opposite of the prediction (turnover
  between 768 and 1,536).
- **GeoTransolver width: still improving at 1,024, at its lower rate.**
  512 to 1,024 gains 2.6% at 1e-3 (0.0417 to 0.0406); at 3e-3, its better
  rate at 256 and 512, the 1,024-wide model is worse than 512 (0.0457, with
  a 12% seed spread), so GeoTransolver's tolerated rate also falls with
  width, more gently than ISLA's and without the plateau (its 3e-3 lane
  degrades to 0.046, not to 0.77). The 2.6% is under the 3% clause that
  would have added a 2,048-wide lane; it is close enough that the lane is
  worth adding once ROUTE-NORM's ISLA ladder exists to compare against.
- **Iso-parameter pairs.** ISLA-384 against GeoTransolver-512 (34M against
  36M): 1.014, **parity**. ISLA-768 against GeoTransolver-1,024 (134M
  against 143M): 0.964, **GeoTransolver leads by 3.6%**, outside the
  parity band. At the top of the two ladders GeoTransolver-1,024 (0.0406,
  73 GB) is 1.2% below ISLA's best (0.0411, 22 GB).
- **Depth.** ISLA at 6 layers is 16% worse than 12 (0.0479): depth is
  binding below 12. ISLA at 24 layers under 5e-4 is the plateau lane
  (0.77, the mean-field prediction; @sec-nb-routingsat-verdict), so the
  depth clause waits on the 2.5e-4 control. GeoTransolver at 24 layers
  gains 2.6% over 12 (0.0417 to 0.0406), within the 3% clause, so its
  depth reading is "within 3%" but at the edge, and it matches its
  1,024-wide lane's error at half the parameters.
- **Slices: null**, as predicted: 1,024 slices score 0.0409 against 0.0411
  at 256.
- **Transolver** gains 9% from 256 to 512 wide (0.0472 to 0.0429): the
  third architecture is also parameter-bound at 435 cars.

**What this says, and what it waits on.** Under the linear routing
parametrization and the learning-rate rule it forces, ISLA cannot use
width beyond 384 at this data size: the rate the wide models tolerate is
too low to train them in 500 epochs, or the wide relative frame does not
convert parameters into accuracy, and the ladder cannot tell which. The
baselines, with a gentler rate ceiling, keep converting parameters at
about 2.6% per doubling past ISLA's turnover, so at matched large parameter
counts GeoTransolver now leads. The efficiency statement of
@sec-nb-isocost-verdict stands unchanged (below 100 GB ISLA's frontier is
ahead; ISLA-384 at 22 GB sits 1.2% behind the best lane in either ladder
at 73 GB), but the scaling statement has a ceiling that is ISLA's own. The
discriminating experiment is running: ROUTE-NORM (@sec-nb-routenorm-prereg)
trains 768 wide at 5e-4 and 1e-3 under bounded routing; if it beats 0.0411,
the turnover was the rate ceiling and the ladder is re-run under cosine
routing, with GeoTransolver at 2,048 added so both are pushed as far. The
rate controls (24 and 48 layers at lower rates, 768 at 3.75e-4 and 5e-4,
384 at 7.5e-4 and 1e-3) complete the depth and width readings when they

## 2026-09-20 — Preregistration, TRAIN-AREA-DR: the DrivAerML twin of the training-law test; do GeoTransolver and Transolver depend on the training sampling law on the cars as they do on the wings, and does ISLA stay indifferent? {#sec-nb-trainarea-dr-prereg}

**Setting.** TRAIN-AREA (@sec-nb-trainarea-verdict) found on the 35-wing
rung that GeoTransolver and Transolver trained under an area-proportional
draw are 2.6x and 2.4x worse on the independent uniform draw than their
uniform-trained twins, while ISLA moves 1%. The wing meshes are the
extreme case (cell-area coefficient of variation 3.3); the two-dataset
rule asks whether the same dependence appears on the cars (coefficient of
variation 2.3), where the area law is closer to the uniform one and the
effect, if it is what it appears to be, should be present but smaller.

**Instrument** (`kernel/trainarea_dr_aga.sbatch`, manifest group `tadr`,
job names `isla.trainarea-dr.<lane>`): ISLA 192 (fused, 1e-3),
GeoTransolver 256 (3e-3) and Transolver 256 (3e-3) trained on 435
DrivAerML cars under `drivaer_ml_surface_area` (a 1,000,000-cell uniform
reader pool followed by an area-proportional Poisson draw with expected
100,000 cells and exact Horvitz-Thompson weights, replacing the uniform
subsample), 500 epochs, bf16, seeds 42 and 43: six lanes. The
uniform-trained twins are the ISO-COST 100,000-cell lanes (ISLA-192,
GeoTransolver-256, Transolver-256), which is why this twin runs at
100,000 cells (cells are flat, @sec-nb-isocost-interim). All twelve
checkpoints are scored by the consistency benchmark on the 48 validation
cars under the independent uniform, stratified and 10:1-biased draws at
100,000 cells from the benchmark's 320,000-cell pool
(`bench/bench_lanes_tadr.tsv`, 36 lanes); at 100,000 cells the pool is
3.2x the count, better than the 1.6x the wing benchmark had at 200,000.

**Bars, written before the runs** (independent uniform draw, two-seed
means, area-trained over uniform-trained per model).

- **Dependence reproduced**: GeoTransolver and Transolver at least 1.2x
  worse when trained on the area law, ISLA within 3% either way; the
  wing finding is then a property of the architectures, not of the wing
  meshes, and the chapter claim stands unqualified.
- **Dependence is a wing property**: both baselines within 1.1x; the
  claim is qualified to non-uniform meshes.
- **ISLA moves**: ISLA more than 5% either way; ISLA's indifference on
  the wings was not general and the statement is withdrawn.
- **Consistency**: ISLA's density factor (biased over uniform) within
  0.95 to 1.3 under both laws.

**Prediction.** Dependence reproduced at a smaller size: GeoTransolver
and Transolver 1.3 to 1.8x worse, ISLA within 2%. Probability 0.7.

## 2026-09-20 — Ruling and repair: no backward-compatibility machinery for ISLA's own pre-merge checkpoints; the passive decoder's local readout was not measure-rescale invariant (a 40% output change under a 137x weight rescale) and now is; `query_mass="source_total"` becomes the default {#sec-nb-no-legacy-compat}

**Ruling (Peter, 2026-09-20).** ISLA is unmerged, so nothing in it needs to
load checkpoints written under its former class name or with retired
research options; that machinery is technical debt and goes. Research is
the primary job; engineering serves it and stays a minority of the effort.
Removed in one pass: the former-name lookup hook on the class, the table
of retired constructor options with its former-default acceptance, the
checkpoint compat mapper and format version that had been added the same
morning, the tests for all of it (five in the checkpoint-utility tests, two
in the contract tests, two in the release tests), and the recipe docstring
sentence about the old name. The general checkpoint utility's
legacy-filename hook, already upstreamed, is untouched.

**A contract failure found on the way.** Three contract tests in the
global-input suite had been failing at HEAD before today's edits: the
passive interior decoder (`query_independent=True`) was not invariant to a
uniform rescale of the measure weights. Measured on a 32-wide, 2-layer
model in float64: a 137x rescale moved the passive output by **1.26**
against an output scale of 3.0, while the boundary-only path and both
query-token conventions moved by 1e-15. The cause was the local Gaussian
readout's legacy form, which multiplied raw weights into the kernel and
clamped the kernel mass at ``eps``; for queries far from every source the
clamp took over and the readout scaled with the absolute weights. That form
had been kept, by its own comment, "so trained passive checkpoints
reproduce". Under the ruling it is deleted: the readout is now the
softmax-over-sources form with logits ``-d^2/rho^2 + log w`` everywhere,
which is exactly invariant to the weights' scale and well defined at any
distance. The three tests pass without changes to their tolerances (1e-9).
The passive decoder is not the interior reference configuration (that is
`query_tokens=True`; the support-token variant already used the log-space
form), so no standing result changes; the golden output for the passive
configuration in the release tests was regenerated.

**Default change.** `query_mass` defaults to `"source_total"` (the
interior and support tokens share a learned fraction of the total source
measure, invariant to how the measure is represented); `"geometric_mean"`
stays available as the refinement-dependent option and is no longer the
default. The RATE-VOL interior lanes trained under `"geometric_mean"` (the
default at launch) and their row will say so; the interior control at
`"source_total"` is queued for when the rate settles.

**Still in the release-readiness set** (kept because they test current
behavior, not history): constructor-attribute, golden-output and
save/`from_checkpoint` round-trip tests, the up-front shape validation in
`forward`, the measure-weight dtype cast, and the once-per-resolution
kernel application. 128 ISLA and checkpoint tests pass.

## 2026-09-20 — Interim, TRAIN-AREA: all six area-draw lanes trained; scored on the area draw itself ISLA's wing deficit is 20% to GeoTransolver and 15% to Transolver against 27% on the uniform draw, a cross-draw reading that the benchmark on the independent uniform draw must confirm {#sec-nb-trainarea-interim}

**Setting.** TRAIN-AREA (@sec-nb-trainarea-prereg) trains ISLA,
GeoTransolver and Transolver on the 35-wing rung with an area-proportional
Poisson draw of 200,000 expected cells (exact Horvitz-Thompson weights) in
place of the uniform-over-cells draw, to test whether the 27% wing deficit
is the variance of the measure weights ISLA reads. All six lanes finished
their 500 epochs and were scored by the fleet pump in float32 on the
dataset's own validation draw, which for these lanes is also the area
draw. The preregistered readout is different: the consistency benchmark's
independent uniform-over-cells draw, area draw and 10:1-biased draw on the
180 validation wings, so that every model is compared on the same points
as the uniform-draw lanes of @sec-nb-wingbench-verdict. Those benchmark
lanes (`bench/bench_lanes_wing200k_area.tsv`, 18 lanes) are prepared; the
numbers below are the pump's and are not the verdict.

**What we saw (area-draw validation, pressure relative L2, seeds 42 /
43).** ISLA 0.1518 / 0.1425, mean **0.1472**; GeoTransolver 0.1114 /
0.1234, mean **0.1174**; Transolver 0.1263 / 0.1253, mean **0.1258**.
Ratios GeoTransolver over ISLA **0.798** and Transolver over ISLA
**0.855**, against 0.732 and 0.734 for the uniform-draw lanes scored on
the uniform draw (@sec-nb-p200k-wings-35). Read model by model against
the uniform-draw lanes: ISLA moved from 0.1500 to 0.1472 (2% lower),
GeoTransolver from 0.1098 to 0.1174 (7% higher), Transolver from 0.1101
to 0.1258 (14% higher). ISLA's two seeds now differ by 6% where they
differed by 0.5% under the uniform draw.

**Why this is not yet a reading against the bars.** The two columns are
scored on different point sets: the area draw concentrates validation
points on large cells, so the relative L2 weights the coarse regions of
the wing more heavily than the uniform draw does, and a model can move
between the columns without its function changing. The bars are written
for the independent uniform draw precisely to remove that. What can be
said now: (1) the direction is the preregistered one, ISLA down and both
baselines up, so the "sampler effect, not mechanism" clause (all three
improve) is unlikely; (2) the size of ISLA's move on its own draw (2%) is
below the 5% the mechanism clause requires, so unless the uniform-draw
benchmark shows a larger gain the likely verdict is the null, with the
baselines' losses under the area draw as a separate finding about the
training law; (3) the baselines' 7% and 14% rises under the area draw
would, if they hold on the independent draw, say the uniform-over-cells
law is the one GeoTransolver and Transolver are tuned for, which is
itself a statement about discretization dependence worth a row.

**What's next.** Launch the 18 benchmark lanes (three draws, six runs),
reduce with the WING-BENCH machinery, and write the verdict against the
preregistered clauses including the density-factor bound (1.05 to 1.3).

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, TRAIN-AREA: null for the weight-variance mechanism (ISLA gains 1.2% on the independent draw), and a new finding: ISLA's trained function does not depend on the training sampling law (1% change) while GeoTransolver's and Transolver's degrade 2.6x and 2.4x when trained on the area draw and scored on the uniform one {#sec-nb-trainarea-verdict}

**Setting.** TRAIN-AREA (@sec-nb-trainarea-prereg) asked whether the 27%
wing deficit at 35 cases is the variance of the measure weights ISLA
reads: train on an area-proportional Poisson draw (exact Horvitz-Thompson
weights, nearly uniform), and the deficit should shrink if it is. The
instrument is the consistency benchmark: every run, trained under the
uniform-over-cells law (the WING-BENCH-200K lanes) or under the area law
(the six new lanes), is scored in float32 on the 180 validation wings
under the same three independent draws at 200,000 cells: uniform over
cells, stratified, and 10:1 front/back biased. Artifact
`results/trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json`; reduction
`results/trainarea_reduce_2026-09-20.py`; 18 benchmark lanes
`bench/bench_lanes_wing200k_area.tsv`, array 799857.

**What we saw** (pressure relative L2, two-seed means; per-seed values
in the artifact).

| model | training law | uniform draw | stratified draw | 10:1-biased draw | density factor (biased ÷ uniform) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA | uniform over cells | 0.1502 | 0.1497 | 0.1498 | 1.00 |
| ISLA | area-proportional | **0.1483** | 0.1480 | 0.1481 | 1.00 |
| GeoTransolver (3e-3) | uniform over cells | 0.1098 | 0.1098 | 0.2716 | 2.47 |
| GeoTransolver (3e-3) | area-proportional | **0.2842** | 0.2842 | 0.3779 | 1.33 |
| Transolver | uniform over cells | 0.1102 | 0.1101 | 0.3080 | 2.80 |
| Transolver | area-proportional | **0.2621** | 0.2621 | 0.2968 | 1.13 |

: TRAIN-AREA: the same six model-and-seed pairs under two training laws, scored under three inference draws on the same 180 wings. {#tbl-trainarea}

**Verdict against the bars.** ISLA under the area law improves on the
independent uniform draw by **1.2%** (0.1502 to 0.1483; seeds 0.1531 and
0.1436 against 0.1507 and 0.1497, so the seed spread, 6%, exceeds the
move). The mechanism clause needed 5%: **null**. The wing deficit is not
the variance of the measure weights. Weight variance was the last
candidate from the 10,000-cell ablations, and the 12% the weights-off
ablation bought (@sec-nb-a35-verdict) is therefore not "less variable
weights"; the candidate now standing is the trained function's response
to the wing geometry itself, the slice-attention form on a multi-element
surface (@sec-nb-p200k-wings-35 lists what has been excluded). The
consistency clause asked ISLA's density factor to stay within 1.05 to 1.3:
it is **1.00**, as it already was under the uniform law
(@sec-nb-wingbench-verdict, 1.00), so the clause's lower edge was
miscalibrated against a factor the program had already measured; the
thing it guarded against, a rise above 1.5, did not happen.

**The finding the instrument produced instead.** GeoTransolver and
Transolver trained on the area draw and scored on the uniform draw are
**2.6x and 2.4x worse** than their uniform-trained twins (0.2842 against
0.1098; 0.2621 against 0.1102), on both seeds, and the same on the
stratified draw. Their trained functions encode the sampling law they were
trained under; move the law and the function moves. ISLA's does not: 0.1483
against 0.1502 on the uniform draw, 0.1480 against 0.1497 stratified,
0.1481 against 0.1498 biased. Read with WING-BENCH-200K, this closes the
second half of the discretization statement: at inference, changing the
draw moves GeoTransolver 2.5x and ISLA 1.00x; in training, changing the
law moves GeoTransolver 2.6x and ISLA 1.01x. The area-trained baselines
are also less draw-sensitive at inference (density factors 1.33 and 1.13
against 2.47 and 2.80), which is the expected face of the same
dependence: their function is now tuned to the area law, so the biased
draw, which is closer to it than the uniform draw is, costs them less.
Under the area training law, ISLA leads GeoTransolver and Transolver by
**1.92x and 1.77x** on the uniform draw; under the uniform law it trails
them by 27%.

**What this changes.** (1) The wing-deficit ledger: weight variance is
closed; the remaining candidate is architectural and is the next study's
subject. (2) The chapter statement on training-law dependence
(@sec-consistency-bench, chapter 6) gains a training-side table: the
baselines' accuracy on the mesher's own draw is conditional on having
been trained on that draw. (3) The recommendation stands as before: the
uniform-over-cells law is the recipe default for every model; ISLA is the
only one of the three for which the choice does not matter, and that is
stated as a pro of the architecture, not as a reason to change the
baselines' training (@sec-nb-geokernel-auto's companion ruling on
released baselines applies).

## 2026-09-19 — Preregistration, CAP-435: how far do width and depth carry at 435 cars? ISLA to 1,536 wide and 48 deep, GeoTransolver to 1,024 wide and 24 deep, Transolver to 512, all at 100,000 cells {#sec-nb-cap435-prereg}

**Setting.** The ISO-COST interim (@sec-nb-isocost-interim) found that at
435 DrivAerML cars the cells axis is flat between 100,000 and 200,000
cells for every model while doubling width buys about 7% for ISLA (192 to
384) and GeoTransolver (256 to 512) alike. The single-case capacity study
(CAP, @sec-nb-cap-verdict) had found the same ordering at one car: width
carries, depth, slices and MLP ratio do not. Peter asked (2026-09-19)
how far width can be pushed and whether depth is worth revisiting now that
the data are abundant. Both models are currently parameter-bound at this
data size, so the question is where each model's width curve turns over,
whether the two curves cross, and whether depth or slice count offers a
cheaper route than width.

**Instrument** (`kernel/cap435_aga.sbatch`, 22 lanes, manifest group
`cap`, job names `isla.cap435.<lane>`; 435 cars, 100,000 cells per case in
training (the scaling-study budget: cells are flat here and 100,000 is the
cheapest point that shows it), 500 epochs, bf16, seeds 42 and 43, float32
scoring at the 200,000-cell reporting protocol through the fleet pump;
per-lane step time and peak memory from the training log as in ISO-COST):

| axis | model | configuration | parameters | learning rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| width | ISLA | 512 wide, 12 layers | 60.3M | 3.75e-4 (width rule) |
| width | ISLA | 1,024 wide | 238M | 1.875e-4 |
| width | ISLA | 1,536 wide | 532M | 1.25e-4 |
| depth | ISLA | 384 wide, 6 layers | 17.3M | 5e-4 |
| depth | ISLA | 384 wide, 24 layers | 68.3M | 5e-4 |
| depth | ISLA | 384 wide, 48 layers | 136M | 5e-4 |
| slices | ISLA | 384 wide, 1,024 slices | 38.1M | 5e-4 |
| width | GeoTransolver | 1,024 wide, 12 layers | 143M | 3e-3 and 1e-3 (better kept) |
| depth | GeoTransolver | 512 wide, 24 layers | 71.1M | 3e-3 |
| width | Transolver | 512 wide, 8 layers | 23.9M | 3e-3 |

Together with the ISO-COST and ISO-MATCH lanes already running (ISLA 192,
384 and 768 wide at 100,000 cells; GeoTransolver 256 and 512), this gives
ISLA a five-point width ladder (192, 384, 512, 768, 1,024, 1,536: six
points) spanning 8.9M to 532M parameters and GeoTransolver a three-point
ladder (9.0M, 35.8M, 143M). The learning rate for ISLA follows the width
rule (@sec-nb-relframe-divergence-mechanism); depth and slice changes keep
the rate of their width. No rate search is run for the depth lanes, and
that is a stated risk, not a control.

**Bars, written before the runs.** Readout is the seed-mean float32
pressure relative L2 on the 48 validation cars; "improves" means a lower
mean by at least the stated fraction.

- **Width turnover (ISLA).** Along 192, 384, 512, 768, 1,024, 1,536 the
  first doubling-equivalent step whose gain is below 1% (or negative) marks
  the turnover. Prediction: 384 to 768 gains 3 to 5%, 768 to 1,536 gains
  under 2%; turnover between 768 and 1,536. If 1,536 still improves on
  1,024 by 2% or more, the ladder is extended.
- **Width turnover (GeoTransolver).** 512 to 1,024 at its better rate.
  Prediction: 2 to 4% gain. If 1,024 gains 3% or more, a 2,048 lane is
  added so the baseline is pushed as far as ISLA.
- **Iso-parameter pairs.** ISLA-768 (134M) against GeoTransolver-1,024
  (143M), and ISLA-384 (34.3M) against GeoTransolver-512 (35.8M, already
  0.0417 against 0.0411): parity if within 3%, otherwise lead or deficit
  named by model. Prediction: ISLA leads both pairs by 1 to 4%.
- **Depth (ISLA).** 24 layers at width 384 improves on 12 by 3% or more:
  depth carries at 435 cars (reversing CAP's single-case null); within
  ±3%: depth null again. 6 layers within 3% of 12: depth is not binding
  at all and the recipe could halve it. 48 layers: reported for the
  turnover and for the training signature (a rise to the mean-field
  plateau at 48 layers marks a depth edge for the width rule, mechanism to
  be measured, not assumed). Prediction: 24 layers within 2% (null), 6
  layers 2 to 4% worse, 48 layers no better than 24.
- **Depth (GeoTransolver).** 24 layers at 512 against 12: same 3% clause.
  Prediction: within 2%.
- **Slices.** ISLA 1,024 slices at 384 within 2% of 256 slices: slices
  null at 435 cars (matching CAP). Prediction: null.
- **Cost.** Every lane's peak memory and step time join the ISO-COST
  frontiers; a lane that does not fit a GB300 is recorded as such (data,
  not failure). Prediction: ISLA-1,536 at 100,000 cells fits (about 80 to
  100 GB); GeoTransolver-1,024 about 100 GB.
- **Training signature.** Every lane is accepted only if its validation
  loss stays below 0.01 after epoch 20 on both seeds; a lane that rises to
  the mean-field plateau is reported with the epoch and value and excluded
  from the ladder with a rate control queued at half its rate.

**Why it matters.** If width keeps paying for ISLA past 768 while
GeoTransolver turns over at 1,024, the equal-budget chapter gains a
scaling statement rather than a point comparison; if both turn over
together, the story is that ISLA reaches the same ceiling at a third of
the memory. Depth is the cheap alternative: if 24 layers at 384 (68M) beat
768 wide (134M), the recommendation for spending parameters changes.

**Addendum, launch acceptance (2026-09-20, 00:20 EDT; 22 lanes at epochs 18
to 24).** Every lane is alive with no traceback and no out-of-memory
event; peak memory 12 GB (384 wide, 6 layers) to 95 GB (GeoTransolver
512 wide, 24 layers), 78 GB for ISLA 1,536 wide and 73 GB for
GeoTransolver 1,024 wide, so every configuration fits a GB300. Eighteen
lanes have validation loss 0.0016 to 0.0022 at epoch about 23, on the
trajectory of their ISO-COST siblings. **The four deep ISLA lanes at 5e-4
are on the mean-field plateau.** At 24 layers both seeds descended
normally to 0.0086 (seed 42, epoch 9) and 0.0050 (seed 43, epoch 10), then
rose over eight epochs, with spikes, to 0.063 and 0.061 by epoch 22 and
stayed there; at 48 layers neither seed left the plateau (validation
loss 0.055 to 0.064 from epoch 0, seed 42 spiking to 0.27 at epoch 1).
The training loss follows the validation loss step for step, so this is
not overfitting; it is the same descend-then-rise signature that
RFDIV measured at width 512 under 1e-3 and that the interior
configuration showed at 200,000 cells under 1e-3, appearing here when
depth is doubled at a rate the 12-layer network trains cleanly at. The
mechanism (RFDIV: routing saturation) is inferred from the signature, not
measured on these runs. Under the preregistered training-signature
clause the four lanes are excluded from the depth ladder and rate
controls are prepared as lanes 22 to 27 of the launcher (job names
`isla.cap435.isla-w384-d24-lr2.5e-4-c100k-s42` and siblings): 24 layers
at 2.5e-4, 48 layers at 2.5e-4 and at 1.25e-4, two seeds each; their
submission is pending (`kernel/cap435_launch.sh 22 27`). The
one-car CAP study trained 24 layers without this signature at 10,000
cells; whether the rate that depth tolerates scales like 1/depth or
1/√depth is what the two 48-layer controls discriminate (1/depth predicts
1.25e-4 clean and 2.5e-4 on the plateau; 1/√depth predicts both clean).

**Addendum, width rate controls added (2026-09-20, 08:30 EDT; lanes 28
to 35).** The ISO-COST second reading (@sec-nb-isocost-interim) found a
5% seed split at widths 512 and 768 under the width rule that width 384
does not show. Eight lanes discriminate the two open explanations: ISLA
768 wide at 100,000 cells under 5e-4 (twice the rule) and 3.75e-4 (1.5x),
and ISLA 384 wide at 100,000 cells under 7.5e-4 and 1e-3 (1.5x and 2x its
rule rate, the latter the 192-wide ceiling), two seeds each.
Preregistered reading: if 768 at a higher rate brings seed 42 to within
1% of seed 43 without a plateau visit, the rule under-trains wide lanes
in 500 epochs and the rule becomes a floor, not a prescription; if seed
42 stays 5% behind at every clean rate, the split is a property of the
wide relative frame's optimization and the width ladder is reported with
seed ranges rather than means. If 384 at 7.5e-4 or 1e-3 improves on its
0.0411 by 2% or more, the best ISLA configuration in the grid moves and
the ISO-MATCH lead is restated; a plateau visit at 1e-3 marks the rate
edge at 384 (RFDIV placed it at 512). The depth controls (lanes 22 to 27)
were submitted at the same time.

**Addendum, acceptance of the rate controls (2026-09-20, 08:15 EDT; epochs
21 to 25).** All fourteen lanes are alive with no traceback. Validation
losses at the reading, seeds 42 / 43: 24 layers at 2.5e-4 **0.0018 /
0.0020** (clean; the 5e-4 pair was at 0.061 / 0.063 by epoch 22); 48
layers at 2.5e-4 **0.057 / 0.061** (on the plateau); 48 layers at 1.25e-4
**0.0035 / 0.0122** (below the plateau, seed 43 elevated and watched).
Read against the preregistered discriminator: the rate depth tolerates
falls with depth like 1/depth (12 layers 5e-4, 24 layers 2.5e-4, 48
layers 1.25e-4), not like 1/√depth, which predicted 2.5e-4 clean at 48
layers. The width controls: ISLA-768 at 5e-4 reads 0.0046 / 0.0022 and at
3.75e-4 0.0019 / 0.0019, against 0.0018 to 0.0022 for the 2.5e-4 lanes at
the same epoch; ISLA-384 at 7.5e-4 reads 0.0024 / 0.0021 and at 1e-3
0.0031 / 0.0045, against 0.002 at 5e-4. Both doubled-rate lanes (768 at
5e-4 seed 42, 384 at 1e-3) sit two times higher than their rule-rate
siblings at epoch 24 without having risen to the plateau; whether they
recover, plateau, or finish worse is the reading that matters, at epoch
500. SCALE-HL (twelve lanes, epoch 2, validation loss 0.062 to 0.082, the
usual wing start) and TRAIN-AREA-DR (six lanes, epoch about 20,
validation loss 0.0022 to 0.0031, on the uniform-law lanes' trajectory)
are accepted as well; the DrivAerML area draw runs from a 1,000,000-cell
pool at 15.6 GB peak memory for ISLA.

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, RATE-VOL: the DrivAerML interior row at the 200,000-cell protocol is written with ISLA at 5e-4; ISLA leads GeoTransolver-volume on velocity by 42% (was 37%), trails on pressure by 13% (was 7%) and on eddy viscosity by 2% (was 14%) {#sec-nb-ratevol-verdict}

**Setting.** The boundary-to-interior task on DrivAerML asks a model to
predict pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity at points inside the flow
domain from the car's surface mesh. ISLA (the architecture under study)
admits the interior query points as interacting tokens; GeoTransolver's
volume configuration is the comparator. The fleet that moves every
evidence lane from the exploration budget of 10,000 sampled cells to the
reporting protocol of 200,000 (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg) found that
ISLA's interior configuration, with 200,000 boundary cells and 200,000
interior queries per car, rose to the mean-field loss plateau at learning
rate 1e-3 on both seeds, while every surface lane at that rate trained
normally (@sec-nb-ratevol-prereg). RATE-VOL retrained the interior
configuration at 5e-4 and 3e-4 with the preregistered rule that the row is
written at the higher rate that never visits the plateau.

**What we saw.** Both rates are clean: no validation loss above 0.01 after
epoch 20 on any of the four lanes through their 500 epochs (the 1e-3
lanes had risen to 0.069 and 0.073). Scored in float32 on the 48
validation cars at 200,000 interior queries, seed means (seeds in
parentheses):

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ISLA, 1e-3 (mean-field plateau) | 0.730 (0.727 / 0.732) | 0.730 (0.720 / 0.741) | 0.968 (0.961 / 0.976) |
| **ISLA, 5e-4 (the row)** | **0.0546** (0.0568 / 0.0523) | **0.0712** (0.0719 / 0.0706) | **0.0857** (0.0859 / 0.0854) |
| ISLA, 3e-4 (rate control) | 0.0579 (0.0591 / 0.0566) | 0.0769 (0.0777 / 0.0762) | 0.0878 (0.0883 / 0.0874) |
| GeoTransolver-volume, unit direction | 0.0477 (0.0478 / 0.0476) | 0.1008 (0.1003 / 0.1013) | 0.0843 (0.0843 / 0.0843) |

: RATE-VOL: interior relative L2 error on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, 200,000 interior queries per car, float32, two seeds. Data: results/ratevol_reduction_2026-09-20.json (reduction results/ratevol_reduce_2026-09-20.py).

The ratios GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA at 5e-4 are **0.874 on pressure,
1.416 on velocity and 0.984 on eddy viscosity**, against 0.933, 1.368 and
0.875 at the 10,000-query exploration budget
(results/relint2_reduction_2026-09-14.json). Against the preregistered
bars: **velocity survives** (a 3.5% change of ratio, within the 5% bar);
**pressure swings 6.3% toward GeoTransolver-volume**, just past the 5% bar,
and is reported as a budget effect with a caveat: ISLA's two pressure
seeds are 8% apart (0.0568 and 0.0523), the widest seed spread on this
board, so the swing is inside the seed range and a third seed would be
needed to call it. Eddy viscosity, not covered by a bar, moved most: ISLA
improved 15% (0.1005 to 0.0857) while GeoTransolver-volume improved 4%,
closing ISLA's 14% deficit to 2%. In absolute terms the twenty-fold
increase in boundary cells and queries moved ISLA by 1% on pressure, 9%
on velocity and 15% on eddy viscosity, and GeoTransolver-volume by 7%, 6%
and 4%. The 3e-4 rate control is 6%, 8% and 3% worse than 5e-4 on the
three fields, in the same direction on both seeds, so the row rate is the
better of the two clean rates and the interior configuration's ceiling
at 200,000 cells sits between 5e-4 and 1e-3.

**Why it matters.** The interior standing of the exploration budget
carries to the reporting protocol in its shape: ISLA ahead on velocity,
behind on pressure, and now level on eddy viscosity. Three qualifications
travel with the row. First, ISLA's interior configuration needs half the
surface configuration's learning rate at this token count; the rate
ceiling is the routing-saturation mechanism ROUTING-SAT measured on the
width and depth lanes (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict), inferred here from the
matching loss signature, not probed on these checkpoints. Second, these
lanes trained under the earlier `query_mass="geometric_mean"` passive
readout (the default is now `source_total`, @sec-nb-no-legacy-compat); the
decoder change is measure-rescale invariant by construction and does not
alter a trained checkpoint's evaluation, but a fresh interior pair under
the current default has not been trained. Third, this is one dataset: the
interior task has no wing twin yet, so the two-dataset rule
(recorded in @sec-nb-scalehl-prereg) leaves the interior standing
single-dataset.

**What's next.** The chapter 3 interior section carries the 200,000-query
row beside the 10,000-query one (@sec-interior-results). The
routing probe extends to the four interior checkpoints when the ROUTE-NORM
verdict lands (bar: the 1e-3 pair at one active slice per block, the 5e-4
pair with 4 or more). An interior pair under cosine routing at 1e-3 is the
natural follow-on if ROUTE-NORM removes the ceiling on the surface lanes.

## 2026-09-20 — Interim, PROTO-200K-FLEET fixed-angle wing rung: at 12° angle of attack and 200,000 cells ISLA reads 0.0300 against GeoTransolver 0.0220 and Transolver 0.0238 at 1e-3; the 3e-3 GeoTransolver control is still training {#sec-nb-fleet-single-aoa-interim}

**Setting.** The HiLiftAeroML fixed-angle rung trains on every wing at a
single angle of attack of 12° and validates on held-out wings at the same
angle, so it isolates geometry generalization from angle generalization.
At the 10,000-cell exploration budget this rung was one of the wing rungs
where ISLA trails the baselines (@sec-program-status).

**What we saw.** The fleet's fixed-angle lanes at 200,000 cells, float32,
seeds 42 / 43: ISLA 0.0302 / 0.0298 (mean 0.0300), GeoTransolver at 1e-3
0.0221 / 0.0218 (0.0220), Transolver at 1e-3 0.0235 / 0.0240 (0.0238).
GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA is 0.73 and Transolver ÷ ISLA is 0.79 at these
rates. GeoTransolver's 3e-3 pair, its better rate on the wing rungs, is
still training; the row is written when it lands, at GeoTransolver's
better rate, per the fleet preregistration. Reading: the fixed-angle rung
keeps the 35-case rung's picture (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.73 at both
budgets there, @tbl-hilift-ladder): the wing deficit is a property
of the trained functions, not of the sampling count. Data:
results/p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json.

## 2026-09-20 — Third readings and an extension: CAP-435's rate controls at epoch 400 leave 48 layers with no clean linear rate; ROUTE-NORM's cosine lanes are clean at epoch 230 at four times the rule rate; six lanes extend cosine routing to 24 and 48 layers and to the interior configuration {#sec-nb-routenorm-depth-prereg}

**Setting.** Two studies are running on the same question from different
sides. CAP-435 (@sec-nb-cap435-prereg) asks how far width and depth carry
ISLA at 435 DrivAerML cars and found that under the width learning-rate
rule (1e-3 × 192 / width) ISLA turns over at width 384 while GeoTransolver
keeps improving (@sec-nb-cap435-interim); its rate controls test whether
the rule under- or over-shoots. ROUTING-SAT (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict)
measured the failure at higher rates as total routing collapse (one active
slice per block, coincident anchors), and ROUTE-NORM
(@sec-nb-routenorm-prereg) tests whether bounding the routing logits with
cosine routing removes that ceiling.

**CAP-435 rate controls at epochs 387 to 424 (validation loss, seeds 42 /
43).** ISLA-384 at 1e-3: **0.059 / 0.052, both on the mean-field plateau**
(the rule rate 5e-4 finished at 0.0411). ISLA-384 at 7.5e-4: 0.043 /
0.0059, seed 42 on the plateau, seed 43 elevated three times above the
5e-4 lanes. ISLA-768 at 5e-4: 0.56 / 0.011, seed 42 on the plateau, seed
43 elevated; ISLA-768 at 3.75e-4: 0.00051 / 0.00050, clean and level with
the rule-rate 2.5e-4 lanes. Depth: 24 layers at 2.5e-4 clean (0.00049 /
0.00050; the 5e-4 pair had plateaued); **48 layers at 2.5e-4 diverged to
NaN on both seeds, and at 1.25e-4 both seeds are on the plateau (0.057 /
0.056)** after reading 0.0035 / 0.0122 at epoch 25. So under linear
routing the 48-layer configuration has no clean rate among those tried,
the rate ceiling falls at least as fast as 1/depth, and at width 384 the
rule rate is within a factor of 1.5 of the ceiling on one seed. The
width-rule verdict waits for the evaluations at epoch 500; nothing here
contradicts the interim reading that ISLA's turnover at 384 is a rate
ceiling, not a capacity limit.

**ROUTE-NORM at epochs 217 to 240 (validation loss, seeds 42 / 43).** Every
cosine lane on the cars is clean: 192 at 1e-3 0.00057 / 0.00057; 384 at
5e-4 0.00051 / 0.00050 and **at 1e-3 0.00054 / 0.00053** (the linear rate
that plateaus on both seeds); 768 at 2.5e-4 0.00048 / 0.00048, at 5e-4
0.00048 / 0.00050 and **at 1e-3 0.00056 / 0.00053**, four times the rule
rate and a rate at which linear 768 is on the plateau by epoch 90. The
ladder extension (1,024 and 1,536 wide at 5e-4 and 1e-3, GeoTransolver
2,048) is at epochs 13 to 57 with validation losses 0.0010 to 0.0041 on
normal trajectories; the wing lanes are at epoch 20. Cosine lanes at the
higher rates read 5% to 15% above the rule-rate lanes at this epoch, so
whether the removed ceiling buys accuracy is still the epoch-500 question.

**Extension, preregistered before launch (lanes 30 to 35 of
`kernel/routenorm_aga.sbatch`, manifest group rn, job names
`isla.routenorm.cos-*`).** Cosine routing is placed exactly where linear
routing had no clean rate:

- **24 layers, width 384, at 5e-4** (two seeds): the rate at which the
  linear 24-layer pair plateaued (0.77 in float32) and the rule rate for
  width 384. Prediction: clean; the 24-layer cosine lane is then compared
  with the linear 24-layer lane at 2.5e-4 when both are scored.
- **48 layers, width 384, at 2.5e-4** (two seeds): the rate at which
  linear routing diverged to NaN. Prediction: clean. If it plateaus or
  diverges, the depth failure has a second mechanism beyond routing
  saturation (the NaN, unlike the plateau, is not the ROUTING-SAT
  signature) and the 48-layer configuration is reported as untrainable in
  this recipe.
- **The interior configuration at 1e-3, 200,000 cells and queries** (two
  seeds): the rate at which the linear interior pair rose to the plateau
  (@sec-nb-ratevol-verdict). The lanes keep the RATE-VOL lanes' eager
  kernel and `geometric_mean` readout (overridden explicitly, because the
  snapshot's default is now `source_total`) so routing is the only change.
  Prediction: clean, with pressure within 5% of the 5e-4 linear row
  (0.0546) and velocity within 5% of 0.0712; a plateau visit falsifies the
  claim that routing saturation is the interior ceiling's mechanism.

Bars for "clean" are the studies' own: no validation loss above 0.01 after
epoch 20. Accuracy is read at epoch 500 in float32 through the fleet pump.
Cost: six lanes on one node each, about 20 to 40 hours of chain time; the
48-layer lane is the most expensive at about 2.5 times the 12-layer cost.

**Addendum, acceptance of the extension (2026-09-20, 16:20 EDT; epochs 26
to 29).** All six lanes are alive, productive and without a traceback or

## 2026-09-20 — Fleet operations: the recipe keeps every checkpoint it writes; running lanes pruned to their newest three epochs and completed lanes to one (14.4 TB freed, quota 94.7 to 81.8 TB); a pruner now runs every 30 minutes {#sec-nb-fleet-ops-prune-2026-09-20}

**Setting.** After the morning's prune of completed runs
(@sec-nb-fleet-ops-quota-2026-09-20) the scratch project quota kept rising
by about 1 TB per hour with roughly 100 lanes training. A size survey of
the user directory located the whole footprint inside the agents task tree
(every other directory holds under 2 TB combined), and a measurement of the
running lanes' checkpoint directories found the cause: **the training
recipe writes a checkpoint pair (`checkpoint.0.<epoch>.pt` and
`<Model>.0.<epoch>.mdlus`, about 1 GB together at width 768) every
`save_interval` epochs and never removes an old one.** The morning prune
had removed only the `.mdlus` files of completed runs and had not touched
running lanes. A 768-wide CAP-435 lane at `save_interval=2` had accumulated
463 files and 243 GB by epoch 447; the 2,048-wide GeoTransolver lanes 200
GB each by epoch 46; the running lanes together held 5.5 TB.

**What was done.** A pruner (`tmp/prune_running.sh`, cluster side in
Python) keeps the newest three epochs of both files for every lane still
training (the chain resumes from the newest checkpoint and the pre-flight
of @sec-nb-fleet-ops-quota-2026-09-20 moves a truncated newest aside, so
three is one spare beyond the safe minimum) and the newest epoch only for
completed lanes; it never touches `norm_stats.pt` or anything outside the
checkpoint directories. Its first pass pruned 955 runs, removed 134,987
files and freed 14.4 TB; the project quota read 81.8 of 100 TB afterwards.
It now runs every 30 minutes in the background alongside the fleet
watcher. No lane was blocked or lost a checkpoint. A recipe-side fix
(rotation at save time) is the right long-term repair and belongs to the
engineering block, not to today's research time.

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, CAP-435 (linear routing): the width rule's rate is the best clean rate at every width and depth tested, so ISLA's turnover at 384 wide (0.0411) is a property of linear routing, not of under-training; depth 24 is null, 48 layers untrainable; GeoTransolver carries to 1,024 wide and 24 layers (0.0406) {#sec-nb-cap435-verdict}

**Setting.** CAP-435 (@sec-nb-cap435-prereg) asked how far width and depth
carry ISLA and GeoTransolver at 435 DrivAerML cars and 100,000 sampled
cells per car (a labeled scaling budget, not the 200,000-cell reporting
protocol), with ISLA's learning rate set by the width rule (1e-3 × 192 /
width, × 12 / layers). The interim (@sec-nb-cap435-interim) found ISLA at
its best at width 384 and worse at every larger width, while GeoTransolver
kept improving. The open alternative was that the rule under-trains wide
and deep lanes in 500 epochs; fourteen rate-control lanes tested it by
training the same configurations at higher rates. All are now scored in
float32 on the 48 validation cars (results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json,
reduction results/cap435_reduce_2026-09-20.py).

**What we saw (surface pressure, seed means, seeds in parentheses).**

| configuration | rate | error |
|---|---|---:|
| ISLA 384 wide, 12 layers | 1e-3 | 0.748 (0.773 / 0.723), mean-field plateau |
| | 7.5e-4 | 0.441 (0.704 / 0.177), both seeds degraded |
| | **5e-4 (rule)** | **0.0411** (0.0409 / 0.0413) |
| ISLA 768 wide, 12 layers | 5e-4 | 0.592 (0.943 / 0.240), both seeds degraded |
| | 3.75e-4 | 0.0428 (0.0430 / 0.0427) |
| | **2.5e-4 (rule)** | **0.0421** (0.0432 / 0.0410) |
| ISLA 384 wide, 24 layers | 5e-4 | 0.770 (0.773 / 0.767), plateau |
| | **2.5e-4 (rule)** | **0.0413** (0.0413 / 0.0413) |
| ISLA 384 wide, 48 layers | 5e-4, 2.5e-4 | NaN |
| | 1.25e-4 (rule) | plateau on both seeds (validation loss 0.056) after a clean start |
| GeoTransolver 1,024 wide | 1e-3 | 0.0406 (0.0409 / 0.0403) |
| GeoTransolver 512 wide, 24 layers | 3e-3 | 0.0406 (0.0402 / 0.0410) |

: CAP-435 rate controls and the best lanes, float32, 48 validation cars, 100,000 cells, 500 epochs. Data: results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json.

**Reading against the preregistered clauses.** The rule does not
under-train: at width 384 and at 24 layers the rule rate is the only clean
rate, and at 768 the one higher clean rate (3.75e-4) is 1.7% worse than the
rule rate. The 768-wide seed split (0.0432 against 0.0410 at 2.5e-4) is
not cured by the higher rate, which brings the seeds together at the worse
seed's level (0.0430 / 0.0427), so the split is a property of the wide
relative frame's optimization and the width ladder is reported with seed
ranges. The 7.5e-4 and 5e-4 controls both degrade: seed 43 at 384 wide
and 7.5e-4 scored 0.177, a partial version of the plateau signature
(ROUTING-SAT measured the full state at 1e-3), so the ceiling at 384 sits
between 5e-4 and 7.5e-4, within a factor of 1.5 of the rule rate. **Under
linear routing ISLA's width ladder is 0.0450 / 0.0411 / 0.0426 / 0.0421 /
0.0429 / 0.0452 at 192 / 384 / 512 / 768 / 1,024 / 1,536, its turnover at
384 is real, depth 24 is null (1.004×), 6 layers cost 16%, 1,024 slices are
null (0.995×), and 48 layers are untrainable in this recipe.** GeoTransolver
improves 6.7% from 256 to 512 wide and 2.6% more to 1,024, and 2.6% from
12 to 24 layers; at matched parameters GeoTransolver-1,024 leads ISLA-768
by 3.6% (143M against 134M), while GeoTransolver-512 and ISLA-384 are at
parity (1.014, 36M against 34M).

**Why it matters.** With linear routing, ISLA's capacity axes stop paying
at about 34M parameters on this task while GeoTransolver's continue to
143M; that is the one place in the program where GeoTransolver's
architecture is ahead of ISLA's, and the mechanism is the routing ceiling
measured by ROUTING-SAT, since every attempt to give the wider or deeper
lanes a higher rate meets the plateau. Whether bounding the routing logits
lifts this ceiling is exactly ROUTE-NORM's question: its cosine lanes at
384 and 768 wide train cleanly at 1e-3 (@sec-nb-routenorm-depth-prereg),
and its 1,024- and 1,536-wide lanes and its 24- and 48-layer lanes will say
whether the ladder then continues. This verdict therefore closes CAP-435
for linear routing and leaves the width and depth question for the cosine
form to ROUTE-NORM. Single dataset: the 510-wing twin of the width picture
is SCALE-HL (@sec-nb-scalehl-prereg), which reads at 100,000 cells at widths
192, 384 and 768.

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, PROTO-200K-FLEET fixed-angle wing rung: at 200,000 cells ISLA scores 0.0300 against GeoTransolver 0.0207 at its better rate (0.69×) and Transolver 0.0238 (0.79×); the ratios at 10,000 cells were 0.68 and 0.75, so the fixed-angle deficit is a property of the trained functions, not of the sampling count {#sec-nb-fleet-single-aoa-verdict}

**Setting.** The HiLiftAeroML fixed-angle rung trains on 126 wing
geometries at a single angle of attack of 12° and validates on 18 held-out
geometries at the same angle, isolating geometry generalization from angle
generalization. The fleet that moves every evidence lane to the 200,000-cell
reporting protocol (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg) writes each wing row at
GeoTransolver's better rate; on this rung the 3e-3 control finished last
(interim in @sec-nb-fleet-single-aoa-interim).

**What we saw (surface pressure, float32, seed means, seeds in
parentheses).** ISLA **0.0300** (0.0302 / 0.0298); GeoTransolver at 3e-3
**0.0207** (0.0206 / 0.0208) and at 1e-3 0.0220 (0.0221 / 0.0218);
Transolver at 3e-3 **0.0238** (0.0235 / 0.0240). GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA at
GeoTransolver's better rate is 0.69 and Transolver ÷ ISLA 0.79. At the
10,000-cell exploration budget the same rung read ISLA 0.0398 (three
seeds, 0.0363 / 0.0405 / 0.0427), GeoTransolver 0.0270 and Transolver
0.0298 (results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_2026-09-09.json,
results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json), ratios 0.68 and 0.75. Twenty
times the sampled cells improved every model by a similar fraction (ISLA
25%, GeoTransolver 23%, Transolver 20%) and moved the ratios by 0.01 and
0.04. On the other logged fields the ordering is the same: velocity 0.80,
wall shear 0.79, temperature 0.87, density 0.70 (GeoTransolver 3e-3 ÷
ISLA). Data: results/p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json.

**Why it matters.** This is the second wing rung to report at the
protocol, and it repeats the 35-case rung's reading
(@tbl-hilift-ladder): the wing deficit is not count noise and does
not shrink with denser sampling. The fixed-angle split removes the angle
axis, so what remains is generalization across wing geometry under a
mesher whose validation geometries recur in training
(@sec-data-efficiency), the mechanism the program points at. ISLA's
three-seed spread at 10,000 cells (16%) collapses to 1% at 200,000, so the
budget also removes ISLA's seed variance on this rung; the baselines'
spread was already small. The remaining wing rungs (105, 510 and 1,260
cases, the geometry ladders, the deflection test) report as their lanes
finish (@sec-program-status).

## 2026-09-20 — Verdict, TRAIN-AREA-DR: on the cars the training-law dependence is far larger than on the wings, not smaller: GeoTransolver and Transolver trained on the area law are 7.9x and 9.6x worse on the uniform draw, ISLA 8% worse; uniform-trained GeoTransolver and Transolver are 8.7x and 5.3x worse under the 10:1 biased draw, ISLA 7% {#sec-nb-trainarea-dr-verdict}

**Setting.** TRAIN-AREA (@sec-nb-trainarea-verdict) found on the 35-wing
rung that GeoTransolver and Transolver trained under an area-proportional
sampling law are 2.6x and 2.4x worse on the independent uniform draw than
their uniform-trained twins, while ISLA moves 1%. The two-dataset rule
required the DrivAerML twin (@sec-nb-trainarea-dr-prereg): ISLA-192,
GeoTransolver-256 and Transolver-256 trained on 435 cars under the area
law at an expected 100,000 cells (six lanes, `tadr`), with the ISO-COST
100,000-cell lanes as the uniform-trained twins, all twelve checkpoints
scored by the consistency benchmark on the 48 validation cars under the
independent uniform, stratified and 10:1-biased draws at 100,000 cells
from the 320,000-cell pool (36 benchmark lanes, job 805750). Float32, two
seeds. Reduction results/trainarea_dr_reduce_2026-09-20.py, artifact
results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json.

**What we saw (surface pressure, seed means; seeds in parentheses).**

| arm | uniform draw | stratified draw | 10:1 biased draw |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ISLA, trained uniform | 0.0458 (0.0450 / 0.0467) | 0.0450 | 0.0489 |
| ISLA, trained area | 0.0496 (0.0491 / 0.0501) | 0.0473 | 0.0601 |
| GeoTransolver, trained uniform | 0.0448 (0.0444 / 0.0452) | 0.0445 | 0.391 (0.354 / 0.428) |
| GeoTransolver, trained area | 0.355 (0.304 / 0.406) | 0.356 | 0.464 |
| Transolver, trained uniform | 0.0473 (0.0472 / 0.0474) | 0.0469 | 0.252 (0.159 / 0.345) |
| Transolver, trained area | 0.454 (0.448 / 0.460) | 0.456 | 0.536 |

: TRAIN-AREA-DR: 48 DrivAerML validation cars, 100,000 cells per draw, float32, two seeds. Data: results/trainarea_dr_reduction_2026-09-20.json.

Area-trained over uniform-trained on the uniform draw: **ISLA 1.08,
GeoTransolver 7.9, Transolver 9.6.** Against the preregistered clauses the
baselines' dependence is reproduced with a factor of thirty to spare
(bar: 1.2x), and **ISLA's clause fires**: it moves 8%, past the 3% "within"
bar and the 5% "ISLA moves" bar, so the wing statement "ISLA's trained
function does not depend on the training sampling law" is not general and
is restated as "depends weakly (8% on the cars, 1% on the wings) where the
baselines' depend by factors of 2.4 to 9.6". The prereg's prediction
(dependence reproduced at a *smaller* size on the cars, 1.3 to 1.8x) was
wrong in direction: the cars, with the smaller cell-area coefficient of
variation (2.3 against 3.3), show the larger dependence. The same table
carries the inference-side statement at 100,000 cells: under the 10:1
biased draw the uniform-trained GeoTransolver is 8.7x its uniform-draw
error (0.391 against 0.0448) and Transolver 5.3x (0.252 against 0.0473),
against ISLA's 1.07 (0.0489 against 0.0458); at 40,000 cells the same
checkpoints' predecessors read about 1.2 for ISLA and the baselines'
factors were of the same order (@sec-consistency-bench). Under the area
law ISLA's density factor is 1.21, inside the 0.95 to 1.3 consistency bar;
under the uniform law 1.07. The stratified draw changes nothing for any
arm (within 2% of the uniform draw for the baselines, 2 to 5% better for
ISLA), which is the count-noise term.

**Why it matters.** Two datasets now say the same thing about the
baselines: **a GeoTransolver or Transolver checkpoint is accurate on the
draw it was trained on and on no other**, and the cars show it at a
severity (0.36 to 0.45, close to the error of predicting the mean field)
that would make the trained model unusable on a mesh from a different
generator. ISLA's error under the same swaps stays within 8% of its native
value on both datasets. The mechanism the book states (the baselines' slice
aggregates are point averages that inherit the sampling pattern, ISLA's
are measure-weighted integrals that do not, @sec-de-limits) predicts the
direction; the size difference between the datasets is not explained by
the cell-area spread alone and is an open question. The one honest
qualification is ISLA's own 8%: the area draw from a 1,000,000-cell pool at
an expected 100,000 cells has a wider weight spread on the cars than the
wings' 200,000-cell draw, and a part of ISLA's 8% may be that quadrature
noise (its stratified-draw error under the area law is 0.0473, 5% above
the uniform-trained 0.0450, so half of the 8% survives the draw's own
variance). The chapter callout (@sec-consistency-bench) is rewritten with
both datasets. Why the dependence is larger on the cars than the wings is
the next question; a cheap discriminator is the same swap on the DrivAerML
interior task, where the sampling law of the interior queries can be
varied independently of the surface's.

## 2026-09-20 — Ruling and repair: the centered frame, the similarity gauge and the constant reference length are removed from ISLA; the class has one frame, origin-free, with the RMS pairwise distance or the total measure as its length unit {#sec-nb-frame-cleanup}

**Setting.** Until today ISLA's constructor carried three frame options
beside the reference configuration: `frame_mode="centered"` (a frame
centered on the plain mean of the sampled points), `similarity_gauge=True`
(the same frame with a measure-weighted centroid and RMS radius) and
`scale_mode="reference_length"` with `reference_length` (a constant length
unit per dataset). All three were the program's configurations at some
point between July and 2026-09-10 and every one of them was measured
against the origin-free frame (the density probe, SG-REF, CORNER-WLR,
CG-WLR); none is used by any live lane, the book reports them only in
collapsed diagnostic notes, and their code paths (a second seed layout,
two extra relational invariants, a centroid branch in the forward pass, a
conditional head frame) were a third of the frame logic. Peter's ruling
this evening: fold them out entirely.

**What was removed.** Constructor parameters `frame_mode`,
`similarity_gauge` and `reference_length`, and the `"reference_length"`
value of `scale_mode`; attributes `frame_mode`, `relative_frame`,
`similarity_gauge`, `reference_length`; the `relative` argument of the
relational-invariant helpers and the `relative_frame` argument of the slice
and read blocks (the geometry width is 5 + K, the seed width K + boundary
scalars + global scalars); the centroid branch and the seed features
$|r|, \log|r|, \hat r \cdot \hat g_k, \hat r \cdot \hat n$ of the forward
pass; the conditional around the head frame. The recipe config
`isla_surface_constant_gauge.yaml` is deleted and `isla_volume_support.yaml`
no longer pins the similarity gauge (its support-token lanes were trained
under it and would need a re-run under the current frame before any
number from that config is quoted again). The Triton kernel keeps its
`RELATIVE` compile-time flag, always set; that branch is the one piece of
dead code left, inside a kernel that is not worth re-validating for it.
The default configuration's arithmetic is unchanged: the committed golden
outputs and reference checkpoint of the release tests still match, and
rigid-motion invariance of the scalar head holds to $5 \times 10^{-7}$ in
float32 across the surface, query-independent, query-token, total-measure,
cosine-routing and no-global-vector modes after the change.

**Consequences.** Checkpoints trained under the removed options no longer
load (ISLA keeps no compatibility shims by the 2026-09-20 ruling); the
measurements made with them stay on file in the results artifacts and the
book's diagnostic notes, labeled as measurements of a removed variant.
Chapters 2 and 9 and the recipe README now describe one frame. The tests
that existed only to exercise the removed branches are deleted; tests of
contracts that still hold (rigid-motion invariance, measure-weight scale
invariance, total-measure scale equivariance, query independence, kernel
agreement, global inputs) are kept and constructed through the current API
(the list is in the addendum below).

**Addendum, the test suite after the cleanup (2026-09-20, 22:10 EDT).** 92
tests pass in the six ISLA test files on CPU and CUDA (fused kernel and
`torch.compile` paths included), none skipped. Removed as tests of the
removed branches: the two similarity-gauge scale-equivariance tests (their
contract is now `test_geometric_scale_equivariance`, four cases over both
length units with and without the passive decoder), the centered
parametrizations of the global-input layout tests, the eight-invariant
fused-kernel case, the centered contrast inside the frame-contract and
sampling-consistency tests, and the `ValueError` checks for option
combinations that no longer exist; `test_frame_contracts` now asserts that
`scale_mode="reference_length"` is refused. Rewritten to the current
constructor: every test that carried the centered defaults only as
boilerplate. One consequence surfaced exactly as the ruling predicts: the
committed reference checkpoint `isla_default_v1.mdlus`, saved before the
cleanup, stored `reference_length` among its constructor arguments and no
longer loaded; it was regenerated through the test's own seeded creation
path, and the committed golden output it must reproduce still matches on
CPU and CUDA, which is the bitwise check that the default arithmetic did not
move. Every ISLA checkpoint written before this cleanup (all cluster lanes
included) fails to load in the current class; their float32 evaluations were
made under the snapshots that trained them and stand.

## 2026-09-20 — Interim verdict, ROUTE-NORM on the cars: cosine routing removes the rate ceiling (every lane clean at epoch 500, including 768 wide at 1e-3, four times the rule rate) at neutral accuracy at the rule rates; cosine 768 at 5e-4 scores 0.0409 with the seed split closed but does not beat 384's 0.0411, so width past 384 still does not pay {#sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict}

**Setting.** ROUTE-NORM (@sec-nb-routenorm-prereg) tests whether bounding
the point-to-slice routing logits (cosine routing at a fixed temperature)
removes the learning-rate ceiling that ROUTING-SAT measured as total
routing collapse (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict) and that CAP-435 showed
capping ISLA's width ladder at 384 (@sec-nb-cap435-verdict). The twelve
DrivAerML lanes (cosine at 192, 384 and 768 wide, at the rule rate and at
the rates that collapse linear routing, two seeds, 100,000 cells) have
finished their 500 epochs and are scored in float32 at the 200,000-cell
protocol (results/routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json, reduction
results/routenorm_reduce_2026-09-20.py). A first pass of the evaluation
pump ran them under the wrong code snapshot and failed at construction;
the pump now selects the snapshot per lane (@sec-nb-fleet-ops-prune-2026-09-20
is the fleet-ops record of the day; the fix is noted there in spirit and
in the pump script). The wing lanes and the width, depth and interior
extensions are still training, so this verdict is interim under the
two-dataset rule.

**What we saw (surface pressure, seed means; seeds in parentheses; the
linear-routing value at the same width and rate from CAP-435 for
comparison).**

| width | rate | cosine | linear | reading |
|--:|--:|---:|---:|---|
| 192 | 1e-3 (rule) | 0.0449 (0.0452 / 0.0446) | 0.0450 | neutral, 0.998 |
| 384 | 5e-4 (rule) | 0.0413 (0.0413 / 0.0413) | 0.0411 | neutral, 1.005 |
| 384 | 1e-3 | 0.0430 (0.0425 / 0.0434) | 0.748 (plateau) | **collapse removed**; 4% worse than the rule rate |
| 768 | 2.5e-4 (rule) | 0.0430 (0.0431 / 0.0428) | 0.0421 (0.0432 / 0.0410) | within 2%, 1.020 |
| 768 | 5e-4 | **0.0409** (0.0410 / 0.0408) | 0.592 (plateau) | **collapse removed**; best cosine lane; seeds 0.6% apart |
| 768 | 1e-3 | 0.0437 (0.0460 / 0.0415) | (linear collapses already at 5e-4) | clean at four times the rule rate; seed split 11% |

: ROUTE-NORM, DrivAerML 435 cars, 100,000 training cells, float32 at 200,000 cells, 48 validation cars. Data: results/routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json; linear values from results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json.

**Against the preregistered clauses (cars only).** *Collapse removed*: yes
on the loss trajectories and the scores; every cosine lane at a collapse
rate finished clean, and the routing-statistics half of the clause (at
least four effective slices per block, ROUTING-SAT probe) is being
measured on these checkpoints now. *Accuracy at the rule rates*: neutral
at 192 and 384 (within 1%), 2.0% worse at 768, on the edge of the 2% bar;
the 768 rule-rate comparison is against a linear pair whose seeds are 5%
apart, so the 2% is inside that pair's spread. *Width beyond 384
recovers*: **no**. The best cosine 768 lane (5e-4) scores 0.0409 against
linear 384's 0.0411, a ratio of 0.995 where the bar asked for 0.98, so the
width turnover at 384 is not an optimization artifact that the bounded
logits cure; it is where this task's capacity axis saturates for ISLA in
either routing form. What cosine routing did buy at 768 is the closing of
the seed split (0.0410 / 0.0408 at 5e-4 against linear's 0.0432 / 0.0410 at
2.5e-4) and a 5% gain over its own rule-rate lane, so the rule rate
under-trains 768 by that much once the ceiling is gone. Above the sweet
spot the rate still costs accuracy without collapsing: 384 at 1e-3 is 4%
worse than at 5e-4, and 768 at 1e-3 is 7% worse than at 5e-4 with an 11%
seed split, the ordinary too-high-a-rate signature rather than the
plateau.

**Why it matters.** The rate ceiling that produced the mean-field plateau
is a property of the linear routing parametrization, as the mechanism
chapter argued: bound the logits and the plateau is gone on every lane
tried, and the width learning-rate rule becomes a recommendation for the
best rate rather than a safety limit. The accuracy ceiling at width 384 is
not a rate artifact; GeoTransolver's continued improvement to 1,024 wide
and 24 layers (0.0406) stands as the one place its architecture is ahead,
now with the rate explanation excluded. Cosine routing therefore becomes
the default candidate on the strength of the removed ceiling at neutral
accuracy; the decision waits for the wing lanes (the second dataset: does
the linear wing control collapse, and are the cosine wing lanes neutral
against SCALE-HL's linear ones), the routing probe on these checkpoints,
and the 1,024- and 1,536-wide cosine lanes, which are the first test of
the ladder above 768 without a rate confound.

float32 scoring at 200,000 cells through the fleet pump under the

- **Second-dataset collapse clause**: the linear 384 wing control's
  validation loss rises above 0.01 after epoch 20 on at least one seed

## 2026-09-21 — Preregistration, three campaigns on the idle cluster: SCALE-LAW (error against training cases and parameters for cosine ISLA and GeoTransolver on two datasets), SEEDS (third and fourth seeds of every headline lane) and COSINE-TWINS (the evidence board under cosine routing) {#sec-nb-campaigns-2026-09-21-prereg}

**Setting.** Peter reports about 1,400 idle nodes on AGA this morning and
asks that the latitude be spent on research that the program has ready.
Three questions are ready and are limited by node count, not by design:
the scaling law the goal asks for (how error depends on training cases and
parameters, for both architectures, on both datasets); the seed count
behind the headline numbers (every reporting-protocol row rests on two
seeds, and two of the book's caveats are 8% seed spreads); and the state of
the evidence board should cosine routing become the default (every ISLA
lane on the board is linear-routed). All three run on one node per lane
with the pinned recipe and the `code_routenorm` snapshot (the class with
`routing_norm`; GeoTransolver and Transolver do not read it), 500 epochs,
bf16, float32 scoring at 200,000 cells through the fleet pump, which now
selects the snapshot per lane for these groups. Lane tables and launchers:
`kernel/{sl,sd,ct}/lanes.{tsv,sbatch}`; 160 lanes, 160 nodes, 640 GPUs,
about one to three days of chain time per lane.

**SCALE-LAW (group `sl`, 80 lanes, 100,000 cells, the scaling budget).**
Cosine ISLA at 192 / 384 / 768 wide (1e-3 / 5e-4 / 5e-4, each width's best
clean rate on the cars) and GeoTransolver at 256 / 512 / 1,024 wide (3e-3 /
3e-3 / 1e-3, its best rate per width at 435 cars) on the DrivAerML rungs of
27, 54, 109 and 218 cars (the 435-car points exist from the routing and
capacity studies) and on the HiLift rungs of 35, 105 and 510 wings (the
510-wing GeoTransolver 256 and 512 points come from the wing scaling study
already running); two seeds. Fit per model and dataset
$\varepsilon(n, P) = a\,n^{-\alpha} + b\,P^{-\beta} + c$ by least squares
on the seed means, with the floor $c$ shared between the two architectures
on a dataset when the fit does not separate them.

- **Bars.** *Data exponent*: $\alpha$ within 0.05 of each other for ISLA and
  GeoTransolver on the same dataset means the architectures convert
  training cases at the same rate and GeoTransolver's small-data lead is
  an offset, not a slope; a difference above 0.1 is a real slope difference
  and is reported with its sign. *Parameter exponent*: $\beta$ is expected
  to vanish for ISLA beyond 384 wide on the cars (the width ladder is flat
  384 to 768 under cosine routing); on the wings the same flatness, within
  3% between 384 and 768 at every rung, means the wing deficit is not
  capacity; a gain above 3% at the largest rung reopens the capacity
  question for the wings. *Two datasets*: the exponents agree between cars
  and wings within 0.1 or the law is stated per dataset. *Cross-over*: a
  rung at which GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA moves from below to above 1 as width
  grows is reported as such.
- **Prediction.** $\alpha \approx 0.3$ for both on the cars (the 200k ladder
  fell 0.83 to 1.00 in ratio, so the slopes are close: within 0.05);
  $\beta_\text{ISLA} \approx 0$ past 384 on both datasets; GeoTransolver's
  wing deficit lead stays about 27% at every width; probability that the
  wings show width recovering more than 3% for ISLA: 0.3.

**SEEDS (group `sd`, 62 lanes, the reporting protocol).** Seeds 44 and 45
of: the 435-car trio (ISLA, GeoTransolver 3e-3, Transolver); ISLA and
GeoTransolver 3e-3 on the 27 / 54 / 109 / 218-car rungs; the pose trio; the
35-wing and fixed-angle trios; the training-law lanes on both datasets
(area-trained trios on the 35-wing rung at 200,000 cells and on the cars at
100,000, with the cars' uniform-trained trio at 100,000); the interior pair
(ISLA at 5e-4, GeoTransolver-volume). Readout: four-seed means and ranges.

- **Bars.** A headline ratio *survives* if the four-seed ratio is within 2%
  of the two-seed ratio (parity 0.998 stays within 0.98 to 1.02; the ladder
  0.83 / 0.86 / 0.92 / 0.97; the wing rungs 0.73 and 0.69; the pose lead
  12% / 21%; the interior 0.87 / 1.42 / 0.98; the training-law factors 2.6x
  / 7.9x, 2.4x / 9.6x, 0.99x / 1.08x). A ratio that moves more than 2% is
  restated at four seeds and the chapter sentence changes. ISLA's interior
  pressure seed spread (8% at two seeds) is reported as the four-seed range.
- **Prediction.** Every ratio survives; the interior pressure range narrows
  to under 6%.

**COSINE-TWINS (group `ct`, 18 lanes, the reporting protocol).** Cosine
ISLA-192 at 1e-3, two seeds, on the 435-car row, the four ladder rungs, the
pose split, the fixed-angle wing rung, the area-trained wing and car lanes
(the 35-wing cosine lanes already run as part of the routing study).

- **Bars.** Cosine within 2% of linear on every row means the board can be
  re-stated under cosine routing without a change of reading if the wing
  lanes of the routing study confirm the default; a row more than 2% worse

  (0.99 wings, 1.08 cars) means the discretization result does not depend

- **Prediction.** Every row within 2% (0.8); the training-law factors within

Acceptance: every lane alive with no traceback at the first validation
(epoch 10 for the cars, 25 for the wings), validation losses on the

## 2026-09-21 — Ruling: extra seeds are not a compute priority; the seed campaign is cut to four lanes and the freed capacity goes to new questions (a second dataset for the interior task, an interpretability study of the slice territories, a routing-resolution probe on the wings) {#sec-nb-seeds-ruling}

**Ruling (Peter, 2026-09-21 morning).** More seeds of the same claim are
not a good use of cluster compute: two seeds are the standard, a third
rarely, more is overkill. Idle capacity should go to new and different
questions: a new dataset, an architectural change, interpretability (what
the slice weights learn), visualizations.

**Repair.** The SEEDS campaign of @sec-nb-campaigns-2026-09-21-prereg (62
lanes) was cancelled forty minutes after launch, except four lanes where a
two-seed spread is load-bearing for a written claim: the interior pair
(ISLA at 5e-4 and GeoTransolver-volume, whose 8% pressure spread carries a
caveat in three chapters) and ISLA's area-trained and uniform-trained lanes
on the cars at 100,000 cells (whose 8% training-law factor fired a
preregistered clause). Each cancelled lane carries a `BLOCKED_<run>` marker
so no chain link restarts it; its manifest row stays for the record. The
SCALE-LAW and COSINE-TWINS campaigns are unaffected: both ask questions the
program has not answered (the data and parameter exponents of both
architectures on two datasets; the evidence board under the candidate
default routing).

**What replaces the seeds.** Three questions, each preregistered in its own
entry as it launches:

- *A second dataset for the interior task.* Every interior claim is single
  dataset (DrivAerML). The cluster holds the HiLiftAeroML volume dataset and
  a GeoTransolver-volume configuration for it; an ISLA interior configuration
  for the wings (query tokens with the signed distance, the wings' five
  output fields) makes the boundary-to-interior standing a two-dataset
  result or refutes it.
- *Slice territories, ISLA against GeoTransolver, under two draws.* The
  discretization results say GeoTransolver's trained function reads the
  point pattern and ISLA's reads the surface. The mechanism claim behind it
  (measure-weighted slices partition the surface, point-averaged slices
  partition the points) has not been looked at. The probe takes trained
  checkpoints of both models, routes the same validation cars under the
  uniform and the 10:1-biased draws, assigns every point to its dominant
  slice, and measures how much each model's slice map moves between the two
  draws (overlap per slice, and a picture of the territories on the car).
- *Routing resolution on the wings.* The 1,024-slice control was null on the
  cars (0.995x, CAP-435) and untested on the wings, where the 27% deficit has
  not responded to width or cells. Four lanes at the reporting protocol
  (ISLA-192 with 1,024 slices on the 35-case and fixed-angle rungs, two
  seeds) against the existing 256-slice rows (0.1502 and 0.0300). Bar: 3%
  better on either rung means routing resolution is a wing lever; within 3%
  is null, as on the cars.

**The setting.** The book's architecture part had one chapter, @sec-isla,
which builds ISLA (Invariant Slice Attention, the soft-slice transformer
this program develops) one idea at a time on the airfoil example, with a
