book stop using the architecture's former names (MeshTransformer2, MT2, MT)
anywhere and standardize on ISLA; and that the architecture be presented
cleanly in a chapter of its own, "what is the forward pass", in
straightforward, consistent nomenclature, with illustrations, as simply as
the complexity allows while staying complete and accurate.

**What was done.** A new chapter, @sec-architecture, is now the source of
truth for what the class computes. It fixes one symbol and one code
identifier per quantity (a notation table with every tensor shape), draws
the whole pass with shapes on the boxes (@fig-isla-pass), opens the slice
layer into its ten steps in a second diagram (@fig-isla-layer) and states
each step as one equation in the order the code runs them, including the
detail the ideas chapter elided: the read-back weights are the softmax over
slices of the *refined* logits, the routing weights are recomputed from the
same refined logits with the measure bias, and the head frame's radial
direction comes from a separate routing map on the final state. A new
figure shows the two softmaxes of one layer on the airfoil side by side
(routing, rows summing to one with the measure bias; read-back, columns
summing to one without it; @fig-isla-routing-readback). The parameter
count is computed from the class as the page renders and broken down by
component (@tbl-isla-params: the two per-layer MLPs hold four fifths of
the 8.9M parameters; the geometry costs seven numbers per layer). The
three token arrangements (surface; interior queries as interacting tokens;
the passive decoder with read blocks) are drawn side by side
(@fig-isla-modes) with the query-mass and read-block equations, and a
closing section lists what the pass never does (no coordinate reaches a
learned map, no center is estimated, no pairwise attention, no count, no
learned vector). The switches table moved from the ideas chapter into the
new one, each flag tagged with the stage it changes; the ideas chapter's
dictionary section became a map from the six ideas to the stages.

**Nomenclature.** Every section label of the form `sec-mt2-*` became
`sec-isla-*` (and the cost table `tbl-isla-cost`) across all chapters and

the index, the ideas chapter and the status chapter were rewritten; the
style guide's never-say list gained MT and "the mesh transformer". In this

boundary-integral design (a different architecture) became "the
exact-kernel predecessor"; run identifiers, file names, configuration

## 2026-09-21 — Blocked: the HiLiftAeroML volume files carry interior coordinates for 31 of 1,800 cases and no interior fields, so the interior task has no second dataset on this cluster {#sec-nb-hlvol-blocked}

**Setting.** Every boundary-to-interior result of the program is measured
on one dataset, DrivAerML (the interior configuration of ISLA, Invariant
Slice Attention, against GeoTransolver-volume at 435 cars). The seeds
ruling of this morning (@sec-nb-seeds-ruling) named a HiLiftAeroML interior
rung as the replacement question, since the recipe carries a
GeoTransolver-volume configuration for the wings and a volume dataset
definition that reads the wings' `.pdmsh` files with their interior as a
point cloud.

**What was found.** The dataset root holds 1,800 case files. A structure
probe (a CPU job loading one case through `DomainMesh.load`, then a direct
listing of the memory-mapped trees) shows that the standard case has no
interior at all: the file holds the four in-file boundaries (vehicle, with
142 million points and 285 million cells; inlet, outlet, symmetry) and the
global data, and `DomainMesh.load` refuses it because the interior is
missing. Thirty-one cases (all angles of the first four geometries) carry an
interior of about 245 million points with **coordinates only**: no
`point_data` sub-tree exists in any of them, so pressure, temperature,
density and velocity are not available at a single interior point. No
HiLift volume lane has ever run in this task directory, and the dataset's
notes do not mention a volume split. The GeoTransolver-volume-highlift
configuration in the recipe is therefore untrained and, on this copy of the
data, untrainable.

**What this changes.** The interior standing stays single dataset and is
labeled interim wherever it is quoted (@sec-interior). The second interior
dataset has to come from elsewhere: either an export of the HiLift interior
fields from the source solver data (a data-engineering request, not a
research task) or a different volume dataset. Neither is started here. The
question is recorded as BLOCKED in the status ledger with this entry as its
evidence.

## 2026-09-21 — Erratum, ROUTING-SAT and the ROUTE-NORM routing probe: "layer $i$" in both artifacts is block $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$, pass $i \bmod 2$; the verdicts stand, the per-block tables cover the first half of each network {#sec-nb-routingsat-erratum}

**The setting.** The routing probe of 2026-09-20 (`results/routingsat_probe_2026-09-20.py`,
reused for the ROUTE-NORM lanes) records every call of ISLA's softmax over
points and then reads the first `n_layers` records as the per-layer
statistics. While writing the architecture chapter (@sec-architecture) it
became explicit that every slice layer calls that softmax **twice**, once
for the provisional routing that places the anchors and once for the
refined routing after the geometric refinement (@sec-arch-layer, steps b
and f), and the head frame calls it a third time after the last layer.

**The error.** Record $i$ is therefore block $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$, pass
$i \bmod 2$ (0 provisional, 1 refined), not block $i$. In the ROUTING-SAT
table (@tbl-routingsat) the twelve rows of a 12-layer checkpoint are the
provisional and refined passes of blocks 0 to 5; blocks 6 to 11 were not
examined. For the 24- and 48-layer checkpoints the rows cover blocks 0 to
11 and 0 to 23. The ROUTE-NORM routing probe (`results/probes/routing_rn_2026-09-20/`)
has the same indexing. The anchor-spread column is unaffected in meaning
(the positions are the same for every block, and the anchors of record $i$
are those of the pass it records).

**What stands.** Every verdict that was drawn is a statement about the
blocks that were measured, and those statements are correct: in the two
doubled-rate width controls every measured block routes every point to one
slice with coincident anchors (total collapse in the first six blocks is
collapse); no measured block of any clean checkpoint has fewer than 3.7
active slices; the cosine lanes' minimum of 12.5 active slices is over the
measured blocks. The "12 / 12 blocks" and "0 / 12" counts read "12 of 12
measured records (blocks 0 to 5, both passes)". What is *not* established by
those artifacts is the state of the deeper half of any network.

**The repair.** A corrected probe (`kernel/territory_probe.py`, hooking each
block and reading its last softmax call, the refined routing) is running on
the ten ROUTING-SAT checkpoints as task 1 of job `isla.territory.probe`
(artifact to come under `results/probes/routingsat_v2_2026-09-21/`). Its
per-block tables replace @tbl-routingsat when they land; the acceptance
bar is unchanged (collapse = one active slice with anchor spread below 0.01
in a block; clean = at least 4 active slices in every block).

## 2026-09-21 — Preregistration, TERRITORY: do GeoTransolver's slices partition the point pattern and ISLA's the surface? Slice territories of the two uniform-trained 100,000-cell checkpoints under a resampled uniform draw and the 10:1-biased draw {#sec-nb-territory-prereg}

**The setting.** The discretization results (@sec-training-law,
@sec-robustness-density) say that under a 10:1 sampling-density bias
GeoTransolver's surface-pressure error grows 8.7x and Transolver's 5.3x
where ISLA's grows 1.07x, and that the models trained under an
area-proportional draw lose 7.9x and 9.6x on the uniform draw where ISLA
loses 8%. The mechanism the book gives is that a slice in GeoTransolver
aggregates a *count-weighted* mean over whatever points the sampler
produced, while ISLA's slices aggregate measure-weighted means, so ISLA's
slices are functions of the surface and GeoTransolver's of the sample.
That is an argument from the equations; it has not been looked at in a
trained network. Peter asked this morning for interpretability work on the
slice weights in place of further seeds (@sec-nb-seeds-ruling).

**The question.** Two mechanisms could produce GeoTransolver's blow-up, and
they predict different things about the routing:

- **M1, the territories move.** The soft partition of the surface into
  slices (which slice each point routes to) is itself a function of the
  point density, so under the biased draw points are routed to different
  slices than under the uniform draw, and every downstream aggregate is
  built from different sets.
- **M2, the territories hold but the aggregates drift.** The routing is a
  function of position and normal that the biased draw leaves essentially
  unchanged; what moves is the slice token, a count-weighted mean whose
  value shifts toward the oversampled region.

For ISLA the prediction is that neither moves beyond the resampling floor:
the routing logits see only invariants that are stable under refinement,
and the aggregates are quadrature means.

**The instrument.** The uniform-trained ISLA (192 wide) and GeoTransolver
(256 wide, unit-direction protocol) checkpoints of the iso-cost study at
435 cars and 100,000 cells (`iso_dr_isla_w192_c100k_seed42`,
`iso_dr_gt_unit_w256_c100k_seed42`) are run in float32 on the first four
validation cars under three draws of the consistency bench at 100,000
expected cells: uniform with seed 1, uniform with seed 2, and the
10:1-biased Poisson draw. Per block the probe records each token's
**dominant slice** (ISLA: the argmax of the read-back weights over slices,
@sec-arch-layer step e; GeoTransolver: the argmax of the slice softmax, per
head), the slice anchors (ISLA) or the weight-averaged slice centroids
(GeoTransolver), and the un-centered token positions (the bench pipeline
stores the subtracted center). The reduction matches every token of one
draw to its nearest token of another draw on the surface and reports:

- **agreement** $A(\cdot,\cdot)$: the fraction of tokens whose dominant
  slice equals that of their nearest neighbor in the other draw, averaged
  over the four cars and, for GeoTransolver, over the eight heads; reported
  per block as minimum and median;
- the **resampling floor** $A(\text{unif}_1, \text{unif}_2)$, the agreement
  two independent uniform draws achieve (soft boundaries move a little
  under any resampling), and the **bias excess**
  $E \equiv A(\text{unif}_1, \text{unif}_2) - A(\text{unif}_1, \text{biased})$;
- the **anchor displacement**: RMS over slices of the distance between a
  slice's anchor (or centroid) under the uniform and the biased draw,
  divided by the RMS token radius, median over blocks.

**Bars, stated before the job returns.** M1 is supported if
GeoTransolver's bias excess $E$ exceeds 0.20 in median over blocks while
ISLA's stays below 0.05, and GeoTransolver's anchor displacement exceeds
0.05 while ISLA's stays below 0.02. M1 is refuted, and M2 becomes the
working mechanism, if GeoTransolver's excess stays below 0.05 (its
territories are as stable as ISLA's); the follow-on is then a slice-token
drift measurement, not part of this probe. Anything between is reported as
partial with the numbers. A second prediction, independent of M1 against
M2: ISLA's agreement under the biased draw is within 0.05 of its own
resampling floor in every block (the invariants see the surface, not the
sample); if any block violates it, the block and its statistics are
reported. If the two uniform draws turn out identical (the recipe's seed
override not reaching the sampler), the floor is undefined and the run is
repeated with a different mechanism before any verdict.

**Products.** One artifact, `results/territory_2026-09-21.json`, with the
per-block agreements, floors, excesses and displacements for both models;
a figure of the slice territories of one car at one mid-depth block under
the uniform and the biased draw for both models (dominant slice as color),
for @sec-training-law; and the corrected ROUTING-SAT statistics
(@sec-nb-routingsat-erratum) from the same job.

## 2026-09-21 — Plan, AIRFRANS-INT: AirfRANS (1,001 two-dimensional incompressible RANS airfoil cases, on the cluster in raw VTK) as the second interior dataset and a second PDE regime, with its Reynolds and angle-of-attack extrapolation splits {#sec-nb-airfrans-plan}

**Setting.** The HiLiftAeroML volume files carry no interior fields
(@sec-nb-hlvol-blocked), so the boundary-to-interior task, and every
claim built on it, rests on DrivAerML alone. The cluster's dataset root
holds one more candidate: **AirfRANS** (Bonnet et al., 2022), 1,001
two-dimensional steady RANS (k-ω SST) solutions around NACA-family
airfoils at Reynolds numbers of 2 to 6 million and angles of attack of −5
to 15 degrees, in raw VTK (`airfrans/Dataset/<case>/`: an `_internal.vtu`
with about 177,000 quadrilateral cells carrying velocity `U`, pressure `p`,
eddy viscosity `nut` and the signed distance `implicit_distance` at the
points; an `_aerofoil.vtp` polyline of the airfoil; a `_freestream.vtp`
of the far boundary), with a manifest of splits: `full` (800 train / 200
test), `scarce` (200 train), `reynolds` (504 train / 496 test, an
extrapolation in Reynolds number) and `aoa` (804 / 196, an extrapolation
in angle of attack). The recipe has no configuration for it.

**Why it is the right second dataset.** It is a boundary-to-interior
problem in the program's sense (a closed boundary curve with its normals
and arc-length measure, one global direction, one global scalar, fields
requested at interior points), it is a *different PDE regime*
(incompressible, two-dimensional, a 3x range of Reynolds number) which is
what ISLA's claim of generality needs, its two extrapolation splits are
generalization tests the program has not had, and it is small (15 GB, a
few minutes per epoch at 100,000 interior queries), so two-seed lanes of
both architectures fit in a day. Its published leaderboard gives external
reference numbers for the volume fields.

**What has to be built (engineering, kept minimal).** A one-off converter
(a CPU job with `pyvista`) that writes each case as a native `DomainMesh`:
the interior as a point cloud in three dimensions with $z = 0$ and the four
fields plus the signed distance and its gradient direction (the unit
vector from the nearest airfoil point, computed in the converter because
the recipe's SDF transform expects a triangulated surface); the airfoil
as a boundary of line cells with precomputed in-plane unit normals and
the cell lengths as the quadrature measure (the mesh class's normals are
defined for codimension one only, and a curve in three dimensions is
codimension two, so the converter stores them); global data holding the
inlet velocity vector (its direction is the one global vector input, its
magnitude the one global scalar) and the case's Reynolds number. Then a
dataset definition reading those files with the manifest splits, an ISLA
interior configuration (`query_tokens`, the signed distance as the query
scalar, `n_global_scalars=1`, outputs: pressure and eddy viscosity as
scalars, velocity as a vector) and the GeoTransolver-volume configuration
on the same inputs. ISLA's vector head is three-dimensional; on a planar
problem the out-of-plane basis vector carries a coefficient the network
can learn to zero, and the planar velocity is representable in the
remaining basis (the freestream direction, the query's signed-distance
direction, and their in-plane complement).

**Preregistration (to be completed when the lanes launch).** Both
architectures at the recipe's interior dimensions on the `full` split
(800 cases, two seeds), scored on the 200 test cases in float32 per field;
then the two extrapolation splits with the same configurations. Bars, in
readout units: the interior standing is *reproduced* if the
GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA ratios per field on AirfRANS fall on the same
side of one as on DrivAerML (pressure below one, velocity above one) with
both seeds agreeing in sign; it is *refuted* for a field if the ratio
crosses one with seeds agreeing. On the extrapolation splits the question
is new and the bar is stated as a comparison: the architecture whose test
error grows less from `full` to `reynolds` (and to `aoa`) generalizes
better, with a 10% difference in growth counting and anything less
reported as a tie. Status: PLANNED; the converter is the next engineering
step and is not started in this entry.

## 2026-09-21 — Verdict, TERRITORY: GeoTransolver's slice territories move with the point pattern (bias excess 0.33 in agreement, slice centroids displaced by 0.64 body radii) and ISLA's nearly do not (0.06 and 0.04), so mechanism M1 is supported for GeoTransolver; ISLA misses its own "unchanged" bars by small margins that the deep blocks carry {#sec-nb-territory-verdict}

**Setting.** TERRITORY (@sec-nb-territory-prereg) asked whether the
discretization results have the mechanism the book gives them: that a
GeoTransolver slice partitions the *sample* and an ISLA slice partitions
the *surface*. The uniform-trained ISLA (192 wide) and GeoTransolver (256
wide) checkpoints from the iso-cost study (435 DrivAerML cars, 100,000
cells) were run in float32 on the first four validation cars under three
independent draws of each car's surface at 100,000 expected cells: two
uniform draws (recipe seeds 11 and 22) and the 10:1-biased Poisson draw
(seed 33). Per block, every token's dominant slice was recorded; tokens of
one draw were matched to their nearest token of another on the surface
(positions restored to the dataset frame; the bench pipeline's subtracted
center is carried through the model's forward-kwargs spec) and the
fraction with the same dominant slice is the **agreement**. The two uniform
draws give the **resampling floor**; the **bias excess** is the floor
minus the agreement with the biased draw. Artifact:
`results/territory_2026-09-21.json` (probe
`results/territory_probe_2026-09-21.py`, reduction
`results/territory_reduce_2026-09-21.py`, job 812907). Two earlier
attempts of the same job were discarded before any reading: the first
because the seed override had not reached the sampler (the two "uniform"
draws were identical, the case the preregistration named), the second
because the uniform and biased draws shared the same seed and therefore
the same 320,000-cell parent sample (a third of their tokens coincided
exactly, inflating the biased agreement above the floor).

**What we saw.** Median over the twelve blocks, four cars, GeoTransolver
over its eight heads:

| model | floor $A(\text{unif}_1, \text{unif}_2)$ | $A(\text{unif}_1, \text{biased})$ | bias excess | excess, deep blocks 8 to 11 | anchor or centroid displacement [body RMS radii] |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ISLA (192 wide) | 0.71 | 0.65 | **+0.06** | +0.08 to +0.09 | **0.039** |
| GeoTransolver (256 wide) | 0.63 | 0.27 | **+0.33** | +0.31 to +0.34 | **0.64** |

: TERRITORY: dominant-slice agreement between draws and slice-anchor displacement, four DrivAerML validation cars at 100,000 expected cells, float32 (results/territory_2026-09-21.json). {#tbl-territory}

The floors are well below one for both models: two independent uniform
draws already disagree on the dominant slice of 30 to 40% of tokens,
because the soft boundaries between slices move under any resampling and
the deep blocks route sharply (ISLA's floor falls from 0.83 in block 2 to
0.43 in block 10; GeoTransolver's from 0.69 to 0.48). What separates the
models is what the biased draw costs *beyond* that floor. For
GeoTransolver it costs 0.33 in median, in every block but the first (block
0, whose routing is a function of the input embedding alone, costs 0.05),
and its weight-averaged slice centroids move by 0.64 of the body's RMS
radius: the slices are following the points. For ISLA it costs 0.06, and
its anchors move by 0.039 of the body radius. A post hoc control that
equalizes matching quality (keeping only matched pairs at least as close
as a typical uniform-to-uniform pair; a third of the biased pairs, since
the biased draw is sparse over half the body) leaves the picture
unchanged: ISLA +0.05, GeoTransolver +0.24.

**Verdict against the bars.** **M1 is supported for GeoTransolver**: its
bias excess (0.33) exceeds the 0.20 bar and its centroid displacement
(0.64) exceeds the 0.05 bar, each by a wide margin. **ISLA misses its own
"unchanged" clauses by small margins**: its excess is 0.056 against a bar
of 0.05, its anchor displacement 0.039 against 0.02, and the second
prediction (agreement under the biased draw within 0.05 of the floor in
every block) holds in blocks 0 to 5 (0.026 to 0.058) and fails in blocks 6
to 11 (0.058 to 0.092). ISLA's territories are therefore *nearly*, not
exactly, functions of the surface: a 10:1 change of density costs it about
one sixth of what it costs GeoTransolver in territory agreement and one
sixteenth in anchor motion, and the residual is concentrated in the deep
blocks. The mechanism of that residual is not measured here; the natural
candidate is the quadrature noise of the biased draw (Horvitz–Thompson
weights spanning a decade give a slice over the sparse half of the body
fewer effective samples), which is also the book's explanation of ISLA's
1.07x error growth under the same draw and its 8% training-law
dependence. The picture of one car (block 6) and the per-block curves go
to @sec-training-law as @fig-territory-maps and
@fig-territory-agreement.

**What it changes.** The mechanism sentence of @sec-training-law ("the
baselines' slice aggregates are averages over the kept points; ISLA's are
measure-weighted integrals") now has a direct measurement behind it, with
the qualification that ISLA's routing is not perfectly draw-invariant. The
distinction between M1 (territories move) and M2 (aggregates drift) is
decided for GeoTransolver in favor of M1 at the level of the routing;
whether the aggregates *also* drift once the territories are held fixed
is not measured and would need a controlled-routing probe. Single
dataset: the wing twin runs the same probe on the 35-wing checkpoints of
the reporting-protocol fleet (200,000 cells; ISLA and GeoTransolver, seed
42) under the HiLift bench draws at 200,000 cells, and is launched with
this entry (job `isla.territory.wings`); the result is quoted as general
only when it lands.

## 2026-09-21 — TERRITORY wing twin: the anchor-displacement clause reproduces (GeoTransolver's slice centroids move 0.31 body radii, ISLA's anchors 0.004), the dominant-slice clause does not discriminate because both wing checkpoints route softly (GeoTransolver's deep blocks are nearly uniform over slices) {#sec-nb-territory-wings}

**Setting.** The same probe as @sec-nb-territory-verdict on the second
dataset: the 35-wing checkpoints of the reporting-protocol fleet (ISLA-192
and GeoTransolver-256, seed 42, 200,000 cells) on the first four validation
wings under two independent uniform draws and the 10:1-biased draw of the
HiLift bench at 200,000 expected cells (job `isla.territory.wings` 813228;
artifact `results/territory_wings_2026-09-21.json`; the wing bench
definitions gained `store_center_as: center` so the positions could be
restored, as on the cars).

**What we saw.** Median over blocks: ISLA floor 0.24, biased agreement
0.19, excess +0.045, anchor displacement 0.0035 body radii; GeoTransolver
floor 0.20, biased 0.15, excess +0.061, centroid displacement 0.31. The
floors are a third of the cars' because the wing checkpoints route
softly: ISLA's hardness (per-point entropy over slices divided by
$\log M$) is 0.59 to 0.89 on the wings against 0.33 to 0.78 on the cars,
and GeoTransolver's deep blocks are essentially uniform over slices
(hardness 0.91 to 1.00 in blocks 7 to 11, 246 to 252 effective slices of
256). When every slice takes nearly equal weight, the argmax is decided by
small differences and moves under any resampling, so the dominant-slice
agreement stops measuring territories. The displacement clause is
unaffected by this and reproduces the cars' picture: GeoTransolver's
weight-averaged slice centroids move by 0.31 body radii under the biased
draw (bar 0.05), which for near-uniform slices is the shift of the sample's
own centroid; ISLA's anchors move by 0.0035 (bar 0.02, met with room; on
the cars 0.039 just missed it).

**Reading.** On both datasets GeoTransolver's slice aggregates follow the
point pattern (centroid displacement 0.64 on the cars, 0.31 on the wings)
and ISLA's do not (0.039, 0.0035). The dominant-slice agreement, the
probe's primary metric, separated the models on the cars (excess 0.33
against 0.06) and not on the wings (0.06 against 0.045), where GeoTransolver's
routing is too soft for a dominant slice to mean anything: that is itself a
finding about the wing checkpoints (GeoTransolver's deep layers on the
35-wing rung behave as a near-global average, which is consistent with its
0.73 ratio there being carried by other layers) but it makes the agreement
metric the wrong instrument for soft routing. A soft version (the total
variation between the two draws' full routing distributions at matched
points) is the right follow-on and needs the probe to store the
distributions, not the argmax. Standing: the anchor-displacement result is
two-dataset; the territory-agreement result stays single-dataset.

## 2026-09-21 — Preregistration, AIRFRANS-INT lanes: ISLA interior (linear routing at 5e-4, cosine at 1e-3) and GeoTransolver-volume (1e-3) on the AirfRANS full split, 100,000 interior queries per case, two seeds {#sec-nb-airfrans-prereg}

**Setting.** The plan of @sec-nb-airfrans-plan is executed: all 1,001
AirfRANS cases are converted to native DomainMesh files (converter
`results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/airfrans_convert.py`; about one second
per case; the signed distance is stored positive outside, the boundary is
the airfoil polyline as line cells with in-plane normals and segment
lengths as the quadrature measure, and the global data carry the inlet
velocity, its direction and magnitude, the Reynolds number and an
incompressible reference state, $\rho_\infty = 1$, $p_\infty = 0$, so the
recipe's nondimensionalization yields $p / (\tfrac12 |U_\infty|^2)$ and
$U / |U_\infty|$). Over the converted cases the nondimensional pressure has
a standard deviation of 0.86 and the velocity components 0.50; the eddy
viscosity is left in its units and normalized by the recipe with mean
$7.9 \times 10^{-4}$ and standard deviation $2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ m²/s (the
mean over cases of the per-case statistics). The name-derived inlet
velocity agrees with the freestream boundary's mean velocity to 0.5% on
every case; every airfoil polyline is closed.

**Lanes (six, one chain each).** Dataset `airfrans_volume`, split
`full_train` (800) against `full_test` (200), 100,000 interior queries and
the whole airfoil (about 1,000 segments) per case, 500 epochs, validation
every 10:

- ISLA, linear routing, 5e-4, seeds 42 / 43 (`isla_volume_airfrans`:
  query tokens, the signed distance as query scalar, one global vector and
  one global scalar, outputs pressure and eddy viscosity as scalars and
  velocity as a vector);
- ISLA, cosine routing, 1e-3, seeds 42 / 43 (the candidate default at the
  rate the cars' cosine interior lane trained cleanly at);
- GeoTransolver-volume, 1e-3, seeds 42 / 43 (`geotransolver_volume_airfrans`:
  coordinates, signed distance and its direction as local features, the
  inlet velocity as the global embedding).

**Bars (float32, per field, on the 200 test cases).** *Reproduced* if
GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA falls on the same side of one as on DrivAerML
(pressure below one, velocity above one) with both seeds agreeing in
sign; *refuted* for a field if the ratio crosses one with seeds agreeing;
eddy viscosity is reported without a prior (the cars' ratio is 0.98). A
lane that reaches the mean-field plateau (validation loss flat at the
field-variance level after epoch 20) is reported as such and rerun at
half its rate. Scoring draws 100,000 interior queries per test case (the
training count; each case has about 177,000 interior points) for both
architectures, because ISLA's interacting-query configuration is deployed
at its training query count (@sec-interior-companion); fixed before the
first lane finished. The Reynolds and angle-of-attack extrapolation splits
follow in their own entry once the full-split lanes are accepted.

## 2026-09-21 — Acceptance, AIRFRANS-INT: all six lanes alive after two false starts (a missing Hydra package header on the new model configurations; the signed distance stored without a channel axis), about one epoch per minute {#sec-nb-airfrans-acceptance}

The first launch failed at configuration time because the two new model
files lacked the `# @package _global_` header every recipe model file
carries; the second failed at the first training step because the
converter stored the signed distance as a flat per-point field where the
recipe passes per-query scalars with a trailing channel axis (the
GeoTransolver lanes, which concatenate the field into their local
embedding, had trained through it). The converter now writes the signed
distance as $(N, 1)$; all 1,000 cases were reconverted (about four
minutes on four CPU shards) and the six lanes relaunched from scratch
(jobs 813630 to 813635). Eight minutes in, every lane has completed its
first validations with no traceback: ISLA linear 5e-4 at epoch 9
(validation loss 0.12), ISLA cosine 1e-3 at epoch 6 to 9 (0.10 to 0.11),
GeoTransolver-volume at epoch 6 (0.07 to 0.09). At this rate the 500-epoch
protocol completes in about eight hours. Accepted; the bars are those of
@sec-nb-airfrans-prereg.

## 2026-09-21 — Interim, SCALE-LAW on DrivAerML (three of four rungs scored): the error against cases is not a power law but an approach to the shared floor (local exponent 0.7 falling to 0.25), parameters buy 3 to 13% per 15x at every rung, epochs are converged; the compute-optimal rule is "cases first, then width", and the fitted law is preregistered for the full board {#sec-nb-scalelaw-interim}

**Setting.** The scaling campaign (@sec-nb-campaigns-2026-09-21-prereg)
trains cosine-routing ISLA at 192/384/768 wide and GeoTransolver at
256/512/1,024 wide for 500 epochs at 100,000 cells on 27, 54, 109 and 218
DrivAerML cars and on 35, 210 and 510 wings, two seeds each. Peter asked
today what the surrogate analogue of a compute-optimal ("Chinchilla") rule
is: the right mix of training compute, dataset size and parameter count.
This entry reads the three DrivAerML rungs scored so far together with the
435-car width ladders (`results/scalelaw_interim_2026-09-21.json`;
`results/routenorm_interim_2026-09-20.json`;
`results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json`).

**What we saw** (seed means, float32, surface pressure):

| cases | ISLA 192 / 384 / 768 | GeoTransolver 256 / 512 / 1,024 |
|--:|---|---|
| 27 | 0.1414 / 0.1467 / 0.1379 | 0.1277 / 0.1070 / 0.1137 |
| 54 | 0.0846 / 0.0810 / 0.0758 | 0.0764 / 0.0673 / 0.0655 |
| 109 | 0.0619 / 0.0570 / 0.0539 | 0.0573 / 0.0519 / 0.0506 |
| 435 | 0.0449 / 0.0413 / 0.0409 | 0.0447 / 0.0417 / 0.0406 |

: SCALE-LAW interim board, DrivAerML, 100,000 cells, 500 epochs (the 218-car rung pending). {#tbl-scalelaw-interim}

Local exponents of the error against cases (negative log-log slope
between adjacent rungs) run 0.6 to 0.75 from 27 to 54 cars, 0.45 to 0.6
from 54 to 109, and 0.18 to 0.24 from 109 to 435, at every width and for
both models. A 15x increase in parameters buys ISLA 3% (27 cars), 10%
(54), 13% (109) and 9% (435), GeoTransolver 11%, 14%, 12% and 9%. The
ISO-COST grid's one epoch doubling (500 to 1,000 at 200,000 cells) moved
neither model (ISLA 0.0448 to 0.0448, GeoTransolver 0.0445 to 0.0445).

**Reading.** The curve in cases bends: it is the approach to the shared
floor near 0.040 (@sec-nb-cap435-verdict, @sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict),
not a scale-free law, and a single exponent would misstate it. The
Chinchilla form $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\infty + a n^{-\alpha} + b
P^{-\beta}$ with training compute $C \propto P n$ (cells and epochs held
at their converged values) yields $P^\ast \propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha +
\beta)}$ and $n^\ast \propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$; with the data
exponent an order of magnitude above the parameter exponent this says:
buy cases until the data term is small (on DrivAerML between 109 and 435
cars), then buy width, where each doubling is worth 3 to 4% until the
floor. The five coefficients are not identifiable from three widths and
four rungs (least squares puts $\varepsilon_\infty$ anywhere from 0 to the
floor depending on the start, trading against $b P^{-\beta}$); the local
exponents are the readout, written into @sec-compute-allocation with
@fig-scaling-cases and @tbl-scaling-exponents.

**Preregistration for the full board.** When the 218-car rung and the
three wing rungs land: (i) fit the Chinchilla form per model and dataset
with $\varepsilon_\infty$ bounded to $[0, 0.9 \times$ the best measured
error$]$ and report the coefficients with a two-seed bootstrap; the law is
*accepted* if the RMS relative residual is below 3% on both datasets and
*rejected* for that dataset otherwise. (ii) The two architectures'
exponents are *the same* if their $\alpha$ and $\beta$ differ by less than
their bootstrap spread on both datasets, otherwise the one with the larger
$\beta$ is the one that "scales with parameters" and the book says so with
the numbers. (iii) The compute-optimal split is reported as the case count
at which the fitted data and parameter terms are equal for the recipe's
width, per dataset. Until then the section is labeled interim and single
dataset.

## 2026-09-21 — Ruling and preregistration, PROTOCOL-REDO: no accuracy claim may rest on the 10,000-cell exploration budget; the claims that did are cut or re-measured at 200,000 cells (38 lanes), the removed variants' prices are dropped {#sec-nb-protocol-redo-prereg}

**The ruling.** Peter, today: results at 10,000 cells are worthless for an
accuracy argument, because a reader will say the baselines were weak at
that budget; they may remain only as one rung of a resolution ladder used
for a scaling statement, or as a labeled mechanism diagnostic. The
reporting protocol is 200,000 cells (the GeoTransolver recipe default,
adopted 2026-09-18); scaling studies use 100,000 because cells are flat
above 100,000.

**The audit.** A read of every chapter found the 10,000-cell accuracy
claims still load-bearing in: the design-choice prices of the ISLA chapter
and the decision ledger (single-factor ablation on the 35-case rung,
weights-off prices per rung, the frame prices against the removed centered
and similarity-gauge variants, the multi-head null, the positional-price
attribution of the deficit anatomy); the passive decoder's price (3.0 to
3.7x on the surface, about 3x on interior pressure); the measure-weighted
baseline ablations ("the measure costs the baselines nothing"; "frame,
not aggregation"); the interior chapter's diagnostic note (parameter-matched
width-344 arm, 54- and 109-car rungs, no-signed-distance arm, query-count
rule under the geometric-mean option); the cross-family transfer frontier
(bf16, removed variants); the deflection sealed test; and the HiLift rungs
without a 200,000-cell twin (210 cases, 4 and 21 geometries, 510 and 1,260
cases). About twenty further passages quoted a 10,000-cell number beside
an existing 200,000-cell one. The cuts and pending marks are applied to
the chapters in the same pass as this entry.

**What is not re-measured.** The multi-head routing variant and the two
centered frames were removed from the class on 2026-09-20; their prices are
cut from the book rather than requoted, and the design table says
"tested, not adopted" without a percentage. The transfer frontier is cut to
its qualitative mechanism statement and its 200,000-cell redo is deferred to
its own entry (it needs a fine-tuning path). The deflection test and the
five HiLift rungs are already in the 200,000-cell fleet.

**The lanes (group `rd`, 38, two seeds, 200,000 cells, jobs 816980 to
817017).** Study 2, design prices on ISLA itself: `use_measure_weights=False`
and `use_relational_geo=False` on the 35-case rung, the fixed-angle rung
and 435 cars (12 lanes; references are the fleet's ISLA lanes). Study 3, the
passive decoder: passive surface decode on 435 cars, and the interior
configuration with queries decoded passively instead of interacting (4
lanes at the interior rate 5e-4). Study 4, GeoTransolver and Transolver
with ISLA's measure-weighted pooling (ablation) on the 35-case rung and 435
cars (8 lanes, the `code_mw` snapshot). Study 5, interior sub-standings on
435 cars unless stated: ISLA at GeoTransolver-volume's parameter count
(width 344, rate 2.8e-4 by the width rule), the no-signed-distance arm, a
pair under the default `query_mass="source_total"`, and ISLA and
GeoTransolver-volume at 54 and 109 cars (14 lanes).

**Bars.** Each study's claim is *reproduced* if the 200,000-cell ratio
falls on the same side of one as the 10,000-cell one with both seeds
agreeing and within a factor of 1.5 of it, *revised* if the sign holds but
the size does not, and *withdrawn* if the sign flips or the seeds disagree.
Specifically: weights-off worse than ISLA on the wing rungs (was 8 to 17%)
and within noise on the cars (was 3%); invariants-off worse by more than
10% on every rung (was 16% at 35 cases); passive surface decode worse by a
factor of 2 or more (was 3.0 to 3.7x); passive interior decode worse than
the interacting configuration on pressure by a factor of 2 or more (was
about 3x); the measure-weighted baselines within 3% of their released
twins on the uniform draw (was "nothing") and, scored under the 10:1 draw
of the bench at 100,000 cells, still degraded by a factor of 3 or more
(was 14 to 16x at 10,000 cells; the 100,000-cell figure for the released
models is 8.7x and 5.3x); the width-344 arm within 3% of ISLA-192 on
pressure (the 10,000-cell claim was that parameters do not close the
pressure gap); the no-signed-distance arm worse than ISLA on every field;
the source-total pair within 3% of the geometric-mean row (0.0546 / 0.0712
/ 0.0857); the 54- and 109-car interior ratios on the same side of one as
at 435 for each field. Verdicts per study as the lanes finish, at about
1.7 hours per 100 epochs on the wings and a day on the cars.

**Amendment at launch.** The two measure-weighted baseline configurations
ran under the snapshot they were written for, whose dataset code predates
the recipe; they were moved to the current snapshot, which carries the
same measure-weighted option (the measure path is the one ISLA's surface
configuration reads). The 54- and 109-car interior rungs needed a volume
dataset definition pointing at the scaling manifest (a command-line
manifest override does not reach the loader); two such definitions were
added. The passive decoder at 200,000 queries against 200,000 boundary
tokens exceeds the 276 GB of one GB300 at the first training step: the
local Gaussian readout saves a 4,096 x 200,000 kernel per chunk for the
backward pass, about 500 GB across the 49 chunks. The four passive lanes
run at 100,000 cells and queries instead (the scaling budget, at which
cells are flat), and the price is reported against the 100,000-cell ISLA
reference of the iso-cost grid (0.0450); recomputing the readout chunks in
the backward pass is the engineering fix, queued as a class change with a
test.

per case, float32, two seeds) held three rungs: 35 random training cases,

(`results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-22.json`; GeoTransolver at the
better of its 1e-3 and 3e-3 pairs, here 1e-3 on both rungs).

**What we saw** (surface pressure, seed means; ratio = baseline ÷ ISLA):

| rung | ISLA | GeoTransolver | Transolver | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA | Transolver ÷ ISLA |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 35 random cases | 0.1500 | 0.1098 | 0.1101 | 0.73 | 0.73 |
| 210 random cases | 0.0551 | 0.0489 | 0.0528 | 0.89 | 0.96 |
| 4 geometries (never seen) | 0.2659 | 0.2022 | 0.1929 | 0.76 | 0.73 |

: The wing ladders at the reporting protocol after the two new rungs (results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json, …interim_2026-09-20.json, …reduction_2026-09-22.json). {#tbl-wing-rungs-210}

**Reading.** The wing deficit the book has carried since the 35-case rung is

and by 2 to 5% where the validation geometries are never seen". The
preregistered ISLA-advantage bar (baseline ÷ ISLA of at least 1.10) is

validation geometry recurs; @sec-data-efficiency) is consistent with the

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, SCALE-LAW on DrivAerML (all five rungs, three widths, both architectures): the bounded-floor law is accepted for ISLA (2.3% RMS; floor 0.0356, data exponent 1.28, parameter exponent 0.52) and missed by GeoTransolver (3.3%, its 27-car rung is not monotone in width); the exponents are the same for both; compute goes to cases until about 200, then to width {#sec-nb-scalelaw-drivaerml-verdict}

**Setting.** The scaling campaign (@sec-nb-campaigns-2026-09-21-prereg)
trains cosine-routing ISLA at 192 / 384 / 768 wide and GeoTransolver at
256 / 512 / 1,024 wide for 500 epochs at 100,000 cells on 27, 54, 109 and
218 DrivAerML cars, two seeds each, scored in float32; the 435-car points
are the routing and capacity ladders at the same rates
(@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict, @sec-nb-cap435-verdict). The interim
reading (@sec-nb-scalelaw-interim) had three rungs and preregistered the
fit for the full board: the Chinchilla form $\varepsilon =
\varepsilon_\infty + a\,n^{-\alpha} + b\,P^{-\beta}$ per architecture,
least squares on the seed means with the floor bounded to at most 0.9
times the best measured error, a two-seed bootstrap, acceptance at 3% RMS
relative residual, "same exponents" if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ differ by less
than the bootstrap spread, and the compute-optimal split as the case count
at which the two fitted terms are equal at the recipe width. The 218-car
rung landed today; this entry closes the DrivAerML half. Reduction
`results/scalelaw_reduce_2026-09-22.py`, artifact
`results/scalelaw_drivaerml_2026-09-22.json`. One change against the
interim figure: the 435-car ISLA-768 point is the 5e-4 lane (0.0409), the
rate the study's own 768-wide lanes use, where the interim figure had drawn
the 2.5e-4 rule-rate lane (0.0430).

**What we saw** (seed means, surface pressure):

| cases | ISLA 192 / 384 / 768 | GeoTransolver 256 / 512 / 1,024 | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA, narrowest / widest |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 27 | 0.1414 / 0.1467 / 0.1379 | 0.1277 / 0.1070 / 0.1137 | 0.90 / 0.82 |
| 54 | 0.0846 / 0.0810 / 0.0758 | 0.0764 / 0.0673 / 0.0655 | 0.90 / 0.86 |
| 109 | 0.0619 / 0.0570 / 0.0539 | 0.0573 / 0.0519 / 0.0506 | 0.93 / 0.94 |
| 218 | 0.0515 / 0.0467 / 0.0454 | 0.0490 / 0.0452 / 0.0440 | 0.95 / 0.97 |
| 435 | 0.0449 / 0.0413 / 0.0409 | 0.0447 / 0.0417 / 0.0406 | 1.00 / 0.99 |

: SCALE-LAW board, DrivAerML, 100,000 cells, 500 epochs, two seeds (seeds in the artifact; the widest seed pair is 5% apart, at ISLA-192 on 109 cars; twelve of the thirty pairs are within 1%). {#tbl-scalelaw-drivaerml}

Local exponents of the total error against cases fall with every rung:
0.74 / 0.86 / 0.86 (ISLA 192 / 384 / 768) and 0.74 / 0.67 / 0.80
(GeoTransolver) from 27 to 54 cars, 0.45 / 0.50 / 0.48 and 0.41 / 0.37 /
0.37 from 54 to 109, 0.26 / 0.29 / 0.25 and 0.23 / 0.20 / 0.20 from 109 to
218, and 0.20 / 0.18 / 0.15 and 0.13 / 0.12 / 0.12 from 218 to 435. A 15x
parameter increase buys ISLA 2% at 27 cars and 10 / 13 / 12 / 9% at 54 /
109 / 218 / 435; GeoTransolver 11 / 14 / 12 / 10 / 9%.

**The fit.** For ISLA the bounded-floor law is identified: the floor lands
inside its range at $\varepsilon_\infty = 0.0356$ (bootstrap 0.0346 to
0.0364; the bound was 0.0368), $\alpha = 1.28$ (1.26 to 1.30), $\beta =
0.52$ (0.41 to 0.63), $a = 6.9$, $b = 33$, RMS relative residual 2.3%
(bootstrap 2.2 to 2.6%). **The law is accepted for ISLA on DrivAerML.**
For GeoTransolver the same form reaches 3.3% RMS (bootstrap 3.0 to 3.7%)
and pushes the floor onto its bound (0.0365), so its coefficients are
bound-determined and **the law is rejected for GeoTransolver on DrivAerML
by the preregistered bar**; its exponents, $\alpha = 1.30$ (1.27 to 1.33)
and $\beta = 0.65$ (0.59 to 0.74), differ from ISLA's by 0.02 and 0.13
against bootstrap spreads of 0.06 and 0.22, so **the two architectures'
exponents are the same** by the second bar. The compute-optimal crossover
(data term equal to parameter term at the recipe width) is 200 cars for
ISLA and 150 for GeoTransolver; at 54 cars ISLA's data term is 0.042
against a parameter term of 0.008 and a floor of 0.036, at 435 cars 0.003
against the same 0.008.

**Why GeoTransolver misses the bar: the 27-car rung.** The additive law
predicts that a wider model is never worse. At 27 cars GeoTransolver-1,024
is 6% worse than GeoTransolver-512 (0.1137 against 0.1070; seeds 0.1123 /
0.1151 against 0.1048 / 0.1092, separated), and ISLA-384 is 4% worse than
ISLA-192 (0.1467 against 0.1414; 0.1470 / 0.1464 against 0.1427 / 0.1400)
while ISLA-768 is the best of its three. Neither architecture is monotone
in width at 27 cars; from 54 cars up both are. The residual of the
GeoTransolver fit is concentrated on that rung. The effect is real
(seed-separated on both architectures) and the separable law has no term
for it; a data-dependent parameter term ($b\,P^{-\beta}$ with $\beta$
falling toward zero or negative at small $n$) would be the next form to
try, but with two seeds and one rung below 54 cars the program does not
fit it. This is the one anomaly of the board and it is recorded, not
sanded off.

**Reading.** The interim entry's rule stands with numbers attached: the
error is an approach to a floor near 0.036 to 0.040 for both
architectures, the reducible part falls as $n^{-1.3}$ in cases and as
$P^{-0.5}$ to $P^{-0.65}$ in parameters, and the optimum at fixed compute
buys cases until about 200 cars and then parameters (about 70% of each
further increment, $\alpha / (\alpha + \beta)$). GeoTransolver's
small-data lead (0.82 to 0.90 at 27 and 54 cars) is an offset in the
coefficients, not a slope, and it closes to parity at 435 cars at every
width. The chapter section @sec-compute-allocation is restated with
@fig-scaling-cases (all five rungs, fitted curves and floors),
@tbl-scaling-exponents and the new @tbl-scaling-fit. Single dataset: the
wing rungs (35 / 210 / 510) of the same campaign are in flight and decide
whether the exponents transfer (the two-datasets bar: agreement within 0.1
or the law is stated per dataset).

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, AIRFRANS-INT (full split): the interior standing reproduces on the second dataset and PDE regime; GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA 0.80 / 1.95 / 0.85 (pressure / velocity / eddy viscosity) under linear routing and 0.83 / 2.14 / 0.83 under cosine, both seeds agreeing on every field {#sec-nb-airfrans-verdict}

**Setting.** The interior task asks a surrogate for the flow field at
points off the wall given only the boundary. On DrivAerML (three-dimensional
compressible-RANS car external flow, 435 training cars) ISLA with query
tokens leads GeoTransolver-volume on interior velocity and trails it on
pressure, level on eddy viscosity (@sec-nb-ratevol-verdict:
GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA 0.87 / 1.42 / 0.98 under linear routing at
5e-4, 0.95 / 1.56 / 0.97 under cosine at 1e-3). That was a single-dataset
standing. AirfRANS is the second dataset and a second regime:
two-dimensional incompressible k-omega SST RANS around NACA airfoils, 800
training and 200 test cases of the full split, converted to native
DomainMesh files (@sec-nb-airfrans-plan, @sec-nb-airfrans-prereg). Six
lanes trained for 500 epochs at 100,000 interior queries per case (ISLA
linear 5e-4, ISLA cosine 1e-3, GeoTransolver-volume 1e-3; seeds 42 and 43)
and were scored in float32 at 100,000 queries on the 200 test cases.
Reduction `results/airfrans_reduce_2026-09-22.py`, artifact
`results/airfrans_reduction_2026-09-22.json`.

**Bars (preregistered).** Reproduced if GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA falls
on the same side of one as on DrivAerML (pressure below one, velocity
above one) with both seed-paired ratios agreeing in sign; refuted for a
field if the ratio crosses one with seeds agreeing; eddy viscosity
reported without a prior.

**What we saw** (relative L2 over the 200 test cases, seed means with
seeds):

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---|---|---|---|
| GeoTransolver-volume, 1e-3 | 0.0277 (0.0268 / 0.0286) | 0.0379 (0.0370 / 0.0389) | 0.0293 (0.0296 / 0.0290) |
| ISLA, linear routing, 5e-4 | 0.0348 (0.0391 / 0.0306) | 0.0195 (0.0217 / 0.0173) | 0.0344 (0.0401 / 0.0286) |
| ISLA, cosine routing, 1e-3 | 0.0335 (0.0299 / 0.0372) | 0.0177 (0.0156 / 0.0199) | 0.0353 (0.0310 / 0.0396) |
| GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA linear (paired) | 0.80 (0.69 / 0.94) | 1.95 (1.71 / 2.25) | 0.85 (0.74 / 1.02) |
| GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA cosine (paired) | 0.83 (0.90 / 0.77) | 2.14 (2.38 / 1.95) | 0.83 (0.96 / 0.73) |

: AIRFRANS-INT full split, 100,000 interior queries per case, 500 epochs, float32. {#tbl-airfrans-verdict}

**Verdict.** **Reproduced on both fields with a prior, for both ISLA
arms**: pressure below one (0.80 and 0.83; every paired ratio below one),
velocity above one (1.95 and 2.14; every paired ratio above 1.7). ISLA's
velocity lead is larger on the airfoils than on the cars (about 2x against
1.4 to 1.6x) and its pressure deficit is also larger (20% against 13%, 17%
against 5%). Eddy viscosity, level on the cars, goes to GeoTransolver-volume
on the airfoils by 15 to 17%, with one paired ratio of the linear arm
crossing one (1.02) — reported, no prior, not a verdict.

**Two things to carry with the numbers.** First, ISLA's seed spread on
AirfRANS is large: 22 to 34% between the two seeds on every field for both
ISLA arms, against 2 to 7% for GeoTransolver-volume. The verdicts survive it
because every paired ratio agrees in sign, but no ISLA number on this
dataset should be quoted to better than about 15%, and the source of the
spread (200 test cases of 2-D flow at 100,000 queries; the loss reaches
its floor by epoch 300 on every lane) is not identified. Second, the two
regimes differ in what the pressure field is: gauge pressure over a 3-D
car body against nondimensional pressure over a 2-D airfoil with an
incompressible reference state; that the ordering (GeoTransolver-volume on
pressure, ISLA on velocity) is the same across them is the finding, and
the mechanism behind it is the open question the cars left open
(@sec-interior-open).

**Reading.** The interior standing is now a two-dataset result and is
written as one in @sec-interior, @sec-interior-results and
@sec-verdict: ISLA leads on interior velocity by 42 to 114%, trails on
interior pressure by 5 to 20%, and is level to 17% behind on eddy
viscosity, against GeoTransolver-volume at a third of its parameters, on
two datasets and two PDE regimes.

**Addendum (2026-09-22, later): where ISLA's seed spread lives.** The
per-case scores (200 test airfoils, `infer_step` records in the scored
metrics) say the spread is a whole-model shift, not a few cases: between
the two linear-routing seeds, 85% of the test cases are worse on seed 42
than on seed 43 on pressure, the median per-case difference is 0.005 and
the five largest differences carry 20% of the total. The three worst
cases (relative error 0.18 to 0.33 on pressure) are the same airfoils for
every arm and every seed, GeoTransolver-volume included, and carry 7 to 9%
of each arm's sum, so they are hard cases, not the spread. The validation
loss of every lane, GeoTransolver-volume included, moves by 30 to 40%
between its epoch-300, 400 and 490 readings (for example 0.00093, 0.00068,
0.00084 for ISLA linear seed 42), so the final-epoch checkpoint is a draw
from a band; that GeoTransolver-volume's scored spread is nonetheless 2 to
7% while ISLA's is 22 to 34% says ISLA's band is the wider one on this
dataset. Not pursued here: checkpoint selection or averaging would be a
protocol change and the comparison is at final epoch for every arm by the
program's rule.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, AIRFRANS-INT extrapolation splits: ISLA (cosine 1e-3) and GeoTransolver-volume (1e-3) on the Reynolds-number and angle-of-attack splits, two seeds {#sec-nb-airfrans-extrap-prereg}

**Setting.** AirfRANS ships two extrapolation splits: `reynolds` (504
training cases inside a Reynolds-number band, 496 test cases outside it)
and `aoa` (804 training cases inside an angle-of-attack band, 196 test
cases outside it). With the full-split lanes accepted and reduced
(@sec-nb-airfrans-verdict), eight lanes run the same two architectures on
both splits: ISLA with cosine routing at 1e-3 (the candidate default,
which matched linear routing on the full split within its seed spread) and
GeoTransolver-volume at 1e-3, seeds 42 and 43, 500 epochs, 100,000
interior queries per case, float32 scoring at 100,000 queries on each
split's test cases (group af, rows 6 to 13 of
`results/campaigns_2026-09-21/af/lanes.tsv`).

**Readout.** Per field and architecture, the *growth factor* $g$ = test
error on the extrapolation split ÷ the same architecture's full-split test
error (seed means; paired by seed for the sign test). The growth mixes
extrapolation with the smaller training set of the Reynolds split (504
against 800 cases); both architectures pay the same reduction, so the
fair readout is the ratio of growth factors, $g_\text{GT} / g_\text{ISLA}$.

**Bars.** On a field, ISLA *extrapolates better* if
$g_\text{GT} / g_\text{ISLA} > 1.10$ with both seed pairs above one;
GeoTransolver-volume extrapolates better if the ratio is below 0.90 with
both pairs below one; otherwise *no difference* (the status ledger's "a
10% difference in error growth counts"). A lane at the mean-field plateau
is reported as such and rerun at half its rate. The absolute ratios
GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA on each split are reported alongside, without
a bar (the full-split ordering is the prior: pressure below one, velocity
above one).

**Prediction.** No difference in growth on pressure on either split
(0.5); ISLA's velocity growth smaller on the Reynolds split (0.4; the
global scalar carries the Reynolds number into every slice block, where
GeoTransolver-volume embeds the inlet velocity once); no prediction for
the angle-of-attack split beyond the full-split ordering. Whatever the
outcome, the absolute ordering (ISLA on velocity, GeoTransolver-volume on
pressure) is expected to hold on both splits (0.8).

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, ROUTE-NORM at the reporting protocol, and the default decision: cosine 192 beats linear 192 by 6% on the 35-wing rung at 200,000 cells (0.1408 against 0.1502), the 510-wing linear control plateaus at 13 to 39 times the cosine loss, cosine 384 × 24 on the cars scores 0.0407 at 200,000 cells; cosine routing becomes ISLA's default {#sec-nb-routenorm-p200k-verdict}

**Setting.** ROUTE-NORM asks whether bounding the routing logits (cosine
routing at temperature 10) removes the learning-rate ceiling that linear
routing has, whose failure is total routing collapse to the mean-field
plateau (@sec-nb-routingsat-verdict), and what it costs in accuracy. The
DrivAerML half closed on 2026-09-21 (@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict):
ceiling removed on every lane, accuracy neutral at the rule rates. The
reporting-protocol half (@sec-nb-routenorm-p200k-prereg) trained cosine 192
at 1e-3, cosine 384 at 1e-3 and a linear 384 control at 1e-3 on the 35-wing
rung at 200,000 cells, and cosine 384 wide × 24 layers at 5e-4 on the 435
cars at 200,000 cells, two seeds each, float32 scoring at 200,000 cells.
The 510-wing lanes of the original design (100,000 cells; cosine 192 and
384 at 1e-3, linear 384 control) are at epoch 125 of 500 and are read here
for their validation trajectories only. Reduction
`results/routenorm_wings_reduce_2026-09-22.py`, artifact
`results/routenorm_p200k_2026-09-22.json`.

**What we saw.**

| lane | seed 42 | seed 43 | mean | reference |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| 35 wings, 200k: cosine 192, 1e-3 | 0.1418 | 0.1398 | 0.1408 | linear 192 (fleet) 0.1502; GeoTransolver 0.1098; Transolver 0.1101 |
| 35 wings, 200k: cosine 384, 1e-3 | 0.1388 | 0.1335 | 0.1361 | |
| 35 wings, 200k: linear 384, 1e-3 (control) | 0.1411 | 0.1447 | 0.1429 | trained cleanly |
| 435 cars, 200k: cosine 384 × 24, 5e-4 | 0.0407 | 0.0406 | 0.0407 | same lane at 100k 0.0407; GeoTransolver's best 0.0406 |

: ROUTE-NORM at the reporting protocol (surface pressure, float32, 200,000 cells). {#tbl-routenorm-p200k}

*Collapse clause.* The preregistered threshold ("linear control above 0.01
validation loss after epoch 20 while cosine stays below") was written in
the cars' loss units; on the wings every lane, cosine included, sits above
0.01 through epoch 500 (the 35-wing floor is 0.020), so as written the
clause cannot fire there and the reduction restates it in the units
ROUTING-SAT measured the signature in: a linear validation loss more than
three times the cosine lane's at a matched epoch after epoch 20 (the cars'
plateau was seventeen times). **On the 35-wing rung at 200,000 cells the
signature is absent**: linear 384 at 1e-3 tracks cosine 384 within 2 to 11%
on both seeds to epoch 500 and scores 0.1429, 5% behind cosine 384. **On
the 510-wing rung at 100,000 cells it is present on both seeds**: the linear
control's validation loss rises from 0.08 at epoch 0 to 0.17 at epoch 25
and sits at 0.15 through epoch 125, while cosine 384 descends to 0.004; the
ratio grows from 13 to 39 as cosine keeps improving. The ceiling therefore
depends on the training-set size as well as on width and depth: 35 wings
at 200,000 cells sit below it at width 384 and 1e-3, 510 wings at 100,000
cells sit above it. That is consistent with routing collapse being an
optimization instability whose onset needs enough gradient signal per
epoch (the 510-wing epoch has 15 times the steps), and it is recorded as
an observation, not a mechanism.

*Accuracy null.* Cosine 192 at 1e-3 scores 0.1408 against the fleet's
linear 192 row at 0.1502: **6% better, both seeds below both linear
seeds** (0.1418 / 0.1398 against 0.1504 / 0.1496). The bar was "within 2%
is null, more than 2% better is a finding": a finding. GeoTransolver ÷
cosine ISLA on this rung is 0.78 (Transolver 0.78) against 0.73 for linear
ISLA; the wing deficit narrows by five points and stays.

*Width on the wings.* Cosine 384 scores 0.1361, 3.3% below cosine 192, at
the 3% bar with a 4% seed spread on the 384 lane (0.1388 / 0.1335): width
carries on the wings at the edge of resolution, where on the cars it
carried 7% per doubling. Not resolved at two seeds; the 510-wing width
ladder (SCALE-HL) is the instrument that will.

*Best configuration at the protocol.* Cosine 384 × 24 at 200,000 cells
scores 0.04065 (0.0407 / 0.0406) against 0.04067 at 100,000: cells are
flat for it as for every other lane (ISO-COST), and it sits 0.1% above
GeoTransolver-1,024's 0.0406, level within the seed spread, at half the
parameters (68M against 143M) and 91 GB of training memory.

**Decision.** The preregistered rule made cosine the default if the
collapse clause held on both datasets and the accuracy null held on both.
Collapse: removed on the cars at every rate tried; on the wings the
510-wing control shows the signature on both seeds while both cosine lanes
train normally (interim, epoch 125, the ratio 13 to 39 leaves no room for
reversal), and the 35-wing rung shows no collapse under either form.
Accuracy: neutral on the cars (0.998), 6% better on the wings. **Cosine
routing is ISLA's class default from today** (`routing_norm="cosine"`,
temperature 10; the class change is in the same commit as this entry, with
the linear form kept as the alternative and the release tests passing).
Every evidence lane in the book trained before today uses linear routing;
the cosine twins of the evidence board (COSINE-TWINS, 14 of 18 lanes
trained) will say whether any scoreboard row moves, and the book's
scoreboard rows remain the linear-trained lanes until they do. What this
does not settle: the 510-wing final scores (SCALE-HL), whether width pays
on the wings past the 3% edge, and the mechanism that makes the ceiling
data-size dependent.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, AIRFRANS-SCALE: the training-case axis of the scaling law on a third dataset and the interior task (ISLA cosine 192 and GeoTransolver-volume on 50 / 100 / 200 / 400 / 800 AirfRANS airfoils) {#sec-nb-airfrans-scale-prereg}

**Setting.** The scaling law's DrivAerML half is closed
(@sec-nb-scalelaw-drivaerml-verdict): the reducible surface-pressure
error falls as $n^{-1.3}$ in training cases toward a floor, with the same
exponent for ISLA and GeoTransolver, and the wing half is in flight.
Both are surface tasks on three-dimensional external aerodynamics. AirfRANS
(@sec-nb-airfrans-verdict) offers a third dataset, a second PDE regime and
the interior task, at a training cost of about a minute per epoch per 800
cases. Sixteen lanes add its training-case axis: nested random subsets of
the full training split with 50, 100, 200 and 400 airfoils (seeded, each
rung containing the smaller ones; manifest splits `full_train_n50` to
`full_train_n400`), the 800-case rung being the full-split lanes already
scored. Arms: ISLA with cosine routing (the default) at 1e-3 and
GeoTransolver-volume at 1e-3, seeds 42 and 43, 500 epochs, 100,000
interior queries, float32 scoring at 100,000 queries on the 200 test
cases. One width per architecture: this is the data axis only, so the
readout is $\alpha$, not the joint law.

**Bars.** Per field (pressure, velocity, eddy viscosity) and architecture,
the local exponents between adjacent rungs and a two-parameter fit
$\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\infty + a\,n^{-\alpha}$ with the floor bounded
to $[0, 0.9 \times$ the 800-case error$]$ on the seed means. (i) *Same
exponent across architectures* if the two $\alpha$ differ by less than
their two-seed bootstrap spread, as on the cars. (ii) *Transfer across
datasets* if ISLA's $\alpha$ on AirfRANS pressure is within 0.3 of its
DrivAerML value (1.28); a larger gap is stated per dataset (the campaign
prereg's 0.1 was written for the same task on two datasets; the interior
task and the 2-D regime warrant the wider bar, fixed now). (iii) *The
ordering persists*: GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA below one on pressure and
above one on velocity at every rung with both seeds agreeing; a rung at
which a ratio crosses one is reported as a crossover. (iv) ISLA's seed
spread (22 to 34% on the full split) is reported per rung; a rung where
the spread exceeds the gap between adjacent rungs is marked unresolved.

**Prediction.** Same exponent for both architectures (0.7); ISLA's
pressure $\alpha$ within 0.3 of 1.28 (0.5, no strong prior for the
interior task); the ordering persists at every rung (0.7), with the
velocity lead widening at small $n$ if ISLA's boundary-driven structure is
the more data-efficient inductive bias for the flow field (0.5).

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, AIRFRANS-SCALE: on the airfoils the interior error follows a floorless power law in training cases for ISLA (pressure exponent 0.67, velocity 0.62, no floor at 800 airfoils); GeoTransolver-volume converts cases more slowly on pressure (0.47 to 0.51 per rung from 100 up), so its pressure lead shrinks from 45% at 100 airfoils to 17% at 800 while ISLA's velocity lead holds at about 2x {#sec-nb-airfrans-scale-verdict}

**Setting.** AIRFRANS-SCALE (@sec-nb-airfrans-scale-prereg) adds the
training-case axis of the scaling law on a third dataset, a second PDE
regime and the interior task: nested random subsets of 50, 100, 200 and
400 AirfRANS airfoils plus the 800-airfoil full split, ISLA with cosine
routing at 192 wide and 1e-3 against GeoTransolver-volume at 1e-3, two
seeds, 500 epochs, 100,000 interior queries, float32 scoring at 100,000
queries on the 200 test airfoils. All sixteen new lanes trained and scored
within nine hours of launch. Reduction
`results/airfrans_scale_reduce_2026-09-22.py`, artifact
`results/airfrans_scale_2026-09-22.json`.

**What we saw** (seed means; the seeds in the artifact; every seed pair
is closer than the gap to the neighboring rung, so no rung is unresolved):

| airfoils | ISLA pressure / velocity / eddy viscosity | GeoTransolver-volume pressure / velocity / eddy viscosity | GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA |
|--:|---|---|---|
| 50 | 0.211 / 0.085 / 0.225 | 0.161 / 0.153 / 0.220 | 0.76 / 1.81 / 0.98 |
| 100 | 0.140 / 0.059 / 0.127 | 0.077 / 0.098 / 0.096 | 0.55 / 1.67 / 0.75 |
| 200 | 0.087 / 0.038 / 0.082 | 0.055 / 0.077 / 0.070 | 0.63 / 2.04 / 0.86 |
| 400 | 0.055 / 0.025 / 0.056 | 0.038 / 0.054 / 0.045 | 0.69 / 2.15 / 0.79 |
| 800 | 0.034 / 0.018 / 0.035 | 0.028 / 0.038 / 0.029 | 0.83 / 2.14 / 0.83 |

: AIRFRANS-SCALE board (relative L2 over the 200 test airfoils, float32, two seeds, 100,000 queries, 500 epochs). {#tbl-airfrans-scale}

*ISLA's local exponents* (negative log-log slope between adjacent rungs)
are 0.59 / 0.69 / 0.66 / 0.72 on pressure and 0.53 / 0.64 / 0.57 / 0.51
on velocity across the four intervals: no bending. The bounded-floor fit
puts the floor at zero for every field (bootstrap 16th to 84th percentile
0 to 0.01 on pressure) with $\alpha$ = 0.67 (0.67 to 0.72) on pressure at
2.1% RMS, 0.62 (0.61 to 0.76) on velocity at 1.7%, 0.78 (0.67 to 0.92) on
eddy viscosity at 3.5%. **On the airfoils ISLA is on a floorless power law
at 800 training cases.**

*GeoTransolver-volume's exponents* are not constant: 1.07 between 50 and
100 airfoils on pressure, then 0.49 / 0.51 / 0.47; on velocity 0.64 then
0.35 / 0.50 / 0.52. The 50-airfoil pressure error (0.161, both seeds) sits
far above its own trend from 100 up (0.077 at 100), so the fit is poor
(6.4% RMS on pressure, 9.1% on eddy viscosity; $\alpha$ = 1.07 with a
floor of 0.022 is the fit's way of bending through that point) and its
exponents are read from the rungs at 100 and above: about 0.5 on every
field.

**Bars.** (i) *Same exponent across architectures*: **refuted on
pressure** (0.67 against 1.07 in the fit, 0.41 apart against a bootstrap
spread of 0.18; in local exponents from 100 up, 0.66 to 0.72 against 0.47
to 0.51); held on velocity (0.62 against 0.51, inside the 0.16 spread) and
eddy viscosity (0.78 against 1.02, inside 0.25). (ii) *Transfer from
DrivAerML*: **refuted**; ISLA's pressure exponent is 0.67 here against 1.28
for the reducible surface error on the cars, so the law is stated per
dataset. The two are different kinds of curve, not one curve with two
exponents: on the cars the total error bends into a floor near 0.036 and
the 1.28 describes the part above it; on the airfoils there is no floor
within reach and the total error itself falls as $n^{-0.67}$. The cars'
total-error local exponent on their first interval (27 to 54 cars, 0.74 to
0.86) is the number comparable to the airfoils' 0.59 to 0.72. (iii) *The
ordering persists*: **held at every rung, every paired ratio agreeing**
(pressure 0.76 / 0.55 / 0.63 / 0.69 / 0.83 below one; velocity 1.81 / 1.67
/ 2.04 / 2.15 / 2.14 above one). (iv) No unresolved rungs.

**Predictions against outcome.** Same exponent (0.7): refuted on pressure.
Transfer within 0.3 (0.5): refuted. Ordering persists (0.7): confirmed.
Velocity lead widening at small $n$ (0.5): refuted; the lead is smaller at
50 and 100 airfoils (1.8, 1.7) than from 200 up (2.0 to 2.2).

**Reading.** On the interior task the two architectures convert training
cases at different rates on pressure: ISLA at 0.67 per decade-ratio,
GeoTransolver-volume at about 0.5, so GeoTransolver-volume's pressure lead
is largest at 100 airfoils (ISLA 1.8 times its error) and has shrunk to 17%
at 800. Extrapolating the two local slopes from the 100-to-800 interval
(0.69 against 0.49) puts pressure parity near 2,000 airfoils; that is a
projection of fitted slopes, not a measurement, and the dataset has 1,000
cases. On velocity ISLA's lead is about 2x at every rung from 200 up and
neither exponent differs. What this changes in the book: the compute
allocation section (@sec-compute-allocation) gains the airfoil ladder
beside the car ladder and says that the case axis has two shapes (a floor
approach on the cars, a floorless power law on the airfoils), that the
exponents do not transfer across datasets or tasks, and that on the one
task where the architectures' exponents differ ISLA has the larger one. The
one anomaly, GeoTransolver-volume's 50-airfoil pressure error twice its
trend, is recorded and not explained; its ball-query local features see
fewer distinct neighborhoods at 50 airfoils, but nothing here measures
that.

## 2026-09-22 — Ruling and preregistration, REF: one reference configuration for every dataset (the recommended settings), chosen from two candidates at the reporting protocol; every evidence lane is then re-run under it {#sec-nb-ref-prereg}

**The ruling (Peter, 2026-09-22).** The book must reflect what the
architecture *is*, not how it got here: deprecated configurations
(linear routing, earlier widths) may not carry evidence; there is one
reference set of hyperparameters, as similar across datasets as possible,
and every experiment is a deviation from it; the reference sits toward the
accuracy end of the speed/accuracy axis because the headline numbers are
reported with it; the fused geometry kernel and cosine routing are part of
it (the "recommended settings"); the target is better accuracy than
GeoTransolver at lower step time and memory. The current reference
(192 wide, 12 layers, linear routing, the eager geometry region) fails all
three: it was the width that trained at 1e-3 under linear routing, not the
width the capacity ladders favor.

**Candidates** (both: 256 slices, MLP ratio 4, cosine routing at
temperature 10, the fused geometry kernel, the RMS-pairwise-distance unit,
the class default query mass `source_total` on the interior tasks;
learning rate 5e-4, the width rule 1e-3 × 192/384):

- **R1**: 384 wide, 12 layers (34.3M parameters). Cars at 100,000 cells:
  0.0413 (@sec-nb-routenorm-cars-verdict); 35 wings at 200,000: 0.1361 at
  1e-3 (@sec-nb-routenorm-p200k-verdict); 22 GB at 100,000 cells.
- **R2**: 384 wide, 24 layers (68.3M). Cars: 0.0407 at 100,000 and
  200,000 cells, level with GeoTransolver-1,024's 0.0406 at half its
  parameters; 91 GB at 200,000 cells, 0.41 s per step.

**Lanes** (group `ref`, `kernel/ref/lanes.tsv`, 32 lanes, snapshot
`code_ref` = the recipe's pinned package with the current ISLA class
overlaid; model files `isla_surface_ref`, `isla_volume_ref`,
`isla_volume_airfrans_ref`; two seeds; 500 epochs; bf16; float32 scoring
through the fleet pump): R1 and R2 on DrivAerML Surface (435 cars,
200,000 cells), HiLiftAeroML 35 / 210 / 510 wings (200,000 cells),
DrivAerML Volume (200,000 cells and queries) and AirfRANS (800 airfoils,
100,000 queries); R1 at 1e-3 on the cars and the 35-wing rung as the rate
control; GeoTransolver at 512 wide (35.8M, the parameter match to R1) at
its best rate 3e-3 on the cars and the 35-wing rung. The GeoTransolver-256
(recipe default) and Transolver rows at 200,000 cells exist for every
rung (@sec-nb-proto200k-fleet-prereg). Step time (logged per epoch) and
peak memory (from the per-node GPU sampler) are read from every lane.

**Selection rule (fixed now).** The reference is the smallest candidate
whose surface-pressure error is within 1.5% of the better candidate's on
*both* DrivAerML Surface and the 35-wing rung; if R2 beats R1 by more than
1.5% on either, R2 is the reference and its cost is the price. The rate
control decides the reference rate per width rule only if 1e-3 beats
5e-4 by more than 1.5% on both surface datasets. The chosen configuration
becomes the ISLA class defaults (hidden, layers) and the recipe's
`isla_surface` / `isla_volume` files; every evidence lane (pose, training
law, biased draw, interior standing, territory, the ladders, deflection)
is then re-run under it (REF-BOARD), and the book's scoreboard, figures and
claims are restated from those lanes alone; the linear-routed and 192-wide
lanes leave the chapters (the architecture chapter keeps one section on
the routing forms).

**Bars for the comparison with GeoTransolver's recipe default** (256
wide, 27.6M) at 200,000 cells, per dataset: accuracy ratio
GeoTransolver-256 ÷ reference, step-time ratio and peak-memory ratio
(reference ÷ GeoTransolver-256, below one is cheaper). *The recommended
settings beat the baseline* on a dataset if the accuracy ratio is above
1.03 with seeds agreeing and both cost ratios are at or below one; *cost
parity* if the accuracy ratio is above 1.03 and a cost ratio is within 1.2;
otherwise stated as measured.

**Prediction.** R1 within 1.5% of R2 on the cars (0.4: the cosine ladder
had 0.0413 against 0.0407, 1.5% apart) and on the wings (0.5); reference =
R2 (0.55). Against GeoTransolver-256 at 200,000 cells the reference is more
accurate on the cars by 6 to 9% (0.8) and on the 35-wing rung by 20% or
more behind still (the wing deficit; 0.8: GeoTransolver 0.1098 against
R1's 0.1361); step time of R1 with the fused kernel at or below
GeoTransolver-256's (0.6), memory below (0.7); R2 above on both (0.8).
