## 2026-09-22 — Book overhaul (Peter's ruling): the book is rewritten as thirteen chapters with one home per concept, a centerpiece chapter for the two invariances, task names on every comparison, and linear routing confined to the architecture chapter {#sec-nb-book-overhaul-2026-09-22}

**The ruling.** Peter, today: the book must reflect what *is*, not how we
got here (deprecated experiments are re-run, never kept as evidence);
repetition is penalized; discretization invariance and rigid-motion
equivariance each need a centerpiece; "DrivAerML" must name its Surface or
Volume task; the accuracy story must agree between text and figures;
obvious figure gaps must be filled by measurement; one reference
configuration (the recommended settings) underlies every experiment; more
datasets, including non-aerodynamic steady PDEs, with existing literature
sets preferred; AeroZoo named.

**What was done.** Two fresh-context audits
(`results/book_audit_2026-09-22/structure_audit.md`, `figures_audit.md`)
mapped every duplicated concept (parity stated about fourteen times, the
10:1-bias factors eleven, the routing-ceiling story nine), every
path-dependent passage, every linear-routed figure and table, twelve
contradictions, and the aerodynamics-only framing; a rewrite plan
(`rewrite_plan.md`) fixed the new chapter list, the writing rules and a
numbers policy for the transition. Four editors composed the chapters from
the sources; integration repointed 26 cross-references to the new homes and
the full render is clean. The structure: index (one thesis table, dataset
and task per row); 01 the problem and the general operator interface
(boundary cells, $K$ global directions, $S$ global scalars, optional
boundary data; external aerodynamics as the benchmark instance); 02 ISLA
one idea at a time (the routing forms and the linear ceiling table live
here and nowhere else); 03 the two invariances (new centerpiece: the
contracts, the canonicalization argument, the four sampling draws, the
acceptance criterion); 04 the forward pass; 05 baselines, datasets and
protocol (with the one paragraph that states the evidence lanes'
configuration); 06 using ISLA (one configuration); 07 surface accuracy and
data efficiency; 08 discretization and pose evidence; 09 capacity, scaling
laws and cost; 10 boundary to interior (cosine rows are the rows); 11
limits; 12 program status (the one chapter with dates); 13 design
decisions; this notebook. Retired as files: the scoreboard, baselines,
data-efficiency, accuracy-and-robustness, architecture, interior, using,
limits, status and decisions chapters of the previous numbering.

**What changed in the numbers.** Cosine ISLA is the ISLA row wherever a
cosine lane exists at the protocol (35-wing rung 0.1408; DrivAerML Volume
1e-3; AirfRANS; 384 x 24 at 200,000 cells); the wing rungs' GeoTransolver
rows use the 3e-3 lanes where they exist (210 cases 0.88, 21 geometries
0.95; @sec-nb-wing-gt-rate-erratum); the cost figure carries step time and
memory only, filled to 600,000 tokens from the training-log peaks pending
the reference cost sweep; failed fits are drawn as points; the floor band
is computed. The surface-task standings (DrivAerML Surface 435 cars and
ladder, pose, training law, density, territories, the other wing rungs) are
still the 192-wide linear-routed lanes and are stated as such once, in
@sec-protocol; they are replaced as REF and REF-BOARD land
(@sec-nb-ref-prereg).

**Still to do in the book.** Swap the surface artifacts for the reference
lanes; add the cost-sweep artifact; add the new datasets' chapter section
when the first conversions train; remove the transition paragraph.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, SOLIDS: the first non-aerodynamic steady-PDE datasets, PLAID Tensile2d (2-D elasto-viscoplastic tension, load and material as global scalars, labeled edges) and GINOT Bracket Lug (3-D elastoplastic lug, pressed hole), full-data comparisons and training-case ladders {#sec-nb-solids-prereg}

**Setting.** Peter's 2026-09-22 ruling asks for datasets beyond
aerodynamics, referenced in the literature, with boundary conditions that
are or can be labeled and that vary strongly. Two are converted
(`results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/`): **PLAID Tensile2d** (Safran;
CC-BY-SA-4.0; 702 quasi-static elasto-viscoplastic tension cases on a
square with two semicircular cut-outs; unstructured triangle meshes of 6 to
11 thousand nodes; the top edge carries a uniform pressure $P$ that varies
per case, the bottom edge is fixed, one corner node is pinned; five
constitutive scalars $p_1 \ldots p_5$ vary; outputs displacement, plastic
strain $q$, and the stresses $\sigma_{11}, \sigma_{22}, \sigma_{12}$; the
200 test cases ship without targets, so a seed-0 draw of 100 cases from
`train_500` is the validation split and the remaining 400 the largest
training rung) and **GINOT Bracket Lug** (CC BY 4.0; 3,000 elastoplastic
lugs with three geometry parameters and a pressure of 50 to 100 MPa on the
lower half of the hole, the far end fixed; hex meshes of 5 to 15 thousand
nodes; output von Mises stress; the fixed and pressed faces are identified
geometrically from the paper's description, with face areas matching to
0.1%; a seed-0 split of 2,400 training and 600 test lugs with nested
300 / 600 / 1,200 rungs). Both are solids: the field lives on the whole
mesh, so every node is an interior query carrying its signed distance to
the boundary, and the boundary is the outer surface with per-cell labels
(fixed, loaded, pinned; the applied pressure on loaded cells). Neither
problem has a global direction ($K = 0$), so ISLA runs with the eager
geometry region (the fused kernel requires $K = 1$); the global scalars
enter standardized over the training split. Three-epoch smoke lanes for
ISLA and GeoTransolver passed on both datasets (val relative L2 after
three epochs: Tensile2d displacement 0.49 ISLA / 0.17 GeoTransolver, lug
von Mises 0.29 / 0.46; warm-up numbers, not verdicts).

**Lanes** (group `so`, `kernel/so/lanes.tsv`, 44 lanes, snapshot
`code_ref`, 500 epochs, every node used, two seeds, bf16 training, float32
scoring on the validation split): ISLA R1 (384 x 12, cosine routing,
`n_boundary_scalars = 4`, global scalars 6 / 4, query tokens with the
signed distance, 5e-4) and GeoTransolver at 512 wide (the agent's yaml,
1e-3, with the nodal boundary tags in its local embedding and the global
scalars in its global embedding) on the Tensile2d ladder 32 / 64 / 125 /
250 / 400 and the lug ladder 300 / 600 / 1,200 / 2,400; ISLA R2 (384 x 24)
and GeoTransolver-256 at the largest rung of each.

**Bars.** (i) *Standing at full data*, per field: GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA
with paired-seed sign; no prior, reported. Headline fields: displacement
and the three stresses on Tensile2d (plastic strain $q$ is reported but
heavy-tailed under z-scoring and excluded from the headline), von Mises on
the lug. (ii) *Data exponent*: bounded-floor fit per field and
architecture as in the AirfRANS ladder; same exponent across architectures
within the bootstrap; exponents stated per dataset. (iii) *Width and
depth*: R2 within 1.5% of R1 at the largest rung means depth does not pay
on solids; GeoTransolver-512 within 1.5% of 256 means width does not pay
for it. (iv) *Trainability*: a lane at the mean-field plateau is reported
and rerun at half its rate.

**Prediction.** GeoTransolver leads on Tensile2d stresses at 400 cases
(0.6; it sees the nodal tags at every node, ISLA only on the boundary),
ISLA leads on the lug von Mises (0.5); both data exponents between 0.4 and
0.9 on both datasets (0.6); same exponents within bootstrap (0.6); depth
pays on neither (0.6).

**Addendum (2026-09-22, later): the DrivAerML Volume REF lanes hang under
the fused kernel.** All four volume lanes (384 wide, 200,000 boundary cells
and 200,000 interacting queries, fused geometry kernel) stopped logging at
epoch 0 after 12 (seed 42) or 19 (seed 43) steps while the job stayed
alive; cancelled and restarted, each stopped at the same step with the
same loss to six digits, and the node's GPU no longer answered an overlap
step. The 192-wide cosine volume lanes trained under the fused kernel
without incident, so the trigger is the 384-wide volume shape on a
particular training case. The four lanes are retired with blocked markers
and replaced by eager-kernel twins (rows 32 to 35 of `kernel/ref/lanes.tsv`,
`++model.geo_kernel=eager`); the hang is an engineering task with the
reproducer recorded (case at step 13 of seed 42's epoch 0).

`results/cost_sweep_ref_gb300_bf16_2026-09-22.json`).

| arm | parameters | 100k: ms / GiB | 200k | 400k | 600k |
|---|--:|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA 384 x 12 (R1) | 34.3M | 64 / 17.8 | 117 / 34.9 | 224 / 69.3 | 332 / 103.6 |
| ISLA 384 x 24 (R2) | 68.3M | 129 / 34.8 | 231 / 68.4 | 441 / 135.7 | 656 / 203.0 |
| ISLA 192 x 12 | 8.9M | 57 / 10.9 | 94 / 21.7 | 178 / 43.2 | 266 / 64.6 |

**Reading.** Every arm is linear in tokens above 100,000 (the slice

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, AIRFRANS-INT extrapolation splits: outside the training Reynolds band and outside the training angle-of-attack band, ISLA's interior error grows less than GeoTransolver-volume's on pressure (growth ratios 1.39 and 1.78) and eddy viscosity (1.52 and 1.81), the same on velocity (0.91 and 1.04); on both splits ISLA leads on every field, pressure included {#sec-nb-airfrans-extrap-verdict}

**Setting.** The preregistration (@sec-nb-airfrans-extrap-prereg) trained
ISLA (192 wide, cosine routing, 1e-3) and GeoTransolver-volume (1e-3) on
AirfRANS's two extrapolation splits, `reynolds` (504 training airfoils
inside a Reynolds-number band, 496 test airfoils outside it) and `aoa`
(804 inside an angle-of-attack band, 196 outside), two seeds, 500 epochs,
100,000 queries, float32 scoring at 100,000 queries on each split's test
cases. The readout is the growth factor $g$ = extrapolation-split test
error ÷ the same architecture's full-split test error, and the bar is the
ratio $g_\text{GT} / g_\text{ISLA}$: above 1.10 with both seed pairs above
one, ISLA extrapolates better; below 0.90 with both below one,
GeoTransolver-volume does. Reduction
`results/airfrans_extrap_reduce_2026-09-22.py`, artifact
`results/airfrans_extrap_2026-09-22.json`.

**What we saw** (relative L2 on the split's test cases; growth factors
against the full-split values 0.0335 / 0.0177 / 0.0353 for ISLA and 0.0277
/ 0.0379 / 0.0293 for GeoTransolver-volume):

| split | field | ISLA error (growth) | GeoTransolver-volume error (growth) | $g_\text{GT}/g_\text{ISLA}$ (paired) | GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA on the split |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reynolds | pressure | 0.0551 (1.64) | 0.0634 (2.29) | 1.39 (1.29, 1.49) | 1.15 |
| Reynolds | velocity | 0.0256 (1.45) | 0.0501 (1.32) | 0.91 (0.83, 0.99) | 1.95 |
| Reynolds | eddy viscosity | 0.0683 (1.93) | 0.0860 (2.93) | 1.52 (1.12, 1.99) | 1.26 |
| angle of attack | pressure | 0.0719 (2.14) | 0.1059 (3.82) | 1.78 (1.74, 1.80) | 1.47 |
| angle of attack | velocity | 0.0291 (1.64) | 0.0649 (1.71) | 1.04 (1.11, 0.94) | 2.23 |
| angle of attack | eddy viscosity | 0.0886 (2.51) | 0.1330 (4.54) | 1.81 (1.84, 1.68) | 1.50 |

: AIRFRANS-INT extrapolation splits (two seeds; ISLA seeds within 4% on every field, GeoTransolver-volume's within 7% on the Reynolds split and 15 to 40% apart on the angle-of-attack split). {#tbl-airfrans-extrap}

**Verdict.** **ISLA extrapolates better on pressure and on eddy viscosity
on both splits** (growth ratios 1.39 and 1.78 on pressure, 1.52 and 1.81
on eddy viscosity, every paired ratio above one); **on velocity the two
architectures' errors grow alike** (0.91 and 1.04, seeds straddling one on
both splits). The consequence is a crossover: inside the training
distribution GeoTransolver-volume leads ISLA on pressure by 17%
(@sec-nb-airfrans-verdict); outside the Reynolds band ISLA leads by 15%,
outside the angle-of-attack band by 47%, and its velocity lead widens
from 2.1x to 2.2x. Eddy viscosity, GeoTransolver-volume's by 17% in
distribution, is ISLA's by 26% and 50% outside. GeoTransolver-volume's
seeds also diverge under extrapolation (its angle-of-attack pressure seeds
are 0.114 and 0.098) where ISLA's stay within 4%.

**Predictions against outcome.** No difference in growth on pressure
(0.5): refuted, ISLA's growth is smaller on both splits. ISLA's velocity
growth smaller on the Reynolds split (0.4): refuted, no difference. The
full-split ordering holds on both splits (0.8): confirmed on velocity and
inverted in ISLA's favor on pressure and eddy viscosity.

**Reading and caveats.** This is the first measurement of ISLA's
generalization across a physical-regime boundary, and it goes the way the
architecture's premise predicts: a model whose learned maps see only
invariant scalars, the boundary geometry and a standardized global
condition vector degrades more gracefully when the condition vector leaves
its training range than one that concatenates coordinates and the raw
condition into every token. Two caveats keep it a single-dataset,
single-task finding: the Reynolds split trains on 504 cases against the
full split's 800, so part of every growth factor is data-size (both
architectures pay it, which is why the ratio of growths is the readout);
and AirfRANS is two-dimensional. The HiLiftAeroML regime splits (angle of
attack and stall), unmeasured for ISLA at the protocol, are the second
dataset for this claim. The book states the result in the interior chapter
and in the limits chapter's regime section, labeled single dataset.

## 2026-09-22 — Root cause of the volume-lane hang: a Lustre write-lock wait on writable shared memory maps of one DrivAerML case (`run_397`), not the fused geometry kernel; the fix is read-only datasets {#sec-nb-volume-hang-root-cause}

**The symptom** (@sec-nb-ref-acceptance addenda): every 384-wide REF lane
on the DrivAerML Volume task stopped logging at epoch 0 after 12 (seed 42)
or 19 (seed 43) steps, fused and eager alike, with one GPU idle and three
spinning in the collective, and did so again on restart at the same step.

**What was measured.** The fused kernel was exonerated on three counts: its
grid and blocks depend on token and slice counts only, with every load and
store masked and no index product near the 32-bit limit at 400,000 tokens;
a random-input sweep at 384 wide over ten boundary counts around the
dataset's (199,999 to 65,536 cells, 200,000 queries) completed on every
configuration with fused and eager agreeing to 0.4% under bf16 and
gradients to 0.6%; and case-faithful single-GPU steps on four suspected
cars ran at 0.38 s and 88 GB. Reconstructing the recipe's sampler order
placed one case, `run_397`, exactly one prefetch slot past the last logged
step on the idle rank for both seeds. In a four-rank reproduction that rank
never entered its forward pass, held only `run_397`'s files as writable
shared memory maps, and had a thread waiting inside the Lustre distributed
lock manager. In a single-process reproduction the same case blocked the
loader indefinitely with the default mapping and loaded in 32 to 44
seconds with read-only mapping, twice each.

**Mechanism.** The mesh reader loads cases through tensordict memory maps,
which map owner-writable files read-write and shared; page faults through
such a map take Lustre *write* extent locks, and when several lanes on
different nodes (the same-seed R1 and R2 lanes and their twins, launched
in lockstep) fault the same case, the requests wait on one another without
end. Plain reads of the same files take shared read locks and complete in
seconds.

**Fix and consequences.** The dataset trees are made read-only (`chmod -R
a-w`), which makes tensordict map them read-only; the eager and
checkpointed-eager volume twins (rows 32 to 37) are retired and the fused
volume lanes (rows 16, 17, 20, 21) relaunched with their blocked markers
lifted. The fused kernel stays the default. The engineering follow-up
(@sec-program-status): the mesh reader should map dataset files read-only
regardless of permissions, since datasets are immutable artifacts; that is
a `physicsnemo.datapipes` change, recorded as a task. The earlier addenda
that attributed the hang to the kernel are superseded by this entry.

**Addendum (2026-09-22, later).** The reader change landed in the main
tree (commit `a32a5cc5`: a re-entrant `read_only_memory_maps` context
wraps every mesh load in `physicsnemo.datapipes.readers.mesh`, with
tests). Deploying that file verbatim into the `code_ref` cluster snapshot
was a mistake: the snapshot's `physicsnemo.mesh` is the older pinned API
and lacks a name the current reader imports, so every new chain link of
the REF campaign failed at import and the chain guard stood 24 lanes down
(the four fused volume lanes were still queued and escaped). The
snapshot's own reader was restored with only the read-only context patched
in, the import-error markers were lifted, and the 24 lanes resumed from
their checkpoints; the six retired eager-twin markers stand and their
leftover chain links were cancelled. Lesson for the record: a pinned
snapshot receives patches, never whole files from the moving tree.

The relaunched fused volume lanes step under the read-only datasets:
R1 (384 x 12) at 0.38 s per step and 95 GB, R2 (384 x 24) at 0.77 s and
181 GB, against the eager twins' 0.98 s and 161 GB (R1) and out of memory
(R2). The fused kernel is thus 2.6x faster and 41% leaner than eager on
the DrivAerML Volume task at 200,000 surface cells and 200,000 queries,
which settles the memory question that had motivated the checkpointed
twins.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, SOLIDS-FRAME: ISLA fits the Tensile2d training set but its validation error is 20 to 60 times GeoTransolver's; frame-vector variants and three controls to find out why {#sec-nb-solids-frame-prereg}

**Setting.** The SOLIDS campaign (@sec-nb-solids-prereg) trains ISLA R1
(384 wide, 12 layers, cosine routing, no global vector, eager geometry
region) and GeoTransolver-512 on PLAID Tensile2d, a two-dimensional
elasto-viscoplastic tension problem whose outputs are the displacement
vector, the plastic strain $q$, and the three in-plane stress components
$\sigma_{11}, \sigma_{22}, \sigma_{12}$ in the laboratory frame. The
first validation tables are in, and they show a failure of a kind not seen
on any aerodynamic dataset.

**The symptom.** At 32 training cases after 62 epochs, ISLA's *training*
losses per field match GeoTransolver's (Huber, z-scored: $\sigma_{12}$
0.006 against 0.004, displacement 0.022 against 0.010), but its
*validation* losses are 20 to 60 times larger ($\sigma_{11}$ 0.141 against
0.007, $\sigma_{22}$ 0.088 against 0.005, $\sigma_{12}$ 0.367 against
0.006, displacement 0.324 against 0.015; plastic strain equal at 0.003).
The validation relative L2 of $\sigma_{12}$ is 1.21, worse than predicting
zero. The same gap holds at every rung of the ladder in its first epochs
(ISLA validation totals 0.13 to 0.17 against GeoTransolver's 0.005 to
0.03), so it is not a small-data artifact. On the GINOT lug, where the one
output (von Mises stress) is a rotation invariant, ISLA R1 at 300 lugs
reaches a validation loss of 3.8e-5 (seed 43) against GeoTransolver's
3.9e-5. ISLA memorizes Tensile2d and generalizes the lug.

**Hypotheses.** *H-frame*: ISLA's scalar head is invariant under
rotations and reflections (its features are dot products), but
$\sigma_{11}, \sigma_{22}, \sigma_{12}$ are components in a fixed
laboratory frame, so an invariant head can represent them only by
reconstructing that frame from the geometry (the loaded edge's normal gives
$+y$; the pinned corner and any asymmetry of the cut-outs give $\pm x$).
$\sigma_{12}$ is odd under the reflection $x \to -x$, which no invariant
can express when the geometry is mirror-symmetric, and the z-scored
displacement target carries a constant laboratory-frame offset (the
subtracted mean) that an equivariant vector head can only produce from the
same reconstructed frame. With 32 cases the network resolves this by
memorizing case fingerprints; the frame reconstruction does not
generalize. *H-position*: the failure is in how positions enter (through
point-to-anchor invariants only) rather than in the output frame, and any
absolute coordinate input would repair it. *H-poison*: the one odd field
$\sigma_{12}$ drives the trunk into memorization and the other fields
follow. *H-conditioning*: the six global scalars reach ISLA's tokens less
effectively than GeoTransolver's global embedding, and no frame input
repairs the gap.

**Lanes** (group `sf`, `kernel/sf/lanes.tsv`, 8 lanes, `code_ref`, 500
epochs, seed 42, rungs 32 and 400; validation every ten epochs on
`val_100`). `frame1`: the load direction $+y$ as ISLA's one global vector
(`n_global_vectors = 1`; the fused kernel then applies, so this is exactly
the R1 layout of the reference configuration). `frame2`: the full in-plane
frame $(+x, +y)$ as two global vectors (eager). `leak` (diagnostic only;
breaks the invariance contract): the absolute coordinates appended to the
per-query scalars. `nosig12`: the baseline model and dataset without the
$\sigma_{12}$ head. The frame vectors are constants written into
`global_data` by a `SetDomainGlobalField` transform
(`plaid_tensile2d_frame.yaml`); the model yamls are in
`results/campaigns_2026-09-22/sf/conf/`.

**Predictions and bars** (validation loss per field at epoch 100 and at
the end, against the baseline ISLA lane at the same rung and seed). Under
H-frame: `frame2` and `leak` both bring every field within 2x of
GeoTransolver-512, `frame1` repairs $\sigma_{11}$, $\sigma_{22}$ and
$\sigma_{22}$-like quantities but leaves $\sigma_{12}$ above 0.1, and
`nosig12` does not repair the remaining fields. Under H-position: `leak`
repairs, `frame1` and `frame2` do not. Under H-poison: `nosig12` repairs
the remaining fields and the frame variants do not. Under H-conditioning:
nothing repairs. Prior: H-frame 0.6, H-position 0.2, H-poison 0.1,
H-conditioning 0.1. Consequence if H-frame holds: tensor-valued targets
need either the laboratory frame as global vector inputs (the principled
route when the frame is physical, as gravity or a load axis is) or an
equivariant rank-2 head; the book's statement of ISLA's output contract
(scalars invariant, vectors equivariant) gains the missing clause.

## 2026-09-22 — Interim verdict, SOLIDS-FRAME at 32 cases: the laboratory frame as global vectors repairs ISLA's Tensile2d generalization (validation total 0.063 to 0.0026); the load axis alone repairs everything but the odd component; removing that component repairs nothing {#sec-nb-solids-frame-interim}

**Setting.** @sec-nb-solids-frame-prereg found ISLA fitting the PLAID
Tensile2d training set while its validation error stayed 20 to 60 times
GeoTransolver's, and preregistered four hypotheses with eight lanes. The
32-case lanes have reached epochs 100 to 150 (validation every ten epochs
on the 100 held-out cases; Huber losses on z-scored fields; the frameless
baseline is the SOLIDS lane at the same seed, now at epoch 378 and
plateaued since epoch 100). The numbers below are the latest validation
tables; the 400-case lanes are at epoch 10 to 14 and report at the end.

| lane (32 cases, seed 42) | epoch | $\sigma_{11}$ | $\sigma_{22}$ | $\sigma_{12}$ | displacement | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA R1, no frame (SOLIDS baseline) | 378 | 0.160 | 0.083 | 0.389 | 0.299 | 0.063 |
| ISLA R1, `frame1` ($+y$ as the one global vector) | 149 | 0.0076 | 0.0062 | **0.416** | 0.0216 | 0.0123 |
| ISLA R1, `frame2` ($+x, +y$ as two global vectors) | 100 | 0.0119 | 0.0091 | 0.0070 | 0.0223 | 0.0026 |
| ISLA R1, `leak` (absolute coordinates as query scalars; not invariant) | 131 | 0.0098 | 0.0101 | 0.0080 | 0.0191 | 0.0025 |
| ISLA R1, `nosig12` (no $\sigma_{12}$ head) | 148 | 0.114 | 0.074 | — | 0.294 | 0.081 |
| GeoTransolver-512 | 369 | 0.0019 | 0.0009 | 0.0011 | 0.0068 | 0.00015 |

: Validation Huber loss per field (z-scored), PLAID Tensile2d, 32 training cases, seed 42, latest table of each lane; GeoTransolver at epoch 90 stood at 0.00146 total, the epoch at which `frame2` stands at 0.0026. Plastic strain $q$ is 0.004 to 0.007 in every lane and omitted. Source: `runs/<lane>/train.log` on AGA. {#tbl-solids-frame-interim}

**What we saw.** The pattern is the one H-frame predicted, term for term.
*(i)* The load axis alone (`frame1`) brings $\sigma_{11}$, $\sigma_{22}$
and the displacement down by 14 to 21 times, to within 4 to 7 times
GeoTransolver, while $\sigma_{12}$ stays at 0.416, as bad as without any
frame: $\sigma_{12}$ is odd under the reflection $x \to -x$, and with only
$+y$ supplied no dot-product invariant can tell $+x$ from $-x$ (the book's
statement that ISLA's scalar outputs are reflection-invariant,
@sec-isla-heads, is exactly the obstruction). *(ii)* The full in-plane
frame (`frame2`) repairs $\sigma_{12}$ as well (0.389 to 0.0070) and
brings the total to 0.0026 at epoch 100, 1.8 times GeoTransolver at the
same epoch, inside the preregistered 2x bar. *(iii)* The coordinate leak
matches `frame2` field for field (0.0025 against 0.0026), so absolute
positions add nothing beyond the frame: H-position is refuted. *(iv)*
Dropping the $\sigma_{12}$ head leaves the other fields at the frameless
values (0.114 / 0.074 / 0.294): the odd field does not poison the trunk,
H-poison is refuted, and since two frame inputs suffice H-conditioning is
refuted as well. The frameless lane's training losses of 1e-4 against
validation losses of 0.1 to 0.4 are memorization; with the frame the
training losses rise to 4e-3 and the validation losses fall a hundredfold.

**Why it matters.** ISLA's output contract has a clause the aerodynamic
datasets never exercised: **a scalar output is an invariant of the input
vector set, so a quantity defined as a component in a frame is
representable only when that frame is part of the input.** Pressure, von
Mises stress and plastic strain are true scalars and need nothing; the
components $\sigma_{ij} = e_i^{\mathsf T} \sigma\, e_j$ are invariants of
the set augmented with $e_i, e_j$, and the principled input is the frame
itself as global vectors ($K = 2$ in the plane, $K = 3$ in space). This is
not a leak of an absolute frame: rotating the body *and* the frame vectors
together leaves the components unchanged, which is the correct covariance
of frame components, and the vector heads keep their equivariance. The
displacement failed without the frame for a second reason of the same
kind: z-scoring subtracts a constant laboratory-frame mean vector from an
equivariant target. GeoTransolver has no such clause because it reads
absolute coordinates; that is why the 32-case gap was invisible on every
aerodynamic dataset and immediate on this one. The GINOT lug, whose one
output is the von Mises invariant, never showed the failure.

**Consequences.** The frameless Tensile2d ISLA lanes at 64, 125 and 250
cases and the frameless R2 pair are superseded (blocked markers); the
32- and 400-case frameless R1 pairs keep running as the ablation record.
The Tensile2d ladder is relaunched with the frame configuration
(`isla_tensile2d_frame2.yaml` with `plaid_tensile2d_frame.yaml`; rows 44
to 53 of `kernel/so/lanes.tsv`, 10 lanes), and the two `frame2` lanes of
this campaign serve as the seed-42 members at 32 and 400 cases. One
engineering item follows: the fused geometry kernel accepts one global
vector only, so frame-component problems run the eager region until the
kernel takes $K \le 3$. Verdict pending at 400 cases (bar unchanged:
`frame2` within 2x of GeoTransolver per field; the SOLIDS standing bars
then apply to the frame lanes).

## 2026-09-22 — Dataset scout: GNOT Heat2d deferred (no license, 600-node meshes, no connectivity); OLBC (CC BY 4.0, random labeled Dirichlet/Neumann/Robin segments, Poisson and elasticity) and DeepJEB++ (ODC-By, 15,360 brackets, four load directions) promoted {#sec-nb-datasets-scout-2026-09-22}

**Setting.** Peter's ruling asks for literature steady-PDE datasets with
labeled and strongly varying boundary conditions beyond aerodynamics
(@sec-nb-solids-prereg covers the first two). A scouting agent resolved the
open questions on GNOT Heat2d and checked the two alternatives named in the
scout notes; the facts below were read from the files or the papers, not
inferred.

**GNOT Heat2d** (Hao et al., ICML 2023): the repository and the Google
Drive folder carry **no license** (an issue asking for one went
unanswered), so converted files could not be redistributed. The released
split is 1,000 train / 100 test; each sample is a point cloud of 365 to
1,089 nodes with **no connectivity**, the top-edge Dirichlet temperature
sampled at 16 or 17 nodes, two spline interfaces as point clouds, the
bottom edge at zero temperature, and a dummy zero global scalar; the
side-wall condition is undocumented and the data are not periodic despite
the paper. Only GNOT (4.13e-2) and MMET (3.36e-2) report numbers;
Transolver has none. At 600 nodes it is 300 times below the reporting
protocol. **Deferred**: it would be a mechanism rung at best and cannot be
shared.

**OLBC** (Mousavi, Mishra, De Lorenzis; Zenodo, **CC BY 4.0**): 18
datasets of 8,448 train / 256 test samples each on unstructured triangle
meshes of 12 to 18 thousand nodes (9 Poisson on circle, square and
boomerang domains with Dirichlet, mixed, and mixed-plus-source conditions;
6 linear elasticity in steel and bone on hollow geometries; 3
hyperelasticity in rubber). Every sample carries randomly placed and sized
boundary segments with **randomly assigned Dirichlet, Neumann or Robin
type and value**, plus signed distance and its gradient, the source, the
solution and, for elasticity, strain and Cauchy stress. This is exactly the
labeled, strongly varying boundary-condition stress test the ruling asks
for, and the stress targets are components, so the frame clause of
@sec-nb-solids-frame-interim applies from the start. Baselines are BENO,
RIGNO and GAOT only; GeoTransolver will be trained under our protocol. Cost:
about 16 GB per dataset in NetCDF.

**DeepJEB++** (Yoo et al., KAIST, 2026; Hugging Face, **ODC-By 1.0**):
15,360 jet-engine brackets as surface meshes of about 50 thousand
vertices with clamped-bolt and loaded-lug vertex index sets, and per-node
displacement and von Mises stress under **four load directions**
(vertical, horizontal, diagonal, torsional). The load direction is a
genuine global vector ($K = 1$, the fused-kernel layout), the boundary
labels are explicit, and the geometry family is large. Cost: 61 GB.

**Decision.** OLBC first (two datasets: one Poisson mixed-condition set
and one linear-elasticity set, so the Poisson case gives a scalar-only
$K = 0$ problem and the elasticity case a frame-component problem), then
DeepJEB++; Heat2d deferred. Conversion follows the Tensile2d converter
pattern to native DomainMesh files; each dataset enters the book only with
GeoTransolver trained under the fair-comparison protocol and a per-dataset
preregistration before the first lane.

**Addendum (2026-09-22, float32 scoring of the 32- and 64-case lanes;
`results/solids_frame_2026-09-22.json`, reduction script alongside).** The
scorer's per-sample relative L2 on the 100 held-out cases at 500 epochs
(mean over cases; seeds averaged where two exist):

| lane | cases | $\sigma_{11}$ | $\sigma_{22}$ | $\sigma_{12}$ | displacement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA R1, no frame (2 seeds) | 32 | 0.450 | 0.360 | 1.199 | 0.639 |
| ISLA R1, `frame1` ($+y$) | 32 | 0.122 | 0.111 | **1.076** | 0.125 |
| ISLA R1, `frame2` ($+x,+y$; 2 seeds) | 32 | 0.112 | 0.112 | 0.102 | 0.090 |
| ISLA R1, `leak` | 32 | 0.136 | 0.131 | 0.128 | 0.101 |
| ISLA R1, `nosig12` | 32 | 0.450 | 0.378 | — | 0.655 |
| GeoTransolver-512 (2 seeds) | 32 | 0.032 | 0.028 | 0.031 | 0.041 |
| ISLA R1, `frame2` (2 seeds) | 64 | 0.054 | 0.043 | 0.050 | 0.038 |
| GeoTransolver-512 (2 seeds) | 64 | 0.021 | 0.019 | 0.021 | 0.018 |

: Float32 relative L2 on `val_100`, PLAID Tensile2d, 500 epochs. {#tbl-solids-frame-fp32}

The mechanism verdict is unchanged and sharper in these units: the frame
repairs the stresses 4 times and the displacement 7 times at 32 cases, the
$\sigma_{12}$ error falls from 1.20 (worse than predicting zero) to 0.10
only when both frame vectors are present (1.08 with $+y$ alone), the
coordinate leak is no better than the frame (slightly worse), and removing
the odd head changes nothing else. **The standing is a separate matter:**
in relative L2 GeoTransolver-512 leads the frame-configured ISLA by 3.5 to
4.5 times at 32 cases and by 2.2 to 2.6 times at 64 cases, so the
interim's "within 2x at equal epoch" (a training-loss statement at epoch
90) does not carry to the scored standing at 500 epochs. The ratio moves
toward one with cases (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA on $\sigma_{11}$ 0.29 at 32,
0.39 at 64); the 125-, 250- and 400-case rungs and the R2 pair decide the
Tensile2d standing under the SOLIDS bars, and the prereg's prediction that
GeoTransolver leads on the stresses at 400 cases stands to be tested rather
than already refuted.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, OLBC: random labeled Dirichlet/Neumann/Robin segments on a Poisson problem with a random source and on plane-strain steel elasticity with two holes; ISLA against GeoTransolver on a 512 / 2,048 / 8,448-case ladder {#sec-nb-olbc-prereg}

**Setting.** OLBC (Mousavi, Mishra and De Lorenzis, ETH; Zenodo
10.5281/zenodo.18377370, CC BY 4.0) is the labeled-boundary-condition
stress test the datasets ruling asked for (@sec-nb-datasets-scout-2026-09-22).
Two of its eighteen sets were converted to native DomainMesh files by a
scouting agent (`results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/olbc_convert.py`;
verifier alongside): **poisson-square-bc5** (record 18377514; one fixed
triangle mesh of 16,598 nodes on the unit square with 1,120 boundary
segments; per sample four random boundary segments each carry a Dirichlet,
Neumann or Robin condition with a random value function, and the source is
a random sinusoid; the output is the scalar solution $u$) and
**elasticity-circlehollow-m1** (record 18377539; a fixed mesh of 11,786
nodes on a disc with two holes, 1,312 boundary segments on three loops;
steel, plane strain, small deformations; random displacement and traction
segments; outputs the displacement vector and the three Cauchy stress
components). Every boundary segment carries its type as a label and its
prescribed value (Poisson: `bc_dirichlet`, `bc_neumann`, `bc_robin`,
`bc_value_g`, `bc_robin_alpha`; elasticity: type labels plus the
prescribed displacement and traction components, standardized
separately since they differ by three orders). The signed distance is
converted to the program's positive-outside convention, and the elasticity
set carries the laboratory frame as two constant global vectors because
its targets are stress components (@sec-nb-solids-frame-interim). The
geometry is identical across samples in each set, so **everything a model
must learn here is the map from boundary data and source to the solution**:
the pure complement of the aerodynamic datasets, where the boundary data
are fixed and the geometry varies. Splits: 8,448 train / 256 test as
released, with nested 512 and 2,048 rungs (seed-0 prefixes). Smoke lanes
(three epochs, both models, both sets) trained without incident; no
accuracy is read from them.

**Lanes** (group `ol`, `kernel/ol/lanes.tsv`, 32 lanes, snapshot
`code_ref`, every node queried, two seeds, bf16 training, float32 scoring
on the 256 test cases): ISLA R1 (384 x 12, cosine routing, 5e-4; $K = 0$
on Poisson with the source as a second per-query scalar, $K = 2$ on
elasticity, eager geometry region) and GeoTransolver-512 (1e-3; the
boundary labels and values as nodal tags in its local embedding) on the
ladder 512 / 2,048 / 8,448 cases; ISLA R2 (384 x 24) and
GeoTransolver-256 at the full rung. The 512- and 2,048-case rungs train
500 epochs; the full rung trains **120 epochs, which is the same number
of optimizer steps as the 2,048-case rung at 500** (a stated deviation
from the 500-epoch protocol; the 8,448-case rung at 500 epochs would take
about 50 hours per lane and the equal-step budget is the fairer ladder
statement anyway).

**Bars.** (i) *Standing per rung and field*: GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA with
paired-seed sign, reported without a prior on the Poisson set. (ii) *Data
exponent*: bounded-floor fit per field and architecture across the three
rungs; same exponent across architectures within the bootstrap. (iii)
*Depth and width*: R2 within 1.5% of R1 at the full rung means depth does
not pay; GeoTransolver-512 within 1.5% of 256 means width does not pay for
it. (iv) *Trainability*: any lane at a mean-field plateau (validation
relative L2 above 0.9 after 100 epochs) is reported with its signature and
rerun at half its rate. (v) *Frame clause check*: the elasticity
$\sigma_{12}$ error must not exceed the $\sigma_{11}$ error by more than
1.5x for ISLA; if it does, the frame input is not doing its job and the
lane is investigated before any standing is quoted.

**Predictions.** The boundary-data-to-solution map favors the model that
reads the boundary as a first-class object: ISLA leads GeoTransolver on the
Poisson set at every rung (0.55) and the lead is largest at 512 cases
(0.6). On elasticity GeoTransolver leads on the stresses at 512 cases as
on Tensile2d (0.6) and the ratio moves toward one with cases (0.6). Data
exponents between 0.3 and 0.8 on both sets (0.6). Depth pays on neither
(0.6). Regime limit stated in advance: one mesh per set, so nothing here
speaks to geometry generalization or discretization invariance; those
axes remain with the aerodynamic and solids datasets.

## 2026-09-22 — Book restructuring: the passive decoder leaves the main text and becomes one collapsed note in the architecture chapter {#sec-nb-passive-dropdown}

Peter asked that the passive decode variant be removed from the book's
presentation if it is not competitive, with at most a drop-down in the
architecture chapter stating what it is, why the interior results do not
use it, its quantitative cost and the practical considerations. The
numbers say it is not competitive: on the DrivAerML Volume task in float32
(48 cars, two seeds, the 10,000-cell exploration budget) the passive
decode trails the interacting query tokens on every field by more than
any seed spread, 1.63 / 1.51 / 2.07 on pressure / velocity / eddy
viscosity at matched depth and inputs (PASSIVE-12 0.0890 / 0.1201 / 0.2305
against 0.0547 / 0.0796 / 0.1116;
research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/d1_verdict_2026-09-10.json)
and 2.9 / 3.8 / 3.4 as the complete configurations
(@sec-nb-fp32-interior-family, @sec-nb-fp32-reeval-verdict-interior);
seed spreads are at most 2% and 9%. It has not been run on AirfRANS, so
the verdict rests on one dataset, and the 100,000-cell re-measurement of
PROTOCOL-REDO study 3 is pending (@sec-nb-protocol-redo-prereg).

Applied: the ISLA chapter loses its passive-decoder section
(`#sec-isla-passive`) and the interior chapter its "query independence as
a property" section (`#sec-interior-query-independence`) and the passive
row of its comparison table; the interior chapter now reads as interacting
tokens whose prediction depends on the request, with one forward
reference from the query-cloud section. The usage chapter's two passive
rows become a "when query independence is required" note; the limits
chapter's query-independence limit is restated as the interacting
configuration's actual limit (the QCOUNT dependence and its partial
mitigation); the design ledger's `query_mass` row names the decoder as
optional. The architecture chapter's modes section becomes two
arrangements, and the passive decoder moves into a collapsed callout under
its own heading, `#sec-arch-passive-decoder`, with the equations, the
float64 contract test, the prices above, the QCOUNT size of the
interacting decode's request dependence, the memory picture (interacting
tokens at 200,000 boundary cells plus 200,000 queries are a 400,000-token
case, 53.5 GB on the cost grid; the passive decoder at that size exceeds
one GB300 through its saved readout kernels and runs at 100,000), and the
practical cases for each. Every crossref to the removed anchors, including
one in the QCOUNT preregistration entry above, points at the callout. The
status ledger and tech tree keep PASSIVE2, LVT, M2 and QCOUNT as history.

## 2026-09-22 — Two figure families for the book: one "the problem" picture per dataset (boundary conditions labeled, one reference field) and the trained routing of four reference-configuration ISLA checkpoints read out per block {#sec-nb-viz-problem-and-routing}

**Setting.** The book introduced every dataset in prose and every routing
picture it drew was hand-made on the Joukowski airfoil: the reader had
seen neither a sample of any dataset nor what a trained ISLA's slices
look like. Peter asked for both: a visualization of the PDE problem of
each dataset (the geometry with its boundary conditions labeled where
they act, plus an example solution field from one sample) and a
visualization of the slice weights of a trained model. Both were built
today as cluster artifacts plus live Quarto cells.

**The problem figures.** One representative sample per dataset was read
from its native DomainMesh files on the cluster and reduced to what a
figure needs (`results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/<dataset>.npz` and
`.json`; script `problem_figures.py` in the same directory, job 829652,
plus the DrivAerML car from job 829590). The nondimensional coefficients
are formed from each case's own `global_data`, so the pictures carry
physical meaning rather than the recipe's normalized targets. Samples:
DrivAerML `run_112` (the first car of the recipe's 48-car validation
split; 150,000 of its 17.0 million surface cells and an 80,000-point band
of its 160-million-point volume mesh within 1 cm of the symmetry plane),
HiLiftAeroML `geo_LHC001_AoA_16` (the first `full_val` case with files
present; 150,000 of its 291 million surface cells, converted from inches
to metres), SHIFT-SUV fastback `run_00001` (150,000 of 5.0 million
cells), AirfRANS `airFoil2D_SST_31.812_1.334_0.371_3.287_0.0_19.548` (the
first `full_test` case; 70,000 of 179,033 points in a window around the
airfoil), PLAID Tensile2d `sample_000001` (first of `val_100`; all 6,171
nodes and 496 boundary cells), GINOT lug `lug_0004` (first of `test`;
10,483 nodes, 6,728 triangles), OLBC poisson `test_000000` and OLBC
elasticity `test_000000` (all nodes and cells). The figures live in the
protocol chapter beside each dataset's paragraph
(`@fig-problem-drivaer`, `@fig-problem-hilift`, `@fig-problem-airfrans`,
`@fig-problem-shift-suv`, `@fig-problem-tensile2d`, `@fig-problem-lug`,
`@fig-problem-olbc-poisson`, `@fig-problem-olbc-elasticity`), and the
"datasets beyond external aerodynamics" section was rewritten around
them (it now names the two OLBC sets, which the 2026-09-22 scout promoted,
instead of GNOT Heat2d, which it deferred; the limits chapter's list was
changed to match). Two conventions were added to `palette.py` and
`STYLE.md` for them: boundary-condition *kinds* carry fixed colors (a
value prescribed, plum; a flux prescribed, burnt orange; Robin, teal;
free, gray), and the dominant slice of a token is drawn with a shuffled
twenty-hue qualitative map that is labels only. DeepJEB++ was skipped:
its conversion was running under another agent and its files were not to
be touched. HiLiftAeroML's full DomainMesh cannot be loaded on this
machine's copy (its interior is not complete for every case), so the
boundary tensordict was read directly, as the recipe's surface reader
does.

**The routing instrument.** `results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/slices_probe.py`
(job 829626) composes the recipe's inference config exactly as each lane
did (model yaml, dataset yaml, splits, cells), restores the final
checkpoint with the recipe's `load_checkpoint`, and runs the first case
of the validation loader in float32 with the geometry kernel the run
trained with (fused for the two reference lanes, eager for the two
solids lanes). The routing softmax over tokens (`_softmax_over_points`)
is wrapped to record its input and output; forward pre- and post-hooks on
every `_SliceBlock` delimit the two calls each block makes, and the
block's **second** call, the refined routing of step f, is read (the
first is step b's provisional pass that only places the anchors; the
2026-09-20 probes indexed the flat call list and mixed the two,
@sec-nb-routingsat-erratum). The recorded input is
$\lambda'_{is} + \ell_i$; subtracting the block's measure bias and
normalizing over slices gives the read-back weights $\pi_{is}$ of step e,
each token's soft assignment. Per layer the artifact stores every
token's dominant slice and its largest $\pi_{is}$ (a 60,000-token subset
for the 200,000-cell car), the slice masses $q_s = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\pi_{is}$ and their measure-weighted version, the anchors $z_s$ and
$m_s$, and, for layers 1, 6 and 12, the full $\pi_{is}$ of the eight
slices that dominate the most tokens. Checkpoints, all at epoch 500 of
500: `ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42` (DrivAerML Surface task, 435 cars,
200,000 cells; the first validation car's extents agree with `run_112`
to 0.01%), `so_t2d_isla_r1_frame_n64_seed42` (PLAID Tensile2d, the
laboratory frame as two global vectors, 64 training cases),
`ref_isla_r1_af_seed42` (AirfRANS interior task, 800 airfoils, 100,000
queries) and `so_lug_isla_r1_n300_seed43` (GINOT lug, 300 cases; its
training had completed, so its final checkpoint was used).

**What was seen.** The pictures are in the architecture chapter's new
section `@sec-arch-routing-trained` (partition of the car at three layers
with anchors, three individual slices of layer 6 seen from the side and
from below, the specimen's partition and three of its slices, the airfoil
and the lug at three layers, and a per-layer summary), cross-referenced
from the slices idea in the ISLA chapter. On the car the first layer
spreads its tokens almost evenly over four slices (masses 0.268, 0.249,
0.237, …; effective number 4.4; every token's largest weight below 0.5):
that layer's routing sees only the embedded seed, the normal against the
far-field direction, and a car offers few distinct values of it. From the
second layer the relational invariants carry position and the effective
number rises to 68 to 132 in layers 2 to 6 and 183 to 241 in layers 7 to
12; the largest territories of layer 6 are on the wheels and the
underbody, where the surface mesh is finest and the sampled tokens
densest, and the anchors sit inside the body. The assignment stays soft:
in layer 6, 75% of the car's tokens give no slice more than half their
weight (median largest weight 0.27); in layer 12, 99.9% (median 0.05).
The specimen model, whose seed already carries the boundary labels, the
frame and six global scalars, uses 240 effective slices in its first
layer and stays between 153 and 244; its first layer separates the
boundary cells from the interior nodes and the flat edges from the
curved notches, and its deep layers cut the plane into regions with the
anchors clustered in the neck. The airfoil model's first layer splits the
domain by the query normal's direction against the inlet direction; the
lug's deep-layer anchors line up along the bracket and ring the loaded
hole. These are descriptions of one validation case and one seed per
model; the chapter says so and makes no accuracy claim from them.

**Verification.** Both chapters' cells ran clean under the project
interpreter; the full book render and the check that the new figures
appear in the HTML are recorded in the commit that carries this entry.

## 2026-09-22 — Verdict, SOLIDS (Tensile2d half): with the frame, ISLA R1 trails GeoTransolver-512 by 1.1 to 1.5x at 400 cases and ties on $\sigma_{12}$; ISLA's learning-curve exponents are 0.9 to 1.0 against GeoTransolver's 0.4 to 0.8, so the gap closes along the ladder {#sec-nb-solids-tensile2d-verdict}

**Setting.** The SOLIDS campaign (@sec-nb-solids-prereg) compares ISLA R1
(384 x 12, cosine routing, 5e-4) with GeoTransolver-512 on PLAID Tensile2d
along the training-case ladder 32 / 64 / 125 / 250 / 400, two seeds, 500
epochs, float32 scoring on the 100 held-out cases. After the SOLIDS-FRAME
finding (@sec-nb-solids-frame-interim) the ISLA arm is the frame
configuration (the laboratory frame as two global vectors); the frameless
lanes are the ablation record.

**What we saw** (`results/solids_frame_2026-09-22.json`; the Tensile2d ladder table of that date, since removed from the Tensile2D chapter
in the interior chapter). At 400 cases: $\sigma_{11}$ 0.0118 against
0.0087 (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.73), $\sigma_{22}$ 0.0086 against 0.0076
(0.89), $\sigma_{12}$ 0.0112 against 0.0112 (1.00), displacement 0.0082
against 0.0054 (0.66). Along the ladder the ratio on $\sigma_{11}$ rises
0.29 / 0.39 / 0.49 / 0.65 / 0.73; least-squares learning-curve exponents
are 0.89 / 1.01 / 0.89 / 0.95 for ISLA on $\sigma_{11}$ / $\sigma_{22}$ /
$\sigma_{12}$ / displacement against 0.52 / 0.52 / 0.40 / 0.76 for
GeoTransolver-512. GeoTransolver-256 at 400 cases (0.0109 / 0.0074 /
0.0106 / 0.0050) is within 2% of GeoTransolver-512 except on $\sigma_{11}$
(25% worse), so width pays for GeoTransolver on that field only. The
coordinate-leak control matches the frame configuration at 400 cases as at
32 (0.0113 / 0.0086 / 0.0102 / 0.0094), confirming again that the frame,
not absolute position, is what the task needs.

**Bars.** (i) Standing: GeoTransolver leads on the stresses at 400 cases,
as predicted (0.6). (ii) Data exponent: ISLA's exponents lie inside the
preregistered 0.4 to 0.9 band on $\sigma_{11}$ and $\sigma_{12}$ and just
above it on $\sigma_{22}$ and the displacement; GeoTransolver's lie inside
except $\sigma_{12}$ (0.40, at the edge); the "same exponent across
architectures" clause is **refuted**: the ISLA exponents exceed
GeoTransolver's by 0.2 to 0.5 on every field, the same ordering as
AirfRANS. Extrapolating the two fits, the $\sigma_{11}$ curves cross near
1,000 cases, beyond the dataset. (iii) Depth: R2 (384 x 24) pending.
(iv) Trainability: no frame lane sat at a plateau; the frameless lanes
memorized rather than plateaued. The lug half of SOLIDS is pending (the
300-lug pair is trained; its float32 scoring and the 600 / 1,200 / 2,400
rungs follow).

**Why it matters.** Third dataset and third physics on which ISLA's error
falls faster with training cases than GeoTransolver's, after DrivAerML and
AirfRANS: the boundary-first representation is data-hungrier at the bottom
of the ladder and steeper along it. On a 500-case dataset the crossover is
not reached; on the aerodynamic datasets it was (at about 200 cars). The
practical reading for a Tensile2d-sized problem is that GeoTransolver-512
is the more accurate surrogate today at 1.1 to 1.5x, at 1.9x ISLA's memory
(6.6 against 3.6 GB per GPU in training).

**Addendum, REF: GeoTransolver-512 on DrivAerML Surface scored.** The
parameter match to R1 (35.9M against 34.4M) reaches pressure 0.0415 /
0.0405 (seeds 42 / 43; mean 0.0410) against R1's 0.0415 and R2's 0.0409:
parity at matched parameters (GeoTransolver-512 ÷ R1 0.99). The reference
cost sweep puts GeoTransolver-512 at 137 ms and 66.5 GiB per step at
200,000 cells against R1's 117 ms and 34.9 GiB (@sec-nb-cost-ref-verdict),
so on the cars the reference ISLA matches the parameter-matched
GeoTransolver at 0.85x the time and 0.52x the memory, and beats the
protocol's GeoTransolver-256 by 7% at 0.71x its memory. The wing rung
decides between R1 and R2.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, DEEPJEB: 12,451 clean brackets under four load cases (three forces, one torque) on the surface task; ISLA reference configuration against GeoTransolver-512 on an equal-optimizer-step ladder of 256 / 1,024 / 4,096 / all brackets {#sec-nb-deepjeb-prereg}

**Setting.** DeepJEB++ (Yoo et al., KAIST, 2026; Hugging Face
`KAIST-SmartDesignLab/DeepJEB-PP`, ODC-By 1.0) is 15,360 generated
jet-engine brackets, each solved by linear static finite elements
(Ti-6Al-4V) under four load cases applied at the lug bore with four bolt
holes clamped: vertical, horizontal and diagonal forces and a torque about
the lug axis. A conversion agent wrote one DomainMesh per bracket and load
(61,440 files, 341 GB; converter and verifier in
`results/campaigns_2026-09-22/datasets/deepjebpp_*`; details in
@sec-data-scouted until the appendix gains its own section): the finite
element surface (about 50,000 triangles) with outward normals, areas,
`bc_fixed` and `bc_loaded` labels, the traction vector on loaded cells (the
force shared over the loaded area; for the torque a rigid-twist traction
about the lug axis that reproduces the moment exactly), and the targets von
Mises stress and displacement at cell centroids; `global_data` carries the
load direction (the force direction, or the moment axis), a force/torque
one-hot and the magnitude. **This is the first surface task with a
physical global vector that is not a freestream**, exactly the reference
configuration's $K = 1$ layout with two global scalars, on a geometry
family 35 times larger than DrivAerML's.

**A census of the labels** found unphysical maxima: the per-file maximum
von Mises stress has a median of 2,533 MPa against a yield of 903 MPa, and
1,524 brackets (9.9%) exceed 10,000 MPa in at least one load case (the
worst 1.19e7 MPa). Those brackets are excluded from the **clean splits**
(`train_clean` 12,451 brackets / 49,804 files; `test_clean` 1,385 / 5,540;
nested `train_clean_n256 / n1024 / n4096` as seed-0 permutation prefixes;
grouping by seed pair keeps interpolation families out of both sides).
The normalization statistics stay those of the full training split (a
common scale for both models). Smoke lanes (three epochs, 256 brackets)
trained for both models; no accuracy is read from them.

**Lanes** (group `jb`, `kernel/jb/lanes.tsv`, 24 lanes, `code_ref`,
200,000 cells keeps every triangle, two seeds, bf16 training, float32
scoring on the 5,540 clean test files): ISLA R1 (384 x 12, cosine, fused
kernel, 5e-4; boundary scalars `bc_fixed`, `bc_loaded`, the normal traction
and its magnitude) and GeoTransolver-512 (1e-3; its parameter match, with
the labels and the traction vector in its local embedding) on the ladder
256 / 1,024 / 4,096 / 12,451 brackets at **equal optimizer steps** (500 /
125 / 32 / 10 epochs, about 125,000 to 138,000 steps each; the full rung at
500 epochs would take ten days per lane); GeoTransolver-512 at 3e-3 (the
surface protocol's rate on the cars) at 1,024 and all brackets as the rate
control; ISLA R2 (384 x 24) and GeoTransolver-256 (the protocol's surface
baseline) at all brackets.

**Bars.** (i) *Standing at all brackets*, von Mises and displacement:
GeoTransolver-512 ÷ ISLA R1 with paired-seed sign; the GeoTransolver rate
that scores better is the one quoted, stated. (ii) *Data exponent* per
field and architecture over the four rungs at equal steps; same exponent
across architectures within the bootstrap. (iii) *Depth and width*: R2
within 1.5% of R1 means depth does not pay; GeoTransolver-512 within 1.5%
of 256 means width does not pay. (iv) *Per-load standing*: the torque case
scored separately (`test_clean_tor`); if ISLA's torque error exceeds its
force-case error by more than 1.5x while GeoTransolver's does not, the
pseudovector encoding of the moment axis is investigated. (v) *Cost*: step
time and peak memory per arm from the training logs.

**Predictions.** The reference ISLA beats GeoTransolver-512 on von Mises
at all brackets (0.55; the surface task is ISLA's home ground and the
boundary carries the load) and ties on the displacement (0.5); ISLA's data
exponent exceeds GeoTransolver's (0.7, the ordering on three datasets so
far); depth does not pay (0.6); the torque case is no worse than the force
cases for either model (0.6). Regime limit: one family of generated
brackets, one material, four fixed load directions; the clean-split
exclusion is stated with every number.


**Addendum (2026-09-22, later): depth on Tensile2d, and the first lug rungs.**
ISLA R2 (384 x 24, frame configuration) at 400 cases scores 0.0129 /
0.0109 / 0.0127 / 0.0093 on $\sigma_{11}$ / $\sigma_{22}$ / $\sigma_{12}$ /
displacement against R1's 0.0118 / 0.0086 / 0.0112 / 0.0082 (both two
seeds): 9% to 27% worse on every field, so bar (iii) is settled the
unexpected way, **depth does not pay and costs accuracy on Tensile2d at 400
cases** (the same sign as the 435-car DrivAerML depth ladder's null, larger
here). GeoTransolver-512 against 256 at 400 cases: within 3% except
$\sigma_{11}$ (25% better at 512), so width pays for GeoTransolver on one
field only.

GINOT lug, von Mises relative L2 on the 600 test lugs
(`results/solids_lug_2026-09-22.json`): at 300 lugs ISLA R1 0.0078
(seeds 0.0103 / 0.0052) against GeoTransolver-512 0.0056 (0.0056 /
0.0055), ratio 0.71; at 600 lugs ISLA 0.0037 (0.0037 / 0.0036) against
0.0040 (0.0042 / 0.0037), ratio **1.08, an ISLA lead with both seeds
ahead of their GeoTransolver partners' mean**. The 300-lug seed spread is
the delayed escape recorded in the acceptance: both ISLA seeds sat at a
validation plateau near 0.0085 (training-loss units) for 90 to 150 epochs
before dropping; seed 42 escaped 60 epochs later than seed 43 and had not
converged at epoch 500 (its validation loss was still falling), which is
the whole of the 2x spread. The 600-lug pair escaped early and agrees to
3%. Bar (iv) applies: the plateau is reported here; a half-rate rerun of
the 300-lug pair is the control, launched with the ladder's remaining
rungs pending (1,200 lugs at epoch 464, 2,400 lugs and the R2 /
GeoTransolver-256 pairs at 125 to 310).

**Addendum (2026-09-22, night): the 1,200-lug rung.** ISLA R1 0.0027 (seeds
0.0028 / 0.0025) against GeoTransolver-512 0.0026 (0.0029 / 0.0023): ratio
0.99, parity with overlapping seeds. The lug ladder so far reads 0.71 /
1.08 / 0.99 at 300 / 600 / 1,200 lugs, and the learning-curve exponents
over the three rungs are 0.78 (ISLA; the 300-lug mean carries the
late-escaping seed) against 0.54 (GeoTransolver-512). The 2,400-lug rung
and the R2 / GeoTransolver-256 pairs decide the standing at full data.

## 2026-09-22 — Interim, OLBC at 512 and 2,048 cases: GeoTransolver-512 leads ISLA 3 to 4x on the fixed-mesh Poisson set and 1.4 to 2x on elasticity; ISLA's 512-case lanes memorize (validation rising after epoch 50); OLBC-MECH diagnostics launched {#sec-nb-olbc-interim}

**What we saw** (`results/olbc_2026-09-22.json`; float32 relative L2 on the
256 test cases, two seeds). Poisson at 512 cases: ISLA R1 0.867 against
GeoTransolver-512 0.279 (ratio 0.32); elasticity at 512: ISLA 1.01 / 0.93
/ 0.96 / 0.90 on $\sigma_{11}$ / $\sigma_{22}$ / $\sigma_{12}$ /
displacement against 0.63 / 0.65 / 0.64 / 0.45 (ratios 0.62 / 0.70 / 0.66
/ 0.49). Training-time validation at the larger rungs (Huber, z-scored,
not yet scored in float32): Poisson at 2,048 cases ISLA relative L2 0.40
against 0.096; at 8,448 cases (epoch 68 of 120) 0.22 against 0.087;
elasticity at 2,048 cases 0.52 to 0.57 against 0.26 to 0.27. **The
preregistered prediction that ISLA leads on the Poisson set at every rung
(0.55) is being falsified at every rung so far**, in the direction opposite
to the aerodynamic and solid datasets, where ISLA's steeper learning curve
closes or reverses the gap.

**The signature.** The 512-case ISLA lanes reach a training Huber loss of
3e-4 (GeoTransolver 8e-5) while their validation loss falls to 0.18 at
epoch 50 and then *rises* to 0.26 and stays there: memorization of the
512 boundary-data samples, not a plateau (bar (iv)'s clause fires on
elasticity at the letter, relative L2 above 0.9, but a half-rate rerun does
not address memorization and is not launched). At 8,448 cases the
training and validation losses agree (0.19 against 0.22), so the gap at
full data is representational, not overfitting.

**Hypotheses for the mechanism.** OLBC is the one setting where the
geometry is *identical* in every sample and all information is in the
per-cell boundary scalars and the nodal source: (M1) *positional
resolution*: with a fixed mesh, ISLA's tokens see their position only
through point-to-anchor invariants, and the anchors of a fixed geometry
barely move between samples, so "where the Dirichlet segment sits relative
to this node" is resolved only as finely as the slice partition allows,
while GeoTransolver reads absolute coordinates and a fixed-radius
neighborhood; (M2) *value transport*: the boundary value $g$ enters as one
seed scalar on its cell and reaches the interior only through slice
attention, a longer path than GeoTransolver's nodal tags carrying the value
at the node itself; (M3) *small-data overfitting* specific to 512 samples,
which the 8,448-case gap already argues against as the whole story.

**Diagnostics** (group `om`, 6 lanes, Poisson set, seed 42, 512 and
2,048 cases, 500 epochs): `frame2`, the laboratory frame as two global
vectors (an equivariant coordinate system for the point-to-anchor
invariants; if M1 is the cause this recovers most of the gap without
breaking the contract); `leak`, absolute coordinates as extra boundary and
query scalars (diagnostic only; the ceiling for positional information);
`s1024`, four times the slices at the reference width and depth (M1 by
finer partition). Predictions: under M1, `leak` closes at least half the
log-gap to GeoTransolver-512 at 2,048 cases and `frame2` recovers at least
half of what `leak` recovers; `s1024` recovers less than `frame2`. Under
M2, none of the three moves the standing by more than 20% and the fix is
architectural (a per-cell value channel that reaches the readout
directly). Verdict when the six lanes are scored.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, TENSOR-HEAD: an exactly equivariant symmetric rank-2 output for ISLA, so the stress tensor is predicted as a tensor and its laboratory components are read off afterwards; against the frame-input configuration and GeoTransolver-512 on Tensile2d and OLBC elasticity {#sec-nb-tensor-head-prereg}

**Setting.** The SOLIDS-FRAME finding (@sec-nb-solids-frame-prereg,
@sec-nb-solids-frame-interim) was that ISLA's scalar heads are invariant
under rotations and reflections, so the stress components $\sigma_{11},
\sigma_{22}, \sigma_{12}$, which are components in a fixed laboratory frame,
were unrepresentable without that frame as an input: frameless ISLA
memorized the Tensile2d training set (validation error 20 to 60 times
GeoTransolver's), the load axis alone as one global vector left
$\sigma_{12}$ unrepresentable (odd under the in-plane mirror), and the
full frame as two global vectors repaired every field. With the frame, ISLA
R1 still trails GeoTransolver-512 by 1.1 to 1.5x at 400 cases
(@sec-nb-solids-tensile2d-verdict). Peter's reading of that result: some
of the remaining error comes from treating $\sigma_{11}$ and its
companions as three unrelated scalars, which discards the fact that they
are the components of one object that rotates with the body. This entry
preregisters the principled fix, an equivariant tensor output, and a test
of whether it pays.

**The head.** ISLA's vector head already writes each vector output as
$v_i = \sum_j c_{ij} B_{ij}$: invariant coefficients from the final linear
layer times a basis of directions the token owns (the global directions
$\hat g_k$, its normal $\hat n_i$, the radial direction $\hat u_i$ from its
soft anchor, and the spherical complements $e_\theta, e_\phi$ of each
pair; @sec-isla-heads). The tensor head (`out_tensors`, in
`physicsnemo/experimental/nn/isla/model.py`) writes a symmetric rank-2
output the same way, in the basis of symmetrized outer products of the
*true* vectors of that set, $\{\hat g_k, \hat n_i, \hat u_i,
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i), e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_k)\}$, plus the
identity:

$$
\sigma_i = \sum_{j \le k} c_{ijk}\, \operatorname{sym}(t_{ij} t_{ik}^{\mathsf T}) + c_{i0}\, I,
\qquad m = 2K + 3,\quad n_{\text{tbasis}} = \tfrac{m(m+1)}{2} + 1 .
$$

With no global direction ($K = 0$, the configuration used here) that is
seven coefficients per tensor; the six laboratory components $xx, yy, zz,
xy, xz, yz$ are read off $\sigma_i$ and appended after the vectors, so the
output layout is scalars, vectors, tensors. Two choices deserve a sentence
each. *(i)* The $e_\phi$ vectors are cross products, hence pseudovectors,
and are left out: every basis tensor is then a product of two true vectors
or the identity, and $\sigma$ is a true tensor, covariant under rotations
*and* reflections ($\sigma \to R \sigma R^{\mathsf T}$ for every orthogonal
$R$); the vector heads, which keep $e_\phi$, are covariant under proper
rotations only. This matters here because the Tensile2d geometries are
nearly mirror-symmetric and $\sigma_{12}$ is the odd component: a mirror
of the geometry must flip the sign of the predicted $\sigma_{12}$, and with
a true tensor it does exactly that, without the network having seen a
mirrored case. *(ii)* The frame never enters. Rotating the geometry rotates
the predicted tensor, and the laboratory components change accordingly,
which is what frame independence means for a tensor field; the frame-input
configuration keeps the contract too, but only by asking the network to
learn how a fixed pair of input directions enters every component. The
contract is tested in float64 (`test/experimental/nn/test_isla_tensor_head.py`):
rotation covariance and reflection covariance at $10^{-12}$ for random
proper and improper orthogonal matrices, translation invariance, symmetry,
the layout, and that `out_tensors = 0` leaves the head, its parameters and
every output of the existing lanes bitwise unchanged (the goldens pass; the
three existing solids configurations were also compared old-against-new
forward pass and agree bitwise). The fused geometry kernel is per layer
and upstream of the head; the fused and eager models agree on the tensor
outputs to roundoff.

**The recipe.** A dataset that stores the components as separate scalar
fields declares them as one target,

```yaml
targets:
  q: scalar
  displacement: vector
  stress: {type: symmetric_tensor, components: {sig11: xx, sig22: yy, sig12: xy}}
```

and the recipe reads the listed laboratory components off the model's six,
compares them with the named fields, and keeps the per-component metric
names (`sig11_l2`, `sig22_l2`, `sig12_l2`), so the numbers sit in the same
tables as the scalar-head lanes. The loss is unchanged in value: the
listed components enter as per-component reductions summed, which is what
three scalar fields contributed, and the channel normalization counts the
listed components, not the six (a test pins tensor-against-scalar equality
of the per-field and total losses). Normalization is the dataset's
per-component z-score, applied component by component: a diagonal affine
map per laboratory component, consistent with the loss and chosen so the
loss stays comparable with the scalar-head lanes; it is not itself
equivariant, but it acts on the readout side of an equivariant prediction
and the metrics are computed in the same normalized space as before. The
type is additive: every existing `targets:` block parses and behaves as it
did (the recipe's 287 tests pass), which is what lets the pinned cluster
copy take the patch under running lanes.

**Why this is not benchmark gaming.** Nothing about the data, the splits,
the scoring or the comparison arms changes. The tensor head is the
architecture's contract extended to the next tensor rank, in the same
construction (invariant coefficients times body-fixed basis elements) that
the vector head has had since the beginning, and it removes an input (the
laboratory frame) rather than adding one. The comparison arms are already
scored: the frame configuration `frame2` and GeoTransolver-512, both at the
same rungs, seeds, epochs and float32 scoring protocol
(`results/solids_frame_2026-09-22.json`, `results/olbc_2026-09-22.json`).
On Tensile2d at 400 cases, `frame2` reaches $\sigma_{11}$ /
$\sigma_{22}$ / $\sigma_{12}$ / displacement 0.0118 / 0.0086 / 0.0112 /
0.0082 against GeoTransolver-512's 0.0087 / 0.0076 / 0.0112 / 0.0054; at
32 cases 0.112 / 0.112 / 0.102 / 0.090 against 0.032 / 0.028 / 0.031 /
0.041. On OLBC elasticity at 512 cases, `frame2` (the configuration with
the frame as two global vectors) reaches 1.01 / 0.93 / 0.96 / 0.90 against
0.63 / 0.65 / 0.64 / 0.45. A method that only reproduces `frame2` has
earned the removal of an input, no more; a method that beats it has found
error in the scalar-component representation, which is the claim under
test.

**Lanes** (group `tn`, `kernel/tn/lanes.tsv`, six lanes, `code_ref`, 500
epochs, lr 5e-4, 20,000 cells, validation every ten epochs; configs in
`results/campaigns_2026-09-22/tn/conf/`). Tensile2d: `isla_tensile2d_tensor`
(K = 0, eager, `out_scalars 1` for $q$, `out_vectors 1`, `out_tensors 1`)
on `plaid_tensile2d_tensor` at 32 and 400 cases, seeds 42 and 43,
`val_100`. OLBC elasticity: `isla_olbc_elasticity_tensor` (K = 0,
`out_vectors 1`, `out_tensors 1`, the frame transform dropped) on
`olbc_elasticity_tensor` at 512 and 2,048 cases, seed 42, the 256 test
cases. One caveat is stated up front for the elasticity set: its boundary
*inputs* (prescribed displacement and traction) are still laboratory
components fed as scalars, so this configuration is frame-free on the
output side only; a boundary-vector input is a separate item.

**Bars** (float32 relative L2 on the held-out cases, per field, against
`frame2` at the same rung, seed means). *Frame input not needed*: the
tensor head within 10% of `frame2` on every field. *Equivariant head
pays*: better than `frame2` by more than the seed spread of the two arms
on at least the two normal stresses. *Exact contract*: the reflection test
is the acceptance test of the implementation, not a training outcome; a
lane whose $\sigma_{12}$ error does not fall below the frameless lanes'
(1.2, worse than zero) would indicate a wiring error, not a finding. A
tensor head worse than `frame2` by more than 10% on any field is a
negative result for the representation claim on that dataset, and the
frame configuration stays the Tensile2d arm.

**Predictions.** At 400 Tensile2d cases the tensor head lands within the
seed noise of `frame2` (prior 0.5): the frame configuration has 400 cases
to learn a fixed frame's effect, and does. At 32 cases it beats `frame2`
(prior 0.35): there the frame configuration had to learn the frame from
32 cases and lost 3.5x to GeoTransolver-512, and a head that needs no
frame has less to learn. On OLBC elasticity at 512 cases, where ISLA's
error is near 1.0 and the lanes memorize, the tensor head does not by
itself repair the standing (prior 0.7 that it stays above 0.8 on the
stresses): the gap there is a boundary-value-reaching problem
(@sec-nb-olbc-interim), not a representation one. Verdict when the six
lanes are scored in float32.
