## 2026-09-22 — Code: ISLA moves to `physicsnemo.experimental.models`, and every input and output becomes a named field of declared tensor rank {#sec-nb-rank-spec-api}

**Setting.** Peter asked whether `out_tensors` was properly generalized:
he wants to hand ISLA a rank-spec dictionary for its output fields and have
the class handle any rank of equivariant tensor, with the input signatures
supporting the same, and no tech debt since ISLA is unreleased. He then
raised the bar on the input side: the per-cell boundary *vector* input
channel had to be implemented, cleanly, in the same style, as the lowest
possible bar for a model that claims to take boundary conditions. This
entry records the API, what changed in the code, the recipe and the book,
and what was verified. Nothing in it is a training result.

**The API.** The class is `physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA`
(`from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA`; the package moved
from `physicsnemo/experimental/nn/isla/` to
`physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/`, tests to
`test/experimental/models/isla/`, no re-export left behind). The
constructor is keyword-only and takes four mappings from a field name to
a *rank spec*: `outputs` (required), `boundary_inputs`, `query_inputs`
and `global_inputs`. A rank spec is an integer rank (0 scalar, 1 vector,
2 rank-2 tensor, ...) or a mapping `{rank, symmetric: false, parity:
"even", channels: 1}`: `symmetric` for a fully symmetric tensor (rank
$\ge 2$), `parity: odd` for a pseudotensor output, `channels` to pack
several independent scalars (a standardized parameter vector) under one
rank-0 name. Outputs take ranks 0 to 4; per-token inputs ranks 0 to 2 and
even parity; global inputs ranks 0 and 1 (a rank-1 global input is a
global direction, normalized inside the model). `forward` takes `points`,
`normals`, `measure_weights` and the same four names as mappings from
field name to tensor (a rank-$r$ per-token field is (B, N, 3, ..., 3)
with $r$ trailing axes; a rank-1 global field (B, 3)), plus
`query_points`, `query_normals`, `support_points`, `support_normals` and
`support_inputs` for the interior modes, and returns `dict[str, Tensor]`
keyed by the output names, a rank-0 field of shape (B, N) and a rank-$r$
field of shape (B, N, 3, ..., 3). The counted channels
(`out_scalars`, `out_vectors`, `out_tensors`, `n_global_vectors`,
`n_global_scalars`, `n_boundary_scalars`, `n_query_scalars`) and the
tensor-valued `global_vectors`, `global_scalars`, `boundary_scalars`,
`query_scalars`, `support_scalars` are gone; nothing is shimmed.

**Outputs (@sec-isla-heads, @sec-arch-head).** One linear head emits every
output's invariant coefficients. With $m = 2K + 3$ true basis vectors
($\hat g_k$, $\hat n_i$, $\hat u_i$, the $e_\theta$ complements) and $p =
\binom{K+2}{2}$ pseudovectors (the cross products of the primaries), an
even output of rank $r$ is contracted over tensor products of $r$ true
vectors plus the isotropic tensors of that rank (the identity at rank 2,
the three products of Kronecker deltas at rank 4, their symmetric sum
under a symmetric spec); an odd output over products with exactly one
pseudovector factor, plus the Levi-Civita symbol at rank 3. A symmetric
spec has one coefficient per unordered multi-index. The coefficient
counts per field are 1 (rank 0); $m$ or $p$ (rank 1, even or odd); $m^2 +
1$, $m(m+1)/2 + 1$, $2pm$, $pm$ (rank 2: general, symmetric, odd, odd
symmetric); $m^3$, $\binom{m+2}{3}$, $3pm^2 + 1$, $p\,m(m+1)/2$ (rank 3);
$m^4 + 3$, $\binom{m+3}{4} + 1$, $4pm^3$, $p\binom{m+2}{3}$ (rank 4). For
$K = 1$: a vector costs 5, a symmetric rank-2 tensor 16, a pseudovector 3.
The code gathers the free coefficients into the full coefficient tensor
and contracts one index at a time, so the $m^r$ basis is never
materialized. The vector head therefore lost the two $e_\phi$
pseudovectors it carried (7 to 5 coefficients with one direction): a true
vector no longer pays for a pseudovector's basis, and every even output
is covariant under reflections as well.

**Inputs (@sec-isla-inputs-rank).** A rank-1 per-token input $v_i$
contributes to the seed its cosines with the token's frame $\{\hat n_i,
\hat g_k\}$, its norm and its dot products with the token's other vector
inputs, and in every slice layer $v_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ beside the
existing $\hat n_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ and $\hat g_k \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$
(`_relational_invariants` now takes the per-token vector stack; the normal
is the first of them). A rank-2 input $T_i$ contributes $a^{\mathsf T} T_i
b$ over the frame pairs, $\operatorname{tr} T_i$ and $\lVert T_i \rVert_F$
to the seed, and $\hat\rho^{\mathsf T} T_i \hat\rho$ plus the contractions
of the derived vectors $T_i \hat n_i$, $T_i \hat g_k$ (and their
transposes for a non-symmetric spec) with $\hat\rho_{is}$ in the layers.
Only true vectors appear on the input side, so every input invariant is
O(3)-invariant and pseudotensor inputs are refused. Boundary-input
invariants widen the boundary tokens' seed (zeros on other tokens);
query-input invariants go through the query, passive-query and support
embeddings; every token carries the union of the two block-level vector
stacks. The geometry width is $5 + K + P' + Q$. The fused Triton kernel
is written for the normal and one global direction: a model with rank-1
or rank-2 per-token inputs runs the eager region (a warning under
`geo_kernel=None`, an error under `geo_kernel="fused"`); extending the
kernel is the standing follow-up.

**What was verified.** The pre-refactor code's `norm_out` state was
recorded with a forward hook for the release-test configurations and
inputs (`test/experimental/models/isla/data/isla_backbone_v1.pth`); the
new class reproduces it bitwise for the default and the passive-decoder
configuration with `outputs={"p": 0, "v": 1}` and `global_inputs={"g":
1}`, so the trunk is unchanged wherever no rank-1 or rank-2 input is
present. Every output spec above (ranks 0 to 4, both parities, symmetric
and general, a two-channel rank-0 field) and rank-0, rank-1, symmetric and
general rank-2 boundary inputs were checked in float64 for covariance to
below $10^{-13}$ under random proper rotations, improper orthogonal maps
(sign $\det R$ for odd parity) and translations of geometry and fields
together; the goldens of the release tests were regenerated by the new
code path (the regeneration command is in the test file's docstring); the
ISLA suite and the recipe suite pass (289 recipe tests). The fused-versus-
eager comparison on a rank-2 output stays as the CUDA-only test.

**Recipe.** A third output type, `output_type: fields`, means the model
returns `{name: tensor}` keyed by the dataset's target names; the model
yaml declares `outputs:` with the same names and their ranks, and the
recipe selects by name (`select_fields_by_target`), reading the listed
laboratory components of a `symmetric_tensor` target off the predicted
(B, N, 3, 3) tensor. The flat six-component tensor layout is deleted
(`field_dim` now refuses a tensor target on a flat model). The yaml's
`global_inputs:`, `boundary_inputs:` and `query_inputs:` blocks under
`forward_kwargs:` map the declared names to dataset paths (the resolver
already produced dict-valued kwargs). A recipe-local `StackScalarFields`
transform stacks component fields into one zero-padded (N, 3) vector, so
OLBC elasticity's `bc_disp_x/y` and `bc_trac_x/y` reach ISLA as ONE
rank-1 `bc_displacement` and ONE rank-1 `bc_traction`; DeepJEB++'s
`bc_load` (already (N, 3)) is declared rank 1 in place of its normal
component and magnitude; the constant laboratory frames become two named
rank-1 globals (`frame_x`, `frame_y`). Every ISLA yaml of the recipe and
of `results/campaigns_2026-09-22` was rewritten (the leak diagnostics
keep their absolute coordinates as a three-channel rank-0 input).

**Cluster.** The running campaigns import the pinned snapshots
`code_ref` and `recipe_globin`, whose yamls speak the old API, and chain
links re-import them every four hours, so neither was touched. New
snapshots `code_v2` (a copy of `code_ref` with `experimental/nn/isla`
removed and only the `experimental/models/isla` package files and the
models `__init__` added) and `recipe_v2` (a copy of `recipe_globin` with
the recipe source changes applied as a patch onto the pinned files and the
ISLA yamls replaced) were created and import-checked on a CPU-partition
job; no training lane was launched. New lanes point their `code` column
at `code_v2` and their recipe at `recipe_v2`.

**Book.** @sec-isla-heads is now "fields of any rank from an equivariant
basis" with the pseudotensor note and the input-side rule
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank); @sec-arch-head states the general head and the
coefficient counts; the notation and switches tables, the seed stage and
the relational invariants carry the new widths; @sec-using-config and
@sec-using-inputs show the yaml; the design-decision ledger
(@tbl-principled-ledger) gains the row "a component is a view of a
tensor, never a channel"; the status chapter's tree and ledger gain
RANK-IO (DONE). The tensor-head lanes of `kernel/tn` (TENSOR-HEAD) were
launched under the old API and keep running on `code_ref`; their
elasticity arm still reads the boundary components as scalars, and the
rerun under `code_v2` with rank-1 boundary inputs is the next lane to
schedule.

## 2026-09-22 — Preregistration, RANK-IO: the rank-spec interface in use; OLBC elasticity with prescribed displacement and traction as rank-1 boundary inputs and the stress as a symmetric rank-2 output, and DeepJEB++ with the load traction as a rank-1 input {#sec-nb-rankio-prereg}

**Setting.** ISLA now declares every input and output as a named field of
a stated tensor rank (@sec-nb-rank-spec-api; `physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA`).
Two of the running campaigns fed frame-dependent data as scalars: on OLBC
elasticity the prescribed displacement and traction entered as their
laboratory-frame components, and on DeepJEB++ the load traction entered as
its normal projection and magnitude. The TENSOR-HEAD lanes (group `tn`,
@sec-nb-tensor-head-prereg) made the *output* frame-free while the inputs
stayed as scalars. This campaign closes the input side with the general
mechanism: a rank-1 boundary field enters through its dot products with the
normal and the global directions at the seed and with the point-to-anchor
direction in every slice block, exactly as the normal itself does.

**Lanes** (group `v2`, snapshot `code_v2` with the pinned recipe patched to
`recipe_v2`; the running campaigns keep `code_ref`): ISLA R1 (384 x 12,
cosine, 5e-4, eager region since the fused kernel does not yet take
per-token vector inputs) on OLBC elasticity with `bc_displacement` and
`bc_traction` as rank-1 inputs and `stress` as a symmetric rank-2 output,
K = 0, 512 and 2,048 cases, two seeds, 500 epochs; and on DeepJEB++ with
`bc_load` as a rank-1 input at 1,024 clean brackets (125 epochs, equal
steps to the `jb` ladder), two seeds.

**Comparisons and bars** (float32 relative L2 on the same test sets).
OLBC elasticity: (a) against the `tn` lanes (tensor output, scalar inputs)
at the same rungs isolates the vector-input channel; (b) against the `ol`
lanes (frame vectors as inputs, scalar outputs) isolates head plus inputs
together; (c) against GeoTransolver-512. Bars: the rank-1 inputs improve
on the `tn` lanes by more than the two-seed spread on the stresses and the
displacement = "vector inputs pay"; within the spread = "the scalar
components sufficed on this fixed-frame dataset" (both are informative:
the dataset's condition tags are still per laboratory component, so a
frame remains implicit in the labels). DeepJEB++: against `jb` ISLA R1 at
1,024 brackets on von Mises and displacement, same bar. Also recorded: the
eager-region cost against the fused `jb` lanes (step time, memory).

**Predictions.** OLBC elasticity: vector inputs pay on the displacement
(0.55) and are within spread on the stresses (0.5); the combined
frame-free configuration is within 10% of the frame-input `ol` lanes
(0.6). DeepJEB++: within spread (0.6; the load direction is already the
global vector, so the traction adds little beyond the normal projection).

## 2026-09-23 — Ops: the scratch project's file-count quota (52.4 million inodes) was hit at 00:00 while bytes stood at 90 of 100 TB; lanes died at checkpoint saves; 2.7 million files of regenerable scorer predictions and raw dataset cache freed {#sec-nb-inode-quota}

**What happened.** Every lane that reached a checkpoint save between about
23:50 and 00:20 died with `OSError: [Errno 122] Disk quota exceeded` (the
RANK-IO lanes among them, at epochs 0 to 5). The byte quota had 10 TB of
headroom; the *file-count* quota of the shared project (52,428,800 inodes)
stood at 52,421,315. The program's own contributions: DomainMesh datasets
are tensordict directory trees of tens of files per case (the 61,440-case
DeepJEB++ conversion alone is about two million), the float32 scorer wrote
one prediction file per test sample per lane (332,000 files across 472
lanes), the routing probes 372,000 files, and the DeepJEB++ raw download
kept both the Hugging Face cache and its extraction.

**What was done.** Deleted, in order of regenerability: every scorer
`predictions/` directory (the per-lane `metrics.jsonl` that every artifact
is built from stays) and the DeepJEB++ Hugging Face cache and extracted
`.obj` surface meshes (the FEA and boundary-condition sources of the
conversion stay). The count fell to 49.7 million. Chain links that died
resume from their last checkpoint on the next singleton link; the guard did
not block any lane because the failure did not repeat. The fleet watcher
now wakes above 51.5 million inodes as it does above 97 TB.

**Standing changes.** The scorer should not write per-sample predictions
unless a study asks for them (engineering item); completed runs keep one
checkpoint and running lanes three (the pruning loop); raw dataset
downloads are deleted once the converted tree is verified. Until the
scorer change lands, the prediction directories are deleted on each
pruning pass.

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, REF: R1 (384 x 12, cosine routing, fused kernel, 5e-4) is the reference configuration; it ties R2 on the 35-wing rung as on the cars, beats GeoTransolver-256 by 7% on the cars at 0.71x its memory, and trails it by 25% on the 35-wing rung {#sec-nb-ref-verdict}

**Selection.** The rule fixed in @sec-nb-ref-prereg chooses the smaller
candidate when it is within 1.5% of the better one on both DrivAerML
Surface (435 cars) and the 35-wing HiLiftAeroML rung, all at 200,000
cells, float32, two seeds. Pressure relative L2: cars R1 0.0416 / 0.0414,
R2 0.0415 / 0.0402 (R1 1.5% behind, at the edge); 35 wings R1 0.1456 /
0.1465, R2 0.1463 / 0.1454 (0.2% apart). **R1 is the reference
configuration**: 384 wide, 12 layers, 256 slices, cosine routing, the
fused geometry kernel, the RMS-pairwise-distance gauge, `source_total`
query mass on interior tasks, learning rate 5e-4. Doubling the depth
buys nothing measurable on either dataset (and costs 9 to 27% on Tensile2d,
@sec-nb-solids-tensile2d-verdict).

**Against the baselines.** Cars: GeoTransolver-256 at the protocol rate
0.0445 ÷ R1 0.0415 = **1.07** with both seeds agreeing, at a step-time
ratio of 1.11 (parity within 1.2) and a memory ratio of 0.71; the
parameter-matched GeoTransolver-512 0.0410 is at parity (0.99) at 1.17x
R1's time and 1.9x its memory. 35 wings: GeoTransolver-256 0.1098 and
Transolver-256 0.1101 (`results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-22.json`)
against R1 0.1461: **GeoTransolver ÷ R1 = 0.75**, the small-recurring-
geometry deficit the wing rungs have shown throughout (@sec-data-efficiency),
unchanged by the reference configuration; GeoTransolver-512 on the wings
is at epoch ~460 and is added when scored (scored 2026-09-23, both seeds:
pressure 0.1022 / 0.1061, mean 0.1042, **GeoTransolver-512 ÷ R1 = 0.71**;
velocity 0.1293 against 0.1679, 0.77; wall shear 0.1963 against 0.2566,
0.77. Doubling GeoTransolver's width buys 5% on this rung against 8% on the
cars, so the parameter match does not change the wing reading: the deficit
is 25 to 29% against either GeoTransolver width). So the prereg's acceptance
clause ("recommended settings beat the baseline") holds on the cars and
fails on the 35-wing rung; both are stated wherever the reference is
quoted.

**Rate.** The 1e-3 control is 2% worse than 5e-4 on the cars (both seeds)
and 3% better on the wings (0.1410 / 0.1420); the reference keeps 5e-4 as
preregistered and the wing-favoring direction is recorded as a
dataset-dependent 2 to 3% effect, not a knob to retune per dataset.

**Consequences.** The class defaults move to the reference (hidden 384,
12 layers, 256 slices; the recipe's ISLA yamls default to R1 and 5e-4);
the scoreboard, cost and scaling chapters quote R1 as "ISLA" from here on,
with the 192-wide lanes of the earlier protocol labeled as such where they
remain load-bearing (REF-BOARD replaces them). Pending under REF: the 210-
and 510-wing rungs, DrivAerML Volume and AirfRANS under R1 (lanes running
after the quota outage relaunch), and GeoTransolver-512 on the wings.

**Addendum to DEEPJEB (2026-09-23): the equal-step ladder is flat for ISLA
above 1,024 brackets.** Float32 von Mises relative L2 on the 5,540 clean
test files, ISLA R1, two seeds: 0.605 / 0.496 / 0.509 / 0.508 at 256 /
1,024 / 4,096 / 12,451 brackets (displacement 0.305 / 0.243 / 0.246 /
0.252); GeoTransolver-512 at 1,024 brackets 0.536 / 0.282, so
GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA = **1.08 / 1.16** there (ISLA leads; the other
GeoTransolver rungs are scoring). The ladder holds optimizer steps fixed
(about 130,000) while multiplying the data, and ISLA's error stops
falling at 1,024 brackets: at equal steps the model is step-limited, not
data-limited, and the "exponent" of 0.04 measures the budget, not the
learning curve. Rows 24 to 27 of `kernel/jb/lanes.tsv` add an
**equal-epoch companion** at the full rung: ISLA R1 and GeoTransolver-512
for 40 epochs (four times the steps, about 500,000), two seeds. Bar: if
ISLA at 40 epochs improves on its 10-epoch full-rung score by more than
the two-seed spread, the ladder's flatness is the step budget and the
data exponent must be read from equal-epoch rungs; the 10-epoch numbers
stay as the equal-compute statement. The load-case breakdown holds at
every rung: the torque case is ISLA's easiest (0.34 to 0.41) and the
diagonal force its hardest (0.58 to 0.71); bar (iv) is met.

÷ native ISLA stays within 1.03 (1.015x at 192 wide,

the draw), area-trained ÷ uniform-trained ISLA stays within 1.05 on both
datasets while the baselines' area-trained errors remain an order of
magnitude above their uniform-trained ones, and the 54 / 109-car interior
rungs improve by the same 5 to 10% as the surface. If any DrivAerML
Surface rung worsens under R1, the width rule (5e-4 at 384) is the first
suspect at small training sets and the rate control of REF is extended
to that rung before the standing is replaced.

GeoTransolver's unchanged"). *Wings*: met with room, biased 0.998 against

*GeoTransolver's factors are unchanged* by construction (released
baseline, not re-run: 8.73 and 0.993 on the cars at 100,000 cells, 2.47
and 1.000 on the wings); the baseline-to-ISLA ratio of biased factors is
8.0 at the matched count and 8.6 against R1 at 200,000, where the earlier
chapter quoted 8.2. One caveat travels with the 100,000-cell row: R1 was
trained at 200,000 cells and is probed at half that, where the 192-wide
lane was trained and probed at 100,000, so the row also carries a small
count shift (its uniform error is 2.3% above the 200,000-cell one).

**Reading.** ISLA's biased-draw residual is the quadrature variance the
chapter has always attributed it to, and R1 shows the count dependence
cleanly on one checkpoint: 1.098 at 100,000 cells, 1.010 at 200,000, where
the sparse half of the biased draw still holds tens of thousands of cells.
The stratified draw is a small free improvement at every count (0.7% at
200,000, 2.4% at 100,000 on the cars; 0.4% on the wings), as QUAD-VAR found
(@sec-nb-quadvar-verdict, @sec-nb-quadvar-hl-verdict). Nothing in the
consistency picture depends on the width or the routing norm; the reference
configuration inherits it.

**Territories.** Medians over the twelve blocks, four validation cases;
GeoTransolver over its eight heads; the displacement floor is new.

*Agreement.* The dominant-slice picture is the 192-wide one: on the cars
R1's bias excess is 0.062 and 0.054 against 0.056 at 192 wide and 0.325 for
GeoTransolver, carried by the deep blocks (0.07 to 0.09 in blocks 8 to 11
against 0.03 to 0.06 in blocks 1 to 5), and it falls to 0.044 when the same
checkpoint is probed at 200,000 cells, the count dependence a quadrature
term should show. The post hoc distance-controlled agreement (pairs at
most a median uniform-uniform match apart, a third of the biased pairs)
leaves it unchanged (ISLA +0.070 / +0.065, GeoTransolver +0.243). Two
details of R1's routing: seed 42's block 0 routes every token to one
dominant slice (4.4 effective slices; floor and biased agreement both 1,
excess 0), and R1 routes over more effective slices than the 192-wide lane
in the deep blocks (170 to 240 in blocks 6 to 11 against 140 to 200,
`territory_*_unif1.json` per-block statistics). On the wings the floors are
0.19 (0.24 at 192 wide) and the excess 0.050 to 0.057 against
GeoTransolver's 0.061: soft routing, where the argmax does not measure
territories, as @sec-nb-territory-wings found; the agreement clause stays
single-dataset.

*Anchor displacement.* Here R1 differs from the 192-wide lane: its anchors
move 0.090 and 0.120 body radii under the bias on the cars, two to three
times the 0.039 of 2026-09-21 and far past the 0.02 the original probe
preregistered, while GeoTransolver's centroids move 0.636. The new floor
column reads it: under two *uniform* draws R1's anchors already move 0.075
and 0.088, so under the bias they move 1.2x and 1.4x as far as under any
resampling, where GeoTransolver's centroids move 17x as far (0.636
against 0.038). The anchor of a slice is the routing-weighted mean
position of its tokens; a network that spreads its mass over more slices
gives each anchor fewer effective tokens, and its anchors are noisier under
every resampling, biased or not. At 200,000 cells the motion halves (0.057
against a floor of 0.055, 1.04x) as a sampling-noise term should. On the
wings the anchors move 0.0045 and 0.0044 (floors 0.0031 and 0.0035, so 1.5x
and 1.3x) against GeoTransolver's 0.311 (floor 0.0044, 71x) and the 192-wide
0.0035, and the displacement clause reproduces on both datasets. The reading of @sec-nb-territory-verdict therefore stands with
one correction of emphasis: the unweighted RMS anchor displacement is
partly a per-slice sample-size statistic, and the bias-specific motion is
the excess over its floor, which is small for ISLA and an order of
magnitude for GeoTransolver. A mass-weighted displacement would remove the
low-mass slices' wander and is the right follow-on if the anchor motion is
to be quoted as a number in its own right; it needs the probe to store the
slice masses.

**Verdict.** Consistency: the bar is met on the wings and on the cars'
stratified factor, and the cars' biased factor at the matched count is at
the bar's edge, three points above the 192-wide lane's (1.10 against
1.07), with both seeds of both lanes agreeing; at the reference
configuration's own protocol the factor is 1.01. GeoTransolver's factors
are unchanged. Territories: the agreement statistics reproduce the
192-wide ones within 0.01 on both datasets; the anchor displacement on the
cars is two to three times the 192-wide value and is mostly the
resampling floor of a network that uses more slices, not a bias-following
motion (1.2 to 1.4x its floor against GeoTransolver's 17x). The

## 2026-09-23 — Interim, TENSOR-HEAD and OLBC-MECH: the equivariant stress head alone does not generalize at 32 Tensile2d cases (it is the load-axis input that carried the frame lanes), and on the fixed-mesh Poisson set absolute coordinates make ISLA better than GeoTransolver, so the gap there is positional resolution {#sec-nb-tensor-mech-interim}

**TENSOR-HEAD at 32 cases** (`tn`, float32 relative L2 on `val_100`, two
seeds): $\sigma_{11}$ 0.609 / 0.593, $\sigma_{22}$ 0.406 / 0.384,
$\sigma_{12}$ 0.459 / 0.438, displacement 0.680 / 0.647. Against the
frame-input configuration (`frame2`: 0.112 / 0.112 / 0.102 / 0.090) the
tensor head alone is 4 to 7 times worse, and against the frameless
configuration (0.450 / 0.360 / 1.199 / 0.639) it repairs only
$\sigma_{12}$ (1.20 to 0.45) and leaves the displacement, a vector head
that the tensor head does not touch, exactly where the frameless lanes had
it. The bar "within 10% of `frame2`" fails by a factor of five, and the
prediction that the tensor head would do *better* at 32 cases is refuted.
**Reading.** The SOLIDS-FRAME ladder already said this in a form I read too
narrowly: `frame1`, the load axis alone, repaired $\sigma_{11}$,
$\sigma_{22}$ and the displacement by 14 to 21 times; the full frame added
only $\sigma_{12}$. What generalizes is the *input*: knowing the load
direction as a global vector lets the network represent "how far along the
load axis" as an invariant of every token; without it the network has to
reconstruct that axis from the labeled-edge normals, and at 32 cases it
memorizes instead. Representability of $\sigma_{12}$ is the second,
smaller issue, and the tensor head is its principled fix. The two are
complementary, not alternatives. Rows 6 to 9 of `kernel/v2/lanes.tsv`
(`tensor_axis`: the symmetric rank-2 stress head plus the load direction
as the one global vector, $K = 1$, fused kernel, no laboratory $x$-axis)
test the combination at 32 and 400 cases, two seeds. Bar: within 10% of
`frame2` on every field means the frame-free-plus-physical-axis
configuration is the canonical one for Tensile2d; the 400-case `tn` and
OLBC elasticity `tn` lanes are scoring.

**OLBC-MECH at 512 cases** (`om`, one seed so far): the coordinate-leak
control reaches $u$ relative L2 **0.203** against the baseline ISLA's 0.867
and GeoTransolver-512's 0.279. Absolute position at every token does not
merely close the gap, it inverts it: with positions, ISLA's routing and
boundary-token path beat GeoTransolver by 27% at this rung. Hypothesis M1
(positional resolution) is confirmed as *a* cause and is sufficient; M2
(value transport) is not needed to explain the gap. Whether the
contract-preserving remedies recover it is what `frame2` (the domain's own
axes as global vectors, legitimate for a fixed domain), `s1024` (finer
slice partition) and `ext` (boundary-value extension) decide when they
score. The reading for the architecture: on a fixed mesh the anchors of a
fixed geometry give every sample the same coordinate scaffold, and 256
slices resolve position on it too coarsely for a boundary-data-to-solution
map that varies on the scale of the boundary segments.

**Addendum (2026-09-23, 06:00): tensor head plus load axis at 32 cases.**
Training-time validation relative L2 at epoch 500 (float32 scoring
follows), `tensor_axis` seeds 42 / 43 against `frame2` seed 42 in the same
units: $\sigma_{11}$ 0.106 / 0.112 vs 0.112; $\sigma_{22}$ 0.074 / 0.077
vs 0.110; $\sigma_{12}$ 0.088 / 0.085 vs 0.101; displacement 0.102 / 0.124
(the `frame2` table did not print this row; float32 gave 0.090). **The
symmetric rank-2 head plus the load direction as the one physical global
vector matches the full-frame configuration on every stress component and
beats it on $\sigma_{22}$ by 30% and on $\sigma_{12}$ by 15%**, with no
laboratory $x$-axis anywhere in the inputs and the fused kernel in use
($K = 1$). Combined with the previous addendum this settles the mechanism:
the load axis is the input that generalizes, the equivariant head is what
makes the shear component representable, and together they are the
canonical Tensile2d configuration; the frame-input lanes stay as the
measured interim. The 400-case pair (epoch ~63) and the float32 scores
close the bar.

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, OLBC-MECH at 512 cases: the boundary-value extension recovers 88% of the log-gap to GeoTransolver without touching the invariance contract; the domain's frame recovers 17%, four times the slices nothing, absolute coordinates overshoot to 27% better than GeoTransolver {#sec-nb-olbc-mech-verdict}

**Setting and numbers** (`om`, Poisson mixed-plus-source set, 512 cases,
seed 42, float32 relative L2 of $u$ on the 256 test cases; baseline ISLA R1
0.867, GeoTransolver-512 0.279, both two-seed means):

| variant | what it adds | $u$ rel. L2 | fraction of the log-gap to GeoTransolver recovered |
|---|---|---|---|
| `s1024` | four times the slices | 0.907 | 0 (slightly worse) |
| `frame2` | the domain's own axes as two global vectors | 0.673 | 0.22 |
| `ext` | parameter-free boundary-value extension: per condition type, the measure-weighted inverse-square-distance average of the prescribed values and the distance to the nearest labeled cell, as six query scalars | **0.318** | **0.88** |
| `leak` | absolute coordinates as boundary and query scalars (diagnostic; breaks the contract) | 0.203 | 1.27 (beats GeoTransolver by 27%) |

: OLBC-MECH at 512 cases, one seed each; recovered fraction = log(baseline ÷ variant) ÷ log(baseline ÷ GeoTransolver-512). {#tbl-olbc-mech}

**Verdict against the preregistered predictions**
(@sec-nb-olbc-interim and its addendum). Under M1 (positional
resolution) `frame2` should have recovered at least half of what `leak`
recovers; it recovers 17%, and `s1024` recovers nothing, so *finer
partition and a coordinate frame are not what is missing*. Under M2
(value transport) `ext` should have recovered at least half the gap; it
recovers 88%, so **the missing ingredient is a direct path from the
prescribed boundary values to the interior query**, which the parameter-
free extension supplies as an invariant, mesh-consistent quadrature. The
leak's overshoot says something further: given position and the extension
is not even needed, ISLA's routing and boundary tokens beat
GeoTransolver's coordinate-reading local embedding on this set. Both
mechanisms are real; the one that can be added without breaking the
contract is the extension, and it does most of the work. Pending: the
2,048-case twins of all four (rows 0 to 2 and 6), and a second seed before
any of these numbers enters a chapter as a standing.

**What it means for the architecture.** The literature idea that
motivated `ext` (the OLBC paper's learned extensions, BENO's boundary
branch) enters ISLA as a **boundary-data extension channel**: for each
labeled condition type, an integral of the prescribed data over the
labeled cells against a distance kernel, evaluated at every query and fed
through the rank-spec input interface (a rank-0 extension per scalar
datum; for vector data such as prescribed displacement or traction the
same construction yields a rank-1 input). The parameter-free kernel is
the control; a learned kernel width per type is the natural next step and
stays within the contract. Entered as the next OLBC lanes: `ext` on the
elasticity set with the vector data extended as rank-1 query inputs under
the v2 API.

**Addendum (2026-09-23, second seeds).** Seed 43 of `ext`, `frame2` and
`leak` scored (`om` rows 8 to 10; `s1024` stays one seed): $u$ relative
L2 0.347 / 0.716 / 0.188 against seed 42's 0.318 / 0.673 / 0.203. Two-seed
means and recovered fractions of the log-gap (baseline 0.867,
GeoTransolver-512 0.279): **`ext` 0.333, 0.84**; `frame2` 0.695, 0.19;
`leak` 0.195, 1.31. The seeds move each fraction by a few points and no
ordering: the verdict stands with the extension recovering 84% of the

**Addendum, TENSOR-HEAD at 400 cases and on OLBC elasticity.** Tensor head

## 2026-09-23 — Code and preregistration, INTERNAL-GEOMETRY: field names may nest with a dot and `forward` returns a TensorDict; an interior query's direction and signed wall distance are computed inside the model from the nearest sampled boundary cell instead of read from a stored SDF; the sampled-boundary price is measured against the full-mesh field on DrivAerML Volume and AirfRANS {#sec-nb-internal-geometry-prereg}

**Two API refinements (Peter's review of the rank-spec interface,
@sec-nb-rank-spec-api).** First, the rank-spec grammar used a mapping
value for `{rank, symmetric, parity, channels}`, which left no way to
declare a nested group of outputs. The resolution is the project's
TensorDict convention (`physicsnemo.datapipes.keys`): a field name may
contain `"."` (`surface.pressure`), every value of `outputs`,
`boundary_inputs`, `query_inputs` and `global_inputs` is a leaf spec, so a
mapping value is never a group and there is no ambiguity. `forward` now
returns a `TensorDict` of batch size `(B, N_out)` with the dotted names
unflattened (`out["surface", "pressure"]`), a name without a dot staying a
top-level leaf; the named input mappings accept a flat dict with dotted
names, a nested dict or a TensorDict. The recipe's `fields` adapter reads
the TensorDict by its (dotted) target names. A name that is a group of
another (`surface` beside `surface.pressure`) is refused at construction.

Second, the interior modes took `query_normals` (the stored SDF gradient)
and the recipe declared `sdf` as a rank-0 query input, although both are
functions of the boundary sample and the query position. The class now
computes them (`interior_geometry="nearest_boundary"`, the default): for
each query the nearest boundary sample $y_{i^*}$ gives the direction $u_q
= (x_q - y_{i^*}) / |x_q - y_{i^*}|$, used as the query's normal, and the
distance $d_q = \pm |x_q - y_{i^*}|$ signed by the nearest sample's normal
(positive on the side the normal points to, the datasets' positive-outside
convention), fed as a built-in rank-0 channel $[d_q / L, \operatorname{sign}
d_q \log(|d_q|/L + \epsilon)]$ ahead of any declared query input (the
layout of one declared `"length"`-scaled scalar, so a `"provided"` model
with the same weights handed the internal $u_q, d_q$ is the same function
to roundoff; tested). The search is an exact chunked nearest-neighbour
pass over the queries (`torch.cdist` without the matmul expansion, one
`(B, chunk, N)` block at a time, chunk from a 512 MiB budget or
`interior_nn_chunk`; the argmin runs without gradient and $d_q, u_q$ are
rebuilt from the gathered sample). At 200,000 queries against 200,000
cells this is about 300 blocks of 640 queries, $4 \times 10^{10}$
distances, some 160 GB of distance traffic on the device: tens of
milliseconds per case, against a training step of order a second, and no
$Q \times N$ matrix ever held. The built-in channel enters the embedding,
not the geometry region, so the fused kernel stays available. Under
`interior_geometry="provided"` the class reproduces the form of every
interior lane trained before today bitwise (the release goldens and the
backbone golden hold under it), so the pinned-snapshot lanes remain
interpretable. Support tokens follow the same switch. Tests: brute-force
match of the geometry, sign convention on a sampled sphere (inside
negative, outside positive, $|d|$ within the sample spacing), on-wall
queries, covariance and scaling of $d, u$, every contract in the internal
mode for all three interior arrangements, the internal-equals-provided
identity, checkpoint round trips, nested names on outputs and inputs with
the covariance holding on the nested values. 153 tests in the ISLA suite,
the recipe suite green.

**The nuance to measure.** The stored SDF is computed on the *full* mesh
(the DrivAerML STL, up to 17 million cells); the internal one sees the
200,000-cell sample, so near the wall $|d_q|$ overestimates the true wall
distance by up to about the sample spacing, and $u_q$ deviates from the
true gradient by the same order. Far from the wall the two agree. Whether
that costs interior accuracy is not assumed.

**Lanes** (group `sg`, snapshot pair `code_v3` = `code_v2` + the ISLA
package overlay and `recipe_v3` = `recipe_v2` + the recipe patch, verified
by a cpu-partition import-and-forward job before launch): ISLA R1 (384 x
12, cosine routing, 5e-4, fused kernel in both arms) on the DrivAerML Volume
task at 200,000 cells and 200,000 queries, 500 epochs, and on the AirfRANS
interior task at 100,000 queries (full split), as the REF lanes
`ref_isla_r1_drvol_*` and `ref_isla_r1_af_*` ran them; two arms, two seeds
each: `sg_{drvol,af}_internal_seed{42,43}` (`interior_geometry:
nearest_boundary`, the dataset's `sdf` / `sdf_normals` not read) against
`sg_{drvol,af}_provided_seed{42,43}` (`isla_volume_*_ref_provided`: the
stored full-mesh field and its gradient). The dataset yamls are identical
between arms. Eight lanes. Acceptance at 15 minutes: every lane stepping,
no Traceback. Scored in float32 by the scorer pump under `code_v3` +
`recipe_v3`.

**Bar** (float32 relative L2 on the validation cars and the 200 test
airfoils, seed means with both seeds agreeing in sign). Internal within 3%
of provided on every interior field (velocity, pressure, eddy viscosity)
on both datasets = the stored SDF is not needed; the internal geometry
stays the default and the `_provided` configurations exist only to load
older checkpoints. Internal worse than provided by more than 3% on any
field on either dataset = the near-wall price of the sampled boundary is
real; it is reported per field and `interior_geometry: provided` stays
documented as the accurate option for datasets that carry a full-mesh
field. Internal better by more than 3% is also recorded (it would mean the
sampled-boundary distance is the more consistent input for a model that
sees the sampled boundary). **Predictions.** DrivAerML: within 3% on
velocity and eddy viscosity (0.6), pressure the field most likely to pay
because it is set near the wall (0.5 that it stays within 3%). AirfRANS:
within 3% on every field (0.8; the airfoil boundary is kept whole at about
a thousand segments, so the sampled and full boundaries coincide and only
the direction convention differs).

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, TENSOR-HEAD at 400 Tensile2d cases: the equivariant stress head with the load axis alone trails the frame-input configuration by 10 to 47%, reversing its 32-case lead; a tensor-head-plus-full-frame lane separates head from input {#sec-nb-tensor-axis-verdict-400}

**Setting.** PLAID Tensile2d is two-dimensional elasto-viscoplastic
tension: a pressure on the top edge and five constitutive scalars vary per
case, and the targets are the displacement and the three in-plane stress
components. Two ISLA configurations are compared, both R1 (384 wide, 12
layers, 256 slices) at 5e-4 and 500 epochs, float32 relative L2 on the 100
held-out cases, two seeds each. `frame2` (the SOLIDS-FRAME lane that the
Tensile2d ladder in @sec-interior-tensile2d reports) receives both
laboratory axes as global vectors and predicts $\sigma_{11}$,
$\sigma_{22}$, $\sigma_{12}$ as three scalar heads. `tensor_axis` (rows 6 to
9 of `kernel/v2/lanes.tsv`) receives the load direction as the one global
vector and predicts the stress as one symmetric rank-2 tensor from the
equivariant head; the laboratory components are read off afterwards. At 32
cases the preregistered bar ("within 10% of `frame2` on every field") was
met on the three stresses with a 4 to 33% lead and missed on the
displacement (@sec-nb-tensor-mech-interim).

**Numbers at 400 cases** (`v2_t2d_isla_r1_tensor_axis_n400_seed42` /
`seed43` from `lane_means_2026-09-23.json`; `frame2` and GeoTransolver-512
from `results/solids_frame_2026-09-22.json`):

| field | `tensor_axis` seeds 42 / 43 | `tensor_axis` mean | `frame2` (two seeds) | `tensor_axis` ÷ `frame2` | GeoTransolver-512 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma_{11}$ | 0.0134 / 0.0126 | 0.0130 | 0.0118 | 1.10 | 0.0087 |
| $\sigma_{22}$ | 0.0140 / 0.0112 | 0.0126 | 0.0086 | 1.47 | 0.0076 |
| $\sigma_{12}$ | 0.0142 / 0.0145 | 0.0144 | 0.0112 | 1.28 | 0.0112 |
| displacement | 0.0097 / 0.0113 | 0.0105 | 0.0082 | 1.28 | 0.0054 |

**Verdict.** The bar fails on every field at 400 cases: the tensor head
with the load axis alone is 10% worse on $\sigma_{11}$ (at the bar, both
seeds above `frame2`), 47% on $\sigma_{22}$, 28% on $\sigma_{12}$ and 28% on
the displacement. Against GeoTransolver-512 the ratios become 0.67 / 0.60 /
0.78 / 0.51 where `frame2` stands at 0.74 / 0.88 / 1.00 / 0.66. **The
32-case lead of the tensor-plus-axis configuration does not carry to the
data-rich rung; `frame2` remains the configuration the Tensile2d ladder
reports**, and the clause that the tensor head plus the physical axis is
"the canonical Tensile2d configuration" (@sec-nb-tensor-mech-interim,
06:00 addendum) is withdrawn as premature: it was written from
training-time validation at 32 cases before the 400-case pair scored.

**What the two configurations differ in.** Two things at once: the
*inputs* (`frame2` sees both laboratory axes, `tensor_axis` only the load
axis; on Tensile2d the second axis is the direction along the loaded edge)
and the *head* (three scalar heads with their per-component z-scores
against one tensor head whose coefficients multiply the basis tensors built
from the query's direction to the boundary, the global vectors and the
identity). The 32-case result says the load axis is what generalizes when
data are scarce; the 400-case result says something in the pairing costs
10 to 47% once the network has enough cases to fit either way, and it does
not say which. Representability is not the candidate: with the load axis,
the direction to the nearest boundary and the identity, the symmetric
rank-2 basis spans the three in-plane degrees of freedom at every query.
The candidates are the missing second axis (an input effect; the frameless
lanes memorized, and the one-axis lanes may still lack a position invariant
along the loaded edge) and the tensor head's optimization (a head effect;
the coefficients' scale depends on the local basis).

**Discriminating lane (launched 2026-09-23).** `tensor_frame2` (rows 14 to
17 of `kernel/v2/lanes.tsv`; `recipe_v2/conf/model/isla_tensile2d_tensor_frame2.yaml`):
the tensor head with *both* laboratory axes as global vectors, i.e.
`frame2`'s inputs with `tensor_axis`'s head, at 400 and 32 cases, two
seeds each, eager kernel ($K = 2$). Bars, stated before the lanes score:
within 5% of `frame2` on every field at 400 cases means the 400-case gap
was the missing axis input and the equivariant head is free; within 5% of
`tensor_axis` means the gap is the head and the scalar-component heads stay
the recommendation for frame-defined components; in between, both
contribute and the split is reported as measured. At 32 cases the same
lane says whether the second axis is what the displacement (25% worse
under `tensor_axis`) was missing.

**For the book.** @sec-interior-tensile2d keeps `frame2` as the ISLA arm
of the ladder; the component clause of @sec-isla-heads stands (a
frame-defined component needs the frame as input); the tensor head remains
the API for tensor-valued targets (it is what makes the OLBC elasticity
stresses learnable together with rank-1 inputs, @sec-nb-rankio-verdict-elasticity),
with the Tensile2d 400-case price recorded beside it until `tensor_frame2`
attributes it.

## 2026-09-23 — Check, TERRITORY metric: weighting slices by the tokens they own changes the anchor displacement by under 10% for both architectures; the unweighted RMS is not dominated by empty slices {#sec-nb-territory-massweighted}

**Question.** The territory table (@tbl-territory) reports the anchor
displacement as the RMS over all 256 slices of how far a slice's anchor
(ISLA) or centroid (GeoTransolver) moves between the uniform and the
10:1-biased draw, divided by the body's RMS token radius. Under cosine
routing R1 spreads its mass over many slices, but a slice that owns almost
no tokens enters that RMS with the same 1/256 weight as one that owns a
whole panel, so the published number could be carried by slices that do
not matter to the prediction. The check re-reduces the same dumps
(`rp_probes/territory/*/dumps`; `probes/territory_*/dumps` for the
released baseline) with each slice weighted by the number of tokens whose
dominant slice it is in the first uniform draw, which under a uniform draw
is proportional to the surface area the slice owns.

**Numbers** (`results/territory_massweighted_2026-09-23.json`; medians
over 12 blocks x 4 validation cases; "floor" = the same displacement
between two independent uniform draws):

| model, dataset, cells | RMS over slices: biased (floor) | token-weighted: biased (floor) | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISLA R1 seed 42, cars, 100k | 0.099 (0.077) | 0.092 (0.073) | -7% |
| ISLA R1 seed 43, cars, 100k | 0.109 (0.082) | 0.099 (0.071) | -10% |
| GeoTransolver-256, cars, 100k | 0.629 (0.038) | 0.619 (0.034) | -2% |
| ISLA R1 seed 42, cars, 200k | 0.056 (0.055) | 0.055 (0.050) | -3% |
| ISLA R1 seeds 42 / 43, wings, 200k | 0.0037 / 0.0041 (0.0032 / 0.0033) | 0.0040 / 0.0040 (0.0029 / 0.0031) | +8% / -2% |
| GeoTransolver-256, wings, 200k | 0.280 (0.004) | 0.281 (0.004) | +1% |

**Verdict.** The weighting moves every entry by 10% or less and none of the
orderings: ISLA's anchors under the bias move by about the resampling floor
(cars 0.09 to 0.10 against a floor of 0.07 to 0.08 at 100,000 cells, equal
to the floor at 200,000; wings at the floor), GeoTransolver's centroids by
6 to 70 times their floor. The published unweighted RMS stands as the
table's metric; this check is cited from its caption. A side reading: by
dominant-token counts the effective number of slices (inverse
Herfindahl of the token shares) is 30 to 36 per block for R1 on the cars
and 16 to 22 on the wings, against 62 and 24 for GeoTransolver-256; the
170 to 240 "effective slices" quoted from the soft routing weights in
@sec-nb-refboard-probes count slices that receive some weight, not
slices that dominate any token, and the two numbers describe different
things.

## 2026-09-23 — Engineering, INTERNAL-GEOMETRY cost: the first nearest-boundary search ran at 46 s per step on DrivAerML Volume (113x the provided-SDF twin); replaced by an exact Triton brute-force kernel, bitwise equal, at matmul-class speed {#sec-nb-internal-geometry-cost}

**Symptom.** The launch-acceptance check of the `sg` lanes
(@sec-nb-internal-geometry-prereg) found the DrivAerML Volume lane with the
internal geometry at epoch 1 while its provided-SDF twin was at epoch 20
after the same 18 minutes: 46.5 s per step against 0.41 s. The AirfRANS
pair, whose airfoil boundary has about a thousand segments, ran at 0.30
against 0.18 s per step.

**Cause.** The search was `torch.cdist` on the element-wise path
(`compute_mode="donot_use_mm_for_euclid_dist"`, chosen for exactness) over
200,000 queries x 200,000 boundary samples in 640-query blocks: 4e10 pairs
through a generic kernel that is two orders of magnitude off the hardware.

**Two fixes, one kept.** (1) The matmul expansion $|y|^2 - 2\,x\cdot y$ is
fast but cancels catastrophically: its squared-distance error is about
$\varepsilon R^2$ ($R$ the body radius), a *distance* resolution of
$\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,R$, which is $2 \times 10^{-4} R$ in float32 (coarser
than the near-wall sample spacing it has to resolve; in a stress test with a
thousand samples within $10^{-3}$ of a point four radii out, 298 of 400
queries picked the wrong sample) and $10^{-8} R$ in float64 (below the
float32 resolution of the coordinates). In float64 it is exact and picked
every sample correctly, but GPUs with reduced float64 throughput make it a
2.8 s step (task 837676), still 7x the twin. It stays as the CPU fallback.
(2) **A Triton kernel** (`physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/nn_kernel.py`):
one program owns 64 queries and streams the boundary in 128-sample tiles,
forming the exact float32 difference $|x_q - y_i|^2$ (whose rounding is set
by the coordinates' own precision, not by $R^2$) and keeping a running
minimum and its index, so no $(Q, N)$ block is ever written and the pass is
compute-bound at about eight flops per pair. On a laptop GPU (RTX 4090
mobile) the full 200,000 x 200,000 search takes 0.36 s and returns indices
bitwise equal to the float64 path; the class's tests compare both paths
with a float64 brute force on the dense-cluster case and at scale
(commit 300ed0ab). The two DrivAerML Volume internal lanes were relaunched
under the kernel (epoch 0 to 1 of the first two links discarded; the
AirfRANS internal lanes pick it up at their next chain link, their results
unchanged since the search is exact either way). **Measured under the kernel (GB300, the relaunched lanes at epoch 9):
0.54 s per step against the provided-SDF twin's 0.41 s**, i.e. the exact
search over 200,000 x 200,000 pairs costs about 0.13 s per step, 1.3x the
twin where the first implementation was 113x. Peak memory unchanged
(93.9 against 93.4 GB).

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, REF-BOARD area-law twin: the reference configuration trained on the area-proportional draw is 5% worse on the uniform draw (seeds 4% and 6%) against 8% for the 192-wide lanes; at the bar, "weakly dependent" stands {#sec-nb-refboard-area-twin}

**Setting.** The training-law study (TRAIN-AREA-DR, @sec-nb-trainarea-dr-verdict)
trains each architecture on 435 DrivAerML cars under an area-proportional
Poisson draw of the surface cells with exact Horvitz–Thompson weights and
scores it on the independent uniform draw the uniform-trained model was
scored on: a trained function that depends on the law its training sample
was drawn by is worse there. The 192-wide ISLA of the earlier protocol
(100,000 cells) came out 8% worse (bar 5%), GeoTransolver-256 and
Transolver-256 7.9x and 9.6x. REF-BOARD re-runs the ISLA arm under the
reference configuration R1 (384 x 12, cosine routing, fused kernel, 5e-4)
at 200,000 cells, two seeds (`rb_dr_isla_area_seed{42,43}`), scored by the
consistency benchmark's three draws (`kernel/rp_bench.sbatch` tasks 6 and
7, job 837636) against the uniform-trained R1 reference
(`ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed{42,43}`) under the same draws.

**Numbers** (`results/trainarea_dr_r1_2026-09-23.json`; float32 pressure
relative L2 on the 48 validation cars at 200,000 cells):

| arm | uniform draw | stratified | 10:1 biased |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 trained on the uniform law | 0.0415 (0.0416 / 0.0414) | 0.0413 | 0.0419 |
| R1 trained on the area law | 0.0436 (0.0434 / 0.0439) | 0.0429 | 0.0448 |
| area-trained ÷ uniform-trained on the uniform draw | **1.051** (1.042 / 1.060) | | |

**Verdict.** The reference configuration's dependence on the training
law is 5.1% by the seed mean, one seed below the 5% bar and one above:
the bar is met by neither reading with margin, so the chapter's statement
stays "weakly dependent" (@sec-training-law), now with the smaller
number beside the earlier protocol's 8%, and the baselines' factors of
2.4 to 9.6 unchanged (released checkpoints, not re-run). The area-trained
R1's own density factor (biased ÷ uniform draw at inference) is 1.026,
against 1.011 for the uniform-trained R1 (@sec-nb-refboard-probes): a
model trained on the area law is also slightly more sensitive to the
inference draw. Both effects are consistent with the quadrature noise of
an area-proportional draw whose weights span four decades; the LIT-MLOSS
idea (@sec-vs-ideas) is the contract-preserving remedy to test if the
residual few percent ever matters.

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict and interims: the vector boundary-value extension does not help on OLBC elasticity at 512 cases (3 to 6% worse than the rank-1 inputs alone, both seeds); tensor head plus full frame at 32 Tensile2d cases; DeepJEB rank-1 load second seed; OLBC elasticity ladder at one seed {#sec-nb-litext-vec-verdict}

**LIT-EXT-vec (falsified at 512 cases).** The Poisson mechanism study
(@sec-nb-olbc-mech-verdict) found that a parameter-free extension of the
prescribed boundary values into the interior recovers 84% of ISLA's
log-gap to GeoTransolver-512. Its vector form on the elasticity set
extends the prescribed displacement and traction per condition label with
the same inverse-square-distance kernel and feeds them as four rank-1
query inputs plus four distances, on top of the RANK-IO configuration
(rank-1 boundary inputs, symmetric rank-2 stress head). Float32 relative
L2 on the 256 test cases, 512 training cases, seeds 42 / 43
(`v2_elasticity_isla_r1_ext_n512_*` against `v2_elasticity_isla_r1_rankio_n512_*`,
`lane_means_2026-09-23.json`):

| field | RANK-IO (rank-1 inputs, tensor head) | + vector extension | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| displacement | 0.673 / 0.667 | 0.713 / 0.700 | +5% |
| $\sigma_{11}$ | 0.724 / 0.756 | 0.780 / 0.770 | +5% |
| $\sigma_{22}$ | 0.737 / 0.766 | 0.786 / 0.783 | +4% |
| $\sigma_{12}$ | 0.770 / 0.789 | 0.789 / 0.783 | +1% |

The preregistered bar ("recovers at least half of the log-gap to
GeoTransolver-512 on every field, as it did for the Poisson scalar")
fails on every field: the extension makes every field 1 to 5% *worse*,
both seeds agreeing on the sign for three of four fields. **The value-transport
mechanism, as the parameter-free extension supplies it, is specific to the
Poisson set at this rung.** A reading, not a measurement: on Poisson the
prescribed values *are* the solution's boundary trace and the extension is
close to a harmonic interpolant of it; on elasticity the prescribed
traction is a derivative datum and the displacement is prescribed on a
few segments, so an inverse-distance average of them is not close to any
field the model must produce, and eight extra query channels at 512 cases
cost more in fit than they give. The 2,048-case twins (rows 12 and 13)
score next; the LIT-EXT ledger row carries the elasticity clause.

**Tensor head plus both laboratory axes at 32 Tensile2d cases (interim;
the 400-case pair decides).** `tensor_frame2` seeds 42 / 43:
$\sigma_{11}$ 0.1165 / 0.1153, $\sigma_{22}$ 0.0779 / 0.0790,
$\sigma_{12}$ 0.0947 / 0.0970, displacement 0.0942 / 0.0954. Against
`frame2` (two scalar-head seeds: 0.112 / 0.112 / 0.102 / 0.090) the tensor
head with the same inputs is 3% worse on $\sigma_{11}$, 30% better on
$\sigma_{22}$, 6% better on $\sigma_{12}$ and 5% worse on the displacement;
against `tensor_axis` (the one-axis tensor lanes, 0.108 / 0.076 / 0.087 /
0.113) the second axis costs 4 to 11% on the stresses and buys 16% on the
displacement. So at 32 cases the second axis is what the displacement was
missing under `tensor_axis`, and the tensor head is what $\sigma_{22}$
gains over scalar heads. The bars of @sec-nb-tensor-axis-verdict-400 are
stated at 400 cases, where rows 14 and 15 are training.

**DeepJEB++ rank-1 load, seed 43** (`v2_jb_isla_r1_rankio_n1024_seed43`,
5,540 clean test brackets): von Mises 0.498, displacement 0.253, against
the R1 lanes with the load as a one-hot-and-magnitude scalar set
(two seeds: 0.496 / 0.242). One seed says the rank-1 load traction is
neutral on von Mises and 4% worse on the displacement at 1,024 brackets;
seed 42 is scoring.

**OLBC elasticity ladder, baseline ISLA at one seed** (`ol_elasticity_isla_r1_n{2048,8448}_seed43`;
GeoTransolver-512 two seeds): at 2,048 cases ISLA 0.344 / 0.537 / 0.518 /
0.484 (displacement / $\sigma_{11}$ / $\sigma_{22}$ / $\sigma_{12}$)
against 0.165 / 0.257 / 0.261 / 0.267, ratios 0.48 / 0.48 / 0.54 / 0.52;
at 8,448 cases 0.086 / 0.220 / 0.211 / 0.211 against 0.050 / 0.102 /
0.105 / 0.098, ratios 0.58 / 0.46 / 0.50 / 0.46. Unlike the 512-case rung,
where ISLA sat at the predict-zero error, it learns the map from 2,048
cases up and trails GeoTransolver-512 by a factor of about two on the
stresses at every rung, with learning-curve exponents 0.84 (displacement)
and 0.53 to 0.54 (stresses) against GeoTransolver's 0.78 and 0.65 to 0.67:
on this set ISLA's stress curve is the *shallower* one (one seed at two
rungs; the second seeds and the RANK-IO 2,048-case lanes decide whether
the rank-1 inputs change the exponent as they changed the 512-case
standing).

**Addendum (2026-09-23, later): DeepJEB++ rank-1 load, both seeds; the
2,048-case elasticity baseline, both seeds; the domain frame at 2,048
Poisson cases, one seed.** (a) `v2_jb_isla_r1_rankio_n1024_seed{42,43}`:
von Mises 0.489 / 0.498 (mean 0.494), displacement 0.246 / 0.253 (0.249),

(0.242). **RANK-IO verdict on DeepJEB++: within the spread on von Mises

against the 2,048-case baseline 0.395 and GeoTransolver-512 0.098, i.e.

mechanism reading changes with the rung: at 512 cases the value channel

**Addendum (2026-09-23, later still).** (d) `om_poisson_isla_r1_leak_n2048_seed42`:

at 8,448 (displacement / $\sigma_{11}$ / $\sigma_{22}$ / $\sigma_{12}$)
against GeoTransolver-512's 0.447 / 0.626 / 0.651 / 0.636, 0.165 / 0.257 /
0.261 / 0.267 and 0.050 / 0.102 / 0.105 / 0.098; GeoTransolver-512 ÷ ISLA
0.49 / 0.62 / 0.70 / 0.66, 0.46 / 0.46 / 0.52 / 0.50, 0.57 / 0.45 / 0.48 /
0.45; learning-curve exponents 0.83 (displacement) and 0.51 to 0.53
(stresses) against 0.78 and 0.65 to 0.67. **On the elasticity set with
scalar boundary inputs ISLA trails GeoTransolver-512 by about two on the
