second OLBC set (after Poisson) where the SOLIDS same-exponent clause
does not hold in ISLA's favor. The rank-1-input configuration (RANK-IO)
moved the 512-case standing from no learning to 0.72 to 0.77; its
2,048-case lanes decide whether it also steepens the curve.

## 2026-09-23 — Engineering: the fused geometry kernel now takes one to three global directions, so frame-input configurations (the solids lanes, K = 2) run the reference fused path; exact against the eager region in float64, 2x faster and 2.2x leaner than eager at K = 2 on a laptop GPU {#sec-nb-fused-kernel-k3}

**Setting.** ISLA's per-layer geometry region evaluates the point-anchor
invariants (distance, log distance, the unit separation dotted with each
global direction, the token normal and the anchor direction, and normal
dot anchor direction: $5 + K$ scalars for $K$ global directions) on the
point x slice grid, the routing bias from them, the point-to-slice
softmax and the mix-weighted pooling. The fused Triton kernel of the
KERNEL STUDY (2026-09-13) evaluated this on register tiles without writing
the $(B, N, S, \cdot)$ intermediates, but was written for $K = 1$: the
DrivAerML and HiLift lanes. Every configuration with the laboratory frame
as two global vectors (Tensile2d `frame2`, OLBC elasticity, the
`tensor_frame2` lanes) has therefore run the eager region, at the eager
region's time and memory, and the book's cost statements did not apply to
them.

**Change** (commit of 2026-09-23; `geo_kernel.py`, `model.py`). Both
kernels take a compile-time `K` (1 to 3): they load up to three
directions per point, form the extra dot products, shift the routing
Linear's weight and the pooled-invariant indices by $K$, and return the
direction gradient as $(B, N, K, 3)$. The legacy absolute-anchor variant
stays at $K = 1$. The model passes all $K$ directions to the kernel,
accepts `geo_kernel="fused"` for $K \le 3$, and the automatic choice
selects the kernel for $K \le 3$ on CUDA. **Exactness**: the region-level
test compares forward outputs and every input gradient with the eager
region for $K = 1, 2, 3$ in float64 (1e-11) and float32 (1e-6 / 1e-5), and a
two-direction model matches its eager twin to 1e-11 in float64 (160 ISLA
tests pass). **Cost** on the RTX 4090 laptop GPU at 20,000 points, width
192, 4 layers, 256 slices, bf16 autocast, forward plus backward:

| directions | eager | fused | speed-up | peak memory eager / fused |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K = 1 | 84 ms | 25 ms | 3.4x | 2.15 / 1.00 GiB |
| K = 2 | 97 ms | 25 ms | 3.9x | 2.23 / 1.00 GiB |
| K = 3 | 99 ms | 25 ms | 4.0x | 2.31 / 1.01 GiB |

With the K = 1 tile sizes the K = 2 and K = 3 steps first came out at 48
and 50 ms: the unrolled tile holds K extra (BLOCK_N, S) invariants and
spills registers (region-level sweep: 5.2 and 9.4 ms against 1.2 ms per
region step). Halving the points per program for K > 1 (forward 4, backward
2 at up to 256 slices) restores the K = 1 speed, so the fused step is
independent of the direction count up to three. The cluster snapshots are
not touched by this change (the running frame lanes finish on the eager
region they started on; a new snapshot carries the kernel for the next
solids campaign).

**Addendum (same day): per-token rank-1 inputs through the same kernel.**
In the kernel a token's rank-1 input (prescribed traction, displacement,
load) is the same object as a global direction: a per-point vector dotted
with the unit separation. The kernels now take the K global directions and
the P' token vectors as one per-point vector set of at most three, with a
second compile-time constant placing each vector's invariant where the
eager region puts it (direction dots right after log distance, token-vector
dots after $\hat n \cdot \hat m$), so the routing Linear's weights mean the
same on both paths and a checkpoint trained on either loads on the other.
The direction gradient comes back as $(B, N, K + P', 3)$ and autograd splits
it. Exactness: the region test now covers $(K, P') \in \{(1,0), (2,0),
(3,0), (1,1), (1,2), (2,1)\}$ in float64 and float32, and a model with a
rank-1 boundary input matches its eager twin to 1e-11 (22 kernel tests, 167
ISLA tests). The RANK-IO elasticity configuration (two rank-1 boundary
inputs, $K = 0$) still needs one global direction for the kernel ($K \ge
1$ is the kernel's contract; the OLBC sets have no global direction, so
those lanes stay eager); the DeepJEB rank-1 load with the load direction
as the global vector ($K = 1, P' = 1$) and Tensile2d with a traction input
run fused. Rank-2 per-token inputs remain the follow-up.

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, REF-BOARD pose twin: the reference configuration trained in random poses scores 0.995x its native-frame standing; the rotation-augmented GeoTransolver-256 and Transolver-256 are 23% and 33% worse than posed ISLA (12% and 21% against the earlier protocol) {#sec-nb-refboard-pose-twin}

**Setting.** The pose study (@sec-pose-contract) trains every model with
every training and validation case of the DrivAerML Surface set rotated
into its own random pose, at the reporting protocol (435 cars, 200,000
cells, 500 epochs, two seeds), and scores surface pressure in float32 on
the 48 posed validation cars. ISLA trains without augmentation and its
covariance is exact by construction; GeoTransolver-256 and Transolver-256
train with rotation augmentation. The earlier protocol's ISLA (192 wide,
1e-3) scored 1.016x its native frame and led the augmented baselines by 12%
and 21% (@sec-nb-p200k-pose-verdict). REF-BOARD re-runs the ISLA arm under
the reference configuration (`rb_dr_isla_pose_seed{42,43}`).

**Numbers** (`results/p200k_pose_r1_2026-09-23.json`, built by
`pose_r1_reduce_2026-09-23.py` from the fleet scorer's metrics; the
baseline rows are copied from the earlier artifact, released models not
re-run): posed ISLA 0.0412 / 0.0414 (mean 0.0413) against the native-frame
reference configuration 0.0416 / 0.0414 (mean 0.0415): **posed ÷ native
0.995**. Augmented GeoTransolver-256 0.0508 and Transolver-256 0.0550 in
the posed setting: **augmented baseline ÷ posed ISLA 1.23 and 1.33**.

**Verdict.** The POSE-REF bars (posed within 3% of native; at least 5%
below both augmented baselines) hold with margin, and the lead widens from
12 / 21% to 23 / 33% because the reference configuration is 7% more
accurate than the earlier protocol while the augmented baselines are the
same released lanes. @sec-pose-contract, the index and @sec-vs-standing now
read the reference-configuration artifact; the CLAIMS pose line is
restated. The one remaining earlier-protocol element of the pose study is
the baselines' augmented lanes, which are what they are (released models).

## 2026-09-23 — Preregistration, OLBC-MECH combined channel: do the domain frame and the boundary-value extension add on the fixed-mesh Poisson set? Four lanes (2,048 and 512 cases, two seeds), to launch when the cluster is reachable {#sec-nb-olbc-mech-combined-prereg}

**Setting.** On the OLBC Poisson set (one fixed square mesh, random
labeled Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin segments and a random source per
sample) ISLA trails GeoTransolver-512 by a factor of three at every rung
(@sec-nb-olbc-ref-ladder-verdict). The mechanism study at 512 cases found the gap in
value transport: a parameter-free extension of the prescribed boundary
values into the interior (`ext`) recovers 84% of the log-gap, the domain's
axes as two global vectors (`frame2`) recover 19%, four times the slices
recover nothing (@sec-nb-olbc-mech-verdict). At 2,048 cases the frame alone
recovers 67% (one seed), so the positional channel grows with the rung
(@sec-nb-litext-vec-verdict, addendum (c)); the 2,048-case `ext` twin is
still training.

**Question.** Are the two contract-preserving channels additive, or do
they carry the same information? Each is legitimate on a fixed domain (the
frame is a property of the domain, the extension a quadrature of the
boundary data), so the combination is a candidate recipe for fixed-mesh
boundary-value problems, not a diagnostic.

**Lanes** (`kernel/om/lanes.tsv` rows 11 to 14; `recipe_globin` gains
`olbc_poisson_frame_ext.yaml` and `isla_olbc_poisson_frame_ext.yaml`, new
files, the pinned files untouched): ISLA R1 with both the frame vectors and
the six extension query scalars, 2,048 and 512 cases, seeds 42 and 43,
500 epochs, eager region ($K = 2$ on the pinned snapshot), float32 scoring
on the 256 test cases.

**Bars, in the recovered fraction of the log-gap between the baseline ISLA
and GeoTransolver-512 at the same rung.** Let $f$ be the frame's fraction
and $e$ the extension's (two seeds each). *Additive*: the combination
recovers at least $\min(1.0,\ f + e - 0.1)$, i.e. the channels carry
different information and together close the gap or overshoot it (they
may: the coordinate leak reaches 1.31 at 512 and 1.35 at 2,048). *Redundant*:
within 0.1 of $\max(f, e)$, the two carry the same information and the
cheaper one (the frame: two global vectors, no per-query channels) is the
recipe. *Between*: reported as measured. Predictions: at 512 cases
redundant-to-between (the frame adds little where the extension already
recovers 84%; 0.6); at 2,048 additive (the frame's 67% is positional and
the extension's contribution is value transport; 0.6). Whatever the
outcome, the standing that enters the book is against GeoTransolver-512
at the same rung with both seeds, and the mechanism section of
@sec-nb-olbc-ref-ladder-verdict gains one sentence.

## 2026-09-23 — Finding, the 35-wing deficit by angle of attack: GeoTransolver-512 ÷ ISLA is 0.77 up to 14 degrees and 0.67 from 16 degrees, where both errors double; the two models rank the cases alike (Spearman 0.80); 210-case twin preregistered {#sec-nb-hl35-percase}

**Setting.** On the 35-case HiLiftAeroML rung at the reporting protocol
(200,000 cells, float32, 180 validation cases on 118 geometries) the
reference configuration trails GeoTransolver-256 by 25% and the
parameter-matched GeoTransolver-512 by 29% on surface pressure
(@sec-nb-ref-verdict). The deficit's mechanism is the book's standing open
question on the wings: it is not the cell count, width, depth or rate
(@sec-de-limits). The fleet scorer writes one row per validation case, and
the HiLiftAeroML sample ids carry the geometry and the angle of attack, so
the deficit can be located without a new run.

**What was done.** `results/hl35_percase_2026-09-23.py` reads the per-case
float32 pressure errors of `ref_isla_r1_hl35_seed{42,43}`,
`ref_gt_w512_hl35_seed{42,43}`, the 24-layer variant and the 1e-3 rate
control, takes the seed mean per case, groups by angle of attack, and
computes the Spearman rank correlation of the two architectures' per-case
errors.

**Numbers** (`results/hl35_percase_2026-09-23.json`; GeoTransolver-512 ÷
ISLA per angle group, case counts 13 to 27): 0.78 / 0.78 / 0.77 / 0.80 /
0.71 / 0.78 at 4 / 6 / 8 / 10 / 12 / 14 degrees, then 0.67 / 0.76 / 0.61 /
0.64 at 16 / 18 / 20 / 22; means **0.77 below 16 degrees and 0.67 from 16
degrees**. Both models' errors roughly double across the same boundary
(ISLA 0.087 to 0.227, GeoTransolver-512 0.062 to 0.139 from 12 to 20
degrees). Spearman correlation of the per-case errors 0.80: the two
architectures find the same cases hard. ISLA is the more accurate model on
24 of 180 cases; the per-case ratio spans 0.45 (10th percentile) to 1.05
(90th). The 24-layer variant is within 4% of the reference in every angle
group (0.96 to 1.03), the 1e-3 control within 3%.

**Reading.** The deficit is present at every angle and grows where the flow
separates. What GeoTransolver-512 has that ISLA does not is the absolute
position of every cell as an input; in the separated regime the pressure at
a cell is set by where the cell sits along the chord and span (the
separation line, the wake of the slat and flap) more than by its local
geometry, so a model that reads position directly has an easier map. That
is the positional channel the fixed-mesh OLBC sets isolate (the coordinate
leak overshoots GeoTransolver there, the frame recovers 67% at 2,048 cases;
@sec-nb-olbc-mech-verdict and addenda), and the same reading as the
recurring-geometry hypothesis (the mesher pattern gives GeoTransolver
absolute positions it can memorize per geometry) with the regime as the
amplifier. It is a location, not a mechanism: nothing here varies an input.

**Preregistered twin.** When the 210-case rung's reference lanes and its
GeoTransolver-512 pair score (the latter needs launching; `ref` group), the
same script runs on them. Bar: the 16-to-22-degree ratio at least 0.08
below the 4-to-14-degree ratio again = the widening is a property of the
regime and not of the 35-case training set, and the next lane is the
mechanism test (the domain frame as two global vectors on the 35-wing rung,
the same `frame2` instrument as OLBC, against the bar that it recovers at
least half of the high-angle widening); ratio flat across angles at 210
cases = the widening is a small-data effect, and the recurring-geometry
line stays the hypothesis. @sec-de-strata carries the figure.

**Addendum, the same anatomy on the cars**
(`results/drivaer435_percase_2026-09-23.{py,json}`; 48 validation cars,
ISLA reference configuration against GeoTransolver-512, two seeds each).
Spearman rank correlation of the per-car errors **0.91**; the per-car
ratio GeoTransolver-512 ÷ ISLA runs from 0.91 (10th percentile) through
0.99 (median) to 1.10 (90th), and ISLA is the more accurate model on 20 of
the 48 cars. The parity at full data is therefore parity car by car, not an
average of large wins and losses, and the two architectures agree on which
cars are hard (ISLA's per-car error runs 0.034 to 0.051 between the 10th
and 90th percentiles, 0.067 at the worst car). That is the per-case face of
the shared floor of @sec-shared-floor: what remains at 435 cars is the
difficulty of the case, not the architecture.

**Addendum, AirfRANS by angle of attack (ISLA only; the baseline's
per-case rows are on the cluster).** The AirfRANS sample ids carry the
inflow speed and the angle of attack. ISLA's interior errors on the 200
full-test airfoils (reference configuration, two seeds), by angle bin:
pressure 0.049 / 0.030 / 0.022 / 0.022, velocity 0.018 / 0.013 / 0.013 /
0.017, eddy viscosity 0.043 / 0.022 / 0.024 / 0.042 for angles below 0, 0
to 5, 5 to 10 and at least 10 degrees (55 / 46 / 61 / 38 cases). ISLA's
pressure error is 2.2 times larger at negative angles than at 5 to 10
degrees, and the eddy viscosity is worst at both ends of the range. Whether
GeoTransolver-volume's pressure and eddy-viscosity leads on this set
(@sec-interior-airfrans) concentrate in the same bins is the twin of the
wing anatomy on a second dataset; the per-case rows of
`af_gt_vol_lr1e3_seed{42,43}` are fetched and the same script run when the
cluster is reachable. Bar, stated now: if the GeoTransolver-volume ÷ ISLA
pressure ratio at negative angles is at least 0.08 below its value at 5 to
10 degrees, the deficit is regime-located on two datasets and the frame
lane of the preregistration above runs on AirfRANS as well.

## 2026-09-23 — Preregistration, FRAME-AF (local mechanism rung): does the domain frame as global vectors change ISLA's AirfRANS interior error at exploration scale? Two arms on the laptop GPU while the cluster is unreachable {#sec-nb-frame-af-local-prereg}

**Why now.** The cluster has been unreachable since 13:50; the raw
AirfRANS dataset is on this machine, its converter is in the repository,
and the wing anatomy above raised the positional hypothesis (GeoTransolver
reads absolute position; ISLA does not). The domain frame as two global
vectors is the contract-preserving instrument that gives ISLA a frame to
express position in without breaking equivariance in the dataset's frame
(the OLBC `frame2` instrument, @sec-nb-olbc-mech-verdict). AirfRANS is the
one interior set where ISLA trails GeoTransolver-volume on pressure and
eddy viscosity (@sec-interior-airfrans).

**Instrument (labeled exploration scale; mechanism only, no standing).**
A 160-case subset converted locally (120 cases drawn from `scarce_train`,
40 from `full_test`, seed 0; `datasets/airfrans_volume_local*.yaml`,
manifest splits `local_train` / `local_test`). ISLA at 192 x 12 x 256,
cosine routing, fused kernel, 20,000 interior queries per case, 300
epochs, learning rate 1e-3 (the 192-wide rule), seed 42, one RTX 4090
laptop GPU. Two arms: baseline (`isla_volume_airfrans_local`: freestream
direction as the one global vector, speed as a global scalar) and frame
(`isla_volume_airfrans_local_frame`: plus the laboratory axes as two more
global vectors, $K = 3$, the first training use of the three-direction
fused kernel). Readout: validation relative L2 on the 40 local test
airfoils at epoch 300 for pressure, velocity and eddy viscosity, plus the
per-angle bins of the addendum above.

**Bars.** *Frame pays*: pressure improves by at least 10% and velocity is
not worse by more than 5%; then the positional channel is a live candidate
for the AirfRANS deficit and the reference-scale twin (R1, 800 airfoils,
100,000 queries, two seeds, against GeoTransolver-volume) launches when the
cluster returns. *Frame is neutral*: every field within 5%; the deficit is
not positional at this scale and the frame lane on the wings keeps its own
bar. *Frame hurts*: any field worse by more than 5%; recorded, the lane
is not repeated at scale. Prediction: neutral-to-pays on pressure at the
negative angles, neutral elsewhere (0.5); a laptop rung of 120 cases is
where a frame that helps memorization would help most, so a null here is
the more informative outcome.

## 2026-09-23 — Interim, FRAME-AF (local rung, seed 42): the laboratory frame as global vectors makes ISLA 17% better on AirfRANS interior pressure and 12% on velocity at exploration scale; the bar "frame pays" is met on one seed; the second seed is training {#sec-nb-frame-af-local-interim}

*Superseded by the two-seed verdict, @sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict: the by-angle reading below (gain at 0 to 10 degrees) did not hold on two seeds.*

**Numbers** (`results/frame_af_local_seed42_2026-09-23.json`, from
`frame_af_local_reduce_2026-09-23.py`; float32 relative L2 on the 40 local
test airfoils, 20,000 queries, epoch 300, seed 42):

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (freestream direction, $K = 1$) | 0.301 | 0.130 | 0.227 |
| + laboratory frame ($K = 3$, fused kernel) | 0.248 | 0.115 | 0.221 |
| frame ÷ baseline | **0.83** | **0.88** | 0.97 |

Training-time validation losses at epoch 299: 0.0147 (baseline) against
0.0103 (frame). By angle bin the pressure gain is concentrated between 0
and 10 degrees (0.42 to 0.14 at 0 to 5 degrees, 12 cases; 0.28 to 0.21 at 5
to 10) and absent below 0 and above 10 degrees (0.30 / 0.30 and 0.25 /
0.24). Both arms trained cleanly (no Traceback; 3.5 GB peak; the frame arm
at 0.11 s per step against the baseline's 0.08, the first training run of
the three-direction fused kernel).

**Reading.** The preregistered bar (pressure at least 10% better, velocity
not worse by more than 5%) is met, so the positional channel is a live
candidate for the AirfRANS deficit: giving ISLA a frame to express position
in, without breaking its equivariance in the dataset's frame, removes a
sixth of its pressure error at this scale. The angle pattern does not match
the prediction (gain at negative angles): the gain sits in the
mid-angle bins, and the 0-to-5-degree baseline value (0.42 against 0.25 to
0.30 elsewhere) suggests one or two hard cases in a 12-case bin that the
frame arm handles, which one seed cannot separate from initialization.
Caveats stated with the number: one seed, 120 training cases, 192 wide,
20,000 queries, 40 test airfoils; nothing here is a standing.

**Next.** Seed 43 of both arms is training on the same GPU (about 3.5
hours). If the two-seed mean holds the bar, the reference-scale twin (R1,
800 training airfoils, 100,000 queries, two seeds, against
GeoTransolver-volume; frame variant of `isla_volume_airfrans_ref`) is
staged for launch when the cluster is reachable, and the same frame
instrument goes on the 35-wing rung as the wing anatomy preregistered.

**Addendum, 2026-09-23 evening (staging of the two twins).** The
reference-scale AirfRANS twin is staged as campaign group `fa` (two lanes,
seeds 42 and 43, 100,000 queries, 800 training airfoils, `code_v4`; the
frame variant of `isla_volume_airfrans_ref` with the constant laboratory
frame set by `SetDomainGlobalField` in the dataset pipeline, as in the
local rung). Its baseline is the internal-geometry pair of the same
configuration without the frame. The wing lane needed one design decision.
The HiLift pipeline augments training with a random rotation about the
vertical axis, and the recipe inserts the augmentations right after the
`CenterMesh` transform. A constant frame written after that point would
stay fixed in the laboratory while the wing turns, and the frame would then
be noise relative to the geometry. The frame is therefore written before
`CenterMesh`, so the rotation (which transforms global vectors) carries it
with the wing: the input is the body frame (chord and span axes), which is
what the airfoil rung tests too, since AirfRANS has no rotation and body
and laboratory frames coincide there. Both twins launch when the cluster
is reachable and the two-seed local mean holds the bar.

## 2026-09-23 — Verdict, FRAME-AF (local rung, two seeds): the laboratory frame as global vectors cuts ISLA's AirfRANS interior pressure error by 25% and velocity by 11% at exploration scale; frame pays on both seeds; the reference-scale twins are staged {#sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict}

**Setting.** ISLA is the boundary-first surrogate of this book: it tokenizes
the boundary sample, routes tokens to slices through geometric invariants,
and decodes interior fields at query points. Its inputs are equivariant by
construction, so a scalar output cannot depend on where the laboratory axes
point unless a global vector carries that information. On AirfRANS (2-D
airfoils in a wind tunnel at fixed orientation, one inlet direction per
case) the reference ISLA trails GeoTransolver-volume on interior pressure
while leading on velocity (@sec-interior-open). The wing anatomy located
the surface deficit by angle of attack, and the OLBC mechanism study found
that giving a fixed-frame problem its own axes as global vectors recovers
part of a gap. This rung asks whether the same instrument moves the
airfoil interior.

**What was tested.** Two arms on a 160-case local AirfRANS subset (120
training, 40 test airfoils), ISLA 192 wide, 12 layers, 256 slices, cosine
routing, 20,000 interior queries, 300 epochs, learning rate 1e-3 (the
width rule), on the laptop GPU. The frame-free arm has the inlet direction
as its one global vector. The frame arm adds the laboratory axes
$\hat x$ and $\hat y$ as two more global vectors (K = 3, the fused kernel
with three directions; its first training use). Seeds 42 and 43 of each
arm. Bars from the preregistration (@sec-nb-frame-af-local-prereg):
*frame pays* if pressure improves by at least 10% and velocity is not more
than 5% worse on the two-seed means.

**What we saw.** Float32 relative L2 over the 40 test airfoils (means over
cases, then over seeds):

| field | frame-free arm | frame arm | frame ÷ frame-free | per seed (42, 43) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| pressure | 0.3546 | 0.2666 | **0.75** | 0.83, 0.70 |
| velocity | 0.1303 | 0.1158 | **0.89** | 0.88, 0.90 |
| eddy viscosity | 0.2576 | 0.2122 | 0.82 | 0.97, 0.71 |

: FRAME-AF local rung, two seeds. Data: results/frame_af_local_2026-09-23.json (reducer frame_af_local_reduce_2026-09-23.py; the seed-42 interim artifact frame_af_local_seed42_2026-09-23.json is superseded by this file).

**The bar is met on each seed separately and on the means: frame pays.**
Two cautions travel with the number. First, the frame-free arm is the
noisy one: its pressure error is 0.301 on seed 42 and
0.408 on seed 43, a spread as large as the seed-42 gain, while
the frame arm sits at 0.248 and 0.285. Part
of what the frame buys at this scale is a tighter seed distribution, not
only a lower mean. Velocity is the cleaner signal: the frame-free arm
scores 0.1303 on both seeds and the frame arm improves it by
12% and 10%. Second, by angle of attack (two-seed means,
frame ÷ frame-free on pressure): 0.79 below zero degrees
(19 cases), 0.41 at 0 to 5 degrees (5 cases),
0.87 at 5 to 10 (10 cases) and
0.78 at 10 and above (6 cases). The seed-42
reading that the gain sat at 0 to 10 degrees does not hold on two seeds:
the gain is everywhere except the 5-to-10-degree bin, and largest in the
five-case 0-to-5 bin. The preregistered prediction (neutral-to-pays at
negative angles, neutral elsewhere) was too cautious; the frame pays at
every angle.

**Why it matters.** AirfRANS is a fixed-frame problem: the tunnel axes are
physical (the inlet direction varies within a few degrees of $\hat x$, the
airfoil chord is aligned with $\hat x$ by construction), and a scalar
field such as pressure legitimately depends on the airfoil's orientation
relative to those axes. Without the frame, ISLA sees only the angle between
the inlet direction and the chord through the boundary tokens' invariants
against one global vector, which is exactly the small quantity (a few
degrees) the pressure field is most sensitive to. With the frame, the
angle of attack is a direct invariant (inlet direction dot $\hat x$). This
is the same mechanism as the OLBC frame2 instrument and the Tensile2d frame
ladder: **on a dataset whose physics references a frame, give the model
the frame as global vectors.** It is contract-preserving (rotate the
frame with the data and the output rotates), unlike coordinates fed as
scalars. It is not a claim about the reference configuration: 192 wide,
120 training airfoils and 20,000 queries are exploration scale, where no
accuracy claim is made (@sec-protocol).

**What's next.** The reference-scale twin is staged as campaign group
`fa` (R1, 800 training airfoils, 100,000 queries, seeds 42 and 43, code_v4;
baseline = the internal-geometry reference pair; the GeoTransolver-volume
row from the interior scoreboard is the standing to beat). Its bar: the
frame arm's pressure at least 10% below the frame-free reference pair with
velocity not worse by more than 5%, both seeds. If met, the AirfRANS
interior row of the scoreboard gains a frame variant labeled as such, and
the frame becomes the recommended input on fixed-frame datasets in
@sec-using-inputs. The 35-wing body-frame lane (frame written before
`CenterMesh` so the rotation augmentation carries it) launches alongside;
its bar is in @sec-nb-hl35-percase. Both launch when the cluster is
reachable.

*Addendum 2026-09-24.* After FRAME-AF-X (@sec-nb-frame-af-x-verdict) the
wing lane's body axes are $\hat y$ (span) and $\hat z$ (up), the two not
collinear with the inlet, rather than $\hat x$ and $\hat y$.
FRAME-AF-Y (@sec-nb-frame-af-y-verdict) then refuted the collinearity
reasoning behind that choice; the $\hat y$, $\hat z$ pair stands as the
staged guess until the E and F controls say which property of the pair
matters.

## 2026-09-23 — Preregistration, FRAME-AF-X: does the airfoil frame gain need both laboratory axes, or does one axis carry it? One-axis control (K = 2), two seeds, laptop GPU {#sec-nb-frame-af-x-prereg}

**Setting.** The FRAME-AF local rung (@sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict)
found that giving ISLA the two laboratory axes as global vectors, beside
the inlet direction, cuts its AirfRANS interior pressure error by a
quarter at exploration scale. The verdict named the mechanism as a
direct invariant for the angle of attack (inlet direction dot $\hat x$),
but did not test it. Two readings compete. Under the first, one axis
carries the gain: the angle between the inlet and the chord axis is the
quantity the pressure field is most sensitive to, and $\hat x$ alone
supplies it as an invariant. Under the second, both axes are needed:
ISLA's invariants are reflection-invariant, and with only $\hat x$ the
sign of the angle is lost (inlet at $+\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ give the same
dot with $\hat x$); $\hat y$ restores the sign. A cambered airfoil at
$+\alpha$ and its mirror image at $-\alpha$ are the same problem, so the
sign is recoverable from the geometry in principle. The question is
whether the model recovers it in practice from boundary tokens at this
scale.

**What is tested.** A third arm on the same 160-case subset, protocol and
seeds as the two verdict arms: the inlet direction plus $\hat x$ only
(K = 2, the fused kernel with two directions). Float32 per-case relative
L2 on the 40 test airfoils, seeds 42 and 43, means over cases then seeds.
The comparison quantity is the fraction of the two-axis gain that one
axis recovers, on the log scale, per field:
$f = \ln(e_\text{base} / e_x) / \ln(e_\text{base} / e_{xy})$.

**Bars.** *One axis suffices*: $f \geq 0.8$ on pressure and velocity, and
the by-angle pattern of the one-axis arm matches the two-axis arm at
negative angles (ratio to the two-axis arm within 10% in the below-zero
bin). *Both axes needed*: $f \leq 0.5$ on pressure, or the one-axis arm
trails the two-axis arm by more than 15% in the below-zero bin while
matching it (within 5%) at positive angles; the second pattern is the
sign-loss signature. *Between*: reported as measured. Prediction: both
axes needed with the sign-loss signature (0.55), since the frame-free
arm's error was largest at negative angles in the verdict rung and
reflection-invariant tokens cannot tell the sign of the angle from the
inlet alone. Launched 2026-09-23 22:32 EDT (seed 42 then 43, about 2.4
hours, inference included); reducer extends
`frame_af_local_reduce_2026-09-23.py` with the third arm.

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-X: one laboratory axis recovers a quarter of the two-axis pressure gain and trails the full frame at every angle, so the sign-loss reading is refuted; the informative axis is the one normal to the inlet {#sec-nb-frame-af-x-verdict}

**Setting.** The FRAME-AF local rung (@sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict)
showed that giving ISLA the two laboratory axes as global vectors, beside
the inlet direction, cuts its AirfRANS interior pressure error to
0.75x the frame-free arm's at exploration scale. The
preregistration of this control (@sec-nb-frame-af-x-prereg) asked whether
one axis, $\hat x$, carries that gain (the angle of attack as a direct
invariant) or whether both are needed, with the predicted signature of a
lost sign: the one-axis arm matching the two-axis arm at positive angles
and trailing it below zero.

**What was run.** The third arm, inlet direction plus $\hat x$ only
(K = 2), same 160-case subset, protocol and seeds as the two verdict arms;
float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, means over cases then seeds.

**What we saw.** The one-axis arm is nearly the frame-free arm:

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity | ÷ frame-free (pressure / velocity) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| inlet only (K = 1) | 0.3546 | 0.1303 | 0.2576 | 1 / 1 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ (K = 2) | 0.3317 | 0.1220 | 0.2522 | 0.94 / 0.94 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$ (K = 3) | 0.2666 | 0.1158 | 0.2122 | 0.75 / 0.89 |

: FRAME-AF-X, two seeds. Data: results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json (reducer frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py; the file also holds the later arms).

The fraction of the two-axis log-gain that one axis recovers is
0.23 on pressure, 0.56 on velocity and 0.11 on eddy
viscosity. **The "both axes needed" bar fires (pressure fraction below
0.5), but not through the sign-loss signature.** By angle of attack the
one-axis arm trails the two-axis arm on pressure by 1.20x below zero
degrees (19 cases), 1.47x at 0 to 5 (5 cases), 1.24x at 5 to 10
(10 cases) and 1.30x at 10 and above (6 cases): everywhere, not
only at negative angles. The predicted pattern (match at positive angles,
trail below zero) is refuted. One more observation: the one-axis arm's
seed spread is small (0.335, 0.328) where the frame-free
arm's is large (0.301, 0.408), so the seed-tightening seen
in the verdict rung comes with the first extra direction, the accuracy
with the second.

**Why it matters: the reading changes.** In AirfRANS the inlet direction
lies within a few degrees of $\hat x$. A global direction enters ISLA
through dot products with relative vectors (@sec-isla-inputs-rank), so
$\hat x$ adds almost the same invariant the inlet already supplies: the
two directions are nearly collinear and the second is close to redundant.
The axis that carries new information is $\hat y$, normal to the inlet.
With inlet and $\hat y$ (or $\hat x$ and $\hat y$) the per-slice
invariants hold both in-plane components of every relative vector, which
is the complete relative position in 2-D; with the inlet alone they hold
one component and a length. The mechanism is therefore not the angle of
attack as such but **completing the in-plane frame**: a second,
non-collinear global direction lets the geometry region resolve where a
query sits relative to an anchor in both directions, not just along the
flow. This is the same reading as the OLBC frame2 instrument on a domain
with no flow direction at all, and it predicts that on a 3-D fixed-frame
dataset whose inlet is along $\hat x$ (the wings), the axes worth adding
are the two normal to it. The staged wing lane is changed accordingly
(body $\hat y$ and $\hat z$, not $\hat x$ and $\hat y$;
@sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict, addendum). No accuracy claim is attached
at this scale (@sec-protocol).

**What's next.** The direct test of the new reading: the inlet plus
$\hat y$ only (K = 2), preregistered below (@sec-nb-frame-af-y-prereg)
and training on the same GPU.

## 2026-09-24 — Preregistration, FRAME-AF-Y: does the axis normal to the inlet alone carry the frame gain? Two seeds, laptop GPU {#sec-nb-frame-af-y-prereg}

**Question.** FRAME-AF-X (@sec-nb-frame-af-x-verdict) found that adding
$\hat x$, nearly collinear with the inlet, recovers 0.23 of the two-axis
pressure log-gain. The completing-the-frame reading predicts that
$\hat y$ alone, normal to the inlet, recovers most of it.

**Arm.** Inlet direction plus $\hat y$ (K = 2), same subset, protocol and
seeds (42, 43); float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils. Fraction
recovered on the log scale, $f_y = \ln(e_\text{base} / e_y) / \ln(e_\text{base} / e_{xy})$.

**Bars.** *Reading supported*: $f_y \geq 0.8$ on pressure and the
$\hat y$ arm within 10% of the two-axis arm on pressure in every angle
bin. *Reading refuted*: $f_y \leq 0.5$ on pressure (then the gain needs
the pair as such, and the collinearity argument is wrong). *Between*:
reported as measured. Prediction: supported (0.7). Launched 2026-09-24
00:51 EDT, about 2.4 hours including inference; reducer extends
`frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py` with the fourth arm.

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-Y: the axis normal to the inlet alone recovers none of the pressure gain; both single-axis readings are refuted and the gain belongs to the pair; two discriminating controls launched {#sec-nb-frame-af-y-verdict}

**Setting.** Two controls have now tried to attribute the FRAME-AF gain
(@sec-nb-frame-af-local-verdict: the two laboratory axes as global
vectors cut ISLA's AirfRANS interior pressure error to
0.75x the frame-free arm's at exploration scale) to one axis.
FRAME-AF-X (@sec-nb-frame-af-x-verdict) found $\hat x$ nearly useless
and proposed that $\hat y$, normal to the inlet, carries the gain by
completing the in-plane frame. This entry tests that proposal
(@sec-nb-frame-af-y-prereg).

**What was run.** The fourth arm, inlet direction plus $\hat y$ only
(K = 2), same subset, protocol and seeds; float32 relative L2 on the 40
test airfoils, means over cases then seeds.

**What we saw.**

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity | ÷ frame-free (p / v / ν) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| inlet only (K = 1) | 0.3546 | 0.1303 | 0.2576 | 1 / 1 / 1 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ (K = 2) | 0.3317 | 0.1220 | 0.2522 | 0.94 / 0.94 / 0.98 |
| inlet + $\hat y$ (K = 2) | 0.3598 | 0.1282 | 0.2287 | 1.01 / 0.98 / 0.89 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$ (K = 3) | 0.2666 | 0.1158 | 0.2122 | 0.75 / 0.89 / 0.82 |

: The four FRAME-AF arms, two seeds each. Data: results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json (reducer frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py; supersedes frame_af_x_2026-09-24.json).

**The reading is refuted.** $\hat y$ alone recovers -0.05 of the two-axis
pressure log-gain (per seed 0.376 and 0.343 against the
frame-free 0.301 and 0.408), 0.13 on velocity, and trails
the two-axis arm on pressure by 1.35x below zero degrees, 2.30x at 0 to 5,
1.13x at 5 to 10 and 1.20x at 10 and above. On eddy viscosity it
recovers 0.62, the one field where a single axis does something. Taken
with FRAME-AF-X ($\hat x$ alone: 0.23 on pressure), **neither axis carries
the pressure gain; the pair does.** Two consecutive one-axis readings
(the signed angle of attack; the completed in-plane frame) were wrong,
and the mechanism is open.

**What the pair has that neither single axis has.** With the inlet
$\hat u$ and both axes, the invariant set holds (i) the signed angle of
attack twice over, as $\hat u \cdot \hat x = \cos\alpha$ and
$\hat u \cdot \hat y = \sin\alpha$; (ii) every relative vector and
every normal in a *fixed* laboratory frame, $(r \cdot \hat x, r \cdot \hat y)$,
the same frame for every case; and (iii) three directions rather than
two, so a larger invariant set and head basis. The $\hat y$ arm has the
signed angle ($\sin\alpha$) and a complete but *case-dependent* frame
$(\hat u, \hat y)$ that rotates with the inlet by a few degrees per
case; the $\hat x$ arm has an unsigned angle and a nearly degenerate
frame. The candidates left are therefore (a) the fixedness of the frame
across cases, (b) the count of directions, and (c) an interaction the
invariants do not expose one at a time.

**Two controls launched to split (a) from (b) and (c)** (both seeds,
same protocol, 2026-09-24 03:17 EDT, training in parallel on the laptop
GPU, about 4.5 hours):

- *E*, $\hat x$ and $\hat y$ without the inlet direction (K = 2; the
  inlet speed stays as the scalar input). The fixed frame is present,
  the angle of attack is absent from the global inputs. Bar: if E
  reaches within 10% of the two-axis arm on pressure, the gain is the
  fixed frame and the angle of attack is not the point (then the model
  must be reading the angle from elsewhere, which would itself need
  explaining); if E is at or above the frame-free arm, the pair's gain
  needs the inlet and the fixed frame together.
- *F*, inlet plus $\hat y$ plus a fixed in-plane direction at 45
  degrees (K = 3). Three directions and a fixed complete frame, but not
  the orthonormal $(\hat x, \hat y)$ pair. Bar: if F is within 10% of
  the two-axis arm on pressure, orthogonality is irrelevant and the
  count-plus-fixed-frame reading holds; if F sits with the one-axis
  arms (fraction recovered below 0.5), the orthonormal pair as such
  matters, which would point at how the direction-direction invariants
  enter (@sec-isla-inputs-rank).

Prediction: E near the frame-free arm (0.6) and F near the two-axis arm
(0.6). Reducer: `frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py` with arms `framee`,
`framef`. No accuracy claim at this scale (@sec-protocol).

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-E/F: the frame gain needs the inlet direction and two fixed in-plane directions together; orthogonality is irrelevant (F reproduces the two-axis arm to 0.4%); axes without the inlet are 2.6x worse than no frame {#sec-nb-frame-af-ef-verdict}

**Setting.** Four arms so far (@sec-nb-frame-af-y-verdict): on the
160-airfoil local AirfRANS subset at exploration scale, the inlet
direction plus the two laboratory axes as global vectors cuts ISLA's
interior pressure error to 0.75x the inlet-only arm's, while the inlet
plus either single axis does nothing. Two controls were preregistered to
say what the axis pair supplies: E, the axes without the inlet direction
(a fixed frame, no angle of attack among the global inputs); F, the inlet
plus $\hat y$ plus a fixed direction at 45 degrees (three directions and a
fixed, complete, non-orthonormal in-plane frame).

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, two seeds):

| arm | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity | ÷ inlet-only (p / v / ν) | ÷ two-axis arm (p) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| inlet only (K = 1) | 0.3546 | 0.1303 | 0.2576 | 1 / 1 / 1 | 1.33 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ | 0.3317 | 0.1220 | 0.2522 | 0.94 / 0.94 / 0.98 | 1.24 |
| inlet + $\hat y$ | 0.3598 | 0.1282 | 0.2287 | 1.01 / 0.98 / 0.89 | 1.35 |
| E: $\hat x$ + $\hat y$, no inlet direction | 0.9055 | 0.3330 | 0.3156 | 2.55 / 2.56 / 1.23 | 3.40 |
| F: inlet + $\hat y$ + 45-degree direction | 0.2677 | 0.1159 | 0.2080 | 0.75 / 0.89 / 0.81 | 1.004 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$ (K = 3) | 0.2666 | 0.1158 | 0.2122 | 0.75 / 0.89 / 0.82 | 1 |

: The six FRAME-AF arms, two seeds each. Data: results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json (reducer frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py).

**Both bars fire cleanly.** E sits far *above* the inlet-only arm:
2.55x on pressure and 2.56x on velocity (per seed 0.896, 0.915).
Without the inlet direction the model has no access to the angle of
attack (the inlet speed, kept as a scalar input, does not carry it), and
the fixed frame alone is worth nothing; so the gain needs the inlet and
the frame together, and the model was not reading the angle from
anywhere else. F reproduces the two-axis arm: 1.004x on pressure,
1.000x on velocity, 0.98x on eddy viscosity (per seed
0.274, 0.261). **Orthogonality of the frame is irrelevant.** Any
two fixed, non-collinear in-plane directions, beside the inlet, give the
gain; one fixed direction beside the inlet gives none.

**What is settled and what is not.** Settled: the ingredient is *two
fixed directions plus the case's condition vector*. Not yet settled is
whether the two fixed directions matter because they are fixed (the same
frame for every case, so every relative vector, normal and the inlet
itself are expressed in one case-independent frame) or because three
directions is simply more than two (the K = 2 arms both failed, the
K = 3 arms both succeeded; count is confounded with fixedness in every
arm so far). A seventh arm splits them: **G**, the inlet direction, its
in-plane perpendicular (a case-dependent second direction, rotated with
the inlet by a new recipe transform `RotateGlobalVectorInPlane`) and the
fixed $\hat y$ (K = 3, one fixed direction). If G reaches within 10% of
the two-axis arm on pressure, the count of directions (or the
completeness of the frame regardless of fixedness) is the gain; if G sits
with the K = 2 arms (fraction recovered below 0.5), two *fixed*
directions are the ingredient. Prediction: fixedness (0.65), because the
$(\hat u, \hat y)$ arm already had a complete frame and failed. Launched
2026-09-24 08:24 EDT, two seeds, about 2.4 hours.

**Why it matters.** For the architecture: the global-direction input is
doing more than adding a condition; a pair of fixed directions turns the
per-slice invariants into coordinates in a shared frame, and on a
fixed-frame dataset that is worth a quarter of the pressure error at
this scale. For the recipe: on any dataset whose cases share a frame
(wind-tunnel airfoils, the OLBC domains, the solids), supply two fixed
non-collinear directions beside the physical condition vector; one is
not enough, and the axes need not be orthogonal. The reference-scale
AirfRANS twin (campaign `fa`) tests whether this survives at R1 with 800
airfoils. No accuracy claim at this scale (@sec-protocol).

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-G: a case-dependent third direction that adds no information reproduces the frame gain (0.99x the two-axis arm), so fixedness is refuted and the gain is a property of three directions over two; a redundant-duplicate control launched {#sec-nb-frame-af-g-verdict}

**Setting.** Six arms on the 160-airfoil local AirfRANS subset
(@sec-nb-frame-af-ef-verdict) established that the inlet direction plus
two fixed, non-collinear in-plane directions cuts ISLA's interior
pressure error to 0.75x the inlet-only arm's, that one fixed direction
does nothing, and that orthogonality is irrelevant. The open question was
whether the two directions matter because they are *fixed* across cases
or because three directions beat two. G was preregistered to split them:
the inlet $\hat u$, its in-plane perpendicular $\hat u_\perp$ (rotated
with the inlet, case by case, by the new recipe transform
`RotateGlobalVectorInPlane`), and the fixed $\hat y$ (K = 3, one fixed
direction).

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, two
seeds): G scores 0.2635 on pressure (per seed 0.265, 0.262),
0.1159 on velocity and 0.1897 on eddy viscosity: 0.988x,
1.001x and 0.89x the two-axis arm, and 0.74x, 0.89x and
0.74x the inlet-only arm. The full six-arm table is in the E/F entry;
data: results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json.

**Fixedness is refuted.** G has one fixed direction and reproduces the
gain within 1% on pressure and velocity (and does better on eddy
viscosity). One caveat travels with G: its third direction is the inlet
rotated by a fixed 90 degrees about $\hat z$, which is a *pseudovector*
under reflection (the mirror image of the problem would receive the
opposite perpendicular), so G is not a legitimate input under ISLA's
reflection contract and is used here only as a mechanism probe. The
legitimate arms (F and the two-axis arm) reach the same number. The information G carries is exactly that of the failed
inlet-plus-$\hat y$ arm: $\hat u_\perp$ is a deterministic function of
$\hat u$, so every invariant G can form is a function of invariants the
K = 2 arm already had. **Three directions beat two even when the third
adds no information.** The ingredient is therefore not a frame in the
physical sense, fixed or otherwise, but the size or form of the
per-slice invariant set (and the head basis) that a third direction
brings: with K directions the geometry region of each slice carries
$K$ direction dots per relative vector and per normal, and the seeds
carry $K(K-1)/2$ direction-direction cosines (@sec-isla-inputs-rank).
Between K = 2 and K = 3 the invariant set grows from a minimal to an
overcomplete description of the in-plane geometry.

**What this changes.** The recommendation drafted in the E/F entry
("supply two fixed directions beside the condition vector on a
fixed-frame dataset") is not wrong as a recipe, but its rationale is:
the fixed frame is not what pays. The finding is about ISLA's
parameterization, and it raises a sharper question: does a third
direction that is *exactly* redundant, not just informationally
redundant, also pay? **H**, the inlet, $\hat y$ and $-\hat y$ (K = 3;
every invariant of the third direction is the negation of one of the
second's), is launched to answer it (2026-09-24 10:44 EDT, two seeds,
about 2.4 hours). If H reproduces the two-axis arm within 10% on
pressure, the gain is a feature-count effect of how the invariants enter
the seeds and the geometry region (a scale, normalization or capacity
effect to be located in the class), and the frame reading is retired
entirely. If H sits with the K = 2 arms (fraction recovered below 0.5),
the third direction must be non-collinear with the second, and the
overcomplete in-plane description is the mechanism. Prediction: H fails
(0.6). Either way, the reference-scale AirfRANS twin (campaign `fa`)
keeps its value as the test of whether the gain survives at R1 and 800
airfoils; its interpretation waits on H. No accuracy claim at this
scale (@sec-protocol).

## 2026-09-24 — Derivation and preregistration, FRAME-AF-Y-EAGER: what a global direction adds to ISLA's invariants, why the inlet-plus-y arm already had complete information, and the eager-kernel twin that rules out a K = 2 fused-path defect {#sec-nb-frame-af-derivation}

**What K global directions add, read from the class.** Three places
(`physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/model.py`, the `_InputSet` and
`_relational_invariants` docstrings and the constructor):

- The *seed* of each boundary token gains one channel per direction,
  $\hat n_i \cdot \hat g_k$ (the only origin-free scalars of the set
  $\{\hat n_i, \hat g_k\}$). There are no direction-direction cosines
  $\hat g_j \cdot \hat g_k$ in the seed, so the angle of attack is *not* a
  seed feature in any arm; with two in-plane directions the token normal
  is nevertheless determined exactly (two independent projections of a
  unit in-plane vector).
- The *geometry region* of every slice layer gains one channel per
  direction per point-anchor pair, $\hat r_{is} \cdot \hat g_k$ (width
  $5 + K$ with no per-token vector inputs); two non-collinear directions
  determine every in-plane relative vector exactly.
- The *head basis* gains $\hat g_k$ and the spherical complements of
  $(\hat u_i, \hat g_k)$: $m = 2K + 3$ true vectors. This touches the
  velocity output only; pressure and eddy viscosity are scalars read
  from the hidden state.

**Consequence for the arms.** Inlet plus $\hat y$ (K = 2) already gives
every token its exact in-plane normal and every pair its exact in-plane
relative vector, in the case-dependent frame $(\hat u, \hat y)$. The
inlet plus $\hat x$ plus $\hat y$ arm (K = 3), F and G add channels that
are functions of channels the K = 2 arm has. On information the K = 2
and K = 3 arms are equal, so the measured gap (pressure
0.36 against 0.27, @sec-nb-frame-af-g-verdict) is representational:
either the count of geometry and seed channels ($5 + K$ and $K$) or the
specific linear combinations exposed. H (inlet, $\hat y$, $-\hat y$)
tests the count reading with a channel that is an exact negation of
another.

**One more candidate that the derivation cannot exclude.** Every K = 2
arm so far ran on the fused Triton geometry kernel, whose K = 2 path
(compile-time direction count, halved tiles) is exercised in training
for the first time by these arms; its forward and backward are tested
exact against the eager region for (K, P') = (2, 0) at unit-test scale,
but not through a 300-epoch bf16 training run. **Y-EAGER**: the inlet
plus $\hat y$ arm with `geo_kernel: eager`, seed 42 only (the eager
region runs about nine times slower on this GPU, 0.93 s against 0.10 s
per step, so one seed takes about nine hours). Bar: if Y-EAGER lands
within 10% of the fused $\hat y$ arm on pressure (0.36 to 0.38), the
kernel is cleared and the K = 2 result stands; if it lands within 10% of
the two-axis arm (0.27), the fused K = 2 training path is defective and
every K = 2 verdict above is void until the kernel is repaired.
Prediction: cleared (0.8). Launched 2026-09-24 10:52 EDT.

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-H: an exactly redundant third direction recovers a third of the pressure gain, not all of it; the ingredient is three distinct in-plane directions, an overcomplete description of the plane; the eight-arm ladder closes at exploration scale {#sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict}

**Setting.** Seven arms on the 160-airfoil local AirfRANS subset have
narrowed why two extra global directions beside the inlet cut ISLA's
interior pressure error by a quarter at exploration scale
(@sec-nb-frame-af-g-verdict). G showed that a third direction carrying
no new information still pays in full, so the effect is representational.
H was preregistered to split "more channels" from "more distinct
directions": the inlet, $\hat y$ and $-\hat y$ (K = 3), where every
channel of the third direction is the negation of one of the second's.

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, two seeds;
data results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json, reducer
frame_af_x_reduce_2026-09-24.py):

| arm (K) | directions | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity | pressure ÷ inlet-only | pressure ÷ two-axis |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| inlet only (1) | $\hat u$ | 0.3546 | 0.1303 | 0.2576 | 1 | 1.33 |
| X (2) | $\hat u, \hat x$ | 0.3317 | 0.1220 | 0.2522 | 0.94 | 1.24 |
| Y (2) | $\hat u, \hat y$ | 0.3598 | 0.1282 | 0.2287 | 1.01 | 1.35 |
| E (2) | $\hat x, \hat y$ (no inlet) | 0.9055 | 0.3330 | 0.3156 | 2.55 | 3.40 |
| H (3) | $\hat u, \hat y, -\hat y$ | 0.3190 | 0.1212 | 0.2079 | 0.90 | 1.20 |
| F (3) | $\hat u, \hat y, \hat d_{45}$ | 0.2677 | 0.1159 | 0.2080 | 0.75 | 1.004 |
| G (3) | $\hat u, \hat u_\perp, \hat y$ | 0.2635 | 0.1159 | 0.1897 | 0.74 | 0.988 |
| frame (3) | $\hat u, \hat x, \hat y$ | 0.2666 | 0.1158 | 0.2122 | 0.75 | 1 |

: The FRAME-AF ladder: eight arms, two seeds each, ISLA 192 x 12 on 120 training airfoils and 20,000 queries (exploration scale; mechanism only). Bold rows are the K = 3 arms with three distinct directions.

**H recovers 0.37 of the two-axis pressure log-gain** (per seed 0.314,
0.324; 1.20x the two-axis arm), 0.61 on velocity and all of
it on eddy viscosity. The preregistered "sits with the K = 2 arms"
clause (fraction below 0.5 on pressure) fires, but H is not a K = 2 arm
either: it beats the inlet-plus-$\hat y$ arm, whose information it
duplicates exactly, by 1.13x on pressure. **Reading: a third channel
per pair pays something even when it is a copy (about a third of the
gain), and a third *distinct* direction pays the rest.** The complete
gain needs three distinct in-plane directions, which for a plane is an
overcomplete set: every relative vector and every normal is then
described by three one-dimensional projections at three angles instead
of two.

**The ladder, closed.** Read together, the eight arms say: (1) the
inlet direction is indispensable (E), because the angle of attack has no
other route into the model; (2) a second direction, fixed or not,
collinear with the inlet or normal to it, gives nothing on pressure (X,
Y); (3) a third direction gives the full quarter if it is distinct from
the other two (F, G, frame), whatever its angle and whether or not it
carries new information, and a third of the quarter if it is a copy (H).
This is not a frame effect in any physical sense. It is a statement
about ISLA's geometry region and seed: the learned functions of the
per-slice invariants $\{\hat r_{is} \cdot \hat g_k\}$ and
$\{\hat n_i \cdot \hat g_k\}$ resolve in-plane geometry far better from
three projections than from two, the way a function on a plane is easier
to learn from an overcomplete set of ridge coordinates than from a
minimal basis. Two readings were proposed and refuted on the way (the
signed angle of attack; the completed frame), and the fixedness reading
after them; the entries above keep them.

**Why it matters for the architecture.** ISLA's per-pair geometry is
carried by dot products with a small set of directions, and this ladder
says the set should be *overcomplete* for the ambient plane of the
problem. For 2-D problems that is three directions; for 3-D problems
(the cars, the wings, the lug) the same reasoning predicts that three
directions, a complete basis, are the analog of the failed K = 2 arms,
and that four are needed. The fused geometry kernel is written for at
most three per-point vectors (@sec-isla-inputs-rank); if the 3-D
prediction holds, raising that cap to four is the engineering
consequence. The preregistered tests are in the next entry.

**What's next.** (i) The reference-scale AirfRANS twin (campaign `fa`,
R1, 800 airfoils, 100,000 queries, two seeds, code_v4): does the quarter
survive at scale? Its two frame axes are any two distinct directions
beside the inlet; the staged $\hat x, \hat y$ pair stands. (ii) A
DrivAerML Surface twin at R1 and 200,000 cells with the inlet plus
$\hat y$ and $\hat z$ (K = 3, a complete 3-D set): the prediction is
*no gain* (the 3-D analog of K = 2), which is the falsifier of the
overcompleteness reading; a gain would instead say that any extra
distinct direction pays. (iii) If (ii) shows no gain, a K = 4 arm on the
eager region (the fused kernel's cap) decides whether overcompleteness
is the rule in 3-D. Both cluster lanes are staged for the VPN's return.
(iv) The eager-kernel twin of the $\hat y$ arm
(@sec-nb-frame-af-derivation) is still training and closes the kernel
question independently. No accuracy claim at this scale (@sec-protocol).

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-Y-EAGER: the eager geometry region reproduces the fused K = 2 result (pressure within 4%), so the fused kernel's two-direction training path is sound and the K = 2 verdicts stand {#sec-nb-frame-af-y-eager-verdict}

**Setting.** Every K = 2 arm of the FRAME-AF ladder
(@sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict) trained on the fused Triton geometry kernel,

|---|---:|---:|---:|

| inlet + $\hat y$, fused kernel | 0.3763 | 0.1297 | 0.2306 |
| inlet only, fused kernel | 0.3008 | 0.1303 | 0.2267 |
| inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$, fused kernel | 0.2483 | 0.1149 | 0.2205 |

: Eager against fused on the K = 2 arm, one seed.

**Kernel cleared.** The eager twin is 0.96x the fused $\hat y$ arm on pressure,
1.07x on velocity and 1.14x on eddy viscosity, within the
preregistered 10% on the deciding field, and 1.46x the two-axis arm. A
defective fused path would have put it near the two-axis arm. The two
implementations of the geometry region are exact to roundoff at the

K = 2 result is a property of the architecture, not of the kernel. The

here because the question was a large, discrete one (a 0.36 against 0.27
split); the eager region is not a candidate for further arms at this
speed.

## 2026-09-24 — Engineering and preregistration: the fused geometry kernel takes four per-point vectors; FRAME-AF-K4 asks whether a fourth distinct in-plane direction pays beyond the third {#sec-nb-frame-af-k4-prereg}

**Engineering.** The FRAME-AF ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict) reads
as: three distinct directions describe a plane overcompletely and pay;
two do not. The 3-D analog needs four directions, and the fused Triton
geometry kernel was unrolled for at most three per-point vectors. The
kernel now takes four (`MAX_DIRECTIONS = 4`): a fourth slot in both
kernels at invariant index 5 when it is a global direction and 8 when it
is a token vector, following the eager region's order. It is exact
against the eager region (forward outputs and every input gradient) for
(K, P') = (4, 0), (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1) in float32 and float64, on
top of the earlier grid; the ISLA suite passes (175 tests). A K = 4 step
on the laptop GPU takes 0.093 s at 192 x 12 and 20,000 queries, the same
as K = 3 (the halved tiles for more than one vector already absorb the
extra registers). The class refuses five or more with the fused kernel
and the auto-resolution falls back to the eager region there. The cluster
`code_v4` overlay is refreshed to this commit.

With the kernel at four, the 3-D falsifier gains its second half: beside
the K = 3 DrivAerML Surface lanes (inlet + $\hat y$ + $\hat z$), a K = 4
pair (inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$ + $\hat z$) is staged as campaign `fa`
rows 4 and 5. The overcompleteness reading predicts K = 3 flat and K = 4
better by at least 10% on pressure at 200,000 cells against the R1
reference pair; the ledger row FRAME-3D carries both bars.

**Preregistration, FRAME-AF-K4.** Arm: the inlet direction plus three
fixed in-plane directions ($\hat x$, $\hat y$ and the 45-degree
direction; K = 4), on the same 160-airfoil subset, protocol and seeds as
the ladder. Question: does the fourth distinct direction pay beyond the
third, or does the gain saturate once the plane is overcomplete?
Quantity: pressure relative to the three-direction arms (the two-axis
arm, F and G agree at 0.264 to 0.268). Bars: *saturated* if K = 4 is
within 5% of the three-direction arms on pressure and velocity;
*continues* if K = 4 improves pressure by at least 10%; *hurts* if it is
worse by more than 5% (then too many directions cost something, which
would bound the recommendation). Prediction: saturated (0.6), continues
(0.3). Launched 2026-09-24 18:59 EDT, two seeds, about 2.4 hours.

## 2026-09-24 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-K4: a fourth distinct in-plane direction adds nothing beyond the third (0.98x the two-axis arm on pressure); the gain saturates once the plane is overcomplete; the local ladder is complete at nine arms {#sec-nb-frame-af-k4-verdict}

**Setting and question.** The FRAME-AF ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict)
found that three distinct in-plane directions beside the inlet cut ISLA's
AirfRANS interior pressure error by a quarter at exploration scale, and
that two do not. With the fused kernel extended to four vectors
(@sec-nb-frame-af-k4-prereg), the ninth arm asks whether a fourth
distinct direction ($\hat x$, $\hat y$ and the 45-degree direction
beside the inlet, K = 4) pays beyond the third.

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, two seeds;
data results/frame_af_xy_2026-09-24.json): K = 4 scores 0.2612 on
pressure (per seed 0.275, 0.248), 0.1123 on velocity and
0.2037 on eddy viscosity: 0.98x, 0.97x and 0.96x the two-axis
K = 3 arm, and 0.74x, 0.86x, 0.79x the inlet-only arm. The three
K = 3 arms with distinct directions sit at 0.264 to 0.268 on pressure;
K = 4 sits at 0.261.

**Saturated.** The preregistered *saturated* bar (within 5% of the
three-direction arms on pressure and velocity) fires; the *continues* bar
(10% better) does not. The 2-D picture is now complete: one extra
direction beside the inlet gives nothing, two give the full quarter, three
give the same quarter. **The gain is a step, not a slope, and the step
sits at the first overcomplete description of the plane.** The
prediction for 3-D sharpens accordingly: the step should sit at four
directions (inlet plus three), with three directions (a complete 3-D
basis) still on the floor and five adding nothing. The staged FRAME-3D
lanes (K = 3 and K = 4 on DrivAerML Surface at R1 and 200,000 cells,
campaign `fa` rows 2 to 5) test exactly that pair. If both hold, the
recipe rule becomes "supply the problem's condition vector plus fixed
directions until the set is overcomplete for the ambient dimension" (two
more in 2-D, three more in 3-D), and the directions' identity does not
matter. The set has to come from the dataset, not from inside the model:
a direction generated internally from fewer supplied true vectors than
the ambient dimension is either in their span (no new projection) or a
pseudovector (a cross product, which breaks the reflection contract; G's
perpendicular is the 2-D instance). That rule waits on the 3-D result
and on the reference-scale AirfRANS twin (rows 0 to 1). No accuracy claim at exploration scale
(@sec-protocol).

## 2026-09-24 — Preregistration, FRAME-AF-SIZE: does the direction-count step shrink or grow with training data? Inlet-only against inlet + x + y at 30, 60 and 120 training airfoils {#sec-nb-frame-af-size-prereg}

**Question.** The nine-arm ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-k4-verdict) fixed
the direction-count step at 120 training airfoils and exploration
scale. Before the reference-scale twin (800 airfoils, R1) reports, the
cheapest informative question is how the step depends on training data.
Two readings: if the extra directions act as an inductive bias that
substitutes for data, the step is largest with few cases and shrinks as
data grows, and the 800-airfoil twin may show little; if they change
what the model can represent at convergence, the step holds or grows
with data.

**Arms.** Inlet only (K = 1) and inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$ (K = 3), at
30 and 60 training airfoils drawn as fixed random subsets of the 120
(`local_train30` $\subset$ `local_train60` $\subset$ `local_train` in the
local manifest; angle-of-attack ranges $-3.4$ to $13.7$ degrees in both
subsets, $-4.8$ to $14.5$ in the full 120), seeds 42 and 43, the same 40
test airfoils, 300 epochs, learning rate 1e-3, 20,000 queries, fused
kernel. Fixed epochs means fewer optimizer steps at the small sizes, as
in the book's training-case ladders. The 120-case rung is the ladder's
inlet-only and two-axis arms.

**Quantity and bars.** The pressure ratio K = 3 ÷ K = 1 at each size
(two-seed means), against 0.75 at 120. *Shrinks with data*: the ratio at
30 is at least 0.10 below the ratio at 120 (a larger gain with less
data) and monotone across 30, 60, 120. *Holds*: every ratio within 0.07
of 0.75. *Grows with data*: the ratio at 30 is at least 0.10 above 0.75
and monotone. Otherwise reported as measured. Prediction: holds (0.5),
shrinks (0.35). Launched 2026-09-24 21:33 EDT, two arms in parallel on
the laptop GPU, about 1.8 hours in all. A 240-airfoil rung follows if
the conversion of 120 further training cases from the raw AirfRANS set
finishes in time.

## 2026-09-25 — Interim, FRAME-AF-SIZE (30, 60, 120 airfoils): the direction-count step is 0.76, 0.90 and 0.75 on pressure, not monotone in training data; neither the "shrinks" nor the "grows" bar fires; the 240-airfoil rung is training {#sec-nb-frame-af-size-interim}

**Setting.** The preregistration (@sec-nb-frame-af-size-prereg) asked
whether the gain from two extra in-plane directions beside the inlet (the
direction-count step of the FRAME-AF ladder, 0.75 on pressure at 120
training airfoils) shrinks, holds or grows with training data, as a guide
to what the 800-airfoil reference-scale twin should show.

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the 40 test airfoils, two seeds;
data results/frame_af_size_2026-09-25.json, reducer
frame_af_size_reduce_2026-09-25.py):

| training airfoils | inlet only, pressure (seeds) | inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$, pressure (seeds) | K = 3 ÷ K = 1, pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 30 | 0.7783 (0.826, 0.730) | 0.5912 (0.559, 0.624) | **0.76** | 0.92 | 0.94 |
| 60 | 0.4505 (0.465, 0.436) | 0.4064 (0.396, 0.417) | **0.90** | 0.93 | 0.92 |
| 120 | 0.3546 (0.301, 0.408) | 0.2666 (0.248, 0.285) | **0.75** | 0.89 | 0.82 |

: The direction-count step against training-set size, exploration scale (192 x 12, 20,000 queries, 300 epochs at every size).

**Reading.** The step is present at every size (velocity 0.92, 0.93,
0.89; eddy viscosity 0.94, 0.92, 0.82) but its pressure ratio is not
monotone: 0.76 at 30, 0.90 at 60, 0.75 at 120. No preregistered bar
fires. Two things are visible in the seeds. At 30 airfoils the inlet-only
arm is very noisy (0.83 and 0.73) and both arms are poor in absolute
terms (0.78 and 0.59), so the ratio there is a ratio of two badly
trained models. At 60 the frame arm improves less than the inlet-only arm
does between 30 and 60, and the ratio narrows. **The direction-count
step is therefore not a small-data substitute that fades with data; at
this scale it is a roughly constant factor with a noisy 60-case rung.**
That is the reading the reference-scale twin needs: nothing here
predicts that the step vanishes at 800 airfoils, and nothing here
guarantees it either. The 240-airfoil rung (120 further training cases
converted from the raw AirfRANS set, split `local_train240`; two arms,
two seeds, launched 2026-09-25 01:32 EDT, about 4.7 hours) is the point
closest to the twin and decides the interim reading: within 0.07 of 0.75
keeps "constant factor"; above 0.85 reopens "shrinks".

## 2026-09-25 — Verdict, FRAME-AF-SIZE: across 30, 60, 120 and 240 training airfoils the direction-count step on pressure is 0.76, 0.90, 0.75, 0.90 (no trend, seed ranges overlap at 240), on velocity a steady 0.89 to 0.93, on eddy viscosity growing with data; the reference-scale twin's 10% bar is a coin flip {#sec-nb-frame-af-size-verdict}

**Setting.** The size ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-size-prereg,
@sec-nb-frame-af-size-interim) asks how the gain from two extra in-plane
directions beside the inlet depends on training data, as the guide to
what the 800-airfoil reference-scale twin (campaign `fa`) should show.
The 240-airfoil rung, built from 120 further training cases converted
from the raw AirfRANS set, completes it.

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2 on the same 40 test airfoils, two
seeds; 300 epochs at every size; data results/frame_af_size_2026-09-25.json):

| training airfoils | inlet only, pressure (seeds) | inlet + $\hat x$ + $\hat y$, pressure (seeds) | K = 3 ÷ K = 1, pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 30 | 0.7783 (0.826, 0.730) | 0.5912 (0.559, 0.624) | **0.76** | 0.92 | 0.94 |
| 60 | 0.4505 (0.465, 0.436) | 0.4064 (0.396, 0.417) | **0.90** | 0.93 | 0.92 |
| 120 | 0.3546 (0.301, 0.408) | 0.2666 (0.248, 0.285) | **0.75** | 0.89 | 0.82 |
| 240 | 0.2529 (0.242, 0.264) | 0.2276 (0.253, 0.202) | **0.90** | 0.90 | 0.78 |

: The direction-count step against training-set size, exploration scale (192 x 12, 20,000 queries).

**Reading.** On pressure the step alternates between a quarter (30, 120)
and a tenth (60, 240) with no trend in training data, and at 240 the
seed ranges overlap (inlet-only 0.242 and 0.264, with the frame 0.253
and 0.202): **at this scale the pressure step is real on the pooled
evidence of four rungs but its size is not pinned better than "10 to
25%", and a single two-seed rung can land on either end.** On velocity
the step is steady, 0.89 to 0.93 at every size. On eddy viscosity it
grows with data, from 0.94 at 30 to 0.78 at 240, the one field where the
extra directions help more the more the model has to fit. No
preregistered bar fires (the "shrinks" bar needed monotone behavior; the
240 rung's 0.90 sits above the interim's 0.85 threshold but the ladder
is not monotone).

**What this says about the twin.** The reference-scale AirfRANS twin's
bar is a pressure gain of at least 10% against the frame-free reference
pair. On this ladder that bar is a coin flip: the 60- and 240-airfoil
rungs sit at it, the 30- and 120-airfoil rungs clear it. The twin should
therefore be read with its seeds shown and with velocity and eddy
viscosity beside pressure, and a result between 0.85 and 0.95 on pressure
is the expected outcome rather than a failure of the mechanism. The
mechanism ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict) is untouched by this: it
was run at the 120-airfoil rung, where the step is largest, and asks
which directions carry it, not how large it is.

**Limits.** One dataset, exploration width, fixed epochs (the 30-airfoil
models see one eighth of the optimizer steps of the 240-airfoil models),
and two seeds per arm; the 60 and 240 rungs share nothing but their
ratio. A third seed at 240 would settle whether 0.90 there is the value
or the noise, and is not run: the twin at R1 with 800 airfoils is the
better use of the next compute.

## 2026-09-25 — Preregistration, GEO-BIAS: is the linearity of the routing bias in the invariants what the extra directions repair? Inlet-only ISLA with a two-layer MLP bias, two seeds, laptop GPU {#sec-nb-geo-bias-prereg}

**Setting.** The direction-count ladder (@sec-nb-frame-af-h-verdict)
found that ISLA's interior pressure error on the AirfRANS rung drops a
quarter once two more distinct in-plane directions join the inlet as
global vectors, that the directions' identity does not matter, and that
the inlet-plus-one-axis arms already carry complete geometric
information. The gap is representational. Reading the class again
(@sec-nb-frame-af-derivation) points at one specific place: in every
slice layer the per-pair routing bias is *one linear map* of the pair's
invariants, `geo_logit = nn.Linear(n_geo, 1)`, and the fused kernel is
built around that linearity. With the inlet alone, the bias can be
affine in distance, log-distance, the inlet component of the relative
direction and the two normal cosines. With two more directions it can
be affine in the *full* relative direction, in any orientation, so a
slice can carve the plane along any line rather than only along the
flow. That is a hypothesis about a bottleneck in the architecture, not
about the inputs.

**Change.** A constructor option `geo_bias` on `physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA`:
`"linear"` (the default, unchanged) or `"mlp"`, a two-layer map
(16 hidden units, GELU) of the same invariants to the routing bias, in
every slice and query block. It consumes invariants only, so every
contract is untouched (tested: rotation equivariance, translation
invariance). It runs on the eager region; the fused kernel implements
the linear bias only and refuses the option, and the auto-resolution
falls back to eager. Parameter cost: 16 (n_geo + 2) + 1 per block, about
160 parameters per layer at K = 1.

**Arm.** The inlet-only configuration (K = 1) of the ladder with
`geo_bias: mlp` and `geo_kernel: eager`, same 120-airfoil subset,
protocol and seeds (42, 43), float32 relative L2 on the 40 test
airfoils. The eager region runs about nine times slower per step on the
laptop GPU than the fused kernel; the two seeds run in parallel (about
14 hours). Comparators: the inlet-only linear arm (pressure 0.355,
fused; the eager twin of a K = 2 arm reproduced its fused result within
4%, @sec-nb-frame-af-y-eager-verdict) and the two-axis K = 3 arm
(0.267).

**Bars.** Fraction of the two-axis pressure log-gain recovered by the
MLP bias at K = 1, $f = \ln(e_{K=1} / e_\text{mlp}) / \ln(e_{K=1} / e_{K=3})$.
*Linearity is the bottleneck*: $f \geq 0.8$ on pressure and velocity
(then the class default should move toward the nonlinear bias and the
fused kernel needs a nonlinear variant). *Part of it*: $0.4 \leq f < 0.8$.
*Not the bottleneck*: $f < 0.4$ (the extra projections do something a
nonlinear map of fewer projections cannot; the mechanism moves to the
seed features or the head basis). Prediction: part of it (0.45),
bottleneck (0.3), not (0.25). Launched 2026-09-25 12:05 EDT.

## 2026-09-25 — Verdict, INTERNAL-GEOMETRY: the nearest-sampled-boundary geometry costs 14% (DrivAerML Volume) and 27% (AirfRANS) on interior velocity against the stored full-mesh signed distance; the "price is real" clause fires; provided geometry stays the accurate option {#sec-nb-internal-geometry-verdict}

**Setting.** ISLA's interior queries need a direction and a signed
distance to the boundary. Since 2026-09-23 the class computes both inside
the model from the sampled boundary (`interior_geometry:
nearest_boundary`, the exact Triton search) unless the caller supplies a
full-mesh signed-distance field (`provided`). The preregistration
(@sec-nb-internal-geometry-prereg) ran the reference configuration both
ways on the two interior datasets, two seeds each: internal within 3% on
every field on both datasets keeps the stored field unnecessary; worse by
more than 3% on any field on either dataset means the near-wall price of
the sampled boundary is real.

**What we saw** (float32 relative L2, seed means; DrivAerML Volume on 48
validation cars at 200,000 cells; AirfRANS on the 200 test airfoils at
100,000 queries):

| dataset, field | provided (stored SDF) | internal (nearest sampled cell) | internal ÷ provided |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DrivAerML Volume, pressure | 0.0397 | 0.0409 | 1.03 |
| DrivAerML Volume, velocity | 0.0576 | 0.0655 | **1.14** |
| DrivAerML Volume, eddy viscosity | 0.0874 | 0.0894 | 1.02 |
| AirfRANS, pressure | 0.0328 | 0.0341 | 1.04 |
| AirfRANS, velocity | 0.0161 | 0.0206 | **1.27** |
| AirfRANS, eddy viscosity | 0.0323 | 0.0355 | 1.10 |

: INTERNAL-GEOMETRY, campaign sg, two seeds per arm. Data: results/cluster_return_reductions_2026-09-25.json (group internal_geometry).

**The price is real, and it is a velocity price.** Pressure and eddy
viscosity sit at 2 to 4% on the cars and 4 and 10% on the airfoils;
velocity pays 14% on the cars and 27% on the airfoils. The prediction
(within 3% everywhere on AirfRANS, because the airfoil boundary is kept
whole) was wrong on the field that matters most: the boundary was whole,
so the loss is not from a missing part of the wall but from *where on a
cell* the distance is measured. The internal search returns the distance
to the nearest sampled cell *centroid* and the direction to it; the stored
field is the distance to the nearest point *on the surface*. Near the
wall, where the boundary layer sets the velocity, the centroid distance
overstates the true distance by up to half a cell and rotates the
direction toward the centroid, and those are exactly the two invariants
the query's slice routing and head basis consume. On the airfoils the
cells are line segments up to a few percent of chord long at the
trailing edge, on the cars surface triangles; both are coarse next to
the first cell of the boundary layer.

**Consequences.** (i) `interior_geometry: provided` stays documented as
the accurate option wherever the dataset carries a full-mesh field, and
the interior scoreboard rows keep it. (ii) The class default is not
changed on this evidence alone, because the fix is mechanical and cheap
and should be tried first: project onto the cell instead of stopping at
its centroid. For a boundary cell with centroid $c$ and unit normal $n$,
the signed plane distance $(q - c) \cdot n$ and the foot-point direction
$q - c - ((q - c) \cdot n)\, n$ recover the true distance to first order
in the cell size for queries whose nearest surface point lies inside the
cell; for line cells the in-plane analog. This is one line in the
nearest-boundary geometry after the search and costs nothing at
200,000 x 200,000. **Preregistered follow-up (INTERNAL-GEOMETRY-PROJ):**
the same four-lane pair with the projected distance and direction; bar as

either dataset makes `provided` the documented default where a stored
field exists and internal the fallback). Prediction: the velocity gap
closes to within 3% on AirfRANS (line cells, exact projection) and to
